examples.text: Residents of a river basin coordinate farming and water use according to the basin's seasonal capacity.
examples.note: The watershed becomes the practical unit because it reflects ecological connections better than an arbitrary boundary.

commonMisreadings: Bioregionalism is not simply localism or a rejection of every wider political institution.

concepts.name: Bizarreness effect
concepts.summary: The bizarreness effect is the tendency for unusual or distinctive information to be remembered better than ordinary information in some conditions.
concepts.body: The bizarreness effect is the tendency for unusual or distinctive information to be remembered better than ordinary information in some conditions. Distinctiveness can make an item more attention-grabbing and provide additional retrieval cues.

examples.text: People often recall a purple cow in a list of common farm animals more accurately than another ordinary cow.
examples.note: The unusual color makes the item stand out from its surrounding material.

commonMisreadings: The effect does not mean that every bizarre event is remembered accurately or permanently.

concepts.name: Bonapartism
concepts.summary: Bonapartism is a political pattern in which a strong executive claims to stand above competing social classes while concentrating authority in personal rule.
concepts.body: Bonapartism is a political pattern in which a strong executive claims to stand above competing social classes while concentrating authority in personal rule. The ruler often appeals directly to the nation and uses plebiscites, administration, or the military to weaken ordinary parliamentary conflict.

examples.text: Louis-Napoleon Bonaparte used a centralized presidency and popular votes to legitimize personal power in nineteenth-century France.
examples.note: His regime exemplifies executive authority presented as a national reconciliation above faction.

commonMisreadings: Bonapartism is not simply any dictatorship or any government led by a military figure.

concepts.name: Boolean algebra
concepts.summary: Boolean algebra is an algebra of values and operations used to represent logical relations.
concepts.body: Boolean algebra is an algebra of values and operations used to represent logical relations. Its basic operations include conjunction, disjunction, and complementation, with identities that support simplification of digital circuits.

examples.text: The expression x AND true simplifies to x under Boolean algebra.
examples.note: The identity preserves the value of x while showing how a redundant logical input can be removed.

commonMisreadings: Boolean algebra is not ordinary arithmetic even though both systems use symbols and equations.

concepts.name: Bound variable
concepts.summary: A bound variable is a variable whose occurrences fall within the scope of a quantifier or another binding operator.
concepts.body: A bound variable is a variable whose occurrences fall within the scope of a quantifier or another binding operator. Its value is determined locally by the binding expression rather than by a free assignment outside that scope.

examples.text: In the formula for every x, x is greater than zero, each occurrence of x is bound by the universal quantifier.
examples.note: The quantifier controls which objects the variable ranges over.

commonMisreadings: A bound variable is distinct from a free variable, whose value depends on an external assignment.

concepts.name: Bounded rationality
concepts.summary: Bounded rationality is the view that decision makers seek satisfactory choices under limits of information, time, and cognitive capacity.
concepts.body: Bounded rationality is the view that decision makers seek satisfactory choices under limits of information, time, and cognitive capacity. Instead of maximizing over every possible option, people often use heuristics and settle for an acceptable alternative.

examples.text: A manager chooses the first supplier meeting minimum quality and price requirements rather than comparing every supplier worldwide.
examples.note: The choice reflects satisficing under practical limits.

commonMisreadings: Bounded rationality does not assert that people are irrational in every decision.

concepts.name: Brahman
concepts.summary: Brahman is the ultimate reality or ground of being in many schools of Hindu philosophy, especially Vedanta.
concepts.body: Brahman is the ultimate reality or ground of being in many schools of Hindu philosophy, especially Vedanta. It is often described as infinite and foundational, though traditions differ over whether it is personal, impersonal, or identical with the self.

examples.text: Advaita Vedanta identifies the deepest self, atman, with Brahman through the claim that ultimate reality is nondual.
examples.note: The example shows Brahman as the reality underlying apparent multiplicity.

commonMisreadings: Brahman is not the same figure as Brahma, the creator deity in Hindu mythology.

concepts.name: Brain in a vat
concepts.summary: The brain-in-a-vat scenario imagines a brain receiving artificial sensory signals that perfectly imitate ordinary experience.
concepts.body: The brain-in-a-vat scenario imagines a brain receiving artificial sensory signals that perfectly imitate ordinary experience. It is used to test whether knowledge of the external world requires a non-deceptive causal connection to that world.

examples.text: A scientist could preserve a brain in nutrient fluid and connect it to a computer generating experiences of walking through a city.
examples.note: The case challenges confidence that experience alone guarantees an external environment.

commonMisreadings: It is a skeptical thought experiment, not an established description of ordinary human biology.

concepts.name: Buddhism
concepts.summary: Buddhism is a family of religious and philosophical traditions centered on understanding suffering and cultivating liberation through the Buddha's teachings.
concepts.body: Buddhism is a family of religious and philosophical traditions centered on understanding suffering and cultivating liberation through the Buddha's teachings. Its traditions commonly emphasize impermanence, ethical conduct, meditation, and insight into the causes of attachment.

examples.text: A practitioner follows the Noble Eightfold Path by combining right conduct with meditation and disciplined understanding.
examples.note: The path links ethical and mental training to the reduction of suffering.

commonMisreadings: Buddhism is not a single uniform doctrine shared identically by every Buddhist school.

concepts.name: Buddhist dependent origination
concepts.summary: Buddhist dependent origination is the teaching that phenomena arise through conditions and relations rather than existing independently.
concepts.body: Buddhist dependent origination is the teaching that phenomena arise through conditions and relations rather than existing independently. The traditional twelve-link formulation explains how ignorance and craving sustain cycles of suffering, while the broader principle applies to conditioned existence generally.

examples.text: A painful resentment persists when an injury is combined with repeated recollection, self-identification, and craving for revenge.
examples.note: The resentment depends on interacting mental conditions rather than an isolated permanent essence.

commonMisreadings: Dependent origination is not the claim that events lack causes or that one linear cause explains everything.

concepts.name: Buddhist emptiness
concepts.summary: Buddhist emptiness is the insight that things lack an independent, permanent, self-sufficient essence.
concepts.body: Buddhist emptiness is the insight that things lack an independent, permanent, self-sufficient essence. Emptiness does not deny conventional existence; it explains that entities exist dependently through causes, parts, concepts, and relations.

examples.text: A clay cup exists conventionally, but its identity depends on material, shape, use, naming, and conditions of production.
examples.note: The cup illustrates how ordinary existence can remain meaningful without an immutable core.

commonMisreadings: Emptiness is not simple nihilism or the claim that nothing exists at all.

concepts.name: Bundle theory
concepts.summary: Bundle theory is the metaphysical view that an object is a bundle of properties or perceptions rather than a separate substance beneath them.
concepts.body: Bundle theory is the metaphysical view that an object is a bundle of properties or perceptions rather than a separate substance beneath them. Applied to personal identity, it explains a person as a succession or collection of experiences, memories, and other mental contents.

examples.text: A supposedly permanent self may be analyzed as changing sensations, thoughts, memories, and dispositions.
examples.note: The analysis treats the self as the organized bundle rather than as an additional hidden entity.

commonMisreadings: Bundle theory differs from substance theories that posit an underlying bearer of properties.

concepts.name: Burden of proof
concepts.summary: The burden of proof is the obligation to provide adequate support for a claim in a particular dispute.
concepts.body: The burden of proof is the obligation to provide adequate support for a claim in a particular dispute. It commonly falls on the person making an affirmative or controversial assertion, though standards and allocations vary by context.

examples.text: A person claiming that a supplement cures a disease must provide evidence rather than demanding that skeptics disprove the claim.
examples.note: The claimant introduced the proposition requiring justification.

commonMisreadings: The burden of proof is not itself proof that a claim is false.

concepts.name: Buridan's ass
concepts.summary: Buridan's ass is a paradox about an agent unable to choose between two equally attractive options.
concepts.body: Buridan's ass is a paradox about an agent unable to choose between two equally attractive options. It illustrates tensions between perfect rational choice, sufficient reasons, and the possibility of action when alternatives are exactly balanced.

examples.text: A donkey placed exactly midway between identical bales of hay could starve if it had no reason to select either bale.
examples.note: The symmetry removes any preference that could initiate movement.

commonMisreadings: The paradox does not show that real animals invariably require unequal reasons before acting.

concepts.name: Bystander effect
concepts.summary: The bystander effect is the tendency for an individual's likelihood of helping to decrease when other observers are present.
concepts.body: The bystander effect is the tendency for an individual's likelihood of helping to decrease when other observers are present. Diffusion of responsibility and uncertainty about how others interpret the situation can inhibit intervention.

examples.text: A person injured in a crowded station may receive slower assistance than an equally injured person seen by one clearly responsible witness.
examples.note: Multiple observers can make each person expect someone else to act.

commonMisreadings: The effect is not universal and can be reduced by assigning responsibility or recognizing a clear emergency.

concepts.name: Capabilities approach
concepts.summary: The capabilities approach evaluates justice by asking what people are genuinely able to be and do.
concepts.body: The capabilities approach evaluates justice by asking what people are genuinely able to be and do. It focuses on substantive opportunities such as health, education, bodily integrity, and political participation rather than resources alone.

examples.text: A policy is judged inadequate if a school technically admits girls but unsafe travel prevents them from attending.
examples.note: The relevant capability is real access to education, not formal permission alone.

commonMisreadings: The approach differs from measuring welfare only by income or reported preference satisfaction.

concepts.name: Capitalism
concepts.summary: Capitalism is an economic system in which private owners control productive assets and coordinate much production through markets and profit-seeking.
concepts.body: Capitalism is an economic system in which private owners control productive assets and coordinate much production through markets and profit-seeking. Its forms vary in regulation, labor relations, ownership concentration, and the role of public institutions.

examples.text: A privately owned company hires workers, sells goods for revenue, and reinvests profits in expanding production.
examples.note: The example combines private control, wage labor, exchange, and a profit motive.

commonMisreadings: Capitalism is not identical to unrestricted markets because capitalist economies can include extensive regulation and public ownership.

concepts.name: Care ethics
concepts.summary: Care ethics is an ethical approach that treats relationships, dependency, attention, and responsiveness to particular people as morally central.
concepts.body: Care ethics is an ethical approach that treats relationships, dependency, attention, and responsiveness to particular people as morally central. It criticizes theories that picture moral agents as detached and interchangeable decision makers.

examples.text: A nurse adjusts support to a patient's fear, family situation, and vulnerability rather than applying a rule without regard to context.
examples.note: The response is guided by an attentive relationship and the patient's concrete needs.

commonMisreadings: Care ethics is not merely being kind or excusing every action performed in the name of care.

concepts.name: Cartesian dualism
concepts.summary: Cartesian dualism is the view that mind and body are distinct kinds of substance.
concepts.body: Cartesian dualism is the view that mind and body are distinct kinds of substance. Descartes characterizes mind by thought and body by spatial extension, creating a problem about how the two interact.

examples.text: A conscious decision to raise an arm appears to produce a bodily movement despite the decision being non-extended.
examples.note: The case illustrates the proposed interaction between mental and physical substances.

commonMisreadings: Cartesian dualism differs from the weaker claim that mental descriptions and physical descriptions are distinct.

concepts.name: Cartesianism
concepts.summary: Cartesianism is the philosophical tradition associated with Descartes's methodic doubt, rationalism, mind-body distinction, and search for indubitable foundations.
concepts.body: Cartesianism is the philosophical tradition associated with Descartes's methodic doubt, rationalism, mind-body distinction, and search for indubitable foundations. It treats disciplined reasoning and clear understanding as central tools for securing knowledge.

examples.text: Descartes doubts sensory appearances while retaining the certainty that doubting is a form of thinking.
examples.note: The cogito demonstrates the Cartesian strategy of finding certainty through reflective reasoning.

commonMisreadings: Cartesianism is broader than the isolated slogan I think, therefore I am.

concepts.name: Carvaka
concepts.summary: Carvaka is an ancient Indian materialist school that privileges perception and rejects the authority of the Vedas and supernatural claims.
concepts.body: Carvaka is an ancient Indian materialist school that privileges perception and rejects the authority of the Vedas and supernatural claims. Its surviving views are known mainly through reports by opponents, so reconstruction of its doctrines is necessarily incomplete.

examples.text: A Carvaka argument may deny an afterlife because no afterlife can be established by ordinary perception.
examples.note: The argument reflects the school's empiricist and anti-religious orientation.

commonMisreadings: Carvaka is not a general name for every materialist view in Indian philosophy.

concepts.name: Casuistry
concepts.summary: Casuistry is a method of ethical reasoning that resolves difficult cases by comparing them with established paradigm cases.
concepts.body: Casuistry is a method of ethical reasoning that resolves difficult cases by comparing them with established paradigm cases. It attends to concrete circumstances and analogies rather than deriving every judgment from a single abstract principle.

examples.text: An ethics committee compares a disputed treatment refusal with prior cases involving competence, risk, and informed choice.
examples.note: The precedent helps identify morally relevant similarities and differences.

commonMisreadings: Casuistry is not arbitrary storytelling because the comparison depends on disciplined case analysis.

concepts.name: Categorical imperative
concepts.summary: The categorical imperative is Kant's unconditional moral requirement to act only on principles that can be willed as universal laws.
concepts.body: The categorical imperative is Kant's unconditional moral requirement to act only on principles that can be willed as universal laws. It also requires treating humanity in oneself and others as an end rather than merely as a means.

examples.text: A person refuses to make a false promise because universalizing deceptive promises would undermine the practice of promising.
examples.note: The maxim fails when imagined as a universal law and also disrespects the other person's rational agency.

commonMisreadings: A categorical imperative differs from a hypothetical imperative, which applies only given a particular goal.

concepts.name: Catharsis
concepts.summary: Catharsis is a process of emotional release, clarification, or purification associated with dramatic art and psychological experience.
concepts.body: Catharsis is a process of emotional release, clarification, or purification associated with dramatic art and psychological experience. In Aristotle's account of tragedy, pity and fear are engaged and transformed through the structure of the drama.

examples.text: An audience leaves a tragedy shaken but more composed after following the consequences of a protagonist's error.
examples.note: The emotional movement is organized by the narrative rather than being a random outburst.

commonMisreadings: Catharsis does not simply mean crying or venting any feeling.

concepts.name: Causal closure
concepts.summary: Causal closure is the principle that events within a specified domain have sufficient causes within that domain.
concepts.body: Causal closure is the principle that events within a specified domain have sufficient causes within that domain. In philosophy of mind, physical causal closure says that physical events have sufficient physical causes, challenging nonphysical mental causation.

examples.text: A neural movement is explained entirely by preceding neural and bodily processes under a strict physical-closure hypothesis.
examples.note: The physical explanation leaves no causal work for an independent nonphysical force.

commonMisreadings: Causal closure is a claim about causal sufficiency, not the claim that the domain contains no outside influences in every context.

concepts.name: Causal determinism
concepts.summary: Causal determinism is the thesis that a complete state of the world together with its laws fixes every later state.
concepts.body: Causal determinism is the thesis that a complete state of the world together with its laws fixes every later state. If true, it concerns the necessity of events given prior conditions and laws, not merely their predictability by human observers.

examples.text: Given an exact physical state and deterministic laws, only one future position of a falling object is possible.
examples.note: The future is fixed by the prior state within the model.

commonMisreadings: Determinism is not the same as fatalism, which does not require causes or laws to explain outcomes.

concepts.name: Causal inference
concepts.summary: Causal inference is reasoning about whether changing one factor would change an outcome.
concepts.body: Causal inference is reasoning about whether changing one factor would change an outcome. It relies on comparisons such as randomized treatments, natural experiments, or carefully adjusted observational designs.

examples.text: Researchers estimate whether a drug lowers blood pressure by comparing randomly assigned users with a control group.
examples.note: Random assignment makes treatment status less entangled with preexisting differences.

commonMisreadings: Causal inference is not the same as observing that two variables are correlated.

concepts.name: Causal power
concepts.summary: Causal power is the capacity of an entity, property, or process to produce or prevent changes under suitable conditions.
concepts.body: Causal power is the capacity of an entity, property, or process to produce or prevent changes under suitable conditions. The notion explains why causes are not merely regular sequences but can make a difference to what occurs.

examples.text: The tensile strength of a cable gives it the power to support a load until a critical force is exceeded.
examples.note: The property changes the range of outcomes available under specified conditions.

commonMisreadings: Causal power is not identical to an observed frequency or a person's intention.

concepts.name: Causation
concepts.summary: Causation is a relation in which one event, condition, or process helps bring about another.
concepts.body: Causation is a relation in which one event, condition, or process helps bring about another. Accounts of causation appeal variously to regularity, counterfactual dependence, mechanisms, intervention, or productive connection.

examples.text: Striking a match causes it to ignite when friction and oxygen are present.
examples.note: The strike contributes to the ignition through a physical process rather than merely preceding it.

commonMisreadings: Causation is not equivalent to temporal order because earlier events can be irrelevant.

concepts.name: Centrism
concepts.summary: Centrism is a political orientation that seeks positions between or beyond established left-right extremes.
concepts.body: Centrism is a political orientation that seeks positions between or beyond established left-right extremes. Centrists may combine policies from different traditions and emphasize compromise, institutional stability, or incremental reform.

examples.text: A party supports regulated markets, a social safety net, and gradual rather than revolutionary change.
examples.note: Its platform occupies a middle position across several contested policy dimensions.

commonMisreadings: Centrism is not a fixed list of policies or proof that a position is objectively moderate.

concepts.name: Certainty
concepts.summary: Certainty is a state or standard in which doubt about a proposition is treated as absent or impossible.
concepts.body: Certainty is a state or standard in which doubt about a proposition is treated as absent or impossible. Philosophers distinguish psychological certainty, evidential certainty, and logical or mathematical necessity.

examples.text: A valid proof can make the conclusion certain relative to its axioms and accepted rules.
examples.note: The proof supplies a necessity that does not depend on changing empirical observations.

commonMisreadings: Certainty is not merely strong confidence or a high probability.

concepts.name: Ceteris paribus
concepts.summary: Ceteris paribus is a qualification meaning that other relevant conditions are held constant for the claim under discussion.
concepts.body: Ceteris paribus is a qualification meaning that other relevant conditions are held constant for the claim under discussion. It lets a theory isolate one relationship while acknowledging that real outcomes may depend on additional variables.

examples.text: Demand tends to fall as price rises, ceteris paribus, when income, tastes, and substitute prices remain unchanged.
examples.note: The qualification identifies which background factors are being controlled.

commonMisreadings: Ceteris paribus does not mean that all other facts are literally frozen in the real world.

concepts.name: Change
concepts.summary: Change is the difference by which something becomes otherwise over time or across states.
concepts.body: Change is the difference by which something becomes otherwise over time or across states. It may involve alteration in properties, relations, location, structure, or existence while preserving some identity or continuity.

examples.text: Water changes from liquid to ice when its temperature falls below the relevant freezing point.
examples.note: The substance retains chemical identity while its physical state changes.

commonMisreadings: Change is not necessarily improvement, decay, or movement from one place to another.

concepts.name: Change blindness
concepts.summary: Change blindness is a failure to notice a significant visual change when attention is interrupted or poorly directed.
concepts.body: Change blindness is a failure to notice a significant visual change when attention is interrupted or poorly directed. The effect shows that visual awareness does not preserve a complete, continuously accessible record of a scene.

examples.text: A viewer may fail to notice that a street sign has changed when the alteration occurs during a brief camera cut.
examples.note: The interruption prevents comparison between the relevant before and after representations.

commonMisreadings: Change blindness is not ordinary poor eyesight and can occur in people with normal vision.

concepts.name: Character
concepts.summary: Character is the relatively stable pattern of dispositions and habits through which a person tends to think, feel, and act.
concepts.body: Character is the relatively stable pattern of dispositions and habits through which a person tends to think, feel, and act. In virtue ethics, character is formed through practice and includes traits such as courage, honesty, generosity, and justice.

examples.text: A person who reliably keeps promises despite inconvenience displays a disposition toward honesty.
examples.note: Repeated conduct reveals a settled trait rather than a single lucky action.

commonMisreadings: Character is not identical to reputation, temperament, or an isolated behavior.

concepts.name: Chesterton's fence
concepts.summary: Chesterton's fence is the principle that an existing rule or institution should not be removed before understanding why it was created.
concepts.body: Chesterton's fence is the principle that an existing rule or institution should not be removed before understanding why it was created. The principle treats inherited arrangements as possible solutions to problems that are no longer visible to a later observer.

examples.text: A city planner investigates a seemingly needless traffic barrier before eliminating it and discovers that it prevents vehicles from entering a pedestrian lane.
examples.note: The barrier's purpose explains why immediate removal would create a new hazard.

commonMisreadings: Chesterton's fence does not prohibit reform or imply that every old practice is justified.

concepts.name: Chinese room
concepts.summary: The Chinese room is a thought experiment arguing that formal symbol manipulation alone does not necessarily produce understanding.
concepts.body: The Chinese room is a thought experiment arguing that formal symbol manipulation alone does not necessarily produce understanding. A person who follows an English rulebook to generate appropriate Chinese responses may appear fluent without knowing what the symbols mean.

examples.text: An operator inside a room receives Chinese characters and returns correct replies by matching them to instructions.
examples.note: The external performance is reproduced without the operator possessing semantic comprehension.

commonMisreadings: The argument targets a claim about sufficient conditions for understanding, not every use of computation.

concepts.name: Christian democracy
concepts.summary: Christian democracy is a political tradition combining Christian social ethics with representative government, social responsibility, and respect for human dignity.
concepts.body: Christian democracy is a political tradition combining Christian social ethics with representative government, social responsibility, and respect for human dignity. It often supports family and community institutions, a social market economy, and limits on both state domination and unrestricted individualism.

examples.text: A Christian democratic party may support private enterprise alongside labor protections and public assistance for families.
examples.note: The program joins market ownership to a duty of social solidarity.

commonMisreadings: Christian democracy is not identical to rule by clergy or to one denomination's government.

concepts.name: Christian existentialism
concepts.summary: Christian existentialism is a Christian philosophical approach that emphasizes individual freedom, anxiety, responsibility, faith, and an encounter with God.
concepts.body: Christian existentialism is a Christian philosophical approach that emphasizes individual freedom, anxiety, responsibility, faith, and an encounter with God. It treats authentic commitment as a personal response that cannot be replaced by conformity or abstract system building.

examples.text: A person chooses faith amid uncertainty while accepting responsibility for the choice rather than hiding behind social convention.
examples.note: The example expresses existential decision and responsibility within a Christian framework.

commonMisreadings: Christian existentialism is not secular existentialism with Christian vocabulary added mechanically.

concepts.name: Christian humanism
concepts.summary: Christian humanism is a tradition that joins Christian faith with confidence in human dignity, learning, moral agency, and cultural development.
concepts.body: Christian humanism is a tradition that joins Christian faith with confidence in human dignity, learning, moral agency, and cultural development. It interprets human flourishing as compatible with religious commitment and often draws on classical education and the humanities.

examples.text: A Christian humanist school teaches rhetoric and philosophy while treating education as a way to cultivate responsible persons before God.
examples.note: The curriculum connects intellectual formation with theological and ethical responsibility.

commonMisreadings: Christian humanism is not the claim that human achievement replaces divine grace or religious belief.

concepts.name: Christian socialism
concepts.summary: Christian socialism is a movement that combines Christian moral commitments with socialist criticism of economic inequality and private domination.
concepts.body: Christian socialism is a movement that combines Christian moral commitments with socialist criticism of economic inequality and private domination. It commonly emphasizes communal ownership, worker solidarity, economic justice, and the obligation to protect the poor.

examples.text: A Christian socialist congregation establishes a cooperative bakery whose profits are shared among workers and used for neighborhood relief.
examples.note: The cooperative expresses both collective economic practice and a Christian duty of solidarity.

commonMisreadings: Christian socialism is not simply charity within capitalism or a claim that all Christians endorse socialism.

concepts.name: Citizenship
concepts.summary: Citizenship is membership in a political community together with the rights, duties, and status that membership entails.
concepts.body: Citizenship is membership in a political community together with the rights, duties, and status that membership entails. It can involve legal nationality, participation in public life, allegiance, and reciprocal protection by institutions.

examples.text: A citizen votes in an election and can seek consular protection while abroad.
examples.note: The vote expresses participation and the protection expresses a reciprocal political status.

commonMisreadings: Citizenship is not identical to residence, ethnicity, or personal loyalty to a government.

concepts.name: Civic nationalism
concepts.summary: Civic nationalism defines national belonging through shared political institutions, laws, and civic commitments rather than ancestry alone.
concepts.body: Civic nationalism defines national belonging through shared political institutions, laws, and civic commitments rather than ancestry alone. It can include people of diverse origins when they participate in a common constitutional and public culture.

examples.text: A republic grants national membership to immigrants who accept its constitution and complete the same civic process as native-born residents.
examples.note: The shared political framework supplies the basis of belonging.

commonMisreadings: Civic nationalism is not automatically free of exclusion or disagreement about who may join.

concepts.name: Civil disobedience
concepts.summary: Civil disobedience is a deliberate, public, conscientious, and usually nonviolent breach of law intended to protest serious injustice.
concepts.body: Civil disobedience is a deliberate, public, conscientious, and usually nonviolent breach of law intended to protest serious injustice. Its practitioners typically accept legal risk to communicate the injustice and appeal to the wider political community.

examples.text: Demonstrators peacefully block an unjustly segregated entrance and remain to be arrested rather than using violence.
examples.note: The public lawbreaking seeks reform while acknowledging the authority of law through nonviolent accountability.

commonMisreadings: Civil disobedience differs from secret evasion, ordinary crime, or violent insurrection.

concepts.name: Civil liberty
concepts.summary: Civil liberty is a protected area of individual freedom from unjustified government interference.
concepts.body: Civil liberty is a protected area of individual freedom from unjustified government interference. Typical civil liberties include freedom of speech, religion, association, movement, and protection against arbitrary detention.

examples.text: A court prevents the government from imprisoning a journalist solely for criticizing public officials.
examples.note: The ruling protects expressive freedom against state punishment.

commonMisreadings: Civil liberty is distinct from a positive welfare entitlement such as guaranteed housing.

concepts.name: Civil society
concepts.summary: Civil society is the sphere of voluntary associations and social relationships between individuals, families, markets, and the state.
concepts.body: Civil society is the sphere of voluntary associations and social relationships between individuals, families, markets, and the state. It includes organizations that pursue shared purposes without being direct organs of government.

examples.text: A neighborhood association organizes flood relief independently of the municipal emergency department.
examples.note: The association coordinates public-minded action through voluntary membership outside the state.

commonMisreadings: Civil society is not the same as society as a whole or as every private business.

concepts.name: Class
concepts.summary: Class is a social category whose members share a position in an economic or social structure.
concepts.body: Class is a social category whose members share a position in an economic or social structure. In Marxist analysis, class is especially tied to relationships to productive property and the control of labor.

examples.text: Wage workers who sell their labor to owners of factories occupy a different class position from those owners.
examples.note: Their contrasting relation to production distinguishes the categories.

commonMisreadings: Class is not reducible to income level, personal taste, or individual occupation alone.

concepts.name: Class consciousness
concepts.summary: Class consciousness is awareness of shared class interests and of the structural position that produces them.
concepts.body: Class consciousness is awareness of shared class interests and of the structural position that produces them. It can transform separate personal grievances into collective interpretation and political organization.

examples.text: Factory workers recognize that recurring wage disputes reflect their common dependence on an employer rather than isolated bad luck.
examples.note: The recognition links individual experiences to a shared class relation.

commonMisreadings: Class consciousness is not simply knowing one's salary or belonging to a demographic group.

concepts.name: Class struggle
concepts.summary: Class struggle is conflict between social classes over labor, property, political power, and the distribution of economic resources.
concepts.body: Class struggle is conflict between social classes over labor, property, political power, and the distribution of economic resources. Marxist theory treats such conflict as a major driver of historical change under class-divided production.

examples.text: Workers strike for higher wages while owners resist because the settlement changes how the product of labor is divided.
examples.note: The opposing interests arise from their positions in production.

commonMisreadings: Class struggle is not limited to open violence and can occur through law, bargaining, or ideology.

concepts.name: Classical Chinese Legalism
concepts.summary: Classical Chinese Legalism is a political philosophy that emphasizes strong centralized authority, clear standards, rewards, punishments, and administrative control.
concepts.body: Classical Chinese Legalism is a political philosophy that emphasizes strong centralized authority, clear standards, rewards, punishments, and administrative control. Legalist thinkers generally distrust reliance on rulers' virtue and seek institutions that make conduct predictable and governable.

examples.text: A ruler publishes uniform penalties and rewards officials according to measurable performance rather than personal loyalty.
examples.note: The system uses impersonal standards to secure state power and discipline.

commonMisreadings: Legalism is not equivalent to modern constitutional rule of law or to any system with written laws.

concepts.name: Classical liberalism
concepts.summary: Classical liberalism is a political tradition emphasizing individual rights, limited government, private property, free exchange, and equality before the law.
concepts.body: Classical liberalism is a political tradition emphasizing individual rights, limited government, private property, free exchange, and equality before the law. It arose partly in opposition to arbitrary authority and inherited privilege, though classical liberals differed about the scope of public provision.

examples.text: A government protects contracts and speech while avoiding censorship and detailed control of ordinary commerce.
examples.note: The arrangement prioritizes individual liberty within a legally constrained state.

commonMisreadings: Classical liberalism is not necessarily identical to contemporary political labels called liberal.

concepts.name: Classical logic
concepts.summary: Classical logic is a formal logical system governed by principles such as bivalence and non-contradiction.
concepts.body: Classical logic is a formal logical system governed by principles such as bivalence and non-contradiction. In standard classical logic, every proposition is either true or false and a contradiction entails every proposition.

examples.text: From p and not p, classical logic permits deriving any proposition under the principle of explosion.
examples.note: The inference follows from the system's treatment of contradiction.

commonMisreadings: Classical logic differs from paraconsistent and many-valued logics that reject one or more of these principles.

concepts.name: Classical pragmatism
concepts.summary: Classical pragmatism is a philosophical tradition that interprets meaning and truth through practical consequences, inquiry, and the habits of action involved in accepting beliefs.
concepts.body: Classical pragmatism is a philosophical tradition that interprets meaning and truth through practical consequences, inquiry, and the habits of action involved in accepting beliefs. Its major figures include Peirce, James, and Dewey, who differ while emphasizing experience and fallible investigation.

examples.text: The meaning of a belief about a medicine includes what observations and actions would follow if the belief were accepted.
examples.note: Practical consequences clarify the belief's content and guide inquiry.

commonMisreadings: Pragmatism is not the claim that whatever is useful is automatically true.

concepts.name: Cognitive architecture
concepts.summary: Cognitive architecture is a theory or model of the fixed structures and processes that organize cognition.
concepts.body: Cognitive architecture is a theory or model of the fixed structures and processes that organize cognition. It specifies components such as memory, perception, learning, attention, and decision mechanisms and how they interact.

examples.text: A model may represent working memory as a limited buffer connected to long-term memory and procedural rules.
examples.note: The architecture explains cognition by assigning functions to interacting structural components.

commonMisreadings: A cognitive architecture is more general than a model of one isolated task.

concepts.name: Cognitive dissonance
concepts.summary: Cognitive dissonance is the uncomfortable tension produced by holding inconsistent cognitions or by acting against an important belief.
concepts.body: Cognitive dissonance is the uncomfortable tension produced by holding inconsistent cognitions or by acting against an important belief. People may reduce the tension by changing a belief, reinterpreting an action, adding justifications, or avoiding conflicting information.

examples.text: A smoker who believes smoking is dangerous may minimize the risk after continuing to smoke.
examples.note: The risk minimization reduces conflict between conduct and belief.

commonMisreadings: Cognitive dissonance is not simply any unpleasant emotion or disagreement with another person.

concepts.name: Cognitive load
concepts.summary: Cognitive load is the amount of mental processing capacity demanded by a task at a given time.
concepts.body: Cognitive load is the amount of mental processing capacity demanded by a task at a given time. Instructional theory distinguishes load inherent in the material, load caused by distracting presentation, and load devoted to learning.

examples.text: A cluttered worksheet makes a simple math problem harder because students must process irrelevant decorations and instructions.
examples.note: The unnecessary presentation demands consume limited working-memory capacity.

commonMisreadings: Cognitive load is not identical to difficulty measured by elapsed time or intelligence.

concepts.name: Cognitive reflection
concepts.summary: Cognitive reflection is the capacity to resist an immediately appealing answer and engage in further analytical thought.
concepts.body: Cognitive reflection is the capacity to resist an immediately appealing answer and engage in further analytical thought. Reflection often matters when an intuitive response is plausible but conflicts with a simple calculation.

examples.text: A person rejects the answer ten cents to a bat-and-ball problem after calculating that the bat costs one dollar more than the ball.
examples.note: The person overrides the tempting but incorrect shortcut.

commonMisreadings: Cognitive reflection is not the same as general intelligence or constant rejection of intuition.

concepts.name: Cognitive science
concepts.summary: Cognitive science is the interdisciplinary study of mental processes and intelligent behavior.
concepts.body: Cognitive science is the interdisciplinary study of mental processes and intelligent behavior. It combines methods and theories from psychology, neuroscience, linguistics, computer science, philosophy, and related fields.

examples.text: Researchers compare human sentence processing with computational models and neural timing measurements.
examples.note: The project integrates behavioral, formal, and biological evidence about cognition.

commonMisreadings: Cognitive science is broader than psychology alone and does not require one theory of mind.

concepts.name: Coherentism
concepts.summary: Coherentism is the epistemological view that a belief is justified by its place within a mutually supporting system of beliefs.
concepts.body: Coherentism is the epistemological view that a belief is justified by its place within a mutually supporting system of beliefs. It contrasts with foundationalism by denying that justification must ultimately rest on beliefs that are justified independently of the network.

examples.text: A scientific hypothesis gains support when it fits observations, background theories, and successful predictions without internal conflict.
examples.note: Its justification comes from systematic coherence among many commitments.

commonMisreadings: Coherentism is not the claim that consistency alone makes a belief true.

concepts.name: Collective action
concepts.summary: Collective action is coordinated activity by multiple people pursuing a shared outcome.
concepts.body: Collective action is coordinated activity by multiple people pursuing a shared outcome. It can be difficult when individuals benefit from the result while preferring others to bear the costs of participation.

examples.text: Residents jointly clean a polluted park even though each resident could prefer that neighbors do all the work.
examples.note: The park's improvement requires coordinated contributions despite incentives to free-ride.

commonMisreadings: Collective action is not any event involving several people; the participants must contribute to a shared objective.

concepts.name: Collective responsibility
concepts.summary: Collective responsibility is responsibility attributed to a group for an outcome or practice because of its members' roles, actions, or shared institutions.
concepts.body: Collective responsibility is responsibility attributed to a group for an outcome or practice because of its members' roles, actions, or shared institutions. It may concern duties to repair or prevent harm even when individual blame is unevenly distributed.

examples.text: A corporation accepts responsibility for cleaning contamination caused by its production system while investigating which managers made the decisions.
examples.note: The organization can owe remediation without assigning identical personal guilt to every employee.

commonMisreadings: Collective responsibility is not the claim that every group member is equally culpable.

concepts.name: Collectivism
concepts.summary: Collectivism is a family of views that gives priority to shared or group interests over isolated individual preference in social organization.
concepts.body: Collectivism is a family of views that gives priority to shared or group interests over isolated individual preference in social organization. It can support common goals, mutual obligations, and collective ownership, but its forms differ greatly in political and economic content.

examples.text: A cooperative allocates surplus according to members' shared decisions rather than distributing it to one private owner.
examples.note: The arrangement treats the group as a significant unit of economic decision.

commonMisreadings: Collectivism is not necessarily total state control or hostility to all individual rights.

concepts.name: Colonialism
concepts.summary: Colonialism is the domination and settlement or exploitation of one people or territory by an external power.
concepts.body: Colonialism is the domination and settlement or exploitation of one people or territory by an external power. It commonly involves political subordination, resource extraction, cultural control, and unequal legal status.

examples.text: An empire governs a distant territory, redirects its minerals to the imperial economy, and restricts local political authority.
examples.note: The external power structures the territory for its own strategic and economic benefit.

commonMisreadings: Colonialism is not limited to formal annexation and is not equivalent to ordinary international trade.

concepts.name: Common good
concepts.summary: The common good is the set of social conditions and shared goods that enable members of a community to flourish together.
concepts.body: The common good is the set of social conditions and shared goods that enable members of a community to flourish together. It concerns benefits that are not adequately secured by isolated private choices, such as public safety, trustworthy institutions, and clean air.

examples.text: A city maintains a public water system that protects residents regardless of which household can pay for a private well.
examples.note: The infrastructure provides a shared condition for health and civic life.

commonMisreadings: The common good is not simply whatever most people currently want or the sum of private advantages.

concepts.name: Common knowledge
concepts.summary: Common knowledge is information that everyone in a group knows, and everyone knows that everyone knows, through arbitrarily many levels.
concepts.body: Common knowledge is information that everyone in a group knows, and everyone knows that everyone knows, through arbitrarily many levels. Its public and recursive structure can coordinate action without each person privately communicating the same fact.

examples.text: In a game, both players know the rules and know that both know the rules.
examples.note: The shared awareness lets each player predict that the other will use the same rules.

commonMisreadings: Common knowledge is stronger than merely having the same information privately.

concepts.name: Common ownership
concepts.summary: Common ownership is an arrangement in which a resource is held by a community or group rather than by exclusive private owners.
concepts.body: Common ownership is an arrangement in which a resource is held by a community or group rather than by exclusive private owners. Rules still determine access, use, maintenance, and decision-making, so common ownership is not the absence of property norms.

examples.text: Members of a village jointly manage a forest and set limits on harvesting.
examples.note: The forest is governed as a shared resource through community rules.

commonMisreadings: Common ownership differs from open access, where no effective group rules restrict use.

concepts.name: Communalism
concepts.summary: Communalism is a political orientation that emphasizes local self-government, participatory democracy, and federated communities.
concepts.body: Communalism is a political orientation that emphasizes local self-government, participatory democracy, and federated communities. In contemporary theory associated with Murray Bookchin, it links ecological concerns with democratic municipal institutions.

examples.text: Neighborhood assemblies elect delegates to a federation that coordinates regional transport and energy policy.
examples.note: The arrangement combines local participation with coordination across communities.

commonMisreadings: Communalism is not merely living communally or sharing a household.

concepts.name: Communism
concepts.summary: Communism is a family of political and economic doctrines seeking a classless society organized around common ownership of productive resources.
concepts.body: Communism is a family of political and economic doctrines seeking a classless society organized around common ownership of productive resources. Marxist communism treats the abolition of class domination as a historical and emancipatory aim, while communist regimes have differed in practice.

examples.text: A cooperative society collectively controls factories and distributes production without a class of private owners hiring wage labor.
examples.note: The example represents common control of production and the absence of owner-worker class relations.

commonMisreadings: Communism is not identical to any single twentieth-century state or to every form of public ownership.

concepts.name: Communitarianism
concepts.summary: Communitarianism is a political and ethical approach that emphasizes the moral importance of communities, social practices, and shared identities.
concepts.body: Communitarianism is a political and ethical approach that emphasizes the moral importance of communities, social practices, and shared identities. It argues that individuals are formed by relationships and traditions rather than existing as wholly detached choosers.

examples.text: A town preserves a local caregiving institution because its responsibilities express a shared civic identity, not only individual contracts.
examples.note: The institution embodies obligations generated through communal membership.

commonMisreadings: Communitarianism does not require rejecting universal rights or endorsing every inherited tradition.

concepts.name: Compactness theorem
concepts.summary: The compactness theorem for first-order logic states that a set of sentences has a model if every finite subset of it has a model.
concepts.body: The compactness theorem for first-order logic states that a set of sentences has a model if every finite subset of it has a model. It connects finite satisfiability with global satisfiability and has consequences for constructing nonstandard models.

examples.text: If every finite collection of constraints on a structure can be satisfied, then all the constraints can be satisfied together in some model.
examples.note: The theorem turns consistent finite approximations into a model for the entire set.

commonMisreadings: It does not say that every finite mathematical object is compact in the topological sense.

concepts.name: Comparative advantage
concepts.summary: Comparative advantage is the ability to produce a good at a lower opportunity cost than another producer.
concepts.body: Comparative advantage is the ability to produce a good at a lower opportunity cost than another producer. Trade can benefit both parties even when one party is more productive in making every good, provided their relative costs differ.

examples.text: A country gives up less wheat than its partner when producing cloth and specializes in cloth while importing wheat.
examples.note: Specialization follows relative sacrifice rather than absolute productivity alone.

commonMisreadings: Comparative advantage is not the same as being the fastest or cheapest producer in absolute terms.

concepts.name: Compatibilism
concepts.summary: Compatibilism is the view that free will and moral responsibility can coexist with causal determinism.
concepts.body: Compatibilism is the view that free will and moral responsibility can coexist with causal determinism. Compatibilists commonly define freedom as acting from one's own reasons or desires without coercive interference, not as being uncaused.

examples.text: A person freely signs a contract after deliberation even if the deliberation has deterministic causes.
examples.note: The action expresses the person's reasons rather than external compulsion.

commonMisreadings: Compatibilism does not claim that determinism is false or that every caused action is free.

concepts.name: Compatibility
concepts.summary: Compatibility is the capacity of two systems, states, or claims to coexist or operate together without contradiction or damaging interference.
concepts.body: Compatibility is the capacity of two systems, states, or claims to coexist or operate together without contradiction or damaging interference. The relevant standard may concern logical consistency, technical interoperability, biological fit, or social coordination.

examples.text: A phone charger is compatible with a device when its connector and electrical specifications allow safe charging.
examples.note: The specifications permit the two systems to function together.

commonMisreadings: Compatibility is not identity and does not guarantee optimal performance.

concepts.name: Completeness
concepts.summary: Completeness is the property of a formal system in which every statement of the relevant kind that is true or semantically valid is derivable within the system.
concepts.body: Completeness is the property of a formal system in which every statement of the relevant kind that is true or semantically valid is derivable within the system. The meaning depends on the logic or theory being discussed, and it differs from consistency, which concerns avoiding contradiction.

examples.text: First-order logic is complete because every logically valid first-order sentence has a formal proof.
examples.note: The proof system captures all semantic validity in that language.

commonMisreadings: Completeness does not mean that every mathematical truth is decidable or that the system has no limits.

concepts.name: Complex adaptive system
concepts.summary: A complex adaptive system is a system of interacting agents whose local responses produce changing collective patterns and adaptation.
concepts.body: A complex adaptive system is a system of interacting agents whose local responses produce changing collective patterns and adaptation. Such systems can learn, reorganize, and generate emergent behavior without a single controller specifying the whole outcome.

examples.text: An ecosystem changes as species alter their behavior in response to predators, resources, and one another.
examples.note: Local adaptations continually reshape the system's larger conditions.

commonMisreadings: A complex adaptive system is not merely a complicated machine with many fixed parts.

concepts.name: Complexity
concepts.summary: Complexity is the degree to which a system contains many interacting elements, dependencies, scales, or possible behaviors that resist simple description.
concepts.body: Complexity is the degree to which a system contains many interacting elements, dependencies, scales, or possible behaviors that resist simple description. Complex systems may exhibit emergence, feedback, nonlinear effects, and sensitivity to initial conditions.

examples.text: A small change in an epidemic's contact network can produce a much larger change in the number of infections.
examples.note: Interactions amplify or suppress effects in ways not captured by a single linear factor.

commonMisreadings: Complexity is not the same as mere size or confusion.

concepts.name: Composition
concepts.summary: Composition is the relation or process by which parts combine to form a whole.
concepts.body: Composition is the relation or process by which parts combine to form a whole. Questions of composition ask what entities are made of and whether the whole has properties beyond those of its components.

examples.text: Several wooden boards and joints compose a table when arranged into a stable usable structure.
examples.note: The organized parts constitute an object with a new functional role.

commonMisreadings: Composition is not identical to physical contact because touching parts need not form a unified whole.

concepts.name: Compositionality
concepts.summary: Compositionality is the principle that the meaning of a complex expression depends on the meanings of its parts and their mode of combination.
concepts.body: Compositionality is the principle that the meaning of a complex expression depends on the meanings of its parts and their mode of combination. It helps explain how speakers understand and generate indefinitely many sentences from finite vocabularies and grammatical rules.

examples.text: The meaning of red boat is derived from the meanings of red and boat plus their attributive relation.
examples.note: Changing either word or the grammatical arrangement changes the resulting interpretation.

commonMisreadings: Compositionality does not imply that every idiom has a fully predictable literal meaning.

concepts.name: Computationalism
concepts.summary: Computationalism is the view that cognition consists in or is explained by computation over representations.
concepts.body: Computationalism is the view that cognition consists in or is explained by computation over representations. It treats mental processes as transformations defined by rules or operations on structured information.

examples.text: A planning system represents possible routes and computes which sequence reaches a destination under specified constraints.
examples.note: The route choice is modeled as information processing over representations.

commonMisreadings: Computationalism is not the claim that every computer program is conscious or that cognition must run on silicon.

concepts.name: Concept
concepts.summary: A concept is a general mental or linguistic representation used to classify, describe, or reason about objects, properties, events, or relations.
concepts.body: A concept is a general mental or linguistic representation used to classify, describe, or reason about objects, properties, events, or relations. Concepts can guide recognition and inference while remaining open to revision and differing across languages and theories.

examples.text: The concept of triangle allows a learner to identify many differently sized three-sided figures.
examples.note: One representation applies across multiple concrete instances by tracking a common structure.

commonMisreadings: A concept is not necessarily a word, a sharply bounded category, or a timeless essence.

concepts.name: Conceptual engineering
concepts.summary: Conceptual engineering is the deliberate assessment, revision, or replacement of concepts to improve their usefulness, justice, clarity, or theoretical performance.
concepts.body: Conceptual engineering is the deliberate assessment, revision, or replacement of concepts to improve their usefulness, justice, clarity, or theoretical performance. It treats inherited concepts as tools that can be redesigned rather than merely described.

examples.text: A legal theorist proposes a narrower concept of consent to exclude apparent agreement produced by coercive threats.
examples.note: The revision aims to make the concept track a morally and legally important distinction.

commonMisreadings: Conceptual engineering is not ordinary word substitution because it evaluates the function and consequences of a concept.

concepts.name: Conceptualism
concepts.summary: Conceptualism is the view that universals or generality depend on concepts rather than existing as mind-independent entities or as mere names alone.
concepts.body: Conceptualism is the view that universals or generality depend on concepts rather than existing as mind-independent entities or as mere names alone. In medieval philosophy, it occupies a position between realism about universals and nominalism.

examples.text: The generality of triangle is explained by the mind's concept applying to many individual triangular objects.
examples.note: The concept accounts for common predication without requiring one universal triangle existing apart from instances.

commonMisreadings: Conceptualism is not the claim that individual objects are unreal.

concepts.name: Conclusion
concepts.summary: A conclusion is a proposition presented as following from one or more premises in an argument or inference.
concepts.body: A conclusion is a proposition presented as following from one or more premises in an argument or inference. Its support depends on the relation between the premises and the conclusion, such as deductive validity or inductive strength.

examples.text: In the argument All mammals breathe and whales are mammals, whales breathe is the conclusion.
examples.note: The final proposition is inferred from the two stated premises.

commonMisreadings: A conclusion is not necessarily true merely because it appears at the end of an argument.

concepts.name: Conditional
concepts.summary: A conditional is a proposition stating that one condition implies or would support another condition.
concepts.body: A conditional is a proposition stating that one condition implies or would support another condition. In the material conditional if p then q, the statement is false only when p is true and q is false, though natural-language conditionals can express richer relations.

examples.text: If a metal is heated sufficiently, it expands expresses a conditional relation between heating and expansion.
examples.note: The statement connects a possible antecedent with a consequent.

commonMisreadings: A conditional does not automatically assert that its antecedent is true.

concepts.name: Confirmation
concepts.summary: Confirmation is the increase in support that evidence gives to a hypothesis or claim.
concepts.body: Confirmation is the increase in support that evidence gives to a hypothesis or claim. Evidence confirms a hypothesis when the evidence is more expected if the hypothesis is true than under relevant alternatives.

examples.text: Finding a fingerprint matching a suspect's print confirms that the suspect handled the object, though it may not prove the entire crime.
examples.note: The print is more expected under contact by that suspect than under many alternatives.

commonMisreadings: Confirmation is not conclusive proof and can depend on background assumptions.

concepts.name: Confounding
concepts.summary: Confounding occurs when a third factor influences both a suspected cause and an outcome, creating a misleading association.
concepts.body: Confounding occurs when a third factor influences both a suspected cause and an outcome, creating a misleading association. A confounder makes it difficult to determine whether the observed relationship reflects the proposed causal effect.

examples.text: Ice cream sales and drowning deaths both rise in summer because warm weather increases swimming and ice cream purchases.
examples.note: Season is associated with both variables and explains their correlation without ice cream causing drowning.

commonMisreadings: Confounding is not the same as random measurement error or any correlation between two variables.

concepts.name: Confucian li
concepts.summary: Confucian li refers to the ritual forms, social norms, etiquette, and patterned practices that shape appropriate conduct.
concepts.body: Confucian li refers to the ritual forms, social norms, etiquette, and patterned practices that shape appropriate conduct. Li is not merely external ceremony because practicing it can cultivate emotions, roles, and moral character.

examples.text: A child bows respectfully to an elder and learns to express gratitude through an established family ritual.
examples.note: The form teaches the relationship and dispositions that make respect socially intelligible.

commonMisreadings: Li is not reducible to empty formalism or to criminal law.

concepts.name: Confucian ren
concepts.summary: Confucian ren is a virtue of humaneness, benevolence, and concern for others that guides ethical relationships.
concepts.body: Confucian ren is a virtue of humaneness, benevolence, and concern for others that guides ethical relationships. It is developed through disciplined conduct, empathy, and the extension of familial concern into wider social responsibility.

examples.text: A magistrate shows ren by tempering a punishment after carefully considering the human consequences while preserving public order.
examples.note: The decision combines humane concern with responsible judgment.

commonMisreadings: Ren is not mere sentimentality or unrestricted favoritism toward one's family.

concepts.name: Confucianism
concepts.summary: Confucianism is a tradition of ethical, social, and political thought centered on cultivated virtue, humane relationships, learning, and responsible roles.
concepts.body: Confucianism is a tradition of ethical, social, and political thought centered on cultivated virtue, humane relationships, learning, and responsible roles. It emphasizes practices such as filial respect, ritual propriety, education, and benevolent governance, with substantial variation across historical schools.

examples.text: A ruler improves public life by cultivating personal virtue and appointing officials who are educated and morally reliable.
examples.note: The example links political legitimacy to character and learning.

commonMisreadings: Confucianism is not simply ancestor worship or a rigid defense of every traditional hierarchy.

concepts.name: Conjecture
concepts.summary: A conjecture is a proposition proposed as plausible but not yet established by proof or decisive evidence.
concepts.body: A conjecture is a proposition proposed as plausible but not yet established by proof or decisive evidence. Conjectures can guide investigation and later be confirmed, revised, or refuted.

examples.text: The Goldbach conjecture claims that every even integer greater than two is the sum of two primes.
examples.note: It remains a precise mathematical proposal whose general proof has not been established.

commonMisreadings: A conjecture is not a random guess and is not equivalent to a theorem.

concepts.name: Connotation
concepts.summary: A connotation is an associated meaning or emotional coloring that a word carries beyond its literal reference.
concepts.body: A connotation is an associated meaning or emotional coloring that a word carries beyond its literal reference. Connotations vary among communities and can change as social attitudes change.

examples.text: The word "slender" often has a more favorable connotation than "skinny".
examples.note: It fits because it distinguishes implied associations from dictionary denotation.

commonMisreadings: Connotation is not the same as denotation, which identifies the literal or referential meaning.

concepts.name: Consciousness
concepts.summary: Consciousness is the condition of having subjective experience or awareness.
concepts.body: Consciousness is the condition of having subjective experience or awareness. Conscious states can include perception, thought, emotion, and wakeful awareness.

examples.text: A person consciously feels pain when the injury is present in their experienced awareness.
examples.note: It fits because it concerns the presence and character of experience.

commonMisreadings: Consciousness is not identical to attention, because some conscious experiences occur outside focused attention.

concepts.name: Consciousness hard problem
concepts.summary: The hard problem of consciousness asks why and how physical processes give rise to subjective experience.
concepts.body: The hard problem of consciousness asks why and how physical processes give rise to subjective experience. It differs from explaining the functions and reportability of mental states.

examples.text: Explaining visual information processing does not by itself explain why seeing red feels like anything.
examples.note: It fits because it targets the explanatory gap between mechanism and phenomenal experience.

commonMisreadings: The hard problem is not simply the practical problem of measuring neural activity.

concepts.name: Consent
concepts.summary: Consent is voluntary and informed agreement to an action or arrangement.
concepts.body: Consent is voluntary and informed agreement to an action or arrangement. Valid consent requires sufficient understanding and freedom from coercion.

examples.text: A patient gives consent to surgery after receiving its risks and alternatives.
examples.note: It fits because it defines the authorization that makes an interaction permissible.

commonMisreadings: Consent is not mere silence when the circumstances do not establish voluntary agreement.

concepts.name: Consequent
concepts.summary: The consequent is the clause that follows the then in a conditional statement.
concepts.body: The consequent is the clause that follows the then in a conditional statement. In the conditional If it rains, the ground is wet, the ground is wet is the consequent.

examples.text: In If a number is divisible by four, it is even, it is even is the consequent.
examples.note: It fits because it identifies the result clause of an implication.

commonMisreadings: The consequent is not the antecedent, which supplies the if-clause.

concepts.name: Consequentialism
concepts.summary: Consequentialism is the moral view that an action is assessed by the value of its consequences.
concepts.body: Consequentialism is the moral view that an action is assessed by the value of its consequences. Different consequentialist theories can disagree about which consequences are valuable.

examples.text: A utilitarian may permit an action when it produces the greatest total well-being.
examples.note: It fits because moral rightness is determined by outcomes in this family of theories.

commonMisreadings: Consequentialism is not equivalent to egoism, since consequences may be evaluated for everyone.

concepts.name: Consequentialist libertarianism
concepts.summary: Consequentialist libertarianism evaluates political arrangements by consequences while treating individual liberty as a central constraint or good.
concepts.body: Consequentialist libertarianism evaluates political arrangements by consequences while treating individual liberty as a central constraint or good. It can support limited government because coercive restrictions are expected to produce harmful consequences.

examples.text: A consequentialist libertarian may defend free expression because broad speech liberty improves social inquiry.
examples.note: It fits because it combines outcome-based justification with a strong commitment to liberty.

commonMisreadings: It is not standard rights-based libertarianism, which grounds restrictions primarily in inviolable rights.

concepts.name: Conservatism
concepts.summary: Conservatism is a political orientation that favors inherited institutions, gradual change, and social continuity.
concepts.body: Conservatism is a political orientation that favors inherited institutions, gradual change, and social continuity. Conservatives can support reform when it preserves order or repairs institutions without abrupt disruption.

examples.text: A conservative may prefer incremental tax reform over a sudden restructuring of the economy.
examples.note: It fits because it emphasizes prudence and continuity in political change.

commonMisreadings: Conservatism is not identical to reaction, which seeks to restore an earlier order.

concepts.name: Consistency
concepts.summary: Consistency is the property of a set of claims that they do not jointly entail a contradiction.
concepts.body: Consistency is the property of a set of claims that they do not jointly entail a contradiction. A consistent set may still be false because consistency alone does not establish truth.

examples.text: The claims All cats are mammals and No cats are mammals are inconsistent if at least one cat exists.
examples.note: It fits because logical compatibility is the central meaning of consistency.

commonMisreadings: Consistency is not completeness, which concerns whether every relevant statement is decided.

concepts.name: Constitution
concepts.summary: A constitution is a fundamental set of rules that establishes and limits a political authority.
concepts.body: A constitution is a fundamental set of rules that establishes and limits a political authority. A constitution commonly allocates powers among institutions and protects certain rights.

examples.text: The United States Constitution creates a federal structure with legislative, executive, and judicial branches.
examples.note: It fits because it defines the basic framework of government.

commonMisreadings: A constitution need not be a single written document, as the United Kingdom illustrates.

concepts.name: Constitutional monarchy
concepts.summary: A constitutional monarchy is a system in which a monarch is head of state while constitutional rules limit political power.
concepts.body: A constitutional monarchy is a system in which a monarch is head of state while constitutional rules limit political power. Elected officials usually exercise government authority under the constitution.

examples.text: In Sweden, the monarch performs mainly ceremonial functions while parliament and the government govern.
examples.note: It fits because monarchy is combined with constitutional limitation and representative government.

commonMisreadings: It is not an absolute monarchy, where the monarch retains much broader governing power.

concepts.name: Constitutionalism
concepts.summary: Constitutionalism is the principle that governmental power must be legally limited and exercised under fundamental rules.
concepts.body: Constitutionalism is the principle that governmental power must be legally limited and exercised under fundamental rules. It includes institutional checks, rights protections, and procedures for lawful government.

examples.text: Judicial review can enforce constitutionalism by invalidating actions that exceed legal authority.
examples.note: It fits because it concerns limits on rulers rather than merely the existence of a constitution.

commonMisreadings: A state can possess a written constitution without practicing constitutionalism.

concepts.name: Constructive dilemma
concepts.summary: A constructive dilemma is an argument form that derives a disjunction from two conditionals and a disjunction of their antecedents.
concepts.body: A constructive dilemma is an argument form that derives a disjunction from two conditionals and a disjunction of their antecedents. Its pattern is If P then R, if Q then S, P or Q, therefore R or S.

examples.text: If rain causes flooding and snow causes closures, and rain or snow occurs, flooding or closures follows.
examples.note: It fits because the inference constructs an alternative conclusion from alternative sufficient conditions.

commonMisreadings: It is not a destructive dilemma, which uses negated consequents to infer negated antecedents.

concepts.name: Constructivism in philosophy
concepts.summary: Constructivism in philosophy holds that some truths, norms, or objects are constituted through procedures, practices, or conceptual activity.
concepts.body: Constructivism in philosophy holds that some truths, norms, or objects are constituted through procedures, practices, or conceptual activity. Moral constructivism can ground principles in what agents would accept under suitable conditions.

examples.text: Kantian constructivism derives moral requirements from the structure of rational agency.
examples.note: It fits because the relevant standards are constructed through a specified standpoint or procedure.

commonMisreadings: It does not necessarily claim that physical reality is invented by human minds.

concepts.name: Content externalism
concepts.summary: Content externalism is the view that the content of some mental states depends partly on factors outside the thinker.
concepts.body: Content externalism is the view that the content of some mental states depends partly on factors outside the thinker. A person can have the same internal physical state while a different environment changes what a word or thought refers to.

examples.text: Twin Earth arguments suggest that the content of water-thoughts depends on whether the surrounding liquid is H2O or XYZ.
