examples.note: It fits because external environmental relations help determine mental content.

commonMisreadings: It differs from internalism, which makes content depend only on factors inside the subject.

concepts.name: Context-dependent memory
concepts.summary: Context-dependent memory is the tendency for recall to improve when the retrieval context resembles the context of learning.
concepts.body: Context-dependent memory is the tendency for recall to improve when the retrieval context resembles the context of learning. The context can include a physical setting, internal state, or surrounding cues.

examples.text: A diver who learns words underwater may recall more of them underwater than on land.
examples.note: It fits because memory retrieval is helped by matching contextual cues.

commonMisreadings: It is not the claim that memories are stored only in the original context.

concepts.name: Contextualism in epistemology
concepts.summary: Contextualism in epistemology holds that the truth conditions of knowledge claims can vary with conversational or practical context.
concepts.body: Contextualism in epistemology holds that the truth conditions of knowledge claims can vary with conversational or practical context. A person may correctly be said to know a fact in an ordinary context but not in a skeptical context with stricter standards.

examples.text: Whether someone knows that a bank is open can depend on how much is at stake in the conversation.
examples.note: It fits because the standards for the verb know shift with context.

commonMisreadings: It does not mean that truth itself changes whenever a speaker changes context.

concepts.name: Continental philosophy
concepts.summary: Continental philosophy is a broad tradition associated with European movements such as phenomenology, existentialism, hermeneutics, and critical theory.
concepts.body: Continental philosophy is a broad tradition associated with European movements such as phenomenology, existentialism, hermeneutics, and critical theory. It often emphasizes history, interpretation, embodiment, society, and lived experience.

examples.text: Heidegger's analysis of being-in-the-world is a work commonly placed in the continental tradition.
examples.note: It fits because the term names a historical and methodological family of philosophical approaches.

commonMisreadings: It is not a precise doctrine shared by every philosopher outside the analytic tradition.

concepts.name: Contingency
concepts.summary: Contingency is the condition of being possible but not necessary, so that something could have been otherwise.
concepts.body: Contingency is the condition of being possible but not necessary, so that something could have been otherwise. A contingent fact is true in the actual world but false in at least one possible world.

examples.text: That a particular tree exists is contingent because the tree might never have grown.
examples.note: It fits because it marks dependence on circumstances rather than inevitability.

commonMisreadings: Contingency is not impossibility, which means that a thing cannot occur in any possible case.

concepts.name: Contingent being
concepts.summary: A contingent being is an entity that exists but could have failed to exist.
concepts.body: A contingent being is an entity that exists but could have failed to exist. Contingent beings depend on conditions or causes outside themselves for their existence.

examples.text: A human being is contingent because the individual would not exist without particular biological and historical conditions.
examples.note: It fits because the concept concerns non-necessary existence.

commonMisreadings: A contingent being is not the same as a dependent object in every philosophical theory, since dependence can be defined more narrowly.

concepts.name: Contractarianism
concepts.summary: Contractarianism is the view that moral or political principles are justified by agreement among rational agents.
concepts.body: Contractarianism is the view that moral or political principles are justified by agreement among rational agents. The agreement may be hypothetical rather than an actual historical contract.

examples.text: Hobbesian contractarianism explains political obligation through an agreement to escape insecurity.
examples.note: It fits because mutual agreement supplies the basis for norms or authority.

commonMisreadings: Contractarianism is distinct from contractualism, which typically derives morality from principles no one could reasonably reject.

concepts.name: Contractualism
concepts.summary: Contractualism is the moral theory that principles are justified when no one could reasonably reject them as a basis for shared conduct.
concepts.body: Contractualism is the moral theory that principles are justified when no one could reasonably reject them as a basis for shared conduct. It evaluates principles from the standpoint of each affected person rather than simply aggregating welfare.

examples.text: A contractualist may reject a policy if its burden on one person cannot be justified to that person.
examples.note: It fits because reasonable rejectability is its central test of moral principles.

commonMisreadings: It is not necessarily based on an actual signed contract or explicit bargain.

concepts.name: Contradiction
concepts.summary: A contradiction is a statement or pair of statements that cannot be true together in the same respect and at the same time.
concepts.body: A contradiction is a statement or pair of statements that cannot be true together in the same respect and at the same time. In classical logic, a proposition and its negation form a contradiction.

examples.text: The claims The door is open and The door is not open contradict when they refer to the same door and time.
examples.note: It fits because incompatibility between truth claims is the defining relation.

commonMisreadings: A contradiction is not merely a disagreement between people, which may arise without logical incompatibility.

concepts.name: Contraposition
concepts.summary: Contraposition is the valid transformation of a conditional into one with the negated consequent as antecedent and negated antecedent as consequent.
concepts.body: Contraposition is the valid transformation of a conditional into one with the negated consequent as antecedent and negated antecedent as consequent. The conditional If P then Q is logically equivalent to If not Q then not P.

examples.text: If a shape is a square then it has four sides entails that if it lacks four sides then it is not a square.
examples.note: It fits because the inference preserves truth by reversing and negating the conditional.

commonMisreadings: Contraposition is not the same as affirming the consequent, which is invalid.

concepts.name: Conventionalism
concepts.summary: Conventionalism is the view that some truths, meanings, or standards depend on human conventions rather than on facts independent of convention.
concepts.body: Conventionalism is the view that some truths, meanings, or standards depend on human conventions rather than on facts independent of convention. It can treat geometrical frameworks or linguistic meanings as selected systems of rules.

examples.text: The meaning of the word bicycle depends on linguistic conventions shared by speakers.
examples.note: It fits because convention is presented as constitutive of the relevant standard.

commonMisreadings: Conventionalism does not imply that every fact is arbitrary or socially chosen.

concepts.name: Cooperative principle
concepts.summary: The cooperative principle is Grice's idea that conversational participants generally contribute what is appropriate to the shared purpose of an exchange.
concepts.body: The cooperative principle is Grice's idea that conversational participants generally contribute what is appropriate to the shared purpose of an exchange. It is expressed through maxims concerning quantity, quality, relation, and manner.

examples.text: Answering a question with relevant information normally follows the maxim of relation.
examples.note: It fits because it explains how shared conversational expectations support interpretation.

commonMisreadings: It does not mean that speakers always cooperate sincerely or obey every maxim literally.

concepts.name: Corporatism
concepts.summary: Corporatism is a political system that organizes representation through occupational or social corporations rather than primarily through individual competition or class conflict.
concepts.body: Corporatism is a political system that organizes representation through occupational or social corporations rather than primarily through individual competition or class conflict. Corporations in this sense can include employers, workers, professions, or other recognized groups.

examples.text: A state may require labor and business associations to negotiate policy through officially recognized councils.
examples.note: It fits because organized social groups are given a formal role in governance.

commonMisreadings: Corporatism is not the same as rule by private corporations or ordinary corporate capitalism.

concepts.name: Correspondence theory of truth
concepts.summary: The correspondence theory of truth holds that a proposition is true when it corresponds to the relevant facts or reality.
concepts.body: The correspondence theory of truth holds that a proposition is true when it corresponds to the relevant facts or reality. Its central idea connects truth with how the world is rather than only with coherence or usefulness.

examples.text: The proposition Snow is white is true when snow is in fact white under the intended conditions.
examples.note: It fits because truth is defined by agreement between statement and fact.

commonMisreadings: Correspondence does not mean that a true statement must resemble its fact pictorially.

concepts.name: Cosmopolitanism
concepts.summary: Cosmopolitanism is the view that all people belong to a shared moral or political community beyond particular nations.
concepts.body: Cosmopolitanism is the view that all people belong to a shared moral or political community beyond particular nations. It gives universal duties or equal moral concern priority over exclusive national loyalty.

examples.text: A cosmopolitan may support international institutions that protect human rights across borders.
examples.note: It fits because the concept treats global membership as morally significant.

commonMisreadings: Cosmopolitanism does not require eliminating all local cultures or political communities.

concepts.name: Cost–benefit analysis
concepts.summary: Cost–benefit analysis compares the expected costs and benefits of an option, often by expressing them in monetary or comparable terms.
concepts.body: Cost–benefit analysis compares the expected costs and benefits of an option, often by expressing them in monetary or comparable terms. It can incorporate discounting, uncertainty, distributional effects, and opportunity costs.

examples.text: A transport agency may compare a bridge's construction cost with monetized travel-time savings and avoided accidents.
examples.note: It fits because systematic comparison guides the choice among policies or projects.

commonMisreadings: It is not a claim that every moral value is inherently reducible to money.

concepts.name: Council communism
concepts.summary: Council communism is a socialist current that advocates workers' councils as the basis of political and economic decision-making.
concepts.body: Council communism is a socialist current that advocates workers' councils as the basis of political and economic decision-making. It rejects party-led state control in favor of direct worker self-management through councils.

examples.text: A council communist model would have workplace councils coordinate production and delegate revocable representatives.
examples.note: It fits because workers' councils are the central institution of the proposed socialism.

commonMisreadings: It is not identical to trade unionism, which can operate within capitalist ownership.

concepts.name: Counterexample
concepts.summary: A counterexample is a specific case that disproves a universal claim or invalidates an alleged general rule.
concepts.body: A counterexample is a specific case that disproves a universal claim or invalidates an alleged general rule. One counterexample is sufficient to refute a statement of the form all objects have property P.

examples.text: The number 9 is a counterexample to the claim that every odd number is prime.
examples.note: It fits because an individual case defeats a universal assertion.

commonMisreadings: A counterexample does not prove the opposite universal claim that no objects have the property.

concepts.name: Counterfactual
concepts.summary: A counterfactual is a conditional statement about what would or might have happened under a condition contrary to fact or not settled as actual.
concepts.body: A counterfactual is a conditional statement about what would or might have happened under a condition contrary to fact or not settled as actual. Counterfactuals are often evaluated using relevant possible-world comparisons.

examples.text: If the alarm had been set, the train would not have been missed is a counterfactual claim.
examples.note: It fits because it reasons about an alternative to the actual course of events.

commonMisreadings: A counterfactual is not simply a prediction about an event that has not happened yet.

concepts.name: Counterfactual thinking
concepts.summary: Counterfactual thinking is the mental process of imagining alternatives to events that actually occurred.
concepts.body: Counterfactual thinking is the mental process of imagining alternatives to events that actually occurred. It can generate upward alternatives that improve on reality or downward alternatives that worsen it.

examples.text: After missing a flight, a traveler may imagine that leaving home ten minutes earlier would have prevented the loss.
examples.note: It fits because it constructs alternative causal paths from an actual outcome.

commonMisreadings: It is not the same as factual recall, which represents what actually happened.

concepts.name: Countermodel
concepts.summary: A countermodel is an interpretation or structure in which premises are true but a proposed conclusion is false.
concepts.body: A countermodel is an interpretation or structure in which premises are true but a proposed conclusion is false. Finding a countermodel demonstrates that an argument form is invalid.

examples.text: An interpretation where P is true and Q is false countermodels the inference from P to Q.
examples.note: It fits because the model provides a formal case against logical consequence.

commonMisreadings: A countermodel is not merely an informal example unless it satisfies the formal interpretation requirements.

concepts.name: Counterpart theory
concepts.summary: Counterpart theory is David Lewis's account of modality in which an object has counterparts in other possible worlds rather than literally existing in them.
concepts.body: Counterpart theory is David Lewis's account of modality in which an object has counterparts in other possible worlds rather than literally existing in them. Counterpart relations are similarity relations and need not be unique or exact identity relations.

examples.text: A person in another possible world may be a counterpart of the actual person without being numerically identical to them.
examples.note: It fits because modal claims are analyzed through counterparts across worlds.

commonMisreadings: It differs from transworld identity, which says one object can literally exist in multiple worlds.

concepts.name: Courage
concepts.summary: Courage is the virtue of facing a significant danger or difficulty for a worthy end despite fear.
concepts.body: Courage is the virtue of facing a significant danger or difficulty for a worthy end despite fear. Courage requires appropriate judgment because reckless exposure to danger is not necessarily virtuous.

examples.text: A firefighter enters a burning building to rescue a trapped person despite recognizing the risk.
examples.note: It fits because courageous action combines fear, risk, and a justified purpose.

commonMisreadings: Courage is not fearlessness, since a person can be courageous while feeling afraid.

concepts.name: Credence
concepts.summary: A credence is a degree of belief represented as a confidence level that a proposition is true.
concepts.body: A credence is a degree of belief represented as a confidence level that a proposition is true. In Bayesian reasoning, credences are commonly represented by probabilities between zero and one.

examples.text: A researcher may assign a credence of 0.8 to the hypothesis that a treatment is effective.
examples.note: It fits because it measures graded belief rather than simple acceptance or rejection.

commonMisreadings: Credence is not evidence itself, but a rational response to evidence may change it.

concepts.name: Critical rationalism
concepts.summary: Critical rationalism is the philosophy that knowledge advances through bold conjectures and attempts at refutation rather than through final verification.
concepts.body: Critical rationalism is the philosophy that knowledge advances through bold conjectures and attempts at refutation rather than through final verification. It treats criticism and falsifiability as central methods for correcting error.

examples.text: A scientific theory survives when repeated tests fail to refute its risky predictions, not because it is proven conclusively.
examples.note: It fits because rational inquiry is organized around criticism of proposed explanations.

commonMisreadings: It does not claim that every idea is equally rational merely because it can be criticized.

concepts.name: Critical theory
concepts.summary: Critical theory is an approach that examines and seeks to transform social structures that produce domination, inequality, or distorted understanding.
concepts.body: Critical theory is an approach that examines and seeks to transform social structures that produce domination, inequality, or distorted understanding. It links social analysis with emancipatory aims rather than treating society as a neutral object of description.

examples.text: A critical theorist may study how workplace rules reproduce class power while appearing impartial.
examples.note: It fits because critique is directed at hidden structures and possibilities for emancipation.

commonMisreadings: It is broader than simply criticizing a particular theory or argument.

concepts.name: Cross-race recognition effect
concepts.summary: The cross-race recognition effect is the tendency to recognize faces of one's own racial group more accurately than faces of unfamiliar racial groups.
concepts.body: The cross-race recognition effect is the tendency to recognize faces of one's own racial group more accurately than faces of unfamiliar racial groups. The effect is influenced by experience, attention, and perceptual learning rather than proving an innate inability.

examples.text: A person who has mostly encountered one racial group may have greater difficulty distinguishing unfamiliar-group faces.
examples.note: It fits because it describes a measurable difference in face recognition across racial categories.

commonMisreadings: It does not mean that people cannot recognize faces from other groups or that race alone determines accuracy.

concepts.name: Cue-dependent forgetting
concepts.summary: Cue-dependent forgetting is failure to retrieve stored information because the cues available at recall do not sufficiently match those present during encoding.
concepts.body: Cue-dependent forgetting is failure to retrieve stored information because the cues available at recall do not sufficiently match those present during encoding. Providing an appropriate cue can recover information that was not erased from memory.

examples.text: A forgotten name may return when a friend mentions the place where the meeting occurred.
examples.note: It fits because retrieval depends on access cues rather than storage failure alone.

commonMisreadings: It is not identical to decay, which attributes forgetting to weakening over time.

concepts.name: Cultural appropriation
concepts.summary: Cultural appropriation is the adoption or use of elements of a culture by outsiders, especially when power inequalities, exploitation, or loss of context are involved.
concepts.body: Cultural appropriation is the adoption or use of elements of a culture by outsiders, especially when power inequalities, exploitation, or loss of context are involved. Assessment depends on factors such as consent, representation, compensation, and whether sacred or marginalized practices are used commercially.

examples.text: Selling sacred Indigenous designs without permission or benefit to the community can constitute cultural appropriation.
examples.note: It fits because the concept concerns unequal cultural borrowing and its consequences.

commonMisreadings: It is not simply any cultural exchange between people from different backgrounds.

concepts.name: Cultural hegemony
concepts.summary: Cultural hegemony is the maintenance of social dominance by making a ruling group's values and assumptions appear natural or universally valid.
concepts.body: Cultural hegemony is the maintenance of social dominance by making a ruling group's values and assumptions appear natural or universally valid. Antonio Gramsci linked hegemony to consent produced through institutions, education, and common sense.

examples.text: A class may accept an economic hierarchy as meritocratic even when its institutions systematically favor that class.
examples.note: It fits because domination operates through accepted meanings as well as direct coercion.

commonMisreadings: Hegemony is not the same as propaganda, which is only one possible means of shaping belief.

concepts.name: Cultural relativism
concepts.summary: Cultural relativism is the methodological or moral view that beliefs and practices should be understood relative to their cultural context rather than judged automatically by another culture's standards.
concepts.body: Cultural relativism is the methodological or moral view that beliefs and practices should be understood relative to their cultural context rather than judged automatically by another culture's standards. Methodological relativism suspends premature judgment, while moral relativism may deny universal moral standards.

examples.text: An anthropologist interprets a marriage ritual through the community's own norms before evaluating it.
examples.note: It fits because cultural context is treated as essential to understanding or assessment.

commonMisreadings: Cultural relativism does not require accepting every practice as morally permissible.

concepts.name: Cynicism
concepts.summary: Cynicism is a skeptical attitude that distrusts the sincerity, motives, or goodness of people and institutions.
concepts.body: Cynicism is a skeptical attitude that distrusts the sincerity, motives, or goodness of people and institutions. Modern cynicism often assumes that apparent altruism conceals self-interest.

examples.text: A cynical observer interprets a charitable campaign mainly as a publicity strategy.
examples.note: It fits because suspicion of professed motives is its defining disposition.

commonMisreadings: Cynicism is not the ancient Cynic philosophy, which criticized convention through austere living.

concepts.name: Daoism
concepts.summary: Daoism is a Chinese philosophical and religious tradition centered on living in accordance with the Dao, the generative way or order of reality.
concepts.body: Daoism is a Chinese philosophical and religious tradition centered on living in accordance with the Dao, the generative way or order of reality. Daoist texts often emphasize wuwei, meaning effective action that avoids forced or artificial striving.

examples.text: A leader practicing wuwei may shape conditions so that a resolution emerges with minimal coercion.
examples.note: It fits because harmony with the Dao and non-forcing are central Daoist themes.

commonMisreadings: Daoism is not simply a synonym for passivity, since wuwei can involve skillful decisive action.

concepts.name: Decision theory
concepts.summary: Decision theory studies how agents should choose among actions under certainty, risk, or uncertainty.
concepts.body: Decision theory studies how agents should choose among actions under certainty, risk, or uncertainty. It commonly represents preferences, probabilities, and utilities to evaluate options.

examples.text: An investor may choose a portfolio by comparing the expected utilities of uncertain returns.
examples.note: It fits because the field analyzes rational choice under different information conditions.

commonMisreadings: Decision theory is not limited to financial decisions or to choices with known probabilities.

concepts.name: Decolonization
concepts.summary: Decolonization is the process of dismantling colonial rule and the political, economic, cultural, and epistemic structures that sustain it.
concepts.body: Decolonization is the process of dismantling colonial rule and the political, economic, cultural, and epistemic structures that sustain it. It can include sovereignty, land restitution, institutional reform, and recovery of suppressed knowledge.

examples.text: A formerly colonized state may replace imposed land laws while restoring authority to Indigenous communities.
examples.note: It fits because it addresses both formal independence and continuing colonial relations.

commonMisreadings: Decolonization is not complete merely because a colony receives a new national flag.

concepts.name: Deconstruction
concepts.summary: Deconstruction is a method of reading that exposes tensions, exclusions, and unstable oppositions within texts or concepts.
concepts.body: Deconstruction is a method of reading that exposes tensions, exclusions, and unstable oppositions within texts or concepts. It shows how a text can undermine the fixed meanings it appears to assert.

examples.text: A deconstructive reading may examine how a text's contrast between speech and writing depends on the supposedly inferior term.
examples.note: It fits because it analyzes internal instability rather than supplying a replacement doctrine.

commonMisreadings: Deconstruction is not the destruction of a text or a claim that texts have no meaning at all.

concepts.name: Deductive reasoning
concepts.summary: Deductive reasoning derives a conclusion that must be true if the premises are true and the inference is valid.
concepts.body: Deductive reasoning derives a conclusion that must be true if the premises are true and the inference is valid. Validity concerns the structure of the inference, while soundness also requires true premises.

examples.text: From All mammals are warm-blooded and whales are mammals, deduction yields that whales are warm-blooded.
examples.note: It fits because necessity of the conclusion is the defining feature.

commonMisreadings: Deduction is not synonymous with certainty about the premises themselves.

concepts.name: Defeasible reasoning
concepts.summary: Defeasible reasoning draws a provisional conclusion that can be withdrawn when new information defeats it.
concepts.body: Defeasible reasoning draws a provisional conclusion that can be withdrawn when new information defeats it. It is useful when generalizations have exceptions and complete information is unavailable.

examples.text: A bird is normally assumed to fly until learning that the bird is a penguin.
examples.note: It fits because the inference remains open to revision by exceptions.

commonMisreadings: Defeasible reasoning is not deductively valid reasoning whose conclusion cannot be overturned by added facts.

concepts.name: Defeater
concepts.summary: A defeater is information that undermines the justification or evidential support for a belief without necessarily making the belief false.
concepts.body: A defeater is information that undermines the justification or evidential support for a belief without necessarily making the belief false. A rebutting defeater supports the belief's negation, while an undercutting defeater attacks the connection between evidence and belief.

examples.text: Learning that a thermometer is broken defeats the reading's support for believing the room is cold.
examples.note: It fits because the new information removes or weakens epistemic justification.

commonMisreadings: A defeater is not automatically a refutation of the proposition believed.

concepts.name: Definite description
concepts.summary: A definite description is a phrase that purports to refer to a unique object by describing it, commonly using the.
concepts.body: A definite description is a phrase that purports to refer to a unique object by describing it, commonly using the. Its standard logical analysis treats it as asserting existence, uniqueness, and possession of the described property.

examples.text: The tallest building in Perth refers only if exactly one building satisfies the description in the relevant context.
examples.note: It fits because the concept concerns uniquely identifying descriptions rather than ordinary names.

commonMisreadings: A definite description is not guaranteed to refer merely because its grammar is definite.

concepts.name: Definitional equivalence
concepts.summary: Definitional equivalence is a relation between formal theories that can define each other's primitive concepts without changing their deductive content.
concepts.body: Definitional equivalence is a relation between formal theories that can define each other's primitive concepts without changing their deductive content. Equivalent theories may use different basic vocabularies while expressing the same structure.

examples.text: Two formulations of geometry can be definitionally equivalent if each system explicitly defines the other's primitive relations.
examples.note: It fits because mutual definability connects the theories at the level of formal language.

commonMisreadings: It is stronger than merely having some logically equivalent theorems.

concepts.name: Deflationism about truth
concepts.summary: Deflationism about truth holds that the truth predicate does not name a substantial property beyond the logical or expressive role captured by instances such as saying that Snow is white is true.
concepts.body: Deflationism about truth holds that the truth predicate does not name a substantial property beyond the logical or expressive role captured by instances such as saying that Snow is white is true. The equivalence schema This proposition is true if and only if the proposition is often does the explanatory work.

examples.text: A deflationist can use true in The theorem is true to endorse the theorem without positing a deep truth substance.
examples.note: It fits because truth is treated as a minimal expressive device rather than a metaphysical relation.

commonMisreadings: Deflationism does not deny that people make true and false assertions.

concepts.name: Deism
concepts.summary: Deism is the theological view that a creator exists but does not ordinarily intervene through revealed miracles or ongoing providential acts.
concepts.body: Deism is the theological view that a creator exists but does not ordinarily intervene through revealed miracles or ongoing providential acts. Deists typically rely on reason and nature rather than institutional revelation as the basis of religious belief.

examples.text: A deist may believe that God created the universe but reject the historical authority of miracle reports.
examples.note: It fits because a creator is affirmed while regular supernatural intervention is denied or minimized.

commonMisreadings: Deism is not atheism, since it retains belief in a creator.

concepts.name: Deliberative democracy
concepts.summary: Deliberative democracy is a model of democracy in which legitimate decisions result from public reasoning among free and equal participants.
concepts.body: Deliberative democracy is a model of democracy in which legitimate decisions result from public reasoning among free and equal participants. Deliberation requires exchanging reasons, listening, and revising views rather than merely counting preferences.

examples.text: A citizens' assembly that studies evidence and publicly justifies its recommendations exemplifies deliberative democracy.
examples.note: It fits because reason-giving discussion is central to democratic legitimacy.

commonMisreadings: It is not identical to direct democracy, which concerns who votes rather than how decisions are reasoned about.

concepts.name: Demarcation problem
concepts.summary: The demarcation problem asks how to distinguish science from non-science or pseudoscience.
concepts.body: The demarcation problem asks how to distinguish science from non-science or pseudoscience. Proposed criteria include falsifiability, empirical testability, methodological norms, and research traditions, but no single criterion is universally accepted.

examples.text: Popper argued that a scientific theory should make predictions that could in principle be falsified.
examples.note: It fits because the concept concerns the boundary of scientific inquiry.

commonMisreadings: It is not the problem of distinguishing one scientific field from another.

concepts.name: Democracy
concepts.summary: Democracy is a form of political rule in which the people exercise ultimate authority, directly or through accountable representatives.
concepts.body: Democracy is a form of political rule in which the people exercise ultimate authority, directly or through accountable representatives. Democratic systems require mechanisms for participation, contestation, and peaceful transfer or accountability of power.

examples.text: A country with competitive elections, universal suffrage, and protected opposition parties has democratic institutions.
examples.note: It fits because popular political authority is the defining principle.

commonMisreadings: Democracy is not guaranteed by elections alone when elections are noncompetitive or unaccountable.

concepts.name: Democratic confederalism
concepts.summary: Democratic confederalism is a decentralized political model based on local assemblies, participatory democracy, gender equality, and ecological responsibility.
concepts.body: Democratic confederalism is a decentralized political model based on local assemblies, participatory democracy, gender equality, and ecological responsibility. It favors a network of self-governing communities over a centralized nation-state.

examples.text: A federation of neighborhood councils that delegates limited, recallable responsibilities illustrates the model.
examples.note: It fits because confederal local autonomy and participatory governance are its organizing principles.

commonMisreadings: It is not conventional federalism, which can retain a powerful central government and representative institutions.

concepts.name: Democratic legitimacy
concepts.summary: Democratic legitimacy is the justified authority of a decision or institution because affected people can participate in, contest, or hold it accountable through democratic procedures.
concepts.body: Democratic legitimacy is the justified authority of a decision or institution because affected people can participate in, contest, or hold it accountable through democratic procedures. Legitimacy can depend on inclusion, representation, transparency, and responsiveness as well as electoral results.

examples.text: A law gains democratic legitimacy when citizens can vote, organize opposition, and challenge its application through independent institutions.
examples.note: It fits because the concept explains why collective decisions deserve political compliance.

commonMisreadings: Democratic legitimacy is not the same as popularity at a single moment.

concepts.name: Democratic socialism
concepts.summary: Democratic socialism is a political tradition seeking social or collective ownership of major productive resources through democratic institutions and civil liberties.
concepts.body: Democratic socialism is a political tradition seeking social or collective ownership of major productive resources through democratic institutions and civil liberties. It differs from authoritarian state socialism by treating political democracy and participation as essential.

examples.text: A democratic socialist program may expand worker ownership while preserving multiparty elections and free association.
examples.note: It fits because socialism is pursued through democratic control rather than one-party rule.

commonMisreadings: It is not simply any welfare-state policy within a predominantly private economy.

concepts.name: Denotation
concepts.summary: Denotation is the literal or referential meaning of a word, distinct from its associated emotional or cultural meanings.
concepts.body: Denotation is the literal or referential meaning of a word, distinct from its associated emotional or cultural meanings. A term's denotation can remain stable while its connotations differ among speakers.

examples.text: The denotation of snake identifies a legless elongated reptile, while fear may be a connotation.
examples.note: It fits because it identifies what an expression directly refers to or means.

commonMisreadings: Denotation is not always identical to a single physical object, since abstract terms can denote properties or concepts.

concepts.name: Deontology
concepts.summary: Deontology is an ethical approach that evaluates actions by duties, rules, or constraints rather than solely by consequences.
concepts.body: Deontology is an ethical approach that evaluates actions by duties, rules, or constraints rather than solely by consequences. Some deontological theories hold that certain actions are wrong even when they would produce better outcomes.

examples.text: A deontologist may reject lying to an innocent person even if the lie would increase overall happiness.
examples.note: It fits because obligation and prohibition are central to moral assessment.

commonMisreadings: Deontology is not the claim that consequences never matter in any moral theory.

concepts.name: Description theory of names
concepts.summary: The description theory of names holds that a proper name refers through an associated description or cluster of descriptions.
concepts.body: The description theory of names holds that a proper name refers through an associated description or cluster of descriptions. It explains reference by treating names as shorthand for identifying information available to speakers.

examples.text: On one version, Aristotle might refer through descriptions such as the ancient Greek philosopher who wrote the Metaphysics.
examples.note: It fits because descriptive content is used to explain how names refer.

commonMisreadings: It is challenged by causal theories that allow reference despite mistaken or incomplete descriptions.

concepts.name: Desert
concepts.summary: Desert is the idea that a person merits a benefit, burden, praise, or blame because of a relevant fact about them.
concepts.body: Desert is the idea that a person merits a benefit, burden, praise, or blame because of a relevant fact about them. Desert differs from entitlement, which can arise from a rule, promise, or legal status without merit.

examples.text: A runner may deserve recognition for completing a difficult race through sustained effort.
examples.note: It fits because it concerns what someone merits rather than what they merely receive.

commonMisreadings: Desert is not identical to need, since a person can need help without having earned it.

concepts.name: Desire theory of well-being
concepts.summary: The desire theory of well-being holds that a person's life goes better when their desires or preferences are fulfilled.
concepts.body: The desire theory of well-being holds that a person's life goes better when their desires or preferences are fulfilled. The theory can count fulfilled desires even when the person is not consciously aware of the fulfillment.

examples.text: A person's well-being may increase when a long-held goal is achieved, even if the person learns of it later.
examples.note: It fits because desire satisfaction supplies the account of welfare.

commonMisreadings: It is not the same as hedonism, which identifies well-being with pleasure and absence of pain.

concepts.name: Despotism
concepts.summary: Despotism is rule by an authority that exercises power with little effective legal, institutional, or popular constraint.
concepts.body: Despotism is rule by an authority that exercises power with little effective legal, institutional, or popular constraint. Despotic rule can be arbitrary even when it maintains formal administrative institutions.

examples.text: A ruler who can confiscate property or imprison opponents without independent review governs despotically.
examples.note: It fits because unchecked arbitrary power is the defining feature.

commonMisreadings: Despotism is not synonymous with monarchy, since a monarchy can be constitutionally limited.

concepts.name: Developmentalism
concepts.summary: Developmentalism is the view or policy approach that prioritizes economic development through active state coordination, industrialization, and structural transformation.
concepts.body: Developmentalism is the view or policy approach that prioritizes economic development through active state coordination, industrialization, and structural transformation. Developmentalist states often use planning, infrastructure investment, trade policy, and targeted industrial support.

examples.text: South Korea's state-directed industrial policies during the late twentieth century are commonly studied as developmentalist.
examples.note: It fits because development is pursued through coordinated transformation rather than laissez-faire alone.

commonMisreadings: Developmentalism is not equivalent to any economic growth, since it names a particular strategy and governing orientation.

concepts.name: Dharma
concepts.summary: Dharma is a concept in Indian traditions referring, depending on context, to duty, moral order, right conduct, or the law that sustains reality.
concepts.body: Dharma is a concept in Indian traditions referring, depending on context, to duty, moral order, right conduct, or the law that sustains reality. Its meaning differs across Hindu, Buddhist, Jain, and other traditions.

examples.text: In the Bhagavad Gita, fulfilling one's dharma is discussed in relation to role, duty, and disciplined action.
examples.note: It fits because it names a normative order connecting conduct and the structure of life.

commonMisreadings: Dharma is not reducible to a single English translation such as religion or duty.

concepts.name: Dialectic
concepts.summary: Dialectic is a method or process of inquiry in which opposing claims, forces, or positions interact to produce clarification or transformation.
concepts.body: Dialectic is a method or process of inquiry in which opposing claims, forces, or positions interact to produce clarification or transformation. Socratic questioning uses dialogue to expose contradictions in a person's assumptions.

examples.text: A discussion may refine a definition by testing it against objections and revising it.
examples.note: It fits because development occurs through structured engagement with opposition.

commonMisreadings: Dialectic is not simply any argument or disagreement without a productive method.

concepts.name: Dialectical materialism
concepts.summary: Dialectical materialism is a Marxist framework that explains social and historical change through material conditions and conflicts developing within systems.
concepts.body: Dialectical materialism is a Marxist framework that explains social and historical change through material conditions and conflicts developing within systems. It treats contradictions in economic and social relations as drivers of transformation.

examples.text: Conflict between capital owners and wage workers is analyzed as a contradiction within capitalism.
examples.note: It fits because material organization and dialectical conflict jointly explain change.

commonMisreadings: It is not merely a synonym for economic determinism, since dialectical relations include active social struggle.

concepts.name: Dialetheism
concepts.summary: Dialetheism is the view that some contradictions are genuinely true.
concepts.body: Dialetheism is the view that some contradictions are genuinely true. It rejects the classical principle that no proposition and its negation can both be true in every case.

examples.text: A dialetheist may treat certain semantic paradoxes as involving both a true statement and its negation.
examples.note: It fits because acceptance of true contradictions is its defining thesis.

commonMisreadings: Dialetheism does not say that every contradiction is true or that reasoning becomes useless.

concepts.name: Direct democracy
concepts.summary: Direct democracy is a system in which citizens decide policies or laws themselves rather than delegating all decisions to representatives.
concepts.body: Direct democracy is a system in which citizens decide policies or laws themselves rather than delegating all decisions to representatives. Referendums, citizen initiatives, and assemblies are common direct-democratic mechanisms.

examples.text: Voters directly approve or reject a proposed constitutional amendment in a referendum.
examples.note: It fits because the electorate exercises decision-making authority on the measure itself.

commonMisreadings: It is not representative democracy, even though representative systems may include direct-democratic tools.

concepts.name: Direct realism
concepts.summary: Direct realism is the view that ordinary perception gives us direct awareness of mind-independent objects and their properties.
concepts.body: Direct realism is the view that ordinary perception gives us direct awareness of mind-independent objects and their properties. It denies that perception always requires awareness of an internal intermediary representation.

examples.text: When someone sees a tree, direct realism says the perceived tree itself is an object of perceptual awareness.
examples.note: It fits because external objects are treated as directly perceived.

commonMisreadings: Direct realism does not claim that perception is infallible or unaffected by conditions.

concepts.name: Disagreement
concepts.summary: Disagreement is a situation in which two or more parties hold incompatible answers, beliefs, judgments, or preferences about a matter.
concepts.body: Disagreement is a situation in which two or more parties hold incompatible answers, beliefs, judgments, or preferences about a matter. Disagreement can concern facts, values, meanings, or practical choices.

examples.text: Two scientists disagree when one accepts a hypothesis and the other rejects it based on competing evidence.
examples.note: It fits because incompatible positions are the essential feature.

commonMisreadings: Disagreement is not necessarily irrational conflict, since reasonable people can disagree under uncertainty.

concepts.name: Discounting
concepts.summary: Discounting is the practice of assigning lower present value to benefits or costs that occur later.
concepts.body: Discounting is the practice of assigning lower present value to benefits or costs that occur later. A discount rate represents the relative weight given to future outcomes in an evaluation.

examples.text: A policy analyst may value a benefit received in twenty years less than the same benefit received today.
examples.note: It fits because temporal distance changes the value assigned to outcomes.

commonMisreadings: Discounting is not the same as ignoring future generations, although high rates can have that effect.

concepts.name: Discourse
concepts.summary: Discourse is an organized use of language or communication that shapes how a subject is understood and discussed.
concepts.body: Discourse is an organized use of language or communication that shapes how a subject is understood and discussed. In social theory, discourse can include institutions, practices, categories, and accepted ways of speaking.

examples.text: Medical discourse can define which conditions count as illness and which treatments are considered legitimate.
examples.note: It fits because meaning is produced through structured patterns of communication.

commonMisreadings: Discourse is broader than a single conversation or speech.

concepts.name: Discourse ethics
concepts.summary: Discourse ethics is the theory that valid moral norms must be justifiable to all affected participants in free and noncoercive practical discourse.
concepts.body: Discourse ethics is the theory that valid moral norms must be justifiable to all affected participants in free and noncoercive practical discourse. It emphasizes equal participation, reasons that others can accept, and the possibility of challenging claims.

examples.text: A law has discourse-ethical support when affected citizens can contest it under fair deliberative conditions.
examples.note: It fits because moral validity is tied to communicative justification.

commonMisreadings: It is not the rule that whatever people happen to agree on is automatically moral.

concepts.name: Discourse theory
concepts.summary: Discourse theory is a social and political approach that studies how language, communication, and shared meaning structure knowledge, identity, and power.
concepts.body: Discourse theory is a social and political approach that studies how language, communication, and shared meaning structure knowledge, identity, and power. It examines how categories and institutions are produced and maintained through communicative practices.

examples.text: A discourse theorist may analyze how the term security frames migration as a threat and enables exceptional policies.
examples.note: It fits because discursive practices are treated as constitutive of social understanding.

commonMisreadings: It is not merely the study of grammar or formal speech patterns.

concepts.name: Disjunction
concepts.summary: A disjunction is a compound proposition formed by joining alternatives with or.
concepts.body: A disjunction is a compound proposition formed by joining alternatives with or. In inclusive logic, P or Q is true when at least one of P and Q is true.

examples.text: The statement The package is at home or at work is true if either location, or both, satisfies the alternatives.
examples.note: It fits because alternatives are combined into one logical proposition.

commonMisreadings: A disjunction need not be exclusive, since ordinary or can allow both alternatives.

concepts.name: Disjunctive syllogism
concepts.summary: Disjunctive syllogism is the inference form from P or Q and not P to Q.
concepts.body: Disjunctive syllogism is the inference form from P or Q and not P to Q. Its validity depends on the disjunction and negation applying to the same alternatives.

examples.text: From The key is in the drawer or the bag and not in the drawer, one may infer that it is in the bag.
examples.note: It fits because eliminating one disjunct leaves the other.

commonMisreadings: It is not valid when or is being used with an unrelated ambiguity or when both alternatives can be false.

concepts.name: Disposition
concepts.summary: A disposition is a stable tendency or capacity of an object or person to behave or react in a certain way under suitable conditions.
concepts.body: A disposition is a stable tendency or capacity of an object or person to behave or react in a certain way under suitable conditions. Dispositions can exist even when they are not currently manifested.

examples.text: A fragile glass has a disposition to shatter when struck with sufficient force.
examples.note: It fits because the concept describes conditional powers rather than only actual events.

commonMisreadings: A disposition is not identical to an occurrence, since the glass can remain unbroken while fragile.

concepts.name: Distributism
concepts.summary: Distributism is an economic view favoring widespread private ownership of productive property among families and small associations.
concepts.body: Distributism is an economic view favoring widespread private ownership of productive property among families and small associations. It criticizes both concentrated capitalism and centralized state ownership.

examples.text: A distributist policy might support small farms, worker cooperatives, and limits on monopolistic landholding.
examples.note: It fits because ownership distribution, rather than only income redistribution, is central.

commonMisreadings: Distributism is not socialism, since it generally preserves private property.

concepts.name: Distributive justice
concepts.summary: Distributive justice concerns the fair allocation of benefits, burdens, opportunities, and resources among members of a society.
concepts.body: Distributive justice concerns the fair allocation of benefits, burdens, opportunities, and resources among members of a society. Theories of distributive justice differ over whether allocation should track equality, need, desert, contribution, or priority to the worst off.

examples.text: A tax system can be evaluated for whether it distributes public burdens fairly across income groups.
examples.note: It fits because it addresses who should receive or bear what.

commonMisreadings: Distributive justice is not identical to corrective justice, which addresses repair after a wrong.

concepts.name: Divine command theory
concepts.summary: Divine command theory holds that moral obligations are grounded in the commands of God or a divine authority.
concepts.body: Divine command theory holds that moral obligations are grounded in the commands of God or a divine authority. On many versions, an action is obligatory because God commands it and wrong because God forbids it.

examples.text: A believer who grounds a duty to give charity in a divine command uses this theory.
examples.note: It fits because divine authority supplies the source of moral requirement.

commonMisreadings: It is not simply the view that God knows moral truths, since knowledge does not itself ground obligation.

concepts.name: Divine foreknowledge
concepts.summary: Divine foreknowledge is the doctrine that God knows in advance all future events, including future human actions.
concepts.body: Divine foreknowledge is the doctrine that God knows in advance all future events, including future human actions. It creates a philosophical problem about how exhaustive knowledge can coexist with human freedom and alternative possibilities.

examples.text: If God infallibly knows tomorrow's choice, philosophers ask whether the agent could choose differently.
examples.note: It fits because complete prior divine knowledge is the defining claim.

commonMisreadings: Foreknowledge is not the same as predestination, which concerns divine determination rather than knowledge alone.

concepts.name: Divine simplicity
concepts.summary: Divine simplicity is the theological doctrine that God has no distinct parts or separable properties and is not composed of act and potentiality.
concepts.body: Divine simplicity is the theological doctrine that God has no distinct parts or separable properties and is not composed of act and potentiality. Classical versions identify God's attributes with one another and with God's being.

examples.text: On a strong doctrine of simplicity, God's goodness is not an added feature but is identical with the divine essence.
examples.note: It fits because it denies metaphysical composition in God.

commonMisreadings: Simplicity does not mean that God is uncomplicated in the ordinary psychological sense.

concepts.name: Doctrine of double effect
concepts.summary: The doctrine of double effect holds that an action with both a foreseen good effect and a foreseen bad effect can be permissible under specified conditions.
concepts.body: The doctrine of double effect holds that an action with both a foreseen good effect and a foreseen bad effect can be permissible under specified conditions. Typical conditions distinguish the intended effect from the merely foreseen harmful effect and require proportionality.

examples.text: Administering high-dose pain relief that foreseeably shortens life may be defended when relieving severe pain is intended and proportionate.
examples.note: It fits because moral evaluation turns partly on intention and side effects.

commonMisreadings: It does not permit any harmful means merely because a good consequence is also expected.

concepts.name: Dogmatism
concepts.summary: Dogmatism is unjustified confidence in a belief or doctrine combined with resistance to relevant criticism or evidence.
concepts.body: Dogmatism is unjustified confidence in a belief or doctrine combined with resistance to relevant criticism or evidence. Dogmatic commitment can occur in religious, political, scientific, or everyday contexts.

examples.text: A person who refuses to examine contrary evidence because a claim is declared unquestionable is dogmatic.
examples.note: It fits because uncritical certainty and closed inquiry define the attitude.

commonMisreadings: Dogmatism is not the same as holding a firm belief supported by strong evidence.

concepts.name: Doing and allowing
concepts.summary: The doing-and-allowing distinction separates actively causing a harm from permitting a harm to occur by failing to intervene.
concepts.body: The doing-and-allowing distinction separates actively causing a harm from permitting a harm to occur by failing to intervene. Some moral theories judge doing harm more strictly than allowing comparable harm, while others reject that distinction.

examples.text: Pushing a person into danger is doing harm, whereas refusing to rescue may be allowing harm.
examples.note: It fits because the concept classifies moral cases by the agent's causal involvement.

commonMisreadings: Allowing is not always morally neutral, especially when the agent has a duty to rescue.

concepts.name: Domain of discourse
concepts.summary: The domain of discourse is the set of objects or values that a formal statement or discussion treats as its possible subjects.
concepts.body: The domain of discourse is the set of objects or values that a formal statement or discussion treats as its possible subjects. Quantifiers range over the domain fixed by the interpretation or conversational context.

examples.text: In a discussion restricted to integers, the domain excludes noninteger real numbers.
examples.note: It fits because it specifies what the variables and claims are about.

commonMisreadings: The domain of discourse is not necessarily the whole universe of everything that exists.

concepts.name: Dominant strategy
concepts.summary: A dominant strategy is an action that gives a player at least as good an outcome as every alternative for every possible action by others, and a better outcome in some case.
concepts.body: A dominant strategy is an action that gives a player at least as good an outcome as every alternative for every possible action by others, and a better outcome in some case. Choosing it does not require predicting what other players will do.

examples.text: In a prisoner's dilemma, confessing is dominant when it yields a better result regardless of the other prisoner's choice.
examples.note: It fits because the strategy is superior or equal across all responses by others.

commonMisreadings: A dominant strategy is not merely the strategy with the highest expected payoff under one probability estimate.

concepts.name: Domination
concepts.summary: Domination is a condition in which one person or group has the power to interfere arbitrarily with another's choices or standing.
concepts.body: Domination is a condition in which one person or group has the power to interfere arbitrarily with another's choices or standing. Republican theories of freedom define domination by dependence on uncontrolled power, even when interference does not occur.

examples.text: A worker dependent on an employer who can arbitrarily withhold essential housing is dominated by that power.
examples.note: It fits because vulnerability to arbitrary control, not only actual coercion, is central.

commonMisreadings: Domination is not identical to any unequal outcome, since inequality can exist without arbitrary power.

concepts.name: Double negation
concepts.summary: Double negation is the logical relation in which negating a negation returns a proposition in classical logic.
concepts.body: Double negation is the logical relation in which negating a negation returns a proposition in classical logic. The classical equivalence is not not P if and only if P.

examples.text: From It is not the case that the switch is not on, one may infer that the switch is on in classical logic.
examples.note: It fits because two negations cancel under the relevant logical rules.

commonMisreadings: Double negation elimination is not accepted in the same form by intuitionistic logic as a general inference.

concepts.name: Drowning child
concepts.summary: The drowning child is a thought experiment in which a person can save a drowning child at a small personal cost but chooses not to do so.
concepts.body: The drowning child is a thought experiment in which a person can save a drowning child at a small personal cost but chooses not to do so. Peter Singer uses it to argue that people should prevent serious suffering when they can do so without sacrificing something of comparable moral importance.

examples.text: Walking around a shallow pond to save a child while ruining inexpensive clothing illustrates the case.
examples.note: It fits because the example tests the moral significance of proximity and small personal sacrifice.

commonMisreadings: The thought experiment does not by itself settle every question about demandingness or institutional responsibility.

concepts.name: Dual-aspect theory
concepts.summary: Dual-aspect theory holds that mental and physical descriptions are two aspects of one underlying reality rather than two separate substances.
concepts.body: Dual-aspect theory holds that mental and physical descriptions are two aspects of one underlying reality rather than two separate substances. It seeks to avoid both reduction of mind to matter and interaction between independent substances.

examples.text: A single event can be described neurally as brain activity and experientially as a pain.
examples.note: It fits because one reality is approached through distinct mental and physical aspects.

commonMisreadings: It is not property dualism if it treats the aspects as descriptions rather than separate fundamental properties.

concepts.name: Dual-process theory
concepts.summary: Dual-process theory proposes that cognition involves at least two interacting modes, one fast and automatic and another slower and more controlled.
concepts.body: Dual-process theory proposes that cognition involves at least two interacting modes, one fast and automatic and another slower and more controlled. The fast mode uses learned associations, while the slower mode can monitor and revise intuitive responses.

examples.text: Recognizing a familiar face is typically rapid, whereas checking a difficult calculation requires deliberate reasoning.
examples.note: It fits because distinct processing modes explain differences in speed and control.

commonMisreadings: It does not imply that all thinking cleanly belongs to exactly two isolated systems.

concepts.name: Dualism
concepts.summary: Dualism is the view that reality or a particular domain contains two fundamentally distinct kinds or principles.
concepts.body: Dualism is the view that reality or a particular domain contains two fundamentally distinct kinds or principles. In philosophy of mind, substance dualism holds that mind and body are different substances.

examples.text: A Cartesian dualist treats thinking mind and extended matter as fundamentally different types of substance.
examples.note: It fits because irreducible twofold structure is the defining commitment.

commonMisreadings: Dualism is not always substance dualism, since it can concern properties, values, or cosmic principles.

concepts.name: Duck test
concepts.summary: The duck test identifies something by whether its observable behavior resembles the kind of thing it is claimed to be.
concepts.body: The duck test identifies something by whether its observable behavior resembles the kind of thing it is claimed to be. It is an abductive heuristic, not deductive proof.

examples.text: A bird that swims, walks, and quacks like a duck is treated as a duck.
examples.note: Several characteristic behaviors jointly support the classification.

commonMisreadings: Resemblance alone does not establish biological identity.

concepts.name: Duhem–Quine thesis
concepts.summary: The Duhem–Quine thesis says a scientific hypothesis is tested with auxiliary assumptions and background conditions.
concepts.body: The Duhem–Quine thesis says a scientific hypothesis is tested with auxiliary assumptions and background conditions. A failed prediction does not uniquely identify which assumption is false.

examples.text: An unexpected orbit could reflect faulty gravity theory or instrument calibration.
examples.note: The observation tests a network rather than one isolated claim.

commonMisreadings: It does not make scientific rejection impossible.

concepts.name: Dukkha
concepts.summary: Dukkha is Buddhist suffering, unsatisfactoriness, and instability in conditioned experience.
concepts.body: Dukkha is Buddhist suffering, unsatisfactoriness, and instability in conditioned experience. It includes pain and frustration caused by attachment to changing things.

examples.text: A new phone’s pleasure becomes anxiety when its owner fears losing it.
examples.note: Impermanence makes satisfaction vulnerable to distress.

commonMisreadings: Dukkha does not mean every moment is equally miserable.

concepts.name: Dunning–Kruger effect
concepts.summary: The Dunning–Kruger effect is impaired self-assessment caused by limited competence in a domain.
concepts.body: The Dunning–Kruger effect is impaired self-assessment caused by limited competence in a domain. It concerns metacognitive calibration rather than universal arrogance.

examples.text: A novice programmer judges flawed code correct because they cannot detect its errors.
examples.note: The missing skill prevents accurate evaluation.

commonMisreadings: It does not affect every domain or every inexperienced person.

concepts.name: Duty
concepts.summary: A duty is an obligation giving an agent a reason to act or refrain from acting.
concepts.body: A duty is an obligation giving an agent a reason to act or refrain from acting. Duties can arise from promises, roles, laws, relationships, or principles.

examples.text: A lifeguard has a duty to respond to a drowning swimmer.
examples.note: The entrusted professional role creates the obligation.

commonMisreadings: A duty is not merely a preferred action.

concepts.name: Dvaita Vedanta
concepts.summary: Dvaita Vedanta, founded by Madhva, holds that God, souls, and matter are really distinct.
concepts.body: Dvaita Vedanta, founded by Madhva, holds that God, souls, and matter are really distinct. It identifies Vishnu as supreme and liberation as dependence on divine grace without identity with God.

examples.text: A liberated soul worships Vishnu while remaining distinct from him.
examples.note: The worship relation depends on real difference.

commonMisreadings: Dvaita is not Advaita nondualism.

concepts.name: Eclecticism
concepts.summary: Eclecticism combines doctrines or methods from different traditions according to perceived merits.
concepts.body: Eclecticism combines doctrines or methods from different traditions according to perceived merits. An eclectic position need not accept every borrowed element.

examples.text: A therapist combines cognitive-behavioral, mindfulness, and family-systems techniques.
examples.note: Different tools are selected for complementary purposes.

commonMisreadings: Eclecticism is not indiscriminate mixing.

concepts.name: Eco-anarchism
concepts.summary: Eco-anarchism links ecological protection with decentralized, non-hierarchical social organization.
concepts.body: Eco-anarchism links ecological protection with decentralized, non-hierarchical social organization. It commonly criticizes state domination and resource systems that treat nature as unlimited.

examples.text: Self-governing communities might manage a watershed through shared ecological rules.
examples.note: Local autonomy and ecological interdependence are combined.

commonMisreadings: It is not simply every environmental movement opposing government.

concepts.name: Eco-socialism
concepts.summary: Eco-socialism combines socialist criticism of capitalism with ecological criticism of profit-driven growth.
concepts.body: Eco-socialism combines socialist criticism of capitalism with ecological criticism of profit-driven growth. It argues that democratic control of production can prevent systematic ecological destruction.

examples.text: A publicly governed energy system could replace fossil-fuel profits with planned renewable transition.
examples.note: Ownership and production decisions are linked to environmental limits.

commonMisreadings: It differs from environmental reform preserving capitalist ownership.

concepts.name: Ecofeminism
concepts.summary: Ecofeminism examines connections between women’s oppression and domination of nature.
concepts.body: Ecofeminism examines connections between women’s oppression and domination of nature. Theories explain those connections through culture, social structure, or political economy.

examples.text: Plantation analysis may connect gendered labor exploitation with deforestation.
examples.note: One economic arrangement burdens people and ecosystems together.

commonMisreadings: It does not claim women are naturally closer to nature.

concepts.name: Ecological rationality
concepts.summary: Ecological rationality means a decision rule fits the structure of the environment where it operates.
concepts.body: Ecological rationality means a decision rule fits the structure of the environment where it operates. Simple heuristics can outperform complex methods when they exploit reliable environmental regularities.

examples.text: Familiarity may help choose the larger of two unknown cities.
examples.note: The environmental cue correlates with city size in that setting.

commonMisreadings: It does not make every instinct rational.

concepts.name: Economic justice
concepts.summary: Economic justice concerns fair distribution and exercise of resources, opportunities, and economic burdens.
concepts.body: Economic justice concerns fair distribution and exercise of resources, opportunities, and economic burdens. It can involve wages, property, taxation, necessities, and decision-making power.

examples.text: A progressive tax funding universal healthcare is defended as economically just.
examples.note: It combines access to care with unequal capacity to pay.

commonMisreadings: It does not require identical incomes.

concepts.name: Effective altruism
concepts.summary: Effective altruism uses evidence and reason to choose actions producing the most good with available resources.
concepts.body: Effective altruism uses evidence and reason to choose actions producing the most good with available resources. It often compares impact, neglectedness, and cost-effectiveness.

examples.text: A donor funds malaria nets after evidence shows they prevent illness cheaply.
examples.note: Estimated outcomes guide the choice more than emotional vividness.

commonMisreadings: It does not require one fixed charity or total self-sacrifice.

concepts.name: Egalitarianism
concepts.summary: Egalitarianism holds that people should be equal in a morally significant respect.
concepts.body: Egalitarianism holds that people should be equal in a morally significant respect. Versions differ over equality of welfare, resources, opportunity, status, or power.

examples.text: Equal voting rights provide equal formal political influence.
examples.note: The specified political dimension is equalized.

commonMisreadings: It need not demand identical outcomes everywhere.

concepts.name: Ego depletion
concepts.summary: Ego-depletion theory proposed that prior self-control temporarily reduces later self-control capacity.
concepts.body: Ego-depletion theory proposed that prior self-control temporarily reduces later self-control capacity. Its original resource model has faced major replication and measurement challenges.

examples.text: Researchers test whether resisting food affects persistence on a tedious task.
examples.note: The tasks examine transfer of regulatory fatigue.

commonMisreadings: Ego depletion is not an established finite mental fuel.

concepts.name: Eleatic philosophy
concepts.summary: Eleatic philosophy, associated with Parmenides, emphasizes the unity and stability of being.
concepts.body: Eleatic philosophy, associated with Parmenides, emphasizes the unity and stability of being. Its arguments challenge the coherence of change, plurality, and coming into existence.

examples.text: Zeno’s motion paradoxes involve infinitely divisible distances.
examples.note: They challenge ordinary assumptions about motion.

commonMisreadings: It is not merely abstract reasoning.

concepts.name: Eliminative materialism
concepts.summary: Eliminative materialism says mature neuroscience may eliminate common-sense psychological categories.
concepts.body: Eliminative materialism says mature neuroscience may eliminate common-sense psychological categories. Beliefs or desires could resemble obsolete scientific entities rather than reduce to neural facts.

examples.text: An eliminativist may expect neuroscience to replace belief with another neural taxonomy.
examples.note: The ordinary category need not map onto a real kind.

commonMisreadings: It is stronger than physical reductionism.

concepts.name: Emancipation
concepts.summary: Emancipation is release from a legal, political, social, or economic condition of domination.
concepts.body: Emancipation is release from a legal, political, social, or economic condition of domination. It can mean formal liberation and practical capacity to use freedom.

examples.text: The Emancipation Proclamation declared enslaved people in specified rebellious areas free.
examples.note: It legally attacked a status of coerced ownership.

commonMisreadings: It does not automatically remove later inequality.

concepts.name: Embodied cognition
concepts.summary: Embodied cognition holds that thought is shaped by bodily, sensory, motor, and environmental interaction.
concepts.body: Embodied cognition holds that thought is shaped by bodily, sensory, motor, and environmental interaction. It rejects explaining cognition solely as detached brain computation.

examples.text: Learning bicycle balance involves continuous corrective movements.
examples.note: The skill is enacted through bodily action and feedback.

commonMisreadings: It does not deny neural involvement.

concepts.name: Emergence
concepts.summary: Emergence is the appearance of system-level patterns arising from component interactions.
concepts.body: Emergence is the appearance of system-level patterns arising from component interactions. An emergent property depends on parts without belonging to one part alone.

examples.text: A fish school’s spiral arises from local spacing and alignment behaviors.
examples.note: No individual fish has the collective formation as its property.

commonMisreadings: Emergence need not be supernatural.

concepts.name: Emergentism
concepts.summary: Emergentism says organized physical systems can have novel properties requiring higher-level concepts.
concepts.body: Emergentism says organized physical systems can have novel properties requiring higher-level concepts. Some emergentists assign higher-level properties new causal powers; others claim only explanatory novelty.

examples.text: Life processes may be emergent from biochemical organization.
examples.note: Organization creates a level not captured by listing molecules.

commonMisreadings: It is not identical to mystery.

concepts.name: Emotivism
concepts.summary: Emotivism says moral judgments express attitudes or emotions rather than report objective moral facts.
concepts.body: Emotivism says moral judgments express attitudes or emotions rather than report objective moral facts. “Stealing is wrong” functions like disapproval or a directive on a classic version.

examples.text: “Do not steal” expresses condemnation and seeks to influence conduct.
examples.note: The utterance performs a motivational function.

commonMisreadings: It is not merely the claim that emotion affects morality.

concepts.name: Empiricism
concepts.summary: Empiricism holds that experience, especially sensory experience, fundamentally contributes to knowledge or justification.
concepts.body: Empiricism holds that experience, especially sensory experience, fundamentally contributes to knowledge or justification. Empiricists may use reasoning while rejecting substantial innate knowledge.

examples.text: A scientist accepts a reaction claim after controlled observations support it.
examples.note: Experience supplies evidence beyond deduction.

commonMisreadings: It does not mean trusting every personal impression.

concepts.name: Enactivism
concepts.summary: Enactivism says cognition arises through active organism-environment engagement, not passive internal representation alone.
concepts.body: Enactivism says cognition arises through active organism-environment engagement, not passive internal representation alone. It emphasizes sensorimotor skill, autonomy, and mutual shaping.

examples.text: Bicycle balance is learned through ongoing action and changing feedback.
examples.note: The skill exists in agent-environment coupling.

commonMisreadings: It does not exclude the brain.

concepts.name: End-of-history illusion
concepts.summary: The end-of-history illusion is underestimating future change in one’s preferences, values, or personality.
concepts.body: The end-of-history illusion is underestimating future change in one’s preferences, values, or personality. People recognize past change while treating the present self as nearly complete.

examples.text: A twenty-year-old predicts identical musical tastes at forty.
examples.note: The prediction ignores earlier transformations.

commonMisreadings: It does not claim people stop changing at a particular age.

concepts.name: Endurantism
concepts.summary: Endurantism says an object is wholly present at every time at which it exists.
concepts.body: Endurantism says an object is wholly present at every time at which it exists. It contrasts with perdurantism, which treats objects as temporal parts.

examples.text: The same tree is wholly present as sapling and mature tree.
examples.note: Persistence consists in complete presence at each time.

commonMisreadings: It allows different properties at different times.

concepts.name: Engaged Buddhism
concepts.summary: Engaged Buddhism applies Buddhist compassion and contemplation to social, political, and environmental suffering.
