concepts.body: Engaged Buddhism applies Buddhist compassion and contemplation to social, political, and environmental suffering. It treats collective action as compatible with personal spiritual cultivation.

examples.text: Buddhists organizing nonviolent refugee relief practice engaged Buddhism.
examples.note: The practice addresses suffering beyond private meditation.

commonMisreadings: It does not say meditation is unnecessary.

concepts.name: Entailment
concepts.summary: Entailment holds when truth of one proposition guarantees truth of another under relevant interpretation.
concepts.body: Entailment holds when truth of one proposition guarantees truth of another under relevant interpretation. The first proposition cannot be true while the entailed proposition is false.

examples.text: “Every raven is a bird” entails “Every raven is an animal.”
examples.note: Raven membership guarantees animal membership.

commonMisreadings: Entailment is stronger than probability.

concepts.name: Environmental ethics
concepts.summary: Environmental ethics studies moral status and obligations concerning nature, organisms, ecosystems, and nonhuman entities.
concepts.body: Environmental ethics studies moral status and obligations concerning nature, organisms, ecosystems, and nonhuman entities. It asks whether value extends beyond human welfare.

examples.text: A forest may be protected because it has value beyond timber.
examples.note: The justification assigns moral significance to an ecosystem.

commonMisreadings: It is broader than pollution policy.

concepts.name: Environmentalism
concepts.summary: Environmentalism is a movement seeking ecological protection and reduced environmental harm.
concepts.body: Environmentalism is a movement seeking ecological protection and reduced environmental harm. Its approaches include conservation, regulation, restoration, activism, and changed consumption.

examples.text: A campaign for lower industrial sulfur emissions is environmentalist.
examples.note: It aims to reduce pollutant damage.

commonMisreadings: It is not one single political theory.

concepts.name: Epicureanism
concepts.summary: Epicureanism teaches that prudent pleasure, friendship, and freedom from irrational fear produce tranquility.
concepts.body: Epicureanism teaches that prudent pleasure, friendship, and freedom from irrational fear produce tranquility. It values simple stable pleasure and absence of disturbance.

examples.text: An Epicurean chooses a modest meal with friends over an anxious lavish feast.
examples.note: The choice favors durable tranquility.

commonMisreadings: It is not unrestricted luxury.

concepts.name: Epiphenomenalism
concepts.summary: Epiphenomenalism says mental events are caused by physical events but do not cause physical events.
concepts.body: Epiphenomenalism says mental events are caused by physical events but do not cause physical events. Conscious experience accompanies neural processes without altering bodily behavior.

examples.text: Neural circuitry causes withdrawal while pain is merely produced alongside it.
examples.note: The mental episode is an effect, not a physical cause.

commonMisreadings: It does not deny mental-physical correlation.

concepts.name: Epistemic closure
concepts.summary: Epistemic closure is the principle that knowledge of a proposition transfers to propositions known to follow from it.
concepts.body: Epistemic closure is the principle that knowledge of a proposition transfers to propositions known to follow from it. A common form says knowing p and knowing p entails q yields knowledge of q.

examples.text: Knowing keys are in a drawer and that this excludes the garden yields knowledge they are not there.
examples.note: A known entailment transmits knowledge.

commonMisreadings: It concerns knowledge, not physical containment.

concepts.name: Epistemic humility
concepts.summary: Epistemic humility is recognizing limits in one’s evidence, competence, and perspective.
concepts.body: Epistemic humility is recognizing limits in one’s evidence, competence, and perspective. It allows confidence when evidence warrants it and openness to correction.

examples.text: A surgeon calls a scan inconclusive and requests another test.
examples.note: The confidence level matches the evidence.

commonMisreadings: It is not refusing every belief.

concepts.name: Epistemic injustice
concepts.summary: Epistemic injustice wrongs someone specifically as a knower or contributor to knowledge.
concepts.body: Epistemic injustice wrongs someone specifically as a knower or contributor to knowledge. Testimonial injustice discounts credibility through prejudice; hermeneutical injustice involves interpretive gaps.

examples.text: A patient’s pain report is dismissed because of a group stereotype.
examples.note: Prejudice creates an unfair credibility deficit.

commonMisreadings: It is not every factual mistake.

concepts.name: Epistemic luck
concepts.summary: Epistemic luck is luck affecting truth or justification in a way relevant to knowledge.
concepts.body: Epistemic luck is luck affecting truth or justification in a way relevant to knowledge. Gettier cases show justified true belief can be true accidentally.

examples.text: A person sees the only real barn among many fake façades.
examples.note: The true perception depends on accidental circumstances.

commonMisreadings: It is not any fortunate life event.

concepts.name: Epistemic modality
concepts.summary: Epistemic modality concerns what is possible, necessary, or certain relative to information or knowledge.
concepts.body: Epistemic modality concerns what is possible, necessary, or certain relative to information or knowledge. It differs from metaphysical modality, which concerns reality’s underlying possibilities.

examples.text: Current evidence leaves it epistemically possible that a suspect is elsewhere.
examples.note: The claim reports compatibility with evidence.

commonMisreadings: Epistemic possibility is not metaphysical possibility.

concepts.name: Epistemic peerhood
concepts.summary: Epistemic peerhood relates agents comparably competent, informed, and conscientious about a question.
concepts.body: Epistemic peerhood relates agents comparably competent, informed, and conscientious about a question. Peer disagreement can give reason to reduce confidence.

examples.text: Two equally qualified climatologists disagree over a forecast using the same data.
examples.note: Neither has an obvious epistemic advantage.

commonMisreadings: A peer need not equal one in every ability.

concepts.name: Epistemic rationality
concepts.summary: Epistemic rationality forms beliefs in ways responsive to evidence and truth-directed reasons.
concepts.body: Epistemic rationality forms beliefs in ways responsive to evidence and truth-directed reasons. It differs from instrumental rationality, which concerns achieving goals.

examples.text: Updating a probability after reliable contrary data is epistemically rational.
examples.note: Evidence rather than convenience drives revision.

commonMisreadings: It does not guarantee truth.

concepts.name: Epistemic relativism
concepts.summary: Epistemic relativism says standards of knowledge or justification vary relative to frameworks, cultures, or conceptual schemes.
concepts.body: Epistemic relativism says standards of knowledge or justification vary relative to frameworks, cultures, or conceptual schemes. Some versions deny one universally binding epistemic standard.

examples.text: A relativist may say laboratory and oral-tradition communities rank evidence differently.
examples.note: Evaluation depends partly on a social framework.

commonMisreadings: It need not say every belief is equally supported.

concepts.name: Epistemic vigilance
concepts.summary: Epistemic vigilance monitors communicated information for reliability, deception, and relevance.
concepts.body: Epistemic vigilance monitors communicated information for reliability, deception, and relevance. It checks a speaker’s competence, intentions, and coherence.

examples.text: A journalist verifies quoted statistics before publication.
examples.note: Verification guards against error and misinformation.

commonMisreadings: It is not automatic distrust.

concepts.name: Epistemology
concepts.summary: Epistemology studies knowledge, belief, justification, evidence, and related concepts.
concepts.body: Epistemology studies knowledge, belief, justification, evidence, and related concepts. It asks what knowledge is and whether skepticism can be answered.

examples.text: Analyzing whether justified true belief suffices for knowledge is epistemological.
examples.note: The inquiry concerns conditions of knowing.

commonMisreadings: It is not merely laboratory method.

concepts.name: Equality
concepts.summary: Equality is sameness of status, treatment, share, or opportunity along a specified relevant dimension.
concepts.body: Equality is sameness of status, treatment, share, or opportunity along a specified relevant dimension. A claim of equality requires identifying the dimension and comparison class.

examples.text: Equal voting rights give each citizen the same formal vote.
examples.note: The political entitlement is equalized.

commonMisreadings: Equality does not mean sameness in every trait.

concepts.name: Equilibrium
concepts.summary: Equilibrium is a state where opposing influences balance and the relevant system has no net change.
concepts.body: Equilibrium is a state where opposing influences balance and the relevant system has no net change. Dynamic equilibrium permits continuing microscopic change with stable aggregate conditions.

examples.text: A chemical reaction has equal forward and reverse rates at equilibrium.
examples.note: Concentrations remain stable while molecules react.

commonMisreadings: Equilibrium does not require total stillness.

concepts.name: Error theory in ethics
concepts.summary: Error theory says moral judgments purport to state objective facts but are all false because no such facts exist.
concepts.body: Error theory says moral judgments purport to state objective facts but are all false because no such facts exist. It combines cognitivist moral language with anti-realist metaphysics.

examples.text: “Cruelty is wrong” asserts a property the error theorist says nothing instantiates.
examples.note: The judgment is false, not merely emotional.

commonMisreadings: It differs from emotivism.

concepts.name: Essence
concepts.summary: An essence is the set of properties making an entity the kind of thing it is.
concepts.body: An essence is the set of properties making an entity the kind of thing it is. Essential properties contrast with accidental properties an entity can lose while remaining itself.

examples.text: Having three sides is essential to a triangle.
examples.note: Removing it makes the object non-triangular.

commonMisreadings: Essence is not the most noticeable feature.

concepts.name: Essentialism
concepts.summary: Essentialism says entities or categories possess necessary underlying properties.
concepts.body: Essentialism says entities or categories possess necessary underlying properties. In social theory it can mean treating groups as fixed and homogeneous.

examples.text: Species essentialism treats every member as sharing one immutable defining nature.
examples.note: Variation is ignored beneath a presumed essence.

commonMisreadings: It is not merely recognizing genetic influence.

concepts.name: Eternalism
concepts.summary: Eternalism about time says past, present, and future events all exist in a tenseless spacetime.
concepts.body: Eternalism about time says past, present, and future events all exist in a tenseless spacetime. It contrasts with presentism, where only the present exists.

examples.text: A past eruption and future eclipse are both spacetime events for an eternalist.
examples.note: Temporal location is treated like spatial location.

commonMisreadings: It does not say all events are simultaneous.

concepts.name: Ethical egoism
concepts.summary: Ethical egoism says each person ought to act in their own self-interest.
concepts.body: Ethical egoism says each person ought to act in their own self-interest. It is normative, unlike the psychological claim that people are actually self-interested.

examples.text: It may judge accepting a profitable opportunity morally required despite no benefit to strangers.
examples.note: Self-interest supplies the fundamental standard.

commonMisreadings: It does not say every person always acts selfishly.

concepts.name: Ethical hedonism
concepts.summary: Ethical hedonism says pleasure is the only intrinsic good and pain the only intrinsic bad, or grounds right action in pleasure over pain.
concepts.body: Ethical hedonism says pleasure is the only intrinsic good and pain the only intrinsic bad, or grounds right action in pleasure over pain. Pleasure need not mean intense physical sensation.

examples.text: A hedonist may choose lasting friendship over a brief thrill.
examples.note: The choice maximizes durable pleasant experience.

commonMisreadings: It is not careless indulgence.

concepts.name: Ethical intuitionism
concepts.summary: Ethical intuitionism says some moral truths are directly knowable through rational intuition.
concepts.body: Ethical intuitionism says some moral truths are directly knowable through rational intuition. It treats some moral properties or principles as irreducible and self-evident.

examples.text: An intuitionist may see gratuitous cruelty as wrong without utility calculation.
examples.note: The judgment is basic rather than derived.

commonMisreadings: It does not equate every feeling with intuition.

concepts.name: Ethical naturalism
concepts.summary: Ethical naturalism says moral facts or properties are natural features of the world.
concepts.body: Ethical naturalism says moral facts or properties are natural features of the world. It rejects a sharp metaphysical divide between moral and natural facts.

examples.text: A theory may identify goodness with natural human flourishing.
examples.note: The moral property is analyzed through worldly conditions.

commonMisreadings: It does not say whatever is natural is good.

concepts.name: Ethical non-naturalism
concepts.summary: Ethical non-naturalism says moral properties are real but irreducible to natural or scientific properties.
concepts.body: Ethical non-naturalism says moral properties are real but irreducible to natural or scientific properties. It is objective moral realism without natural reduction.

examples.text: Justice’s goodness may not equal any measurable amount of pleasure.
examples.note: The moral property remains objective but non-natural.

commonMisreadings: It is not moral nihilism.

concepts.name: Ethics
concepts.summary: Ethics studies right action, character, value, obligation, and the good life.
concepts.body: Ethics studies right action, character, value, obligation, and the good life. It includes normative ethics, applied ethics, and metaethics.

examples.text: Allocating scarce organs by urgency is an applied ethical problem.
examples.note: The case requires reasoning about competing values.

commonMisreadings: Ethics is not etiquette alone.

concepts.name: Ethnic nationalism
concepts.summary: Ethnic nationalism defines a nation through shared ancestry, culture, language, or inherited identity.
concepts.body: Ethnic nationalism defines a nation through shared ancestry, culture, language, or inherited identity. It makes political membership depend on an ethnic community rather than only citizenship.

examples.text: A movement seeks a state for people sharing a language and historical origin.
examples.note: Ethnic belonging grounds sovereignty.

commonMisreadings: It differs from civic nationalism.

concepts.name: Ethnonationalism
concepts.summary: Ethnonationalism seeks political authority or borders to correspond to an ethnically defined people.
concepts.body: Ethnonationalism seeks political authority or borders to correspond to an ethnically defined people. It can support autonomy, separation, assimilation, or exclusion.

examples.text: A party restricts citizenship to members of a favored ethnicity.
examples.note: Ethnic membership controls political belonging.

commonMisreadings: It is not ordinary cultural pride.

concepts.name: Eudaimonia
concepts.summary: Eudaimonia is the Greek ideal of flourishing through a complete and excellent human life.
concepts.body: Eudaimonia is the Greek ideal of flourishing through a complete and excellent human life. Aristotle treats it as virtuous activity rather than a passing feeling.

examples.text: A person cultivating courage, practical wisdom, friendship, and civic responsibility exemplifies it.
examples.note: The whole life is judged successful in human activity.

commonMisreadings: It is not momentary pleasure.

concepts.name: Eudaimonism
concepts.summary: Eudaimonism says human flourishing or well-being is the ultimate moral standard.
concepts.body: Eudaimonism says human flourishing or well-being is the ultimate moral standard. Virtues may be valued as constituents or conditions of flourishing.

examples.text: Honesty is praised because it supports trust and practical excellence.
examples.note: The virtue contributes to a good human life.

commonMisreadings: It is broader than psychological egoism.

concepts.name: Euroscepticism
concepts.summary: Euroscepticism is skepticism or opposition toward some or all European Union integration.
concepts.body: Euroscepticism is skepticism or opposition toward some or all European Union integration. It ranges from policy criticism to support for withdrawal.

examples.text: A party supports the single market but opposes transferring more powers to EU institutions.
examples.note: The stance rejects deeper integration without rejecting every European link.

commonMisreadings: It is not hostility to all European countries.

concepts.name: Euthyphro dilemma
concepts.summary: The Euthyphro dilemma asks whether actions are good because a deity commands them or commanded because they are good.
concepts.body: The Euthyphro dilemma asks whether actions are good because a deity commands them or commanded because they are good. It challenges simple divine-command foundations through arbitrariness or dependence concerns.

examples.text: If command alone makes generosity good, command could seemingly make cruelty good.
examples.note: The example raises the arbitrariness problem.

commonMisreadings: It does not prove religious people lack moral reasons.

concepts.name: Event
concepts.summary: An event is a happening located in a temporal and sometimes spatial framework.
concepts.body: An event is a happening located in a temporal and sometimes spatial framework. Events differ from enduring objects that participate in them.

examples.text: A bridge collapse at noon is an event.
examples.note: It occurs rather than persists as a thing.

commonMisreadings: An event need not be planned.

concepts.name: Evidence
concepts.summary: Evidence is information that supports, undermines, or bears on a claim’s truth or justification.
concepts.body: Evidence is information that supports, undermines, or bears on a claim’s truth or justification. Its force depends on relevance, reliability, background assumptions, and alternatives.

examples.text: A DNA match links a suspect to biological material.
examples.note: Reliable matching changes the probability of involvement.

commonMisreadings: Evidence is not always certainty.

concepts.name: Evidentialism
concepts.summary: Evidentialism says belief justification depends on evidence available to the believer.
concepts.body: Evidentialism says belief justification depends on evidence available to the believer. A common principle requires confidence to track evidential strength.

examples.text: A researcher lowers confidence after a controlled contrary experiment.
examples.note: Evidence governs revision rather than attachment.

commonMisreadings: It need not require only verbal evidence.

concepts.name: Existence
concepts.summary: Existence is being real or instantiated, though theories disagree about abstract entities.
concepts.body: Existence is being real or instantiated, though theories disagree about abstract entities. Platonists and nominalists disagree whether numbers exist independently.

examples.text: A Platonist treats numbers as abstract objects, unlike a nominalist.
examples.note: The dispute concerns which entities are real.

commonMisreadings: Existence is not limited to observability.

concepts.name: Existential import
concepts.summary: Existential import is an assumption that a categorical statement presupposes or entails subject-class members exist.
concepts.body: Existential import is an assumption that a categorical statement presupposes or entails subject-class members exist. Modern predicate logic gives universal statements no existential import.

examples.text: “All unicorns are white” is true in an empty-unicorn domain.
examples.note: Universal quantification does not require a witness.

commonMisreadings: It differs from existential quantification.

concepts.name: Existential quantification
concepts.summary: Existential quantification asserts that at least one object satisfies a predicate or formula.
concepts.body: Existential quantification asserts that at least one object satisfies a predicate or formula. Predicate logic represents it with ∃.

examples.text: ∃x(Penguin(x) and Swims(x)) says some penguin swims.
examples.note: A particular penguin can witness the formula.

commonMisreadings: It does not say every object swims.

concepts.name: Existentialism
concepts.summary: Existentialism emphasizes freedom, responsibility, situated choice, anxiety, and meaning.
concepts.body: Existentialism emphasizes freedom, responsibility, situated choice, anxiety, and meaning. Its thinkers disagree about God but often reject predetermined personal essence.

examples.text: Sartre’s person choosing between caring for a parent and joining resistance faces conflicting responsibility.
examples.note: Concrete choice shapes identity under uncertainty.

commonMisreadings: It is not simply pessimism.

concepts.name: Expected utility
concepts.summary: Expected utility is the probability-weighted average of utilities across possible outcomes.
concepts.body: Expected utility is the probability-weighted average of utilities across possible outcomes. Decision theory prefers higher expected utility when probabilities and utilities are accepted.

examples.text: A fair $100-or-$0 gamble has expected monetary utility of $50 under linear utility.
examples.note: Each outcome is weighted before summing.

commonMisreadings: It is not necessarily the most probable outcome.

concepts.name: Expected value
concepts.summary: Expected value is the probability-weighted average numerical outcome of a random variable.
concepts.body: Expected value is the probability-weighted average numerical outcome of a random variable. It may be a value no single trial can produce.

examples.text: A fair die has expected value 3.5 although no roll does.
examples.note: The number describes the long-run average.

commonMisreadings: It is not a one-trial prediction.

concepts.name: Experience machine
concepts.summary: The experience machine is Nozick’s device producing any desired pleasurable experience.
concepts.body: The experience machine is Nozick’s device producing any desired pleasurable experience. It tests whether pleasure alone makes a life good.

examples.text: Someone refusing permanent connection may value doing real things and being a certain person.
examples.note: The refusal assigns value to authenticity or reality.

commonMisreadings: It does not prove pleasure has no value.

concepts.name: Explanation
concepts.summary: An explanation accounts for why or how something occurs through causes, mechanisms, laws, reasons, or structures.
concepts.body: An explanation accounts for why or how something occurs through causes, mechanisms, laws, reasons, or structures. Standards differ among science, history, action, and mathematics.

examples.text: An infection and its physiological effects explain a fever.
examples.note: The account identifies a producing mechanism.

commonMisreadings: Restatement is not explanation.

concepts.name: Explanatory power
concepts.summary: Explanatory power is a theory’s capacity to account for evidence and diverse phenomena.
concepts.body: Explanatory power is a theory’s capacity to account for evidence and diverse phenomena. It increases when one framework unifies facts with few ad hoc assumptions.

examples.text: Natural selection explains adaptation, homologous structures, and fossil succession.
examples.note: One mechanism connects several observations.

commonMisreadings: It is not identical to simplicity.

concepts.name: Exploitation
concepts.summary: Exploitation is unfair use of another’s vulnerability, labor, or resources for disproportionate benefit.
concepts.body: Exploitation is unfair use of another’s vulnerability, labor, or resources for disproportionate benefit. Theories disagree whether coercion or unequal bargaining is required.

examples.text: An employer pays migrant workers illegally low wages while threatening retaliation.
examples.note: Constrained options make refusal costly while the employer gains.

commonMisreadings: It is not every unequal mutually beneficial exchange.

concepts.name: Explosion principle
concepts.summary: The explosion principle says a contradiction entails any proposition in classical logic.
concepts.body: The explosion principle says a contradiction entails any proposition in classical logic. It is also called ex falso quodlibet.

examples.text: From P and not-P, classical logic derives unrelated Q.
examples.note: An inconsistent premise set becomes deductively trivial.

commonMisreadings: Explosion is not a physical claim.

concepts.name: Expression theory of art
concepts.summary: Expression theory says an artwork’s artistic identity or value centrally involves expressing emotion or experience.
concepts.body: Expression theory says an artwork’s artistic identity or value centrally involves expressing emotion or experience. Some versions require emotion to be clarified or communicated.

examples.text: A composer’s dissonant slow piece conveys mourning.
examples.note: Musical form communicates an emotional quality.

commonMisreadings: Art need not express autobiography.

concepts.name: Expressivism
concepts.summary: Expressivism says normative statements express attitudes, commitments, or plans rather than describe normative facts.
concepts.body: Expressivism says normative statements express attitudes, commitments, or plans rather than describe normative facts. It explains moral disagreement without ordinary factual moral properties.

examples.text: “Cheating is wrong” expresses opposition and a practical commitment.
examples.note: The statement guides action without describing a moral object.

commonMisreadings: It does not make moral language meaningless.

concepts.name: Extended mind
concepts.summary: The extended-mind thesis says cognitive processes can include suitably integrated external resources.
concepts.body: The extended-mind thesis says cognitive processes can include suitably integrated external resources. An external resource must reliably and readily perform a cognitive function.

examples.text: Otto’s constantly consulted notebook functions as external memory.
examples.note: It performs retrieval work that internal memory performs for another agent.

commonMisreadings: Not every tool automatically becomes part of mind.

concepts.name: Extension
concepts.summary: The extension of a term is the set of things to which it correctly applies.
concepts.body: The extension of a term is the set of things to which it correctly applies. It contrasts with intension, the term’s meaning or conditions.

examples.text: The extension of “planet” includes bodies satisfying the chosen astronomical definition.
examples.note: Those bodies are the term’s members.

commonMisreadings: Extension is not word length.

concepts.name: Externalism in epistemology
concepts.summary: Epistemic externalism says factors outside conscious access can contribute to knowledge or justification.
concepts.body: Epistemic externalism says factors outside conscious access can contribute to knowledge or justification. Reliabilism evaluates belief-forming processes partly by objective truth reliability.

examples.text: Normal perception can yield knowledge even when a person cannot prove perception reliable.
examples.note: The process’s truth connection is externally relevant.

commonMisreadings: It does not deny internal reasons.

concepts.name: Externality
concepts.summary: An externality is an unpriced cost or benefit of an activity imposed on third parties.
concepts.body: An externality is an unpriced cost or benefit of an activity imposed on third parties. Negative externalities can make markets produce too much harm.

examples.text: Factory smoke imposes respiratory costs on nearby residents.
examples.note: Outsiders bear harm absent from the product price.

commonMisreadings: It is not any unpaid producer cost.

concepts.name: Fabianism
concepts.summary: Fabianism is a socialist tradition favoring gradual democratic institutional reform over revolution.
concepts.body: Fabianism is a socialist tradition favoring gradual democratic institutional reform over revolution. The Fabian Society promoted research, education, municipal action, and legislation.

examples.text: A Fabian strategy expands public ownership through parliamentary reforms.
examples.note: Socialist objectives are pursued incrementally.

commonMisreadings: It is not opposition to all state intervention.

concepts.name: Fairness
concepts.summary: Fairness treats people by impartial, relevant, and consistently applied standards.
concepts.body: Fairness treats people by impartial, relevant, and consistently applied standards. It can require unequal treatment when circumstances differ relevantly.

examples.text: Extra exam time for a student with a disability can be fair.
examples.note: The adjustment equalizes opportunity rather than treatment.

commonMisreadings: Fairness is not always identical treatment.

concepts.name: Fallibilism
concepts.summary: Fallibilism says justified beliefs remain open to error.
concepts.body: Fallibilism says justified beliefs remain open to error. It rejects certainty as a requirement for knowledge or rational belief.

examples.text: A geologist accepts a fault model while allowing future revision.
examples.note: The belief is responsible without being guaranteed true.

commonMisreadings: It is not total skepticism.

concepts.name: False fame effect
concepts.summary: The false fame effect is judging an unfamiliar previously seen name as famous because it feels familiar.
concepts.body: The false fame effect is judging an unfamiliar previously seen name as famous because it feels familiar. It often results from source-monitoring failure.

examples.text: After seeing a fictional author’s name, participants may call it a celebrity name.
examples.note: Exposure creates familiarity without fame evidence.

commonMisreadings: It does not make the person famous.

concepts.name: Falsifiability
concepts.summary: Falsifiability is vulnerability of a claim to observations that could show it false.
concepts.body: Falsifiability is vulnerability of a claim to observations that could show it false. Popper used potential refutation to distinguish scientific conjectures from insulated claims.

examples.text: “One measured metal contracts when heated” could challenge “all metals expand.”
examples.note: The universal claim permits a counterexample.

commonMisreadings: Falsifiable does not mean false.

concepts.name: Family resemblance
concepts.summary: Family resemblance is category membership through overlapping similarities without one feature common to all members.
concepts.body: Family resemblance is category membership through overlapping similarities without one feature common to all members. Wittgenstein used it against universal defining essences.

examples.text: Games include sports, board games, and solitary puzzles sharing different features.
examples.note: No one feature must define every game.

commonMisreadings: The category is not thereby arbitrary.

concepts.name: Fascism
concepts.summary: Fascism is authoritarian ultranationalism subordinating individuals to a mythic national community and often using leader rule and violence.
concepts.body: Fascism is authoritarian ultranationalism subordinating individuals to a mythic national community and often using leader rule and violence. Fascist movements reject liberal pluralism and mobilize against internal enemies.

examples.text: Mussolini’s regime combined one-party rule, censorship, paramilitaries, and nationalism.
examples.note: The institutions express authoritarian militant nationalism.

commonMisreadings: Fascism is not every dictatorship or patriotism.

concepts.name: Fatalism
concepts.summary: Fatalism says some outcomes occur regardless of what agents choose or do.
concepts.body: Fatalism says some outcomes occur regardless of what agents choose or do. It differs from determinism, which allows actions to be causes within a determined chain.

examples.text: A fatalist refuses exam study because the result is fixed anyway.
examples.note: Deliberation is treated as causally irrelevant.

commonMisreadings: It is not merely difficulty changing an outcome.

concepts.name: Federalism
concepts.summary: Federalism divides constitutional authority between central and regional governments.
concepts.body: Federalism divides constitutional authority between central and regional governments. Each level has some protected sphere of competence.

examples.text: The United States assigns national defense federally and many local matters to states.
examples.note: Both government levels possess legally assigned authority.

commonMisreadings: It differs from a unitary state.

concepts.name: Feedback loop
concepts.summary: A feedback loop returns a system’s output as input that alters later behavior.
concepts.body: A feedback loop returns a system’s output as input that alters later behavior. Positive feedback amplifies change; negative feedback counteracts deviation.

examples.text: A thermostat turns heating on when measured temperature falls below its set point.
examples.note: Measurement controls action that reduces deviation.

commonMisreadings: It is not every temporal sequence.

concepts.name: Feminism
concepts.summary: Feminism seeks to understand and end gender-based subordination and secure gender justice.
concepts.body: Feminism seeks to understand and end gender-based subordination and secure gender justice. Its theories examine intersections with race, class, sexuality, disability, and colonial power.

examples.text: Equal-pay campaigns challenge gendered workplace disadvantage.
examples.note: They target institutional effects of gender roles.

commonMisreadings: Feminism does not seek women’s domination.

concepts.name: Feminist epistemology
concepts.summary: Feminist epistemology studies how gendered power shapes knowledge, credibility, inquiry, and justification.
concepts.body: Feminist epistemology studies how gendered power shapes knowledge, credibility, inquiry, and justification. It analyzes situated knowledge, exclusion, epistemic privilege, and testimonial injustice.

examples.text: Studying women’s exclusion from drug trials reveals distorted medical knowledge.
examples.note: Research design affects what is known and for whom.

commonMisreadings: It does not claim only women know.

concepts.name: Feminist ethics
concepts.summary: Feminist ethics critiques moral theories neglecting dependency, unequal power, emotion, and care.
concepts.body: Feminist ethics critiques moral theories neglecting dependency, unequal power, emotion, and care. It emphasizes contextual responsibility alongside justice principles.

examples.text: Discharge planning may consider an unpaid caregiver’s constrained labor.
examples.note: Relationships and structural burdens become morally relevant.

commonMisreadings: It is not simply kindness over rules.

concepts.name: Fermi paradox
concepts.summary: The Fermi paradox is the tension between probable extraterrestrial life and absence of clear advanced-civilization evidence.
concepts.body: The Fermi paradox is the tension between probable extraterrestrial life and absence of clear advanced-civilization evidence. It asks why a populous galaxy has yielded no unambiguous signals or probes.

examples.text: The Drake equation may suggest many communicators while searches find no confirmed technosignatures.
examples.note: Expectation conflicts with observation.

commonMisreadings: It does not prove aliens do not exist.

concepts.name: Feudalism
concepts.summary: Feudalism is a label for landholding, military obligation, and hierarchical dependence especially associated with medieval Europe.
concepts.body: Feudalism is a label for landholding, military obligation, and hierarchical dependence especially associated with medieval Europe. Historians dispute its precision and geographic scope.

examples.text: A lord grants a fief to a vassal for military service.
examples.note: Land tenure is tied to personal political obligation.

commonMisreadings: It was not one identical universal system.

concepts.name: Fictional discourse
concepts.summary: Fictional discourse discusses entities and events represented in stories.
concepts.body: Fictional discourse discusses entities and events represented in stories. It raises how meaningful claims can concern nonactual entities.

examples.text: Readers infer that Sherlock Holmes is a detective from the stories.
examples.note: The inference uses information authorized by the fiction.

commonMisreadings: It is not necessarily deceptive real-world speech.

concepts.name: Fictionalism
concepts.summary: Fictionalism uses a discourse as useful make-believe while denying literal existence of its entities.
concepts.body: Fictionalism uses a discourse as useful make-believe while denying literal existence of its entities. A fictionalist can reason within a theory instrumentally without ontological commitment.

examples.text: A mathematical fictionalist calculates with numbers while denying abstract numbers exist.
examples.note: Mathematical practice is retained without Platonist commitment.

commonMisreadings: It does not deny truth within fiction.

concepts.name: Fideism
concepts.summary: Fideism holds that faith is independent of or superior to reason for certain religious commitments.
concepts.body: Fideism holds that faith is independent of or superior to reason for certain religious commitments. It may deny that rational proof supplies religious trust.

examples.text: A fideist grounds belief in God in faith rather than cosmological demonstration.
examples.note: Trust, not inference, supplies the commitment.

commonMisreadings: It is not merely faith cooperating with reason.

concepts.name: Filial piety
concepts.summary: Filial piety is respect, care, and obligation toward parents and ancestors.
concepts.body: Filial piety is respect, care, and obligation toward parents and ancestors. Confucian thought connects it to roles, ritual, cultivation, and social harmony.

examples.text: An adult child caring for an ill parent while preserving dignity exemplifies it.
examples.note: The conduct expresses sustained family responsibility.

commonMisreadings: It does not require obeying every harmful demand.

concepts.name: Final cause
concepts.summary: A final cause is the end or purpose for which something occurs in Aristotelian teleology.
concepts.body: A final cause is the end or purpose for which something occurs in Aristotelian teleology. It differs from an efficient cause, which produces an event.

examples.text: The heart’s final cause is circulating blood, while contraction is an efficient process.
examples.note: Function explains what the organ is for.

commonMisreadings: A final cause need not be a conscious intention.

concepts.name: First-order logic
concepts.summary: First-order logic quantifies over individual objects but not over predicates or properties.
concepts.body: First-order logic quantifies over individual objects but not over predicates or properties. Its syntax includes variables, predicates, connectives, and quantifiers such as universal and existential quantification.

examples.text: “All mammals are animals” can be formalized as every object that is a mammal being an animal.
examples.note: The formula quantifies over objects and applies predicates to them, which is the defining scope of first-order logic.

commonMisreadings: It is not propositional logic, because it represents internal subject-predicate structure.

concepts.name: First-person perspective
concepts.summary: A first-person perspective presents experience or narration from the standpoint of an experiencing subject.
concepts.body: A first-person perspective presents experience or narration from the standpoint of an experiencing subject. It uses indexicals such as “I” and makes the subject’s situated access to events central.

examples.text: A diary entry describing the writer’s fear during an earthquake uses a first-person perspective.
examples.note: The account reports the event through the writer’s own point of view rather than an external observer.

commonMisreadings: It is not merely a story containing a character, because the relevant perspective is the character’s own.

concepts.name: First-principles reasoning
concepts.summary: First-principles reasoning analyzes a problem by reducing it to basic facts and deriving conclusions from them.
concepts.body: First-principles reasoning analyzes a problem by reducing it to basic facts and deriving conclusions from them. It separates fundamental constraints from inherited assumptions, conventions, and analogies.

examples.text: A battery designer may derive a pack’s cost from cell price, materials, assembly, and losses instead of copying an existing pack price.
examples.note: The calculation rebuilds the answer from underlying components rather than accepting a conventional design as given.

commonMisreadings: It is not simply being skeptical, because it requires constructive derivation after questioning assumptions.

concepts.name: Flourishing
concepts.summary: Flourishing is a condition of living well in which a person develops capabilities and exercises them across a worthwhile life.
concepts.body: Flourishing is a condition of living well in which a person develops capabilities and exercises them across a worthwhile life. Aristotelian accounts connect flourishing with virtue, practical judgment, relationships, and sustained activity rather than momentary pleasure.

examples.text: A community nurse who cultivates skill, friendship, civic responsibility, and personal health illustrates flourishing.
examples.note: The example includes integrated activity and development, not just a temporary pleasant feeling.

commonMisreadings: Flourishing is broader than happiness understood as positive mood alone.

concepts.name: Folk psychology
concepts.summary: Folk psychology is the ordinary framework of beliefs, desires, intentions, and emotions used to explain and predict behavior.
concepts.body: Folk psychology is the ordinary framework of beliefs, desires, intentions, and emotions used to explain and predict behavior. It treats mental states as reasons for action in everyday interpretation.

examples.text: Saying that Maya took an umbrella because she believed it would rain is a folk-psychological explanation.
examples.note: The explanation uses an ordinary belief and desire vocabulary rather than a laboratory theory.

commonMisreadings: Folk psychology is not necessarily primitive science; it is the common interpretive framework people routinely use.

concepts.name: Forer effect
concepts.summary: The Forer effect is the tendency to accept vague, broadly applicable personality descriptions as uniquely accurate.
concepts.body: The Forer effect is the tendency to accept vague, broadly applicable personality descriptions as uniquely accurate. It helps explain why generalized statements can make horoscopes or personality readings seem personally tailored.

examples.text: A person may rate “You sometimes doubt yourself but value independence” as an unusually precise assessment.
examples.note: The statement combines common traits and flexible wording, allowing the reader to fit it to personal experience.

commonMisreadings: It is not evidence that the assessment measured an individual trait with high specificity.

concepts.name: Forgiveness
concepts.summary: Forgiveness is the deliberate relinquishing of resentment or a demand for retaliation after a wrong.
concepts.body: Forgiveness is the deliberate relinquishing of resentment or a demand for retaliation after a wrong. It can occur without excusing the wrong, restoring trust, or abandoning justified accountability.

examples.text: A victim may stop seeking revenge against an apologetic offender while still reporting the crime.
examples.note: The victim releases personal vengeance but does not deny harm or remove institutional consequences.

commonMisreadings: Forgiveness is distinct from reconciliation, which requires renewed relationship and usually mutual participation.

concepts.name: Formal language
concepts.summary: A formal language is a set of strings generated or recognized according to explicit symbolic rules.
concepts.body: A formal language is a set of strings generated or recognized according to explicit symbolic rules. Its alphabet and formation conditions are specified independently of ordinary conversational meaning.

examples.text: The language of balanced parentheses contains strings such as “()()” and “(())” but excludes “)(”.
examples.note: Membership is determined by a formal rule for matching delimiters rather than by interpretation.

commonMisreadings: A formal language need not be a natural human language or have semantic content.

concepts.name: Formalism in aesthetics
concepts.summary: Formalism in aesthetics evaluates artworks primarily through perceptible relations such as form, composition, color, rhythm, or structure.
concepts.body: Formalism in aesthetics evaluates artworks primarily through perceptible relations such as form, composition, color, rhythm, or structure. It gives those properties analytical priority over biography, representation, or moral effects.

examples.text: A formalist analysis of a painting may focus on geometric balance and contrast without discussing its political subject.
examples.note: The analysis explains the work’s aesthetic organization through features directly present in its arrangement.

commonMisreadings: Formalism does not mean that an artwork must lack meaning; it means meaning is not the primary evaluative basis.

concepts.name: Formalism in mathematics
concepts.summary: Formalism in mathematics treats mathematical practice as manipulation of symbols according to stipulated rules, with consistency as a central concern.
concepts.body: Formalism in mathematics treats mathematical practice as manipulation of symbols according to stipulated rules, with consistency as a central concern. David Hilbert’s program sought finitary proofs that formal systems do not derive contradictions.

examples.text: In a formal arithmetic system, a proof is a finite sequence of formulas each licensed by an axiom or inference rule.
examples.note: The proof’s validity depends on syntactic derivability rather than intuitive reference to numbers.

commonMisreadings: Formalism is not the claim that mathematicians never use intuition or interpretation in practice.

concepts.name: Foundationalism
concepts.summary: Foundationalism is the epistemological view that some beliefs are basic and support other justified beliefs without depending on them.
concepts.body: Foundationalism is the epistemological view that some beliefs are basic and support other justified beliefs without depending on them. It explains justification as having a structure with foundational beliefs and inferentially supported beliefs.

examples.text: A foundationalist may hold that a present perceptual experience directly justifies belief that a red object is visible.
examples.note: That perceptual belief is treated as an immediate support from which further beliefs can be inferred.

commonMisreadings: Foundationalism differs from coherentism, which makes mutual fit within a belief system central.

concepts.name: Four noble truths
concepts.summary: The Four Noble Truths state that suffering or unsatisfactoriness exists, has craving as a cause, can cease, and has a path leading to cessation.
concepts.body: The Four Noble Truths state that suffering or unsatisfactoriness exists, has craving as a cause, can cease, and has a path leading to cessation. They organize early Buddhist teaching as a diagnosis, cause, prognosis, and treatment.

examples.text: The Noble Eightfold Path is presented as the practical path associated with ending suffering.
examples.note: It supplies the fourth truth’s prescribed route rather than merely describing Buddhist ethics in general.

commonMisreadings: The first truth does not assert that every experience is equally painful; it concerns pervasive unsatisfactoriness and vulnerability.

concepts.name: Four-dimensionalism
concepts.summary: Four-dimensionalism is the metaphysical view that objects extend through time as well as through the three spatial dimensions.
concepts.body: Four-dimensionalism is the metaphysical view that objects extend through time as well as through the three spatial dimensions. It treats temporal parts, such as an object’s childhood stage, as constituents of a spacetime whole.

examples.text: A four-dimensionalist can describe a tree as a spacetime worm containing distinct temporal parts across its life.
examples.note: The tree’s change is represented as differences among temporal parts rather than alteration of one wholly present object.

commonMisreadings: Four-dimensionalism is not the claim that physical space has four spatial dimensions.

concepts.name: Frankfurt cases
concepts.summary: Frankfurt cases are thought experiments in which an agent acts freely even though a counterfactual mechanism would have prevented alternative action if needed.
concepts.body: Frankfurt cases are thought experiments in which an agent acts freely even though a counterfactual mechanism would have prevented alternative action if needed. They challenge the principle that moral responsibility requires the genuine ability to do otherwise.

examples.text: A hidden controller would intervene only if Jones began choosing differently, but Jones chooses for his own reasons and the controller never acts.
examples.note: Because the intervention is inactive, the actual choice appears responsible despite the absence of a live alternative.

commonMisreadings: A Frankfurt case is not simply any deterministic scenario; its distinctive feature is the nonintervening backup mechanism.

concepts.name: Frankfurt School
concepts.summary: The Frankfurt School was a tradition of critical social theory associated with the Institute for Social Research and analyses of capitalism, culture, and domination.
concepts.body: The Frankfurt School was a tradition of critical social theory associated with the Institute for Social Research and analyses of capitalism, culture, and domination. Its major figures developed Marxist theory alongside psychoanalysis, sociology, and philosophy.

examples.text: Adorno and Horkheimer’s analysis of the culture industry examines how mass-produced entertainment can reproduce social conformity.
examples.note: The example connects cultural production with the maintenance of power, a characteristic Frankfurt School concern.

commonMisreadings: The name does not refer to a university department or a single uniform doctrine.

concepts.name: Free variable
concepts.summary: A free variable is a variable occurrence not bound by a quantifier or another binding operator within its scope.
concepts.body: A free variable is a variable occurrence not bound by a quantifier or another binding operator within its scope. A formula containing a free variable is generally an open formula rather than a complete sentence.

examples.text: In “x is taller than y,” both x and y are free if no quantifier governs them.
examples.note: Their values must be supplied by an assignment before the formula receives a truth value.

commonMisreadings: A free variable is not the same as a variable that happens to be unquantified in an informal sentence.

concepts.name: Free will
concepts.summary: Free will is the capacity to exercise control over choices or actions in a way relevant to agency and responsibility.
concepts.body: Free will is the capacity to exercise control over choices or actions in a way relevant to agency and responsibility. Philosophical accounts disagree about whether this capacity requires alternatives, sourcehood, or reasons-responsiveness.

examples.text: A person who considers reasons and voluntarily signs a contract is commonly described as exercising free will.
examples.note: The decision is attributed to the person’s deliberation rather than to coercion or reflex.

commonMisreadings: Free will is not identical to doing whatever one desires, since desires may be manipulated or compulsive.

concepts.name: Freedom
concepts.summary: Freedom is the condition of having meaningful scope to act, choose, or develop without unjustified constraint.
concepts.body: Freedom is the condition of having meaningful scope to act, choose, or develop without unjustified constraint. Political theories distinguish freedom from interference, domination, and the effective capacity to pursue ends.

examples.text: A worker is freer when leaving a job is legally permitted and economically feasible than when exit is formally legal but impossible.
examples.note: The example shows that formal noninterference can differ from practical power to act.

commonMisreadings: Freedom is not equivalent to unlimited choice, because social rules can protect everyone’s agency.

concepts.name: Freedom of association
concepts.summary: Freedom of association is the liberty to form, join, maintain, or leave groups for lawful shared purposes.
concepts.body: Freedom of association is the liberty to form, join, maintain, or leave groups for lawful shared purposes. It protects collective organization in areas such as unions, political parties, clubs, and religious communities.

examples.text: Employees forming a union exercise freedom of association by organizing around shared workplace interests.
examples.note: Their coordinated membership creates a group through which they pursue a common purpose.

commonMisreadings: It does not guarantee every group access to public resources or exemption from generally applicable law.

concepts.name: Freedom of expression
concepts.summary: Freedom of expression is the right to communicate ideas, information, opinions, and artistic or symbolic messages without unjustified state restriction.
concepts.body: Freedom of expression is the right to communicate ideas, information, opinions, and artistic or symbolic messages without unjustified state restriction. Its protection can coexist with narrow rules addressing threats, defamation, or direct incitement.

examples.text: Publishing criticism of a government policy in a newspaper is an exercise of freedom of expression.
examples.note: The communication conveys a political opinion, a core protected use of expressive liberty.

commonMisreadings: It is not a guarantee that private platforms must publish every message.

concepts.name: Freedom of religion
concepts.summary: Freedom of religion protects a person’s liberty to hold, change, practice, or decline religious beliefs.
concepts.body: Freedom of religion protects a person’s liberty to hold, change, practice, or decline religious beliefs. It commonly includes both freedom of belief and freedom from compelled religious observance.

examples.text: A state that permits a citizen to convert and attend worship without penalty protects religious freedom.
examples.note: The citizen’s belief and practice remain voluntary rather than imposed by government.

commonMisreadings: Religious freedom does not automatically exempt conduct from neutral laws that protect others.

concepts.name: Friendship
concepts.summary: Friendship is a voluntary relationship involving mutual goodwill, personal concern, and shared recognition between people.
concepts.body: Friendship is a voluntary relationship involving mutual goodwill, personal concern, and shared recognition between people. Philosophical accounts often distinguish friendships of utility or pleasure from friendships grounded in appreciation of character.

examples.text: Two neighbors who reliably support one another and enjoy candid conversation exemplify friendship.
examples.note: Their relationship includes mutual concern and companionship rather than a merely transactional exchange.

commonMisreadings: Friendship is not identical to familiarity, popularity, or any relationship that happens to feel pleasant.

concepts.name: Functionalism in philosophy of mind
concepts.summary: Functionalism in philosophy of mind identifies mental states by the causal roles they play among inputs, internal states, and behavior.
concepts.body: Functionalism in philosophy of mind identifies mental states by the causal roles they play among inputs, internal states, and behavior. It allows the same mental function to be realized by different physical substrates.

examples.text: A functionalist can regard an appropriately organized silicon system as capable of pain if it occupies the relevant causal role.
examples.note: The theory defines pain by its response and interaction pattern rather than by biological tissue alone.

commonMisreadings: Functionalism is not behaviorism, because it includes internal causal states rather than only observable behavior.

concepts.name: Fundamentalism
concepts.summary: Fundamentalism is a movement that insists on authoritative foundational doctrines and often opposes perceived dilution by modern interpretation.
concepts.body: Fundamentalism is a movement that insists on authoritative foundational doctrines and often opposes perceived dilution by modern interpretation. The term can apply to religious or political movements, though its historical use is context-dependent.

examples.text: Christian fundamentalism in the early twentieth century defended selected doctrines against liberal Protestant reinterpretation.
examples.note: The movement treated those doctrines as nonnegotiable foundations of religious authority.

commonMisreadings: Fundamentalism does not simply mean intense religious commitment or literal reading in every context.

concepts.name: Fuzzy logic
concepts.summary: Fuzzy logic represents degrees of membership or truth between the binary values of completely false and completely true.
concepts.body: Fuzzy logic represents degrees of membership or truth between the binary values of completely false and completely true. Its membership functions permit an object to belong to a category to a specified degree.

examples.text: A thermostat can use the rule that if a room is somewhat cold, heating should increase moderately.
examples.note: The rule handles gradual temperature categories instead of forcing a sharp cold-versus-not-cold boundary.

commonMisreadings: Fuzzy truth is not the same as probability, which measures uncertainty about whether a proposition is true.

concepts.name: Game theory
concepts.summary: Game theory studies strategic situations in which each participant’s outcome depends partly on the choices of others.
concepts.body: Game theory studies strategic situations in which each participant’s outcome depends partly on the choices of others. It models players, available strategies, preferences or payoffs, and sometimes information conditions.

examples.text: In the prisoner’s dilemma, each prisoner’s best individual response can produce a worse joint outcome than cooperation.
examples.note: The payoff structure makes the conflict between individual incentives and collective benefit explicit.

commonMisreadings: Game theory is not limited to recreational games or necessarily to competitive situations.

concepts.name: Generation effect
concepts.summary: The generation effect is the memory advantage that occurs when people produce information themselves rather than merely read it.
concepts.body: The generation effect is the memory advantage that occurs when people produce information themselves rather than merely read it. Self-generated material is often encoded with more distinctive retrieval cues.

examples.text: A student usually remembers a definition better after completing a missing word than after copying the completed sentence.
examples.note: The act of generating the word adds an active encoding operation that supports later recall.

commonMisreadings: It does not mean every generated answer is accurate or better than every form of study.

concepts.name: Georgism
concepts.summary: Georgism is the economic view that individuals should retain the value they create while socially generated land value should be captured for public benefit.
concepts.body: Georgism is the economic view that individuals should retain the value they create while socially generated land value should be captured for public benefit. It commonly proposes a tax on unimproved land value rather than on buildings or labor.

examples.text: A city may fund services with a land-value tax that charges more for a centrally located vacant lot than for a remote lot of equal size.
examples.note: The tax targets location value created by community activity while avoiding a direct penalty on construction.

commonMisreadings: Georgism is not a general ban on private property in land.

concepts.name: German idealism
concepts.summary: German idealism is an early modern philosophical movement emphasizing the conditions under which reason, subjectivity, and freedom structure experience and reality.
concepts.body: German idealism is an early modern philosophical movement emphasizing the conditions under which reason, subjectivity, and freedom structure experience and reality. Kant, Fichte, Schelling, and Hegel are commonly associated with its development.

examples.text: Hegel’s account of history as the development of freedom is a German idealist approach to social and metaphysical change.
examples.note: It treats rational self-development as central to understanding both thought and historical reality.

commonMisreadings: German idealism is not one claim that only private ideas exist; several of its thinkers defended objective structures.

concepts.name: Gettier cases
concepts.summary: Gettier cases are examples in which a person has justified true belief but seems not to know because the belief is true by luck.
concepts.body: Gettier cases are examples in which a person has justified true belief but seems not to know because the belief is true by luck. They typically introduce misleading evidence while preserving a true conclusion.

examples.text: A person sees a stopped clock showing the correct time and believes it is noon, but the clock is correct only by coincidence.
examples.note: The belief is true and perceptually supported, yet its truth is disconnected from the evidence in the relevant way.

commonMisreadings: A Gettier case is not merely a false justified belief, because its defining conclusion is true.

concepts.name: Gettier problem
concepts.summary: The Gettier problem is the challenge to the claim that knowledge is simply justified true belief.
concepts.body: The Gettier problem is the challenge to the claim that knowledge is simply justified true belief. It asks what additional condition would exclude accidentally true justified beliefs.

examples.text: The stopped-clock example motivates searching for a no-luck, causal, or safety condition on knowledge.
examples.note: The problem arises because truth, belief, and justification can all be present while knowledge still seems absent.

commonMisreadings: It does not show that justification is irrelevant to knowledge; it shows that the three-part analysis is insufficient.

concepts.name: Global justice
concepts.summary: Global justice concerns the fair distribution of rights, duties, resources, and political consideration across national borders.
concepts.body: Global justice concerns the fair distribution of rights, duties, resources, and political consideration across national borders. It asks whether principles of justice apply to all persons regardless of citizenship.

examples.text: A global justice argument may require affluent states to reduce emissions because poorer populations bear disproportionate climate harms.
examples.note: The proposed duty crosses borders and responds to unequal effects on people worldwide.

commonMisreadings: Global justice is broader than international charity, because it also examines institutions and structural power.

concepts.name: Globalism
concepts.summary: Globalism is a perspective that emphasizes worldwide interdependence and cooperation across national boundaries.
concepts.body: Globalism is a perspective that emphasizes worldwide interdependence and cooperation across national boundaries. It can describe economic, political, cultural, or institutional projects that treat global connections as significant.

examples.text: Support for an international climate agreement is a globalist policy orientation.
examples.note: The agreement addresses a shared planetary problem through coordinated action among states.

commonMisreadings: Globalism is not identical to globalization, which describes processes rather than a normative or political viewpoint.

concepts.name: Gnosticism
concepts.summary: Gnosticism refers to religious movements that make salvific knowledge of divine reality central and often portray the material world as deficient or alienating.
concepts.body: Gnosticism refers to religious movements that make salvific knowledge of divine reality central and often portray the material world as deficient or alienating. Many groups called Gnostic combined Jewish, Christian, and Hellenistic elements, so the category is historically diverse.

examples.text: The Valentinian tradition presented spiritual knowledge as a route toward restoration to the divine realm.
examples.note: Its emphasis on revealed knowledge and a problematic material order fits recurring Gnostic themes.

commonMisreadings: Gnosticism is not simply any religion that values knowledge or private spiritual experience.

concepts.name: Goodhart's law
concepts.summary: Goodhart’s law states that when a measure becomes a target, it can cease to be a good measure.
concepts.body: Goodhart’s law states that when a measure becomes a target, it can cease to be a good measure. Targeting changes behavior toward optimizing the indicator rather than the underlying objective.

examples.text: If a hospital rewards low average treatment time, staff may discharge patients prematurely to improve the metric.
examples.note: The metric becomes gameable and no longer reliably represents quality of care.

commonMisreadings: The law is not a mathematical theorem that every metric inevitably fails when used as a target.

concepts.name: Google effect
concepts.summary: The Google effect is the tendency to remember information less well when people expect to be able to retrieve it online.
concepts.body: The Google effect is the tendency to remember information less well when people expect to be able to retrieve it online. People may retain where information can be found rather than the information’s content.

examples.text: After searching a fact repeatedly, a student may remember the website location but not the fact itself.
examples.note: External availability reduces the perceived need to encode the fact in durable memory.

commonMisreadings: It is not identical to ordinary forgetting caused by time or lack of attention.

concepts.name: Governance
concepts.summary: Governance is the process by which collective affairs are directed, regulated, and held accountable through institutions and practices.
concepts.body: Governance is the process by which collective affairs are directed, regulated, and held accountable through institutions and practices. It includes state and nonstate actors, rules, decision procedures, and mechanisms of oversight.

examples.text: A city’s governance includes elected officials, agencies, public consultations, courts, and service contractors.
examples.note: These actors jointly shape decisions and accountability rather than government alone issuing every action.

commonMisreadings: Governance is broader than government, which usually denotes the formal public authority.

concepts.name: Grandfather paradox
concepts.summary: The grandfather paradox is a time-travel puzzle in which changing the past could prevent the traveler’s own existence.
concepts.body: The grandfather paradox is a time-travel puzzle in which changing the past could prevent the traveler’s own existence. It exposes tension between backward time travel, causal consistency, and a single determinate history.

examples.text: A traveler who kills their grandparent before their parent is conceived would remove the condition for the traveler’s journey.
examples.note: The action creates a causal contradiction between the traveler’s existence and the altered past.

commonMisreadings: It is not merely any time-travel story involving family history; the contradiction concerns self-undermining causation.

concepts.name: Green politics
concepts.summary: Green politics is a political tradition that prioritizes ecological sustainability, interdependence, social justice, and participatory democracy.
concepts.body: Green politics is a political tradition that prioritizes ecological sustainability, interdependence, social justice, and participatory democracy. It treats environmental degradation as connected to economic structures and political power.

examples.text: A green platform may combine renewable energy investment, public transit, habitat protection, and community decision-making.
examples.note: The package links ecological limits with social and democratic reforms rather than treating pollution as an isolated technical issue.

commonMisreadings: Green politics is not reducible to conservation alone, because it includes institutional and distributive concerns.

concepts.name: Grounding
concepts.summary: Grounding is a metaphysical relation in which one fact or entity explains why another exists or obtains.
concepts.body: Grounding is a metaphysical relation in which one fact or entity explains why another exists or obtains. It is often described as a noncausal, constitutive relation of dependence.

examples.text: The fact that a triangle has three sides is grounded in what it is to be a triangle.
examples.note: The definitional nature of triangularity explains the fact without one event causing another.

commonMisreadings: Grounding is not simply causal explanation, because causes operate through temporal or productive dependence.

concepts.name: Groupthink
concepts.summary: Groupthink is a pattern in which a cohesive group suppresses dissent and critical evaluation in pursuit of apparent agreement.
concepts.body: Groupthink is a pattern in which a cohesive group suppresses dissent and critical evaluation in pursuit of apparent agreement. It can produce overconfidence, self-censorship, and poor decisions despite capable members.

examples.text: A committee may ignore warnings about a failed launch because members fear appearing disloyal.
examples.note: Pressure for unanimity prevents the group from examining serious contrary evidence.

commonMisreadings: Groupthink is not the same as ordinary consensus reached after open disagreement.

concepts.name: Guild socialism
concepts.summary: Guild socialism is a socialist theory proposing worker control of industry through self-governing occupational guilds coordinated within a democratic state.
concepts.body: Guild socialism is a socialist theory proposing worker control of industry through self-governing occupational guilds coordinated within a democratic state. It rejects both private capitalist control and centralized state management as the sole form of industrial organization.

examples.text: A transport guild could manage rail operations through elected workers while a public council coordinates regional needs.
examples.note: The arrangement gives producers institutional control while retaining broader democratic coordination.

commonMisreadings: Guild socialism is not simply trade-union bargaining within an otherwise unchanged capitalist system.

concepts.name: Haecceitism
concepts.summary: Haecceitism is the view that individual things possess primitive nonqualitative identities or thisnesses.
concepts.body: Haecceitism is the view that individual things possess primitive nonqualitative identities or thisnesses. It holds that two entities could share all qualitative properties while differing in which individual each is.

examples.text: A haecceitist may say two intrinsically identical particles are nevertheless distinct because each has its own thisness.
examples.note: Their numerical difference is not reduced to a difference in observable qualities.

commonMisreadings: Haecceitism differs from the identity of indiscernibles, which denies such possibility under its strongest reading.

concepts.name: Haecceity
concepts.summary: Haecceity is the nonqualitative property or principle that makes an individual that particular individual.
concepts.body: Haecceity is the nonqualitative property or principle that makes an individual that particular individual. The term derives from the idea of “thisness” and contrasts with properties shared by kinds or classes.

examples.text: Socrates’s haecceity would be what makes him Socrates even if another person matched his qualitative description.
examples.note: It individuates the subject independently of general features such as height or occupation.

commonMisreadings: Haecceity is not simply a person’s distinctive collection of qualitative traits.

concepts.name: Harm principle
concepts.summary: The harm principle holds that coercive interference with a person’s liberty is justified primarily to prevent harm to others.
concepts.body: The harm principle holds that coercive interference with a person’s liberty is justified primarily to prevent harm to others. John Stuart Mill used it to distinguish self-regarding conduct from conduct that threatens others.

examples.text: A law against reckless driving can be justified because the conduct creates an unjustifiable risk to other road users.
examples.note: The restriction targets danger imposed on others rather than mere moral disapproval of the driver’s choice.

commonMisreadings: The principle does not define every form of harm or settle all disputes about paternalism.

concepts.name: Hawthorne effect
concepts.summary: The Hawthorne effect is the change in behavior that occurs because people know they are being observed or studied.
concepts.body: The Hawthorne effect is the change in behavior that occurs because people know they are being observed or studied. The observation itself can become an experimental influence that complicates causal interpretation.

examples.text: Factory workers may increase effort temporarily after learning that researchers are monitoring their productivity.
examples.note: The productivity change could reflect attention from researchers rather than the tested workplace intervention.

commonMisreadings: It is not a universal law that observation always improves performance.

concepts.name: Heap paradox
concepts.summary: The heap paradox is a sorites paradox arising when repeated removal of one grain appears unable to turn a heap into a non-heap.
concepts.body: The heap paradox is a sorites paradox arising when repeated removal of one grain appears unable to turn a heap into a non-heap. It exposes the difficulty of applying vague predicates with borderline cases and apparently harmless small changes.

examples.text: If one million grains form a heap, removing one grain seems to leave a heap, yet repeating that reasoning reaches zero grains.
examples.note: The chain of individually plausible steps conflicts with the clear endpoint.

commonMisreadings: The paradox is about vagueness and reasoning, not about the physical mechanics of grain piles.

concepts.name: Hedonic utilitarianism
concepts.summary: Hedonic utilitarianism evaluates actions by their consequences for aggregate pleasure and pain.
concepts.body: Hedonic utilitarianism evaluates actions by their consequences for aggregate pleasure and pain. It treats the balance of pleasant and unpleasant experience as the fundamental value to maximize.

examples.text: A policy that produces more total enjoyment than suffering is favored even if the benefits are distributed unevenly.
examples.note: The policy is assessed by summed experiential welfare rather than by rights or intentions alone.

commonMisreadings: Hedonic utilitarianism is a form of consequentialism, but not every consequentialist theory measures value in pleasure and pain.

concepts.name: Hedonism
concepts.summary: Hedonism is the view that pleasure is intrinsically valuable or that pleasure and absence of pain fundamentally determine well-being.
concepts.body: Hedonism is the view that pleasure is intrinsically valuable or that pleasure and absence of pain fundamentally determine well-being. Ethical hedonism concerns value, while psychological hedonism claims that people are motivated by pleasure.

examples.text: An ethical hedonist may judge a life better when it contains more intense and sustained enjoyment.
examples.note: The judgment treats pleasurable experience as a basic component of what makes life go well.

commonMisreadings: Hedonism is not necessarily the claim that people should pursue every immediate appetite.

concepts.name: Hegelianism
concepts.summary: Hegelianism is a family of approaches inspired by Hegel’s account of dialectical development, social recognition, and historical rationality.
concepts.body: Hegelianism is a family of approaches inspired by Hegel’s account of dialectical development, social recognition, and historical rationality. It interprets contradictions and their transformations as drivers of conceptual or social change.

examples.text: A Hegelian analysis may explain freedom as developing through institutions that secure mutual recognition.
examples.note: The analysis treats individual autonomy as dependent on historically formed social relations.

commonMisreadings: Hegelianism is not simply admiration for Hegel or the belief that history always improves smoothly.

concepts.name: Hegemony
concepts.summary: Hegemony is dominance maintained partly through consent and the normalization of a ruling group’s worldview.
concepts.body: Hegemony is dominance maintained partly through consent and the normalization of a ruling group’s worldview. Antonio Gramsci used the concept to explain how cultural institutions can stabilize class power.

examples.text: A dominant class may make its economic assumptions seem like common sense through schools, media, and political institutions.
