examples.note: Its legal status rests on recognized social sources rather than its goodness.

commonMisreadings: Legal positivism does not claim that judges should ignore morality in every decision or that law is always just.

concepts.name: Legal realism
concepts.summary: Legal realism is the jurisprudential view that law in practice is shaped by judicial behavior, institutional context, facts, and social consequences, not only written rules.
concepts.body: Legal realism is the jurisprudential view that law in practice is shaped by judicial behavior, institutional context, facts, and social consequences, not only written rules. American legal realists emphasized that formal rules often underdetermine outcomes in difficult cases.

examples.text: A judge's prediction of how an appellate court will treat evidence may matter more to a lawyer than an abstract rule's wording.
examples.note: The prediction focuses on law as administered by institutions and people.

commonMisreadings: Legal realism is not the claim that rules never matter because realists study how rules interact with actual decision-making.

concepts.name: Legitimacy
concepts.summary: Legitimacy is the quality that makes a rule, institution, or exercise of power accepted as rightful or justified by relevant people or standards.
concepts.body: Legitimacy is the quality that makes a rule, institution, or exercise of power accepted as rightful or justified by relevant people or standards. Political legitimacy can arise from consent, lawful procedure, democratic authorization, justice, tradition, or performance, depending on the theory.

examples.text: An elected government gains democratic legitimacy through a free and fair election.
examples.note: The procedure gives citizens a recognized basis for treating the government's authority as rightful.

commonMisreadings: Legitimacy is not identical to coercive effectiveness because a regime can control people without being regarded as rightful.

concepts.name: Leibniz's principle of plenitude
concepts.summary: Leibniz's principle of plenitude is the metaphysical idea that reality contains or expresses every genuine possibility in some form or across the full order of creation.
concepts.body: Leibniz's principle of plenitude is the metaphysical idea that reality contains or expresses every genuine possibility in some form or across the full order of creation. The principle is associated with the thought that a complete universe realizes a vast range of possible forms and perfections.

examples.text: A Leibnizian may regard the diversity of species and worlds as evidence that divine creation realizes many possibilities.
examples.note: The example treats variety as part of a maximal order rather than as accidental scarcity.

commonMisreadings: The principle of plenitude is not the claim that every imagined description is possible or exists exactly as conceived.

concepts.name: Leninism
concepts.summary: Leninism is a revolutionary Marxist theory emphasizing a disciplined vanguard party, imperialism, and the seizure of state power by a proletarian revolution.
concepts.body: Leninism is a revolutionary Marxist theory emphasizing a disciplined vanguard party, imperialism, and the seizure of state power by a proletarian revolution. Lenin argued that a professional revolutionary organization could develop class consciousness and coordinate action against the capitalist state.

examples.text: The Bolshevik Party's organization and leadership during the 1917 Russian Revolution are associated with Leninist practice.
examples.note: The party sought centralized coordination for revolutionary transformation.

commonMisreadings: Leninism is not simply any belief in socialism because its distinctive strategy centers on the vanguard party and revolutionary state power.

concepts.name: Leveling and sharpening
concepts.summary: Leveling and sharpening are memory distortions in which recall omits details and emphasizes or exaggerates other details.
concepts.body: Leveling and sharpening are memory distortions in which recall omits details and emphasizes or exaggerates other details. Leveling reduces distinctive information over time, while sharpening preserves or intensifies selected features.

examples.text: After retelling a story, a witness forgets minor background details but repeatedly emphasizes the suspect's red jacket.
examples.note: The account shows both loss of peripheral information and increased salience of one feature.

commonMisreadings: The terms do not mean improving or worsening a memory in an objective sense; they describe systematic changes in recall.

concepts.name: Levels-of-processing effect
concepts.summary: The levels-of-processing effect is the finding that information processed for meaning is generally remembered better than information processed only for superficial features.
concepts.body: The levels-of-processing effect is the finding that information processed for meaning is generally remembered better than information processed only for superficial features. Craik and Lockhart's framework distinguishes shallow structural or phonemic processing from deeper semantic processing.

examples.text: A learner remembers the word “apple” better after deciding whether it names a fruit than after counting its letters.
examples.note: The semantic judgment creates deeper encoding than the orthographic task.

commonMisreadings: The effect does not mean that every semantic task guarantees memory or that depth is independent of task and context.

concepts.name: Liar paradox
concepts.summary: The liar paradox arises when a sentence appears to assert its own falsity, producing a conflict if it is treated as either true or false.
concepts.body: The liar paradox arises when a sentence appears to assert its own falsity, producing a conflict if it is treated as either true or false. The sentence “This sentence is false” is true only if it is false and false only if it is true under ordinary assumptions.

examples.text: If the sentence is true, what it says makes it false; if it is false, what it says makes it true.
examples.note: Each assigned truth value reverses itself through the sentence's self-reference.

commonMisreadings: The liar paradox is not simply an ordinary lie because its semantic self-reference creates the contradiction.

concepts.name: Liberal conservatism
concepts.summary: Liberal conservatism combines support for individual liberty and constitutional government with preference for gradual change, social continuity, and restrained state power.
concepts.body: Liberal conservatism combines support for individual liberty and constitutional government with preference for gradual change, social continuity, and restrained state power. It accepts reform when necessary but treats inherited institutions and social order as goods that require protection.

examples.text: A liberal conservative may support free speech and market competition while opposing abrupt revolutionary restructuring.
examples.note: The position joins liberal rights with conservative caution about rapid institutional change.

commonMisreadings: Liberal conservatism is not identical to either unrestricted laissez-faire or traditionalist rejection of liberal rights.

concepts.name: Liberal democracy
concepts.summary: Liberal democracy is a political system combining popular elections with constitutional limits, individual rights, pluralism, and rule of law.
concepts.body: Liberal democracy is a political system combining popular elections with constitutional limits, individual rights, pluralism, and rule of law. Majority rule is constrained so that elected authorities cannot normally abolish basic rights or eliminate lawful opposition.

examples.text: A parliament elected by universal suffrage remains subject to an independent court enforcing freedom of expression.
examples.note: Elections and rights-protecting institutions jointly define the system.

commonMisreadings: Liberal democracy is not mere majority voting because liberal constitutional constraints are essential.

concepts.name: Liberal feminism
concepts.summary: Liberal feminism seeks women's equality through individual rights, equal opportunity, legal reform, education, and access to institutions.
concepts.body: Liberal feminism seeks women's equality through individual rights, equal opportunity, legal reform, education, and access to institutions. It generally emphasizes removing discriminatory barriers rather than abolishing all hierarchical social or economic structures.

examples.text: A liberal feminist campaign supports equal pay laws and nondiscriminatory hiring procedures.
examples.note: The reforms aim to secure equal civic and economic opportunities under law.

commonMisreadings: Liberal feminism differs from radical feminism by not necessarily treating patriarchy as a total system requiring comprehensive social transformation.

concepts.name: Liberal nationalism
concepts.summary: Liberal nationalism holds that national belonging can support democratic self-government while remaining constrained by individual rights and civic equality.
concepts.body: Liberal nationalism holds that national belonging can support democratic self-government while remaining constrained by individual rights and civic equality. It typically defines the nation through shared political membership or public culture rather than ethnic hierarchy alone.

examples.text: A liberal nationalist supports a common language for public institutions while protecting minority citizenship and religious freedom.
examples.note: Shared civic practices coexist with equal rights for members of diverse backgrounds.

commonMisreadings: Liberal nationalism is not ethnic nationalism because national membership need not depend on ancestry.

concepts.name: Liberal socialism
concepts.summary: Liberal socialism combines liberal rights and democratic institutions with socialist aims such as social ownership, economic equality, or worker control.
concepts.body: Liberal socialism combines liberal rights and democratic institutions with socialist aims such as social ownership, economic equality, or worker control. It rejects both authoritarian socialism and the idea that formal liberties are sufficient under severe economic dependence.

examples.text: A liberal socialist may support constitutional free speech alongside worker cooperatives and universal public services.
examples.note: Political liberties and egalitarian economic institutions are treated as mutually supporting.

commonMisreadings: Liberal socialism is not social liberalism because it generally seeks more extensive changes in ownership or control of production.

concepts.name: Liberalism
concepts.summary: Liberalism is a political tradition centered on individual liberty, equal civic status, limited government, and institutions that protect rights.
concepts.body: Liberalism is a political tradition centered on individual liberty, equal civic status, limited government, and institutions that protect rights. Different liberalisms disagree about property, markets, welfare, democracy, and the extent of state action needed to secure freedom.

examples.text: A constitutional liberal state protects speech and religious exercise while applying laws through independent courts.
examples.note: The institutions limit arbitrary power and recognize citizens as rights-bearing individuals.

commonMisreadings: Liberalism is not simply permissive individualism because many liberals support public institutions that make freedom effective.

concepts.name: Libertarian communism
concepts.summary: Libertarian communism advocates a classless, stateless society based on common ownership, voluntary association, and decentralized self-management.
concepts.body: Libertarian communism advocates a classless, stateless society based on common ownership, voluntary association, and decentralized self-management. It combines communist opposition to private domination of production with libertarian opposition to coercive centralized government.

examples.text: An anarcho-communist federation distributes goods through worker and neighborhood assemblies without a permanent state bureaucracy.
examples.note: Common resources and self-governing associations replace both capitalist ownership and hierarchical state command.

commonMisreadings: Libertarian communism is not state socialism because it rejects centralized state ownership as the route to liberation.

concepts.name: Libertarian free will
concepts.summary: Libertarian free will is the view that genuine free choice requires indeterminism and that agents can originate alternative actions.
concepts.body: Libertarian free will is the view that genuine free choice requires indeterminism and that agents can originate alternative actions. It contrasts with determinism and with compatibilism, which defines freedom without requiring metaphysical alternatives of this kind.

examples.text: A person deciding whether to donate may, with the same prior conditions, genuinely choose either donation or refusal.
examples.note: The agent's choice is treated as an undetermined source of action rather than a predetermined outcome.

commonMisreadings: Libertarian free will does not mean arbitrary behavior because reasons and character can still guide the choice.

concepts.name: Libertarian municipalism
concepts.summary: Libertarian municipalism is a political program of democratic local assemblies linked in confederations to replace hierarchical state administration.
concepts.body: Libertarian municipalism is a political program of democratic local assemblies linked in confederations to replace hierarchical state administration. Associated with Murray Bookchin, it treats municipalities as sites for ecological and participatory self-government.

examples.text: Residents of several towns deliberate in neighborhood assemblies and send recallable delegates to a regional confederation.
examples.note: Decision-making remains local while coordination occurs through accountable delegation.

commonMisreadings: Libertarian municipalism is not ordinary municipal administration because it aims to transform political authority and economic relations.

concepts.name: Libertarian socialism
concepts.summary: Libertarian socialism seeks social ownership and worker self-management without a coercive centralized state or capitalist class hierarchy.
concepts.body: Libertarian socialism seeks social ownership and worker self-management without a coercive centralized state or capitalist class hierarchy. It includes anarchist and councilist traditions that emphasize voluntary association, decentralized federation, and direct democracy.

examples.text: Workers in a federation of cooperatives govern their workplaces and coordinate production through elected councils.
examples.note: The producers exercise control over economic decisions without private owners or state managers.

commonMisreadings: Libertarian socialism is not identical to laissez-faire libertarianism because it rejects capitalist ownership of productive assets.

concepts.name: Libertarianism in politics
concepts.summary: Libertarianism in politics gives primary importance to individual liberty, voluntary exchange, property rights, and limiting coercive government power.
concepts.body: Libertarianism in politics gives primary importance to individual liberty, voluntary exchange, property rights, and limiting coercive government power. Its versions range from minimal-state views to anarchism and differ over taxation, public goods, and the status of property.

examples.text: A minarchist supports courts, police, and national defense but opposes most other compulsory government programs.
examples.note: The state is limited to functions thought necessary for protecting rights and contracts.

commonMisreadings: Political libertarianism is not simply a preference for personal freedom because it includes institutional claims about coercion and authority.

concepts.name: Liberty
concepts.summary: Liberty is the condition of being free from undue coercion or able to direct one's conduct and participate in collective self-rule.
concepts.body: Liberty is the condition of being free from undue coercion or able to direct one's conduct and participate in collective self-rule. Negative liberty emphasizes absence of interference, while positive liberty emphasizes effective capacity or self-government.

examples.text: Freedom of speech protects a person's ability to criticize the government without legal punishment.
examples.note: The protection removes a form of state interference in expression.

commonMisreadings: Liberty is not identical to doing whatever one wants because rights and other people's liberty can limit action.

concepts.name: Lindy effect
concepts.summary: The Lindy effect is the heuristic that the expected remaining lifespan of a non-perishable thing increases with the length of time it has already survived.
concepts.body: The Lindy effect is the heuristic that the expected remaining lifespan of a non-perishable thing increases with the length of time it has already survived. It is applied to technologies, institutions, and ideas whose future survival is not consumed by use in the way perishable goods are.

examples.text: A programming language used successfully for fifty years may be expected to remain relevant longer than a newly released language.
examples.note: Past survival is treated as evidence of robustness or continued adoption.

commonMisreadings: The Lindy effect is a probabilistic heuristic, not a law that guarantees old things will outlast new ones.

concepts.name: Linguistic relativity
concepts.summary: Linguistic relativity is the view that the structures and categories of a language can influence how its speakers perceive, remember, or conceptualize experience.
concepts.body: Linguistic relativity is the view that the structures and categories of a language can influence how its speakers perceive, remember, or conceptualize experience. The moderate view allows cognitive effects without claiming that language makes alternative thoughts impossible.

examples.text: Speakers of languages that grammatically mark evidential sources may attend more consistently to how they know a reported fact.
examples.note: The grammatical distinction can guide habitual attention to evidence.

commonMisreadings: Linguistic relativity is not linguistic determinism because influence does not entail that language fixes all thought.

concepts.name: List-length effect
concepts.summary: The list-length effect is the tendency for the proportion of correctly recalled items to decrease as the number of studied items increases.
concepts.body: The list-length effect is the tendency for the proportion of correctly recalled items to decrease as the number of studied items increases. It is often discussed with serial position effects, which make early and late list items easier to recall than middle items.

examples.text: People usually recall a larger percentage of a ten-word list than of a forty-word list under the same testing conditions.
examples.note: The longer list creates greater competition and memory load.

commonMisreadings: The list-length effect concerns recall proportion or performance as list size changes, not merely the fact that a longer list contains more items.

concepts.name: Literal meaning
concepts.summary: Literal meaning is the conventional semantic content of an expression apart from figurative, pragmatic, or ironic implications.
concepts.body: Literal meaning is the conventional semantic content of an expression apart from figurative, pragmatic, or ironic implications. Literal meaning is shaped by vocabulary and grammar but can remain incomplete without contextual disambiguation.

examples.text: The literal meaning of “The cat is on the mat” states that a cat is located on a mat.
examples.note: The sentence directly describes a spatial relation rather than implying a metaphorical condition.

commonMisreadings: Literal meaning is not always the total communicated meaning because context can add implicatures.

concepts.name: Logical atomism
concepts.summary: Logical atomism is the philosophical view that reality consists of atomic facts and that meaningful propositions can be analyzed into logically independent elementary components.
concepts.body: Logical atomism is the philosophical view that reality consists of atomic facts and that meaningful propositions can be analyzed into logically independent elementary components. Bertrand Russell and the early Ludwig Wittgenstein associated language analysis with uncovering the logical structure of facts.

examples.text: The statement “Socrates is mortal” may be treated as representing a simple fact involving an object and a property.
examples.note: The proposition is analyzed as a basic correspondence rather than as an unanalyzed whole.

commonMisreadings: Logical atomism is not the claim that physical matter consists of indivisible atoms because its atoms are logical or factual units.

concepts.name: Logical consequence
concepts.summary: Logical consequence is the relation in which a conclusion must be true whenever the premises are true under the relevant semantics.
concepts.body: Logical consequence is the relation in which a conclusion must be true whenever the premises are true under the relevant semantics. The relation depends on form and interpretation, not on whether the premises are actually true in the world.

examples.text: From “All mammals are animals” and “All dogs are mammals,” it follows logically that all dogs are animals.
examples.note: Every model satisfying the premises also satisfies the conclusion.

commonMisreadings: Logical consequence differs from causal consequence because validity concerns truth preservation rather than production of events.

concepts.name: Logical empiricism
concepts.summary: Logical empiricism is a twentieth-century movement combining formal logical analysis with the view that meaningful knowledge is grounded in experience and scientific method.
concepts.body: Logical empiricism is a twentieth-century movement combining formal logical analysis with the view that meaningful knowledge is grounded in experience and scientific method. It developed from logical positivism while allowing more nuanced accounts of theory, confirmation, and the limits of verification.

examples.text: A logical empiricist analyzes a scientific claim's logical form and asks how observation could support it.
examples.note: Formal clarification and empirical testing operate together in evaluating the claim.

commonMisreadings: Logical empiricism is not a rejection of all theoretical entities because many members accepted theories that organize observable evidence.

concepts.name: Logical equivalence
concepts.summary: Logical equivalence is the relation between propositions that have the same truth value under every possible interpretation.
concepts.body: Logical equivalence is the relation between propositions that have the same truth value under every possible interpretation. Equivalent formulas can replace one another in valid arguments without changing the resulting truth conditions.

examples.text: P and not-not-P are classically logically equivalent.
examples.note: Both formulas are true in exactly the same classical valuations.

commonMisreadings: Logical equivalence is stronger than having the same truth value in one actual situation.

concepts.name: Logical form
concepts.summary: Logical form is the abstract structural pattern that determines how the parts of an expression combine for inferential or semantic purposes.
concepts.body: Logical form is the abstract structural pattern that determines how the parts of an expression combine for inferential or semantic purposes. Different sentences can share a logical form even when their subject matter and words differ.

examples.text: “All birds are animals” and “All roses are plants” share a universal conditional structure.
examples.note: Their common form explains why the same deductive pattern applies to both.

commonMisreadings: Logical form is not identical to surface word order because grammatical appearance can conceal relevant structure.

concepts.name: Logical necessity
concepts.summary: Logical necessity is the status of a proposition that cannot be false under the relevant logical rules or interpretations.
concepts.body: Logical necessity is the status of a proposition that cannot be false under the relevant logical rules or interpretations. A logically necessary truth follows from form alone rather than from contingent facts about the world.

examples.text: The proposition “Either it is raining or it is not raining” is classically logically necessary.
examples.note: No classical truth assignment makes both disjunctive alternatives false.

commonMisreadings: Logical necessity differs from physical necessity because a physically impossible event can still be logically describable.

concepts.name: Logical positivism
concepts.summary: Logical positivism is the view that meaningful factual claims are tied to possible empirical verification or confirmation and that formal logic clarifies language.
concepts.body: Logical positivism is the view that meaningful factual claims are tied to possible empirical verification or confirmation and that formal logic clarifies language. The Vienna Circle used the verification principle to criticize metaphysical statements as lacking empirical meaning.

examples.text: A logical positivist treats “Water boils at standard pressure near 100 degrees Celsius” as meaningful because observations can test it.
examples.note: The statement has an identifiable observational connection.

commonMisreadings: Logical positivism is not the claim that every meaningful sentence is itself an observation report because logical and mathematical statements are treated separately.

concepts.name: Logical possibility
concepts.summary: Logical possibility is the status of a proposition or scenario that contains no contradiction under a specified logical framework.
concepts.body: Logical possibility is the status of a proposition or scenario that contains no contradiction under a specified logical framework. A logically possible situation may be physically impossible if it conflicts with the laws of nature.

examples.text: A world in which gravity is weaker than on Earth is logically possible even if it is not physically accessible from Earth.
examples.note: The description is coherent without being compatible with actual physical laws or history.

commonMisreadings: Logical possibility is not the same as conceivability in every theory because some apparently conceivable descriptions may hide contradictions.

concepts.name: Logicism
concepts.summary: Logicism is the philosophical program that mathematics can be reduced to logic and definitions of mathematical objects.
concepts.body: Logicism is the philosophical program that mathematics can be reduced to logic and definitions of mathematical objects. Frege, Russell, and Whitehead pursued versions of logicism, though paradoxes and technical limitations complicated the program.

examples.text: Principia Mathematica attempts to derive arithmetic within a formal logical system.
examples.note: The derivation seeks to show that numerical truths follow from logical principles and definitions.

commonMisreadings: Logicism is not merely the use of logic in mathematics because it claims a foundational reduction of mathematics to logic.

concepts.name: Longtermism
concepts.summary: Longtermism is the ethical view that improving the long-run future of humanity has very great moral importance.
concepts.body: Longtermism is the ethical view that improving the long-run future of humanity has very great moral importance. It often emphasizes the enormous number of possible future people and the risk of permanently damaging civilization's potential.

examples.text: A longtermist may support reducing the probability of a civilization-ending catastrophe even when near-term benefits are modest.
examples.note: The policy is justified by protecting many future generations and their opportunities.

commonMisreadings: Longtermism is not identical to ordinary long-term planning because it is a claim about moral priority, not only prudential foresight.

concepts.name: Luxemburgism
concepts.summary: Luxemburgism is the revolutionary socialist tradition associated with Rosa Luxemburg's emphasis on mass strikes, working-class democracy, and opposition to authoritarian party rule.
concepts.body: Luxemburgism is the revolutionary socialist tradition associated with Rosa Luxemburg's emphasis on mass strikes, working-class democracy, and opposition to authoritarian party rule. It criticizes both reformist gradualism and excessive centralization that suppresses spontaneous workers' activity.

examples.text: Luxemburg's criticism of the Bolsheviks warned that restricting political freedom could weaken socialist democracy.
examples.note: The critique treats autonomous mass participation as essential to revolutionary liberation.

commonMisreadings: Luxemburgism is not simply support for Rosa Luxemburg personally because it names a broader strategic and democratic tradition.

concepts.name: Machism
concepts.summary: Machism is the philosophical position associated with Ernst Mach that treats scientific concepts as economical descriptions of experience and is skeptical of metaphysical claims beyond possible observation.
concepts.body: Machism is the philosophical position associated with Ernst Mach that treats scientific concepts as economical descriptions of experience and is skeptical of metaphysical claims beyond possible observation. Mach emphasized relations among sensations and criticized absolute space, absolute time, and unobservable metaphysical entities.

examples.text: Mach analyzes mechanics as a system for summarizing observable relations among bodies rather than as a final picture of reality in itself.
examples.note: The theory's value is tied to its economy and empirical coordination.

commonMisreadings: Machism is not identical to all forms of empiricism because its distinctive emphasis is on economy of description and anti-metaphysical critique.

concepts.name: Madhyamaka
concepts.summary: Madhyamaka is a Mahayana Buddhist philosophical tradition that argues phenomena are empty of inherent existence and arise dependently.
concepts.body: Madhyamaka is a Mahayana Buddhist philosophical tradition that argues phenomena are empty of inherent existence and arise dependently. Nagarjuna's analysis avoids both essentialism and nihilism by using dependent origination to reject independent essence.

examples.text: A chariot exists conventionally through the arrangement and designation of parts but lacks a self-existing chariot essence.
examples.note: The example distinguishes conventional existence from intrinsic existence.

commonMisreadings: Madhyamaka's emptiness is not the claim that nothing exists because it preserves conventional truth and causal practice.

concepts.name: Mahayana Buddhism
concepts.summary: Mahayana Buddhism is a broad Buddhist movement emphasizing the bodhisattva ideal, universal liberation, and expanded scriptural traditions.
concepts.body: Mahayana Buddhism is a broad Buddhist movement emphasizing the bodhisattva ideal, universal liberation, and expanded scriptural traditions. It develops doctrines such as buddha-nature, emptiness, and skillful means in diverse schools.

examples.text: A bodhisattva postpones final nirvana to assist other beings toward liberation.
examples.note: The vow expresses Mahayana's ideal of compassionate awakening for all sentient beings.

commonMisreadings: Mahayana is not a single uniform denomination because Zen, Pure Land, and other schools differ in doctrine and practice.

concepts.name: Many-valued logic
concepts.summary: Many-valued logic is a logical system with more than two truth values or semantic statuses.
concepts.body: Many-valued logic is a logical system with more than two truth values or semantic statuses. It can represent indeterminacy, partial truth, vagueness, or other conditions that binary true-false logic does not distinguish.

examples.text: In a three-valued logic, a statement about an undecided future event may receive true, false, or indeterminate.
examples.note: The third value records the unresolved status without forcing a classical binary assignment.

commonMisreadings: Many-valued logic is not automatically fuzzy logic because its additional values need not represent graded degrees of truth.

concepts.name: Maoism
concepts.summary: Maoism is a revolutionary communist theory associated with Mao Zedong that emphasizes peasant mobilization, protracted people's war, and continuing class struggle.
concepts.body: Maoism is a revolutionary communist theory associated with Mao Zedong that emphasizes peasant mobilization, protracted people's war, and continuing class struggle. It adapts Marxism-Leninism to predominantly rural societies and treats political mass participation as a source of revolutionary power.

examples.text: The Chinese Communist Party's rural base-building and guerrilla war before 1949 exemplify Maoist strategy.
examples.note: Peasant organization and prolonged territorial struggle substitute for an initially urban industrial uprising.

commonMisreadings: Maoism is not simply Chinese nationalism because its theory claims a general revolutionary method grounded in class struggle.

concepts.name: Marginal utility
concepts.summary: Marginal utility is the additional satisfaction or value a person receives from consuming one more unit of a good or service.
concepts.body: Marginal utility is the additional satisfaction or value a person receives from consuming one more unit of a good or service. The marginal utility of a good often decreases as a person consumes more units, producing diminishing marginal utility.

examples.text: The first glass of water for a thirsty person provides more marginal utility than the fourth glass.
examples.note: The additional benefit falls as the person's urgent need is relieved.

commonMisreadings: Marginal utility is not the total utility of all units consumed.

concepts.name: Market anarchism
concepts.summary: Market anarchism is the view that voluntary markets can coordinate production and exchange without a coercive state.
concepts.body: Market anarchism is the view that voluntary markets can coordinate production and exchange without a coercive state. Market anarchists differ over property, contract, competition, and whether capitalist firms or cooperative arrangements would predominate.

examples.text: An anarchist community might use voluntary cooperatives and mutually agreed exchanges while relying on private arbitration rather than state courts.
examples.note: Market coordination and dispute resolution occur through non-state association.

commonMisreadings: Market anarchism is not identical to ordinary capitalism because it rejects state authority and may reject capitalist wage relations.

concepts.name: Market liberalism
concepts.summary: Market liberalism is a political-economic view favoring competitive markets, private property, voluntary exchange, and limited government intervention.
concepts.body: Market liberalism is a political-economic view favoring competitive markets, private property, voluntary exchange, and limited government intervention. It generally accepts a legal framework and public institutions needed to protect contracts, competition, and property rights.

examples.text: A market-liberal government removes price controls while maintaining courts that enforce contracts.
examples.note: The policy relies on decentralized exchange within a supporting legal order.

commonMisreadings: Market liberalism is not pure laissez-faire because even limited markets require rules and institutions.

concepts.name: Market socialism
concepts.summary: Market socialism combines social or worker ownership of productive assets with markets for allocating goods, services, or investment.
concepts.body: Market socialism combines social or worker ownership of productive assets with markets for allocating goods, services, or investment. It seeks to preserve price signals while preventing private capital owners from controlling production and appropriating all profits.

examples.text: Worker cooperatives compete to sell products while their members collectively own each firm.
examples.note: Markets coordinate exchange, but ownership and governance remain socialized.

commonMisreadings: Market socialism is not state socialism because market allocation remains central and ownership need not be centralized in the state.

concepts.name: Marxism
concepts.summary: Marxism is a tradition of social theory and political economy analyzing history through material production, class relations, and conflict.
concepts.body: Marxism is a tradition of social theory and political economy analyzing history through material production, class relations, and conflict. It criticizes capitalism for separating workers from control of production and for organizing labor around capital accumulation.

examples.text: A Marxist analyzes a factory by examining ownership, wage labor, surplus value, and class power.
examples.note: The analysis explains economic activity through relations between capital and workers rather than only individual transactions.

commonMisreadings: Marxism is not a single political program because Marxist traditions disagree about reform, revolution, state power, and culture.

concepts.name: Marxism–Leninism
concepts.summary: Marxism–Leninism is a twentieth-century communist doctrine combining Marxist class analysis with Leninist party organization and revolutionary state power.
concepts.body: Marxism–Leninism is a twentieth-century communist doctrine combining Marxist class analysis with Leninist party organization and revolutionary state power. It commonly presents a vanguard party and a transitional socialist state as necessary for building communism.

examples.text: The Soviet Communist Party's one-party state was officially justified through Marxism–Leninism.
examples.note: Party leadership was treated as the institutional vehicle for proletarian rule and socialist construction.

commonMisreadings: Marxism–Leninism is not identical to Marx's own writings because it is a later codified doctrine shaped by Leninist and state-socialist practice.

concepts.name: Mary's room
concepts.summary: Mary's room is Frank Jackson's thought experiment in which a scientist with complete physical knowledge of color learns something apparently new on seeing red.
concepts.body: Mary's room is Frank Jackson's thought experiment in which a scientist with complete physical knowledge of color learns something apparently new on seeing red. The case is used to argue that physical descriptions may omit phenomenal facts about what experiences are like.

examples.text: Mary knows every physical fact about color vision while living in a black-and-white environment, then experiences a red tomato.
examples.note: Her apparent new knowledge is intended to challenge the completeness of physicalism.

commonMisreadings: Mary's room is not an empirical claim that real scientists can know every physical fact; it is an argument about knowledge and consciousness.

concepts.name: Material implication
concepts.summary: Material implication is the classical truth-functional connective represented by P implies Q, which is false only when P is true and Q is false.
concepts.body: Material implication is the classical truth-functional connective represented by P implies Q, which is false only when P is true and Q is false. It is equivalent in classical logic to not-P or Q, regardless of any causal or explanatory connection between the propositions.

examples.text: “If it rains, the ground is wet” is materially true whenever it does not rain or the ground is wet.
examples.note: The truth table makes the conditional true in those three cases even without a causal relation.

commonMisreadings: Material implication is not the same as an ordinary-language conditional because natural language often carries relevance or causation.

concepts.name: Materialism
concepts.summary: Materialism is the metaphysical view that reality is fundamentally material or physical and that mental and other phenomena depend on physical processes.
concepts.body: Materialism is the metaphysical view that reality is fundamentally material or physical and that mental and other phenomena depend on physical processes. Contemporary physicalism includes positions that use properties or laws not described by ordinary matter while still denying a separate nonphysical substance.

examples.text: A materialist explains pain as dependent on neural activity rather than as an immaterial substance.
examples.note: The account makes physical processes fundamental to the existence of the mental state.

commonMisreadings: Materialism is not necessarily the claim that current physics is complete because a materialist can accept future revisions of physical theory.

concepts.name: Maximin
concepts.summary: Maximin is a decision rule that chooses the option with the best worst-case outcome.
concepts.body: Maximin is a decision rule that chooses the option with the best worst-case outcome. It evaluates each available action by its minimum possible payoff and then maximizes that minimum.

examples.text: A cautious investor chooses the bond whose worst plausible return exceeds the worst plausible return of every stock option.
examples.note: The choice protects the best guaranteed floor among the alternatives.

commonMisreadings: Maximin differs from minimax because it maximizes a decision maker's minimum payoff rather than minimizing an opponent's maximum loss.

concepts.name: Meaning
concepts.summary: Meaning is the content, significance, or reference conveyed by a sign, expression, practice, or event.
concepts.body: Meaning is the content, significance, or reference conveyed by a sign, expression, practice, or event. Meaning can depend on linguistic conventions, context, speaker intention, and the role of an expression in a wider system.

examples.text: The word “bank” means a financial institution in “deposit money at the bank” but a river margin in “sit on the bank.”
examples.note: Context selects which content the ambiguous word conveys.

commonMisreadings: Meaning is not always identical to a speaker's private intention because public conventions can constrain interpretation.

concepts.name: Mechanism
concepts.summary: A mechanism is an organized process in which interacting parts produce a phenomenon.
concepts.body: A mechanism is an organized process in which interacting parts produce a phenomenon. Mechanistic explanations identify entities, activities, organization, and the way their interaction generates an outcome.

examples.text: A bicycle brake mechanism converts hand-lever movement into friction at the wheel rim.
examples.note: The linked movements of the lever, cable, caliper, and pads explain how braking occurs.

commonMisreadings: A mechanism is more specific than a mere correlation because it describes the productive process.

concepts.name: Mental causation
concepts.summary: Mental causation is the relation by which mental states, events, or properties bring about or influence physical events.
concepts.body: Mental causation is the relation by which mental states, events, or properties bring about or influence physical events. It raises questions about how beliefs and intentions can cause bodily movements if physical events already have physical causes.

examples.text: A driver's intention to turn left causes the hand movement that rotates the steering wheel.
examples.note: The intention helps explain the action while neural and muscular processes implement it.

commonMisreadings: Mental causation is not simply causation by a brain state unless the mental description has explanatory relevance.

concepts.name: Mental representation
concepts.summary: A mental representation is an internal state or structure that stands for, models, or carries information about something.
concepts.body: A mental representation is an internal state or structure that stands for, models, or carries information about something. Mental representations are often invoked to explain perception, memory, imagery, language, and action planning.

examples.text: A remembered map of a neighborhood represents streets and landmarks without being a physical map of the neighborhood.
examples.note: The memory guides navigation by preserving information about spatial relations.

commonMisreadings: A mental representation need not resemble its object because symbolic representations can represent by convention.

concepts.name: Mere-exposure effect
concepts.summary: The mere-exposure effect is the tendency for repeated exposure to a stimulus to increase liking or familiarity with it.
concepts.body: The mere-exposure effect is the tendency for repeated exposure to a stimulus to increase liking or familiarity with it. The effect can occur without conscious recognition, although excessive repetition can produce boredom or saturation.

examples.text: People may rate an unfamiliar-looking nonsense word more favorably after seeing it several times.
examples.note: Repeated exposure increases processing fluency, making the item feel easier and safer to process.

commonMisreadings: The effect is not proof that repeated exposure always improves preference under every condition.

concepts.name: Mereological nihilism
concepts.summary: Mereological nihilism is the view that composite objects do not exist and that reality contains only simples, if it contains simples at all.
concepts.body: Mereological nihilism is the view that composite objects do not exist and that reality contains only simples, if it contains simples at all. On this view, an apparent table is not an additional object beyond the particles arranged tablewise.

examples.text: A nihilist may say that there are particles arranged as a chair rather than that a chair exists as a composite.
examples.note: The description preserves the arrangement while denying a further chair entity.

commonMisreadings: Mereological nihilism is not the claim that ordinary talk about chairs is meaningless.

concepts.name: Mereological universalism
concepts.summary: Mereological universalism is the view that any collection of objects composes a further object.
concepts.body: Mereological universalism is the view that any collection of objects composes a further object. It allows composition without requiring spatial contact, causal interaction, or functional unity between the parts.

examples.text: Under universalism, the Eiffel Tower and a distant coin can together compose a scattered object.
examples.note: The theory accepts that object because the parts are objects, despite their lack of ordinary unity.

commonMisreadings: Universalism differs from restricted composition theories that allow wholes only under special conditions.

concepts.name: Mereology
concepts.summary: Mereology is the philosophical study of part–whole relations and the principles governing composition.
concepts.body: Mereology is the philosophical study of part–whole relations and the principles governing composition. It examines relations such as proper part, overlap, sum, fusion, and the conditions under which objects compose wholes.

examples.text: A mereologist can ask whether two planks and their arrangement constitute one boat.
examples.note: The question concerns composition and identity rather than the boat's material history alone.

commonMisreadings: Mereology is not simply the study of physical objects because it also treats abstract and scattered compositions.

concepts.name: Meritocracy
concepts.summary: Meritocracy is a social ideal in which positions or rewards are allocated according to relevant ability, achievement, or performance.
concepts.body: Meritocracy is a social ideal in which positions or rewards are allocated according to relevant ability, achievement, or performance. Meritocratic systems require judgments about what counts as merit and can reproduce inequality when opportunities are unequal.

examples.text: A civil-service examination that ranks applicants by demonstrated administrative competence is a meritocratic procedure.
examples.note: The procedure assigns selection weight to measured performance rather than family status.

commonMisreadings: Meritocracy is not identical to equality of outcome because it permits differing rewards for differing assessed merit.

concepts.name: Metaethics
concepts.summary: Metaethics is the branch of ethics that studies the meaning, truth, justification, and metaphysical status of moral judgments.
concepts.body: Metaethics is the branch of ethics that studies the meaning, truth, justification, and metaphysical status of moral judgments. It asks whether moral claims describe facts, express attitudes, prescribe actions, or arise from practical construction.

examples.text: The question “Are torturing innocents wrong?” is normative, while “What makes ‘wrong’ true?” is metaethical.
examples.note: The second question investigates moral discourse rather than directly issuing a moral verdict.

commonMisreadings: Metaethics differs from normative ethics, which develops principles about what ought to be done.

concepts.name: Metalanguage
concepts.summary: A metalanguage is a language used to describe, analyze, or reason about another language called the object language.
concepts.body: A metalanguage is a language used to describe, analyze, or reason about another language called the object language. Metalanguages can state rules, define expressions, and formulate truth predicates for the language they discuss.

examples.text: English functions as a metalanguage when it says that the sentence “Snow is white” is true.
examples.note: The English sentence talks about a sentence rather than asserting snow's color directly.

commonMisreadings: A metalanguage is not necessarily a separate spoken language because a language can discuss itself in a controlled hierarchy.

concepts.name: Metaphor
concepts.summary: A metaphor is an expression that presents one thing in terms of another to invite a nonliteral comparison or transfer of understanding.
concepts.body: A metaphor is an expression that presents one thing in terms of another to invite a nonliteral comparison or transfer of understanding. Metaphors can highlight selected similarities while suppressing others and need not assert literal identity.

examples.text: Calling a difficult negotiation “a chess game” emphasizes strategic moves and countermoves.
examples.note: The phrase transfers features of chess to negotiation without claiming that negotiators are literally chess pieces.

commonMisreadings: A metaphor differs from a simile because it normally makes the comparison without using “like” or “as.”

concepts.name: Metaphysical necessity
concepts.summary: Metaphysical necessity is necessity that holds in every metaphysically possible world.
concepts.body: Metaphysical necessity is necessity that holds in every metaphysically possible world. A proposition can be metaphysically necessary even if it is not knowable a priori or guaranteed by linguistic convention.

examples.text: If water is necessarily H2O, then no metaphysically possible world contains water with a different chemical composition.
examples.note: The claim treats the chemical identity as fixed across possible ways reality could have been.

commonMisreadings: Metaphysical necessity differs from logical necessity because some necessary truths may depend on the nature of things rather than form alone.

concepts.name: Metaphysical nihilism
concepts.summary: Metaphysical nihilism is the view that there are no concrete objects or entities of the relevant kind, often including the claim that nothing exists.
concepts.body: Metaphysical nihilism is the view that there are no concrete objects or entities of the relevant kind, often including the claim that nothing exists. Different versions deny all entities, all concrete entities, or the existence of ordinary objects while allowing abstract items.

examples.text: A radical metaphysical nihilist asserts that no tables, planets, people, or other concrete things exist.
examples.note: The position rejects the existence of the ordinary world rather than merely denying a particular category.

commonMisreadings: Metaphysical nihilism is stronger than mereological nihilism, which can accept simples while denying composites.

concepts.name: Metaphysical possibility
concepts.summary: Metaphysical possibility concerns what could exist or occur according to the fundamental nature of reality.
concepts.body: Metaphysical possibility concerns what could exist or occur according to the fundamental nature of reality. A metaphysically possible scenario need not be physically realizable under the actual laws of nature.

examples.text: A world containing a different distribution of matter may be metaphysically possible even if our universe cannot evolve into it.
examples.note: The scenario is allowed as a way reality could have been, independently of actual historical laws.

commonMisreadings: Metaphysical possibility is not the same as conceivability because some apparently conceivable descriptions may be incoherent.

concepts.name: Metaphysical realism
concepts.summary: Metaphysical realism is the view that reality exists independently of our thoughts, language, or conceptual schemes.
concepts.body: Metaphysical realism is the view that reality exists independently of our thoughts, language, or conceptual schemes. It generally holds that truth is constrained by a mind-independent world rather than created wholly by our representational practices.

examples.text: A realist about mountains holds that a mountain existed before anyone named or perceived it.
examples.note: The mountain's existence does not depend on a human observer's conceptual activity.

commonMisreadings: Metaphysical realism does not require that humans have perfect or direct access to reality.

concepts.name: Metaphysics
concepts.summary: Metaphysics is the branch of philosophy that investigates the most general features and structure of reality.
concepts.body: Metaphysics is the branch of philosophy that investigates the most general features and structure of reality. Its topics include existence, identity, possibility, causation, time, substance, properties, and dependence.

examples.text: The question whether persons remain the same through radical bodily change is a metaphysical question about identity.
examples.note: It concerns what makes an entity persist rather than how a particular person happens to remember their past.

commonMisreadings: Metaphysics is not merely speculation because arguments can analyze definitions, commitments, and explanatory consequences.

concepts.name: Methodological holism
concepts.summary: Methodological holism explains phenomena by treating systems, structures, or groups as relevant units of analysis.
concepts.body: Methodological holism explains phenomena by treating systems, structures, or groups as relevant units of analysis. It does not necessarily deny that components matter, but it claims that system-level relations can be indispensable to explanation.

examples.text: An economist may explain a recession through credit institutions and aggregate demand rather than only individual spending choices.
examples.note: The institutional structure supplies explanatory variables not captured by isolated biographies.

commonMisreadings: Methodological holism differs from ontological holism because it is a strategy of inquiry rather than a claim that wholes are the only things that exist.

concepts.name: Methodological individualism
concepts.summary: Methodological individualism explains social phenomena through individuals, their actions, and their interactions rather than treating groups as irreducible agents.
concepts.body: Methodological individualism explains social phenomena through individuals, their actions, and their interactions rather than treating groups as irreducible agents. It can still use social institutions as descriptions of patterned individual behavior and expectations.

examples.text: A market price can be explained by buyers' and sellers' choices under shared rules.
examples.note: The account derives the social outcome from interacting persons instead of assigning an independent choosing mind to the market.

commonMisreadings: Methodological individualism does not require psychological egoism or deny that institutions constrain individuals.

concepts.name: Methodological naturalism
concepts.summary: Methodological naturalism is the rule that scientific inquiry should seek natural causes and publicly testable explanations.
concepts.body: Methodological naturalism is the rule that scientific inquiry should seek natural causes and publicly testable explanations. It brackets supernatural explanations as methods of science without necessarily claiming that no supernatural reality exists.

examples.text: A biologist explains a disease through pathogens, genetics, or physiology rather than divine intervention.
examples.note: Those causes can be investigated with observation, experiment, and reproducible evidence.

commonMisreadings: Methodological naturalism differs from metaphysical naturalism, which asserts that nature is all that exists.

concepts.name: Methodological skepticism
concepts.summary: Methodological skepticism uses systematic doubt to test whether beliefs have adequate grounds.
concepts.body: Methodological skepticism uses systematic doubt to test whether beliefs have adequate grounds. It suspends or challenges assumptions as an investigative method rather than necessarily endorsing permanent disbelief.

examples.text: A historian checks a widely repeated anecdote against contemporaneous documents before accepting it.
examples.note: The historian uses doubt to separate evidence from inherited confidence.

commonMisreadings: Methodological skepticism differs from global skepticism, which may conclude that knowledge is impossible in general.

concepts.name: Mimamsa
concepts.summary: Mimamsa is an Indian philosophical tradition centered on interpreting Vedic ritual, language, duty, and knowledge.
concepts.body: Mimamsa is an Indian philosophical tradition centered on interpreting Vedic ritual, language, duty, and knowledge. The school, especially Purva Mimamsa, defends the authority of the Veda and analyzes how injunctions generate obligations.

examples.text: Jaimini's Mimamsa tradition treats a Vedic injunction to perform a sacrifice as prescribing a duty rather than merely reporting a fact.
examples.note: The analysis focuses on the action-guiding force and interpretation of ritual language.

commonMisreadings: Mimamsa is not identical to Vedanta, whose classical focus is the Upanishadic teaching about ultimate reality.

concepts.name: Mimesis
concepts.summary: Mimesis is representation or imitation, especially the depiction of human action in art or narrative.
concepts.body: Mimesis is representation or imitation, especially the depiction of human action in art or narrative. The term can mean copying appearances, presenting actions, or creatively modeling reality depending on the theory using it.

examples.text: A novel that portrays a family conflict through dialogue and events uses mimesis.
examples.note: The narrative represents action by staging or describing what characters do rather than merely listing abstract propositions.

commonMisreadings: Mimesis is not simple duplication because artistic representation selects, orders, and transforms its subject.

concepts.name: Minarchism
concepts.summary: Minarchism is the libertarian view that the state should be limited to essential protective functions such as defense, policing, and courts.
concepts.body: Minarchism is the libertarian view that the state should be limited to essential protective functions such as defense, policing, and courts. It rejects extensive economic management and many welfare activities while retaining a minimal coercive government.

examples.text: A minarchist may support publicly funded courts and police but oppose state ownership of most industries.
examples.note: The institutions are restricted to protecting persons and property under the minimal-state ideal.

commonMisreadings: Minarchism differs from anarcho-capitalism because it retains a state rather than abolishing government.

concepts.name: Mind–body problem
concepts.summary: The mind–body problem asks how mental phenomena relate to physical bodies and brains.
concepts.body: The mind–body problem asks how mental phenomena relate to physical bodies and brains. Its central issues include whether mind and matter are distinct, identical, emergent, or related in another way.

examples.text: The experience of pain and the neural activity accompanying it create a mind–body problem about their relationship.
examples.note: The case requires an account of both subjective experience and physical process.

commonMisreadings: The mind–body problem is broader than the question of whether the brain causes behavior.

concepts.name: Minimax
concepts.summary: Minimax is a decision rule that chooses the option whose worst possible loss is as small as possible.
concepts.body: Minimax is a decision rule that chooses the option whose worst possible loss is as small as possible. In zero-sum games, minimax advises a player to minimize the opponent's maximum guaranteed gain.

examples.text: A chess player selects a move that limits the largest loss available to the opponent's best reply.
examples.note: The choice evaluates adverse responses and protects against the worst-case outcome.

commonMisreadings: Minimax differs from maximin because it minimizes maximum loss, whereas maximin maximizes minimum gain.

concepts.name: Minority rights
concepts.summary: Minority rights are legal or political protections for groups that could be disadvantaged by majority rule.
concepts.body: Minority rights are legal or political protections for groups that could be disadvantaged by majority rule. They may protect language, religion, association, representation, equal treatment, and cultural practice.

examples.text: A constitution guaranteeing a linguistic minority the right to educate children in its language protects a minority right.
examples.note: The guarantee prevents a numerical majority from eliminating the minority's language through ordinary legislation.

commonMisreadings: Minority rights do not necessarily grant minorities power to veto every majority decision.

concepts.name: Modal realism
concepts.summary: Modal realism is David Lewis's view that possible worlds are concrete realities as real as the actual world.
concepts.body: Modal realism is David Lewis's view that possible worlds are concrete realities as real as the actual world. On this view, “actual” is an indexical term for the world occupied by the speaker rather than a mark of superior existence.

examples.text: A modal realist treats a world where dinosaurs survived as a concrete world that is spatially or causally disconnected from ours.
examples.note: The dinosaur world is not merely a description or abstract object under the theory.

commonMisreadings: Modal realism differs from ersatz theories that regard possible worlds as abstract representations or sets of propositions.

concepts.name: Modality effect
concepts.summary: The modality effect is the memory advantage or disadvantage caused by presenting information in an auditory or visual mode relative to another mode.
concepts.body: The modality effect is the memory advantage or disadvantage caused by presenting information in an auditory or visual mode relative to another mode. In multimedia learning, spoken words can be remembered differently from written words because they recruit partly distinct processing channels.

examples.text: A learner may recall a diagram better when its explanation is spoken than when identical text is displayed beside it.
examples.note: The auditory and visual streams can reduce competition for the same limited representational channel.

commonMisreadings: The modality effect is not the mere preference for one medium because it concerns measurable effects on learning or recall.

concepts.name: Model theory
concepts.summary: Model theory is the study of the relationships between formal languages, axioms, and the mathematical structures that satisfy them.
concepts.body: Model theory is the study of the relationships between formal languages, axioms, and the mathematical structures that satisfy them. It investigates notions such as truth in a structure, satisfiability, elementary equivalence, and definability.

examples.text: The real numbers with their usual addition and order form a model of suitable axioms for an ordered field.
examples.note: The structure makes the formal sentences true under a specified interpretation.

commonMisreadings: Model theory differs from model building in science because its primary objects are formal theories and mathematical structures.

concepts.name: Modernism
concepts.summary: Modernism is a broad cultural movement that sought new forms in response to industrialization, urban life, mass society, and inherited traditions.
concepts.body: Modernism is a broad cultural movement that sought new forms in response to industrialization, urban life, mass society, and inherited traditions. Modernist works often use fragmentation, formal experimentation, abstraction, and distrust of conventional narrative or representation.

examples.text: T. S. Eliot's “The Waste Land” uses fragmented voices and allusions characteristic of literary modernism.
examples.note: Its discontinuous structure represents modern experience through deliberate formal disruption.

commonMisreadings: Modernism is not simply anything produced after 1900 because it names a historically specific aesthetic orientation.

concepts.name: Modus ponens
concepts.summary: Modus ponens is the valid inference form that affirms a conditional's antecedent and concludes its consequent.
concepts.body: Modus ponens is the valid inference form that affirms a conditional's antecedent and concludes its consequent. Its pattern is “If P then Q; P; therefore Q.”

examples.text: From “If the alarm is armed, the light flashes” and “the alarm is armed,” one concludes that the light flashes.
examples.note: The conclusion follows by applying the stated conditional to its confirmed antecedent.

commonMisreadings: Modus ponens is not affirming the consequent, which would wrongly infer P from Q.

concepts.name: Modus tollens
concepts.summary: Modus tollens is the valid inference form that denies a conditional's consequent and concludes that its antecedent is false.
concepts.body: Modus tollens is the valid inference form that denies a conditional's consequent and concludes that its antecedent is false. Its pattern is “If P then Q; not Q; therefore not P.”

examples.text: From “If the server is online, it responds to a ping” and “it does not respond,” one may infer that the server is not online, assuming the conditional is exhaustive.
examples.note: The absent consequent rules out the stated antecedent under the conditional premise.

commonMisreadings: Modus tollens is not denying the antecedent, which does not validly establish the denial of the consequent.

concepts.name: Mohism
concepts.summary: Mohism was an ancient Chinese philosophical school associated with Mozi that emphasized impartial care, practical benefit, and opposition to aggressive war.
concepts.body: Mohism was an ancient Chinese philosophical school associated with Mozi that emphasized impartial care, practical benefit, and opposition to aggressive war. Mohists defended standards of conduct by their effects on social order and criticized lavish ritual and music when they harmed people.

examples.text: A Mohist argument may condemn an offensive war because it causes widespread loss without benefiting the population.
examples.note: The judgment applies concern for welfare impartially rather than favoring one's own state.

commonMisreadings: Mohism differs from Confucianism in its stronger criticism of inherited ritual hierarchy and partial familial preference.

concepts.name: Moksha
concepts.summary: Moksha is liberation from the cycle of birth and death in Indian religious and philosophical traditions.
concepts.body: Moksha is liberation from the cycle of birth and death in Indian religious and philosophical traditions. Its interpretation varies, including release from karma, realization of the self's relation to ultimate reality, or freedom from ignorance and suffering.

examples.text: In Advaita Vedanta, moksha involves realizing that the individual self is not ultimately separate from Brahman.
examples.note: The realization removes the ignorance that sustains bondage and repeated rebirth.

commonMisreadings: Moksha is not simply temporary pleasure or ordinary worldly success.

concepts.name: Monarchism
concepts.summary: Monarchism is the political view that a monarch should hold a central constitutional or governing role.
concepts.body: Monarchism is the political view that a monarch should hold a central constitutional or governing role. It includes absolute, constitutional, elective, and ceremonial forms, so monarchists need not support unlimited royal power.

examples.text: A constitutional monarchist supports a hereditary king as head of state while elected ministers govern.
examples.note: The monarch's political role is preserved without making the crown the sole source of executive policy.

commonMisreadings: Monarchism differs from royal absolutism because a monarchy can be constrained by law and representative institutions.

concepts.name: Monism
concepts.summary: Monism is the metaphysical view that reality is fundamentally one kind of substance, entity, or principle.
concepts.body: Monism is the metaphysical view that reality is fundamentally one kind of substance, entity, or principle. Materialism, idealism, and neutral monism are different monist accounts of what the single fundamental basis is.

examples.text: An idealist monist holds that mind or experience is fundamental and physical objects depend on it.
examples.note: The view explains apparent plurality as forms or manifestations of one underlying reality.

commonMisreadings: Monism is not the claim that only one individual object exists in everyday experience.

concepts.name: Monotheism
concepts.summary: Monotheism is belief in one God as the sole or ultimate deity.
concepts.body: Monotheism is belief in one God as the sole or ultimate deity. Some monotheistic traditions distinguish one creator from angels, saints, or other spiritual beings that are not gods.

examples.text: Islam is monotheistic because it affirms one God, Allah, rather than a plurality of deities.
examples.note: The existence of angels in Islamic theology does not undermine the doctrine because angels are created beings, not gods.

commonMisreadings: Monotheism differs from henotheism, which may worship one god without denying that other gods exist.

concepts.name: Monotonic reasoning
concepts.summary: Monotonic reasoning is reasoning in which adding premises never invalidates a conclusion already derived.
concepts.body: Monotonic reasoning is reasoning in which adding premises never invalidates a conclusion already derived. Classical deductive entailment is monotonic, while reasoning from defaults or incomplete information is often nonmonotonic.

examples.text: If “Tweety is a bird” supports “Tweety can fly” in a default system, learning that Tweety is a penguin may retract the conclusion.
examples.note: The retraction shows that the reasoning pattern is nonmonotonic rather than monotonic.

commonMisreadings: Monotonic reasoning does not mean that conclusions increase numerically with every added premise.

concepts.name: Moral absolutism
concepts.summary: Moral absolutism is the view that at least some moral rules hold without exception across relevant circumstances.
concepts.body: Moral absolutism is the view that at least some moral rules hold without exception across relevant circumstances. An absolutist can maintain that certain actions are always wrong even when obeying the rule has severe consequences.

examples.text: A strict absolutist may hold that intentionally torturing an innocent person is wrong in every circumstance.
examples.note: The rule's validity does not depend on local custom or a calculated exception.

commonMisreadings: Moral absolutism differs from moral universalism because a universalist may endorse common moral standards without making every rule exceptionless.

concepts.name: Moral agency
concepts.summary: Moral agency is the capacity to understand moral reasons, deliberate about them, and control conduct accordingly.
concepts.body: Moral agency is the capacity to understand moral reasons, deliberate about them, and control conduct accordingly. Moral agency is often linked to rational competence, freedom from coercion, and accountability for choices.

examples.text: An adult who understands a duty, weighs reasons, and intentionally breaks it exercises moral agency.
examples.note: The person can be assessed as responsible because the action was guided by understood reasons.

commonMisreadings: Moral agency differs from moral status, which concerns how an entity may be treated rather than whether it can choose morally.

concepts.name: Moral anti-realism
concepts.summary: Moral anti-realism is the family of views denying that objective, mind-independent moral facts exist in the realist sense.
concepts.body: Moral anti-realism is the family of views denying that objective, mind-independent moral facts exist in the realist sense. Anti-realist theories include expressivism, error theory, subjectivism, and some forms of constructivism.

examples.text: An expressivist interprets “lying is wrong” as expressing disapproval of lying rather than reporting a stance-independent moral property.
examples.note: The utterance functions primarily as an attitude or practical commitment under that theory.

commonMisreadings: Moral anti-realism is not identical to moral skepticism because an anti-realist may still accept moral reasoning and condemnation.

concepts.name: Moral cognitivism
concepts.summary: Moral cognitivism is the view that moral judgments are beliefs or propositions capable of being true or false.
concepts.body: Moral cognitivism is the view that moral judgments are beliefs or propositions capable of being true or false. Cognitivism does not by itself decide whether moral truths are objective, constructed, or dependent on attitudes.

examples.text: A cognitivist treats “charity is required” as a claim that can be assessed for truth rather than only an expression of emotion.
examples.note: The judgment has propositional content suitable for truth evaluation.

commonMisreadings: Moral cognitivism differs from noncognitivism, which treats moral utterances as attitudes, prescriptions, or commitments rather than truth-apt beliefs.

concepts.name: Moral constructivism
concepts.summary: Moral constructivism holds that moral principles are generated or justified through an appropriate procedure of practical reasoning rather than discovered as independent facts.
concepts.body: Moral constructivism holds that moral principles are generated or justified through an appropriate procedure of practical reasoning rather than discovered as independent facts. Different constructivists specify procedures involving rational agreement, universalization, autonomy, or conditions of fair deliberation.

examples.text: A Kantian constructivist may justify a duty by asking whether every rational agent could will its principle as universal law.
examples.note: The principle's authority arises from the structure of justified practical reasoning.

commonMisreadings: Constructivism differs from subjectivism because its standards need not vary with each person's arbitrary preference.

concepts.name: Moral hazard
concepts.summary: Moral hazard is the increased risk-taking that occurs when a person is protected from the full consequences of their actions.
concepts.body: Moral hazard is the increased risk-taking that occurs when a person is protected from the full consequences of their actions. Insurance, bailouts, and limited liability can create moral hazard when protection weakens incentives for care.

examples.text: A fully insured driver may leave a car unlocked more often because theft losses are largely covered.
examples.note: The coverage shifts part of the cost of carelessness to the insurer.

commonMisreadings: Moral hazard concerns behavior after protection is provided, unlike adverse selection, which concerns hidden traits before a contract.

concepts.name: Moral particularism
concepts.summary: Moral particularism is the view that moral judgment does not require general principles whose reasons retain the same relevance in every case.
concepts.body: Moral particularism is the view that moral judgment does not require general principles whose reasons retain the same relevance in every case. A feature such as honesty can count for or against an action depending on the particular circumstances.

examples.text: Breaking a promise to prevent an imminent murder may be permissible even if promise-breaking normally counts against an action.
examples.note: The emergency changes the practical relevance of the promise without applying a fixed exception list.

commonMisreadings: Particularism differs from moral generalism, which explains judgment through stable principles or rules.

concepts.name: Moral perfectionism
concepts.summary: Moral perfectionism is the ethical ideal that agents should cultivate excellence, capacities, or higher forms of human development.
concepts.body: Moral perfectionism is the ethical ideal that agents should cultivate excellence, capacities, or higher forms of human development. Perfectionist theories often value rational, creative, civic, or virtuous activity beyond the satisfaction of preferences.

examples.text: A perfectionist policy may fund public education because it develops citizens' reasoning and artistic capacities.
examples.note: The policy treats capability development as intrinsically valuable rather than merely as a means to consumer choice.

commonMisreadings: Moral perfectionism differs from hedonism because it does not identify the good solely with pleasure.

concepts.name: Moral pluralism
concepts.summary: Moral pluralism holds that several distinct moral values or principles are genuinely important and may conflict.
concepts.body: Moral pluralism holds that several distinct moral values or principles are genuinely important and may conflict. Pluralists often reject reducing all moral reasons to one measure such as pleasure, preference satisfaction, or duty.

examples.text: A decision to allocate a scarce organ may weigh fairness, medical benefit, respect for choice, and compassion.
examples.note: The conflict requires judgment about multiple values rather than calculation under one complete ranking.

commonMisreadings: Moral pluralism differs from moral relativism because plural values can be defended as valid beyond a particular culture.

concepts.name: Moral realism
concepts.summary: Moral realism is the view that at least some moral claims are true because of objective moral facts or properties.
