concepts.body: Moral realism is the view that at least some moral claims are true because of objective moral facts or properties. Realists disagree about whether moral facts are natural, nonnatural, relational, or otherwise grounded.

examples.text: A realist may hold that gratuitously torturing a child is wrong even if a society approves of it.
examples.note: The act's wrongness is treated as independent of collective endorsement.

commonMisreadings: Moral realism is not the same as moral absolutism because a realist may allow context-sensitive or defeasible moral truths.

concepts.name: Moral relativism
concepts.summary: Moral relativism is the view that the truth or justification of moral judgments depends on a framework such as a culture, society, or individual standpoint.
concepts.body: Moral relativism is the view that the truth or justification of moral judgments depends on a framework such as a culture, society, or individual standpoint. Relativists may deny a single universally binding moral standard while allowing criticism within a framework.

examples.text: A cultural relativist may judge a burial practice by the norms of the community that performs it.
examples.note: The practice's moral assessment is indexed to local standards rather than imposed by one external code.

commonMisreadings: Moral relativism differs from pluralism because pluralism can affirm several values as objectively valid.

concepts.name: Moral responsibility
concepts.summary: Moral responsibility is the status of being appropriately subject to praise, blame, obligation, or accountability for conduct.
concepts.body: Moral responsibility is the status of being appropriately subject to praise, blame, obligation, or accountability for conduct. Responsibility commonly requires relevant knowledge, control, and the absence of excusing conditions.

examples.text: A person who knowingly and freely damages a neighbor's property can be held morally responsible for the harm.
examples.note: The agent understood the act and could have refrained from it under ordinary assumptions.

commonMisreadings: Moral responsibility is not identical to causal responsibility because a person may cause an event accidentally without blame.

concepts.name: Moral status
concepts.summary: Moral status is the standing that determines whether an entity's interests or treatment require moral consideration.
concepts.body: Moral status is the standing that determines whether an entity's interests or treatment require moral consideration. Theories of moral status appeal to sentience, rationality, relationships, species membership, or other properties.

examples.text: A sentient animal may have moral status because its capacity for pain gives humans reasons not to harm it needlessly.
examples.note: Its suffering counts morally even though it may lack human language or legal personhood.

commonMisreadings: Moral status differs from moral agency because an entity can deserve consideration without making responsible choices.

concepts.name: Moral uncertainty
concepts.summary: Moral uncertainty is uncertainty about which moral theory, principle, or judgment is correct.
concepts.body: Moral uncertainty is uncertainty about which moral theory, principle, or judgment is correct. Decision makers under moral uncertainty may compare options across competing ethical frameworks rather than ignore unresolved disagreement.

examples.text: A philanthropist uncertain between utilitarianism and rights theory may choose a donation that performs well under both views.
examples.note: The action manages uncertainty about moral reasons instead of treating one theory as settled.

commonMisreadings: Moral uncertainty is not merely uncertainty about factual consequences, though factual uncertainty can contribute to it.

concepts.name: Moral universalism
concepts.summary: Moral universalism is the view that some moral standards apply to all persons regardless of culture, status, or location.
concepts.body: Moral universalism is the view that some moral standards apply to all persons regardless of culture, status, or location. Universalists can allow contextual variation while maintaining a common basis for condemning certain harms.

examples.text: A universalist may hold that deliberately enslaving innocent people is wrong whether practiced by a monarchy or a tribe.
examples.note: The judgment applies the same fundamental standard across social boundaries.

commonMisreadings: Moral universalism differs from moral absolutism because universal application does not require that every rule have no exceptions.

concepts.name: Moralism in aesthetics
concepts.summary: Moralism in aesthetics is the view that an artwork's moral character can affect its aesthetic value or evaluation.
concepts.body: Moralism in aesthetics is the view that an artwork's moral character can affect its aesthetic value or evaluation. Moralists may argue that a work's ethically defective perspective can impair its artistic achievement, while moderate versions allow other values to outweigh it.

examples.text: A novel that glamorizes cruelty through an unreliable narrator may be judged aesthetically weaker if the glamorization is artistically unearned.
examples.note: The moral defect matters because it distorts the work's response and interpretive design.

commonMisreadings: Aesthetic moralism differs from censorship because evaluating artistic value does not itself require suppressing the work.

concepts.name: Morgan's canon
concepts.summary: Morgan's canon is the methodological principle that an animal's behavior should not be explained by a higher psychological faculty when a lower faculty suffices.
concepts.body: Morgan's canon is the methodological principle that an animal's behavior should not be explained by a higher psychological faculty when a lower faculty suffices. It cautions researchers against attributing humanlike reasoning to animals without evidence that simpler mechanisms cannot explain behavior.

examples.text: A horse opening a gate by repeating a learned movement need not be credited with abstract mechanical insight.
examples.note: Conditioning or trial-and-error may explain the behavior more economically than complex reasoning.

commonMisreadings: Morgan's canon is a parsimony rule, not the claim that animals never reason.

concepts.name: Multiple realizability
concepts.summary: Multiple realizability is the thesis that one mental, functional, or higher-level state can be implemented by different physical structures.
concepts.body: Multiple realizability is the thesis that one mental, functional, or higher-level state can be implemented by different physical structures. It challenges identities that define a mental state as one particular neural or material state.

examples.text: Pain could be realized by human neurons, an octopus nervous system, or a suitably organized artificial system.
examples.note: The systems differ physically but share the functional organization associated with pain.

commonMisreadings: Multiple realizability does not imply that realizations have nothing in common because they can share a causal organization.

concepts.name: Mutualism
concepts.summary: Mutualism is a political theory advocating cooperative association and reciprocal exchange rather than centralized state control or capitalist domination.
concepts.body: Mutualism is a political theory advocating cooperative association and reciprocal exchange rather than centralized state control or capitalist domination. In the tradition of Pierre-Joseph Proudhon, mutualists support worker or consumer cooperatives, federated self-management, and reciprocal credit.

examples.text: A mutualist community might organize a credit union and worker-owned workshops linked by voluntary federation.
examples.note: The institutions distribute control through reciprocal association instead of a state bureaucracy or absentee owner.

commonMisreadings: Mutualism is not biological mutualism, which describes a relationship in which different species benefit.

concepts.name: Mysticism
concepts.summary: Mysticism is a family of practices and claims concerning direct, transformative experience of ultimate reality or the divine.
concepts.body: Mysticism is a family of practices and claims concerning direct, transformative experience of ultimate reality or the divine. Mystical traditions often describe union, presence, emptiness, or insight that exceeds ordinary discursive knowledge.

examples.text: A Sufi practitioner who reports losing ordinary ego boundaries in an experience of divine unity gives a mystical report.
examples.note: The experience is presented as immediate and transformative rather than as an inference from doctrine.

commonMisreadings: Mysticism is not simply belief in the supernatural because it centers on experiential encounter or disciplined practice.

concepts.name: Naive realism in perception
concepts.summary: Naive realism in perception is the view that perception directly presents ordinary objects and their properties as they exist independently in the world.
concepts.body: Naive realism in perception is the view that perception directly presents ordinary objects and their properties as they exist independently in the world. It treats colors, shapes, and tables as mind-independent features perceived without an intervening representational construction.

examples.text: A naive realist says that seeing a red apple presents the apple's redness itself rather than a brain-generated visual representation.
examples.note: The perceptual experience is understood as direct awareness of the external property.

commonMisreadings: Naive realism differs from representationalism, which places a mental representation between perceiver and external object.

concepts.name: Naming
concepts.summary: Naming is the linguistic practice of assigning an expression to identify, refer to, or classify a person, object, kind, or idea.
concepts.body: Naming is the linguistic practice of assigning an expression to identify, refer to, or classify a person, object, kind, or idea. Philosophical theories distinguish names that rigidly refer to an individual from descriptions whose reference depends on associated properties.

examples.text: The name “Aristotle” refers to a particular historical person across statements about him.
examples.note: Its reference is not normally replaced by whichever person happens to fit a description such as “the teacher of Alexander.”

commonMisreadings: Naming is not the same as defining because a name can refer without specifying a complete descriptive meaning.

concepts.name: Nash equilibrium
concepts.summary: A Nash equilibrium is a profile of strategies in which no player can improve their payoff by changing strategy alone.
concepts.body: A Nash equilibrium is a profile of strategies in which no player can improve their payoff by changing strategy alone. It represents mutual best responses given the strategies chosen by the other players.

examples.text: In the Prisoner's Dilemma, mutual defection is a Nash equilibrium even though mutual cooperation would benefit both prisoners.
examples.note: Each prisoner would lose relative to the other player's defection by switching alone.

commonMisreadings: A Nash equilibrium need not be socially optimal or unique.

concepts.name: Nation
concepts.summary: A nation is a community of people who understand themselves as sharing a common identity, history, culture, or political aspiration.
concepts.body: A nation is a community of people who understand themselves as sharing a common identity, history, culture, or political aspiration. Nationhood can be based on civic membership, ethnicity, language, religion, or combinations of these factors.

examples.text: The Québécois can be described as a nation through shared language, historical memory, and political identity within Canada.
examples.note: The collective identity persists even though the group does not possess a fully sovereign state.

commonMisreadings: A nation is not automatically a nation-state because nations and state borders need not coincide.

concepts.name: Nation-state
concepts.summary: A nation-state is a sovereign state that claims to represent and govern a corresponding national community.
concepts.body: A nation-state is a sovereign state that claims to represent and govern a corresponding national community. The ideal assumes substantial overlap between political territory, citizenship, and national identity, although actual states are usually multinational.

examples.text: Japan is often described as a nation-state because the state and a dominant Japanese national identity largely overlap.
examples.note: The political institutions present themselves as the government of a national people rather than merely a dynasty or empire.

commonMisreadings: A nation-state is not simply any state containing a nation because the defining claim is representational alignment.

concepts.name: National bolshevism
concepts.summary: National Bolshevism is a syncretic ideology combining radical nationalism with elements of Bolshevik or communist economic and political rhetoric.
concepts.body: National Bolshevism is a syncretic ideology combining radical nationalism with elements of Bolshevik or communist economic and political rhetoric. Its variants have appeared in different historical settings and can reject both liberal capitalism and conventional internationalist communism.

examples.text: The German National Bolshevik current of the early Weimar period combined nationalist revisionism with advocacy of cooperation with Soviet Russia.
examples.note: The combination links national power and anti-capitalist revolution in one program.

commonMisreadings: National Bolshevism is not ordinary Bolshevism because it makes national identity central rather than treating proletarian internationalism as primary.

concepts.name: National conservatism
concepts.summary: National conservatism is a political outlook that emphasizes national sovereignty, cultural continuity, social order, and restrictive approaches to immigration or supranational governance.
concepts.body: National conservatism is a political outlook that emphasizes national sovereignty, cultural continuity, social order, and restrictive approaches to immigration or supranational governance. It can combine conservative social policy with economic positions that reject unrestricted global markets.

examples.text: A national-conservative party may defend traditional family norms while opposing the transfer of legislative power to a regional union.
examples.note: The program treats the nation-state and inherited culture as primary political reference points.

commonMisreadings: National conservatism differs from classical conservatism when it gives national sovereignty a stronger organizing role.

concepts.name: National liberalism
concepts.summary: National liberalism is a political tradition combining liberal rights or constitutional government with commitment to national self-determination and state building.
concepts.body: National liberalism is a political tradition combining liberal rights or constitutional government with commitment to national self-determination and state building. Its adherents may support civil equality and markets while insisting that political institutions serve a distinct national community.

examples.text: A nineteenth-century movement can demand parliamentary liberties and an independent national state at the same time.
examples.note: The program unites individual rights with the project of national political independence.

commonMisreadings: National liberalism differs from cosmopolitan liberalism when national membership remains a central source of political legitimacy.

concepts.name: National syndicalism
concepts.summary: National syndicalism is an ideology that combines syndicalist organization and economic corporatism with intense nationalism.
concepts.body: National syndicalism is an ideology that combines syndicalist organization and economic corporatism with intense nationalism. It favors mobilizing workers through national unions or corporative bodies rather than class struggle directed toward international socialism.

examples.text: The Italian revolutionary-syndicalist currents that influenced early fascism used strikes and worker organization in service of national power.
examples.note: The example connects labor mobilization to the nation instead of to an international proletarian movement.

commonMisreadings: National syndicalism differs from anarcho-syndicalism because it subordinates syndicalist organization to nationalist state aims.

concepts.name: Nationalism
concepts.summary: Nationalism is the doctrine or movement that treats the nation as a primary basis of political identity, loyalty, and legitimate self-government.
concepts.body: Nationalism is the doctrine or movement that treats the nation as a primary basis of political identity, loyalty, and legitimate self-government. Nationalists may seek independence, cultural preservation, state power, or solidarity among citizens identified as one people.

examples.text: The Indian independence movement used national identity to oppose British colonial rule and demand self-government.
examples.note: The movement made political sovereignty for the Indian nation its central objective.

commonMisreadings: Nationalism is not identical to patriotism because nationalism usually includes a political claim about the nation and state.

concepts.name: Natural deduction
concepts.summary: Natural deduction is a formal proof system that derives conclusions from premises using introduction and elimination rules for logical connectives and quantifiers.
concepts.body: Natural deduction is a formal proof system that derives conclusions from premises using introduction and elimination rules for logical connectives and quantifiers. Its proof steps model ordinary reasoning by temporarily assuming formulas and discharging those assumptions in subproofs.

examples.text: To prove “if P then P,” a natural-deduction proof assumes P and then introduces the conditional from that same assumption.
examples.note: The conditional-introduction rule records the dependency and discharges the temporary premise.

commonMisreadings: Natural deduction differs from a truth table because it demonstrates derivability through structured proof steps.

concepts.name: Natural kind
concepts.summary: A natural kind is a category whose members are grouped by underlying structure or causal properties rather than by arbitrary convention alone.
concepts.body: A natural kind is a category whose members are grouped by underlying structure or causal properties rather than by arbitrary convention alone. Examples often include chemical elements and biological species, although philosophers dispute which categories are genuinely natural.

examples.text: Gold is treated as a natural kind because instances share atomic number 79 and characteristic chemical behavior.
examples.note: The classification tracks a stable underlying property that supports explanations and predictions.

commonMisreadings: A natural kind is not simply any useful category because usefulness alone does not establish objective unity.

concepts.name: Natural law theory
concepts.summary: Natural law theory holds that moral norms are grounded in facts about human nature, practical reason, or the natural order.
concepts.body: Natural law theory holds that moral norms are grounded in facts about human nature, practical reason, or the natural order. Classical versions claim that reason can identify basic goods and norms even apart from enacted law.

examples.text: A natural-law theorist may argue that deliberately targeting innocent civilians is wrong because it violates a basic requirement of practical reason.
examples.note: The prohibition is justified by a norm considered valid independently of a legislature's command.

commonMisreadings: Natural law theory differs from legal positivism, which separates a law's legal validity from its moral merit.

concepts.name: Natural rights
concepts.summary: Natural rights are rights held by persons by virtue of their humanity or nature rather than granted by a government.
concepts.body: Natural rights are rights held by persons by virtue of their humanity or nature rather than granted by a government. They are commonly described as universal and inalienable, though theories disagree about their foundation and scope.

examples.text: The claim that every person has a right not to be enslaved exemplifies a natural-rights argument.
examples.note: The right is said to bind governments even before a constitution recognizes it.

commonMisreadings: Natural rights differ from civil rights because civil rights are typically created or specified by a legal system.

concepts.name: Natural theology
concepts.summary: Natural theology seeks knowledge or arguments about God from reason, observation, or the natural world rather than from revealed scripture alone.
concepts.body: Natural theology seeks knowledge or arguments about God from reason, observation, or the natural world rather than from revealed scripture alone. Its arguments include versions of cosmological, teleological, and moral arguments, alongside arguments from religious experience.

examples.text: An argument from the apparent order of biological systems to an intelligent designer is a piece of natural theology.
examples.note: The reasoning begins from features accessible to ordinary inquiry instead of citing a sacred revelation as its sole premise.

commonMisreadings: Natural theology differs from revealed theology because revelation is not its necessary starting point.

concepts.name: Naturalism
concepts.summary: Naturalism is the general philosophical stance that explanations should appeal to the natural world and its regularities, often rejecting supernatural entities or methods.
concepts.body: Naturalism is the general philosophical stance that explanations should appeal to the natural world and its regularities, often rejecting supernatural entities or methods. Metaphysical naturalism says only natural entities exist, whereas methodological naturalism limits the methods of inquiry without settling ultimate ontology.

examples.text: A naturalist explains consciousness through evolved biological and physical processes rather than an immaterial soul.
examples.note: The explanation places mental life within the causal order studied by the natural sciences.

commonMisreadings: Naturalism is broader than physicalism because some naturalists allow emergent or nonreducible properties.

concepts.name: Nazism
concepts.summary: Nazism was the totalitarian, racist, ultranationalist ideology and regime associated with Adolf Hitler's National Socialist German Workers' Party.
concepts.body: Nazism was the totalitarian, racist, ultranationalist ideology and regime associated with Adolf Hitler's National Socialist German Workers' Party. It promoted dictatorship, racial hierarchy, antisemitism, militarism, territorial expansion, and the subordination of individuals to the racial nation.

examples.text: The Nazi regime's Nuremberg Laws stripped Jews of citizenship and institutionalized racial persecution.
examples.note: The laws show how Nazi racial ideology became coercive state policy.

commonMisreadings: Nazism is not simply generic authoritarianism because its defining program centered on racial nationalism and genocidal antisemitism.

concepts.name: Necessary being
concepts.summary: A necessary being is an entity that cannot fail to exist and exists in every metaphysically possible world.
concepts.body: A necessary being is an entity that cannot fail to exist and exists in every metaphysically possible world. Arguments for such a being often claim that contingent reality requires an ultimate noncontingent ground, though the arguments are disputed.

examples.text: Classical theism identifies God as a necessary being rather than as one more contingent object in the universe.
examples.note: The identification explains divine existence as not dependent on external conditions.

commonMisreadings: A necessary being differs from a physically indestructible object because physical durability does not imply existence in every possible world.

concepts.name: Necessary condition
concepts.summary: A necessary condition is a requirement that must be present for a state or event to occur.
concepts.body: A necessary condition is a requirement that must be present for a state or event to occur. If A is necessary for B, B cannot occur without A, although A alone may not produce B.

examples.text: Oxygen is necessary for an ordinary fire to burn, but oxygen alone does not create a fire.
examples.note: The absence of oxygen prevents the specified combustion while its presence leaves other requirements open.

commonMisreadings: A necessary condition differs from a sufficient condition, which guarantees the outcome when present.

concepts.name: Necessity
concepts.summary: Necessity is the modal status of being unable to be otherwise within a specified system or range of possibilities.
concepts.body: Necessity is the modal status of being unable to be otherwise within a specified system or range of possibilities. Logical, metaphysical, physical, and deontic necessity differ according to the constraints that rule out alternatives.

examples.text: It is logically necessary that a triangle has three sides under the standard definition of triangle.
examples.note: The denial creates a contradiction in the relevant concept rather than merely describing an unusual triangle.

commonMisreadings: Necessity is not the same as certainty because a person can be certain of a contingent claim.

concepts.name: Negation
concepts.summary: Negation is the logical operation that changes a proposition into the proposition that it is not the case.
concepts.body: Negation is the logical operation that changes a proposition into the proposition that it is not the case. The negation of P is commonly written not-P and is true exactly when P is false in classical logic.

examples.text: The negation of “the switch is on” is “the switch is not on.”
examples.note: The second proposition reverses the truth condition of the first.

commonMisreadings: Negation differs from contradiction because a contradiction combines a proposition and its negation in one claim or set.

concepts.name: Negative liberty
concepts.summary: Negative liberty is freedom from interference, coercion, or obstruction by other agents.
concepts.body: Negative liberty is freedom from interference, coercion, or obstruction by other agents. A person has negative liberty to the extent that others do not prevent them from choosing and acting within a protected sphere.

examples.text: A government respects negative liberty when it does not censor a peaceful political opinion.
examples.note: The absence of state interference leaves the speaker free to express the view.

commonMisreadings: Negative liberty differs from positive liberty, which concerns having the power or resources to achieve an end.

concepts.name: Negative utilitarianism
concepts.summary: Negative utilitarianism is the ethical view that reducing suffering has priority over increasing happiness or other positive value.
concepts.body: Negative utilitarianism is the ethical view that reducing suffering has priority over increasing happiness or other positive value. Some versions treat the minimization of suffering as the sole goal, while others give it lexical or strong priority.

examples.text: A negative utilitarian may support a policy that prevents severe chronic pain even if it produces little additional pleasure.
examples.note: The policy is justified by the suffering avoided rather than by a larger quantity of happiness created.

commonMisreadings: Negative utilitarianism is not ordinary utilitarianism with a pessimistic attitude because it changes the value structure of the theory.

concepts.name: Neo-Aristotelianism
concepts.summary: Neo-Aristotelianism is a modern philosophical revival of Aristotelian ideas about virtue, flourishing, form, causation, and human nature.
concepts.body: Neo-Aristotelianism is a modern philosophical revival of Aristotelian ideas about virtue, flourishing, form, causation, and human nature. Neo-Aristotelians adapt Aristotle's concepts to contemporary debates in ethics, metaphysics, philosophy of mind, and political theory.

examples.text: A neo-Aristotelian ethicist may define courage as a virtue enabling appropriate response to danger within a flourishing life.
examples.note: The account treats character and practical judgment as central rather than reducing morality to rule-following.

commonMisreadings: Neo-Aristotelianism is not simple historical commentary because it develops Aristotelian resources for current problems.

concepts.name: Neo-Confucianism
concepts.summary: Neo-Confucianism is a Song-era and later revival of Confucian philosophy that engages Buddhist and Daoist metaphysics while emphasizing ethical cultivation.
concepts.body: Neo-Confucianism is a Song-era and later revival of Confucian philosophy that engages Buddhist and Daoist metaphysics while emphasizing ethical cultivation. Thinkers such as Zhu Xi developed accounts of principle, material force, moral knowledge, and self-cultivation.

examples.text: Zhu Xi's interpretation of the Four Books made disciplined study and investigation of things part of moral development.
examples.note: Knowledge is integrated with the formation of a virtuous person rather than treated as detached information.

commonMisreadings: Neo-Confucianism differs from early Confucianism through its developed metaphysical vocabulary and sustained response to Buddhism.

concepts.name: Neo-Hegelianism
concepts.summary: Neo-Hegelianism is a modern revival or reinterpretation of Hegelian themes such as social recognition, historical development, ideality, and systematic thought.
concepts.body: Neo-Hegelianism is a modern revival or reinterpretation of Hegelian themes such as social recognition, historical development, ideality, and systematic thought. It includes diverse thinkers who use Hegel to analyze ethics, society, religion, or logic without accepting every part of Hegel's original system.

examples.text: British neo-Hegelians such as F. H. Bradley treated social relations and an integrated whole as central to reality and ethics.
examples.note: Their work uses Hegelian ideas to challenge atomistic accounts of persons and values.

commonMisreadings: Neo-Hegelianism is not a single uniform doctrine because its members reinterpret Hegel in different national and philosophical contexts.

concepts.name: Neo-Kantianism
concepts.summary: Neo-Kantianism was a nineteenth- and early-twentieth-century movement that returned to Kant to address science, knowledge, ethics, and culture.
concepts.body: Neo-Kantianism was a nineteenth- and early-twentieth-century movement that returned to Kant to address science, knowledge, ethics, and culture. The Marburg school emphasized the conditions of scientific knowledge, while the Baden school stressed values and the cultural sciences.

examples.text: Hermann Cohen's Marburg neo-Kantianism interpreted scientific objects through the conceptual activity that makes knowledge possible.
examples.note: The account preserves Kant's concern with conditions of objectivity while engaging modern science.

commonMisreadings: Neo-Kantianism differs from Kant's original philosophy because it selectively reconstructs his project for later intellectual problems.

concepts.name: Neo-Marxism
concepts.summary: Neo-Marxism is a set of twentieth-century Marxist approaches that revise classical Marxism to analyze culture, ideology, politics, race, or bureaucracy.
concepts.body: Neo-Marxism is a set of twentieth-century Marxist approaches that revise classical Marxism to analyze culture, ideology, politics, race, or bureaucracy. Neo-Marxists often supplement economic analysis with theories of hegemony, mass culture, state autonomy, or social reproduction.

examples.text: The Frankfurt School's critique of the culture industry explains how commercial media can stabilize domination beyond direct workplace exploitation.
examples.note: The analysis extends Marxist critique into cultural production and everyday consciousness.

commonMisreadings: Neo-Marxism is not a single school because its approaches can disagree about class, culture, and revolutionary strategy.

concepts.name: Neo-reaction
concepts.summary: Neo-reaction is an anti-democratic political current that criticizes egalitarian liberal democracy and favors hierarchical or authoritarian forms of governance.
concepts.body: Neo-reaction is an anti-democratic political current that criticizes egalitarian liberal democracy and favors hierarchical or authoritarian forms of governance. Some neo-reactionary writers advocate replacing electoral states with corporate or monarchic sovereignty and emphasize technological governance.

examples.text: A neo-reactionary proposal may compare a private city governed by an owner to a firm with a chief executive rather than to a democratic municipality.
examples.note: The proposal treats exit and managerial competence as alternatives to popular sovereignty.

commonMisreadings: Neo-reaction is not merely conservatism because it rejects core democratic equality and electoral accountability.

concepts.name: Neo-Scholasticism
concepts.summary: Neo-Scholasticism is the nineteenth- and twentieth-century revival of medieval scholastic philosophy, especially its Aristotelian and Thomistic traditions.
concepts.body: Neo-Scholasticism is the nineteenth- and twentieth-century revival of medieval scholastic philosophy, especially its Aristotelian and Thomistic traditions. It sought to renew systematic metaphysics, natural theology, ethics, and philosophy of nature in response to modern philosophy and science.

examples.text: A neo-scholastic college may teach act and potency as metaphysical principles while engaging contemporary debates about evolution.
examples.note: The curriculum preserves scholastic conceptual tools while addressing modern intellectual conditions.

commonMisreadings: Neo-Scholasticism is broader than neo-Thomism because it includes revivals of several scholastic schools.

concepts.name: Neo-Thomism
concepts.summary: Neo-Thomism is a modern revival and development of the philosophy and theology of Thomas Aquinas.
concepts.body: Neo-Thomism is a modern revival and development of the philosophy and theology of Thomas Aquinas. It commonly emphasizes act and potency, natural law, analogy, realist epistemology, and the compatibility of faith with reason.

examples.text: Jacques Maritain used Thomistic natural-law theory to defend human dignity and democratic rights.
examples.note: The application extends Aquinas's framework to modern political questions.

commonMisreadings: Neo-Thomism differs from medieval Thomism because it interprets and adapts Aquinas under modern philosophical and social conditions.

concepts.name: Neo-Vedanta
concepts.summary: Neo-Vedanta is a modern interpretation of Vedanta that presents Hindu philosophy, often Advaita, in universalist and reformist terms.
concepts.body: Neo-Vedanta is a modern interpretation of Vedanta that presents Hindu philosophy, often Advaita, in universalist and reformist terms. It frequently recasts liberation and nonduality for engagement with modern science, comparative religion, nationalism, and global audiences.

examples.text: Swami Vivekananda presented the realization of the divine self as a universal spiritual possibility compatible with service to humanity.
examples.note: The presentation translates Vedantic ideas into a modern pluralistic and socially engaged framework.

commonMisreadings: Neo-Vedanta is not identical to every premodern Vedanta school because its universalist framing is historically modern.

concepts.name: Neoconservatism
concepts.summary: Neoconservatism is a political movement that emphasizes anti-communism, national strength, social order, and an active foreign policy, especially in its American forms.
concepts.body: Neoconservatism is a political movement that emphasizes anti-communism, national strength, social order, and an active foreign policy, especially in its American forms. Neoconservatives often support liberal democracy abroad but are skeptical of isolationism and revolutionary social engineering at home.

examples.text: A neoconservative may support using American power to contain an expansionist dictatorship and defend allied democracies.
examples.note: The policy combines international activism with concern for political order and national security.

commonMisreadings: Neoconservatism differs from traditional conservatism when it gives foreign intervention and democratic state power a larger role.

concepts.name: Neoliberalism
concepts.summary: Neoliberalism is a family of political-economic ideas favoring markets, competition, private enterprise, trade, and limits on some forms of state control.
concepts.body: Neoliberalism is a family of political-economic ideas favoring markets, competition, private enterprise, trade, and limits on some forms of state control. Historical uses vary, but contemporary criticism often associates it with deregulation, privatization, fiscal restraint, and market-oriented governance.

examples.text: A government that privatizes a state-owned utility and introduces competition follows a neoliberal policy direction.
examples.note: The reform treats market competition and private ownership as tools for improving allocation.

commonMisreadings: Neoliberalism is not identical to laissez-faire because many neoliberal programs retain active regulation and state institutions.

concepts.name: Neoplatonism
concepts.summary: Neoplatonism is a late-antique philosophical tradition that describes reality as flowing from the transcendent One through Intellect and Soul.
concepts.body: Neoplatonism is a late-antique philosophical tradition that describes reality as flowing from the transcendent One through Intellect and Soul. Plotinus and later thinkers combine Platonic metaphysics with a hierarchical account of emanation, return, and spiritual ascent.

examples.text: Plotinus describes the intellective world as an emanation from the One and the soul's contemplation as a path of return.
examples.note: The structure explains multiplicity as dependent on a higher unified source.

commonMisreadings: Neoplatonism differs from Plato's original writings because it develops a more explicit emanationist and hierarchical system.

concepts.name: Neopragmatism
concepts.summary: Neopragmatism is a contemporary form of pragmatism that emphasizes language, social practice, interpretation, and the rejection of fixed foundations.
concepts.body: Neopragmatism is a contemporary form of pragmatism that emphasizes language, social practice, interpretation, and the rejection of fixed foundations. Neopragmatists such as Richard Rorty often treat vocabularies as tools for coping and coordination rather than mirrors of intrinsic reality.

examples.text: A neopragmatist may judge a scientific vocabulary by how well it supports prediction, explanation, and inquiry instead of asking whether it copies reality's final structure.
examples.note: The evaluation focuses on practical and conversational success rather than foundational representation.

commonMisreadings: Neopragmatism differs from classical pragmatism in its stronger engagement with linguistic and post-analytic philosophy.

concepts.name: Neopythagoreanism
concepts.summary: Neopythagoreanism was a Hellenistic and Roman revival of Pythagorean themes involving number, mathematical order, ascetic practice, and cosmic harmony.
concepts.body: Neopythagoreanism was a Hellenistic and Roman revival of Pythagorean themes involving number, mathematical order, ascetic practice, and cosmic harmony. It often combined Pythagorean ideas with Platonism and treated mathematics as a route to understanding the structure of reality.

examples.text: A neopythagorean writer may interpret the numerical ratios of musical intervals as evidence of an ordered cosmos.
examples.note: The example links mathematical proportion with metaphysical and ethical significance.

commonMisreadings: Neopythagoreanism is not identical to the historical Pythagorean community because later authors reconstructed Pythagorean teachings from new philosophical contexts.

concepts.name: Network effect
concepts.summary: A network effect occurs when a product or service becomes more valuable to each user as the number of users increases.
concepts.body: A network effect occurs when a product or service becomes more valuable to each user as the number of users increases. Direct network effects arise from user-to-user interaction, while indirect effects arise when growth attracts complementary products or services.

examples.text: A messaging application becomes more useful to a person when more friends and relatives use the same application.
examples.note: The larger user network creates more possible communication partners for every participant.

commonMisreadings: A network effect differs from a general popularity effect because its value increase is tied to the network's size or connectivity.

concepts.name: Neutral monism
concepts.summary: Neutral monism is the metaphysical view that mind and matter are two aspects or organizations of a more basic neutral reality.
concepts.body: Neutral monism is the metaphysical view that mind and matter are two aspects or organizations of a more basic neutral reality. It rejects both substance dualism and the reduction of everything to purely mental or purely physical substance.

examples.text: Bertrand Russell's neutral-monist approach treats events as having mental and physical descriptions without making either description fundamental.
examples.note: The same underlying event can enter psychological and physical causal accounts under different relations.

commonMisreadings: Neutral monism differs from property dualism because it posits a neutral basis rather than two fundamental kinds of properties alone.

concepts.name: New Left
concepts.summary: The New Left was a mid-twentieth-century political movement that challenged both traditional conservatism and the established communist left.
concepts.body: The New Left was a mid-twentieth-century political movement that challenged both traditional conservatism and the established communist left. It emphasized civil rights, antiwar activism, participatory democracy, feminism, student power, and criticism of bureaucratic domination.

examples.text: The 1960s Students for a Democratic Society organized against militarism and for participatory democracy as part of the New Left.
examples.note: The organization joined opposition to war with a demand for more democratic control of social institutions.

commonMisreadings: The New Left differed from the Old Left by broadening political struggle beyond industrial class politics and party discipline.

concepts.name: Newcomb's problem
concepts.summary: Newcomb's problem is a decision puzzle involving one-boxing or two-boxing after a predictor forecasts the choice.
concepts.body: Newcomb's problem is a decision puzzle involving one-boxing or two-boxing after a predictor forecasts the choice. Its opaque box was filled according to that forecast.

examples.text: Choosing one box when prediction is accurate illustrates the puzzle.
examples.note: The choice appears to affect both reward and evidence about the prediction.

commonMisreadings: It is not ordinary optimization because causal and evidential reasoning conflict.

concepts.name: Next-in-line effect
concepts.summary: The next-in-line effect is impaired memory for material presented immediately before one's own expected turn.
concepts.body: The next-in-line effect is impaired memory for material presented immediately before one's own expected turn. Attention shifts from encoding the preceding material to preparing performance.

examples.text: A student may poorly recall the talk before their own.
examples.note: The imminent turn creates the characteristic attentional shift.

commonMisreadings: It is not merely general stage fright because the memory loss is selective.

concepts.name: Nirvana
concepts.summary: Nirvana is Buddhist liberation from craving, suffering, and rebirth.
concepts.body: Nirvana is Buddhist liberation from craving, suffering, and rebirth. Early Buddhism explains it through extinguishing the causes of suffering.

examples.text: An awakened monk attaining release exemplifies nirvana.
examples.note: Craving and ignorance have been overcome in the case.

commonMisreadings: It is not simply annihilation in every Buddhist tradition.

concepts.name: Nominalism
concepts.summary: Nominalism denies that universals exist independently of their particular instances or names.
concepts.body: Nominalism denies that universals exist independently of their particular instances or names. It may explain common predicates through resemblance or linguistic convention.

examples.text: A nominalist calls several apples red without positing redness itself.
examples.note: The classification uses a predicate without an abstract universal.

commonMisreadings: It is not the claim that names lack meaning.

concepts.name: Non-interventionism
concepts.summary: Non-interventionism rejects coercive interference in another state's affairs.
concepts.body: Non-interventionism rejects coercive interference in another state's affairs. It can permit diplomacy, trade, and defensive alliances.

examples.text: A government refusing troops in a foreign civil war follows it.
examples.note: The policy limits coercion while allowing external relations.

commonMisreadings: It is not complete isolationism.

concepts.name: Nonclassical logic
concepts.summary: Nonclassical logic revises at least one principle or feature of classical logic.
concepts.body: Nonclassical logic revises at least one principle or feature of classical logic. Examples include intuitionistic, fuzzy, relevant, and paraconsistent logics.

examples.text: Three-valued logic adds an indeterminate truth status.
examples.note: The extra status changes classical semantics.

commonMisreadings: It is not irrational reasoning because its rules are formal.

concepts.name: Nondualism
concepts.summary: Nondualism denies that subject and object are fundamentally independent opposites.
concepts.body: Nondualism denies that subject and object are fundamentally independent opposites. Advaita Vedanta identifies deepest self with ultimate reality.

examples.text: A meditator seeing observer and observed as one reality expresses nondualism.
examples.note: The apparent separation is treated as derivative.

commonMisreadings: It is not necessarily simple substance monism.

concepts.name: Nonmaleficence
concepts.summary: Nonmaleficence is the duty to avoid unjustified harm.
concepts.body: Nonmaleficence is the duty to avoid unjustified harm. Medical ethics uses it to reject interventions whose burdens exceed benefits.

examples.text: A clinician declining a dangerous futile treatment follows it.
examples.note: The decision prevents injury rather than merely withholding aid.

commonMisreadings: It differs from beneficence, which requires producing benefit.

concepts.name: Nonmonotonic logic
concepts.summary: Nonmonotonic logic permits new information to defeat an earlier conclusion.
concepts.body: Nonmonotonic logic permits new information to defeat an earlier conclusion. It models defeasible inferences about typical cases.

examples.text: From birds usually fly one may retract Tweety flies after learning Tweety is a penguin.
examples.note: The exception defeats the default inference.

commonMisreadings: It is not simply inconsistent logic.

concepts.name: Normative ethics
concepts.summary: Normative ethics studies standards for what actions, motives, or lives are morally right.
concepts.body: Normative ethics studies standards for what actions, motives, or lives are morally right. Its major approaches include consequentialism, deontology, and virtue ethics.

examples.text: Comparing whether lying is wrong by consequence or duty is normative ethics.
examples.note: The comparison evaluates standards rather than describing beliefs.

commonMisreadings: It is not moral psychology.

concepts.name: Nothingness
concepts.summary: Nothingness is the alleged absence of entities, properties, events, or structure.
concepts.body: Nothingness is the alleged absence of entities, properties, events, or structure. Philosophers dispute whether absolute nothingness is coherent.

examples.text: The question why there is something rather than nothing invokes it.
examples.note: Nothingness supplies the contrast to existence.

commonMisreadings: It is not empty space, which still has structure.

concepts.name: Nyaya
concepts.summary: Nyaya is an Indian tradition focused on logic, epistemology, and valid knowledge.
concepts.body: Nyaya is an Indian tradition focused on logic, epistemology, and valid knowledge. It recognizes perception, inference, comparison, and testimony as knowledge sources.

examples.text: Inferring fire from smoke illustrates Nyaya inference.
examples.note: A reliable relation connects observed sign and hidden fact.

commonMisreadings: It is broader than a debate technique.

concepts.name: Object
concepts.summary: An object is an entity treated as a bearer of properties or target of reference.
concepts.body: An object is an entity treated as a bearer of properties or target of reference. Objects may be concrete, abstract, events, or intentional entities.

examples.text: A bronze statue is an object with shape and location.
examples.note: It is a distinct referent supporting predication.

commonMisreadings: Object does not always mean physical thing.

concepts.name: Object language
concepts.summary: An object language is the language being described by a metalanguage.
concepts.body: An object language is the language being described by a metalanguage. The distinction separates a sentence from a statement about it.

examples.text: Snow is white may be object-language, while its truth claim is metalanguage.
examples.note: The latter discusses an expression in the former.

commonMisreadings: It need not discuss physical objects.

concepts.name: Objective-list theory
concepts.summary: Objective-list theory says well-being contains goods valuable independently of personal preference.
concepts.body: Objective-list theory says well-being contains goods valuable independently of personal preference. Knowledge, friendship, achievement, and health are common proposed goods.

examples.text: Learning a skill can improve a person's life despite no prior desire.
examples.note: The skill is valuable beyond preference satisfaction.

commonMisreadings: It is not hedonism because pleasure is not its only good.

concepts.name: Objectivism
concepts.summary: Objectivism is a view emphasizing mind-independent reality and truth, especially Ayn Rand's rationalist ethical system.
concepts.body: Objectivism is a view emphasizing mind-independent reality and truth, especially Ayn Rand's rationalist ethical system. Randian Objectivism endorses reason, rational self-interest, and individual rights.

examples.text: Choosing productive work to sustain rational independence fits Randian Objectivism.
examples.note: Productivity is linked to rational flourishing.

commonMisreadings: The label can also mean other forms of realism.

concepts.name: Objectivity
concepts.summary: Objectivity is judging by evidence and standards not dependent on private preference.
concepts.body: Objectivity is judging by evidence and standards not dependent on private preference. Science pursues it through public methods, reproducibility, and criticism.

examples.text: Two blinded laboratories comparing measurements illustrate objectivity.
examples.note: Shared procedures limit personal expectations.

commonMisreadings: It does not require observers to have no perspectives.

concepts.name: Obligation
concepts.summary: An obligation is a binding requirement to act or refrain from acting.
concepts.body: An obligation is a binding requirement to act or refrain from acting. It can arise from promises, law, roles, relationships, or morality.

examples.text: Returning a borrowed book fulfills an obligation created by a promise.
examples.note: The promise creates a requirement owed to another.

commonMisreadings: It is more than a strong preference.

concepts.name: Occasionalism
concepts.summary: Occasionalism says created things do not genuinely cause events; God directly produces them.
concepts.body: Occasionalism says created things do not genuinely cause events; God directly produces them. The view is associated with Islamic theology and Malebranche.

examples.text: A hand's movement occasions a ball's motion without causing it.
examples.note: Divine action supplies the efficient cause.

commonMisreadings: It is not deism's hands-off creator.

concepts.name: Omnipotence paradox
concepts.summary: The omnipotence paradox asks whether an all-powerful being can create a stone it cannot lift.
concepts.body: The omnipotence paradox asks whether an all-powerful being can create a stone it cannot lift. Many replies restrict omnipotence to logically possible actions.

examples.text: Calling the task contradictory resolves it for a classical theologian.
examples.note: The problem is treated as incoherent description.

commonMisreadings: It does not refute every definition of omnipotence.

concepts.name: Ontic structural realism
concepts.summary: Ontic structural realism treats relational structure as fundamental and objects as derivative.
concepts.body: Ontic structural realism treats relational structure as fundamental and objects as derivative. It is motivated partly by the relational character of modern physics.

examples.text: An electron may be identified by its position in a physical structure.
examples.note: Relations explain identity more basically than intrinsic essence.

commonMisreadings: It is stronger than epistemic structural realism.

concepts.name: Ontological argument
concepts.summary: An ontological argument seeks God's existence from the concept of a perfect or necessary being.
concepts.body: An ontological argument seeks God's existence from the concept of a perfect or necessary being. Anselm and modal versions use different premises about perfection or necessity.

examples.text: If a necessarily existing perfect being is possible, modal reasoning entails its actual existence.
examples.note: The argument is conceptual rather than empirical.

commonMisreadings: It is not a cosmological argument from contingent causes.

concepts.name: Ontological commitment
concepts.summary: Ontological commitment is the set of entities a theory must accept for its claims to be true.
concepts.body: Ontological commitment is the set of entities a theory must accept for its claims to be true. Quine connects commitment to what a theory's quantified variables range over.

examples.text: There are prime numbers commits mathematical theory to numbers.
examples.note: The variables require mathematical entities in the interpretation.

commonMisreadings: Mentioning a thing alone does not establish commitment.

concepts.name: Ontology
concepts.summary: Ontology studies what exists and how existing kinds are structured.
concepts.body: Ontology studies what exists and how existing kinds are structured. It considers objects, properties, events, relations, minds, and numbers.

examples.text: Asking whether events are entities distinct from substances is ontology.
examples.note: The question concerns reality's inventory.

commonMisreadings: It is not merely taxonomy.

concepts.name: Operationalism
concepts.summary: Operationalism defines a concept through the operations used to measure or test it.
concepts.body: Operationalism defines a concept through the operations used to measure or test it. Percy Bridgman associated it with specifying reproducible procedures.

examples.text: Temperature can be defined by a calibrated thermometer reading.
examples.note: The operation gives the term experimental use.

commonMisreadings: It need not deny theoretical entities.

concepts.name: Opportunity cost
concepts.summary: Opportunity cost is the value of the best alternative forgone by a choice.
concepts.body: Opportunity cost is the value of the best alternative forgone by a choice. It applies to time and resources even without monetary payment.

examples.text: Studying instead of working costs the best available paid shift.
examples.note: The rejected best alternative is the relevant cost.

commonMisreadings: It is not the value of every rejected option.

concepts.name: Ordinary language philosophy
concepts.summary: Ordinary-language philosophy examines how words function in everyday contexts.
concepts.body: Ordinary-language philosophy examines how words function in everyday contexts. It often diagnoses problems created by removing expressions from their practical use.

examples.text: Comparing ordinary uses of know analyzes a knowledge puzzle.
examples.note: Usage distinctions replace an assumed hidden entity.

commonMisreadings: It can still employ rigorous argument.

concepts.name: Organicism
concepts.summary: Organicism explains organisms or societies as integrated wholes whose parts depend on organization.
concepts.body: Organicism explains organisms or societies as integrated wholes whose parts depend on organization. Social organicism opposes reducing society to isolated individuals.

examples.text: A heart is understood through its role in maintaining the body.
examples.note: Its function depends on the whole.

commonMisreadings: It does not say every system is literally biological.

concepts.name: Original position
concepts.summary: The original position is Rawls's hypothetical choice situation behind a veil of ignorance.
concepts.body: The original position is Rawls's hypothetical choice situation behind a veil of ignorance. Representatives do not know their class, talents, gender, or religion.

examples.text: Choosing rules without knowing whether one will be rich illustrates it.
examples.note: Ignorance blocks bargaining for actual advantage.

commonMisreadings: It is not a historical founding meeting.

concepts.name: Pacifism
concepts.summary: Pacifism rejects war and, in stronger forms, intentional violence.
concepts.body: Pacifism rejects war and, in stronger forms, intentional violence. Its arguments may appeal to killing's wrongness or nonviolent alternatives.

examples.text: Civil disobedience without armed retaliation exemplifies pacifism.
examples.note: Political resistance occurs without violence.

commonMisreadings: It is not passivity.

concepts.name: Paleoconservatism
concepts.summary: Paleoconservatism emphasizes national sovereignty, tradition, and skepticism toward interventionist foreign policy.
concepts.body: Paleoconservatism emphasizes national sovereignty, tradition, and skepticism toward interventionist foreign policy. It often criticizes cosmopolitan institutions and expansive federal power.

examples.text: A politician favoring strict immigration limits and non-intervention expresses it.
examples.note: Traditionalism and foreign-policy restraint combine here.

commonMisreadings: It is not all conservatism.

concepts.name: Pan-Africanism
concepts.summary: Pan-Africanism promotes solidarity among African peoples and their global descendants.
concepts.body: Pan-Africanism promotes solidarity among African peoples and their global descendants. It has opposed colonialism, racism, and political fragmentation.

examples.text: The Organization of African Unity expressed continental solidarity.
examples.note: Independent states coordinated around shared African interests.

commonMisreadings: It is transnational rather than ethnic to one group.

concepts.name: Pan-Arabism
concepts.summary: Pan-Arabism holds that Arabs share a cultural and political nation deserving solidarity or unity.
concepts.body: Pan-Arabism holds that Arabs share a cultural and political nation deserving solidarity or unity. Nasserism and Ba'athism gave it major twentieth-century influence.

examples.text: The 1958 United Arab Republic was a unification project.
examples.note: Egypt and Syria joined under shared Arab identity.

commonMisreadings: It is not Islamism.

concepts.name: Pan-Slavism
concepts.summary: Pan-Slavism promotes cultural or political unity among Slavic peoples.
concepts.body: Pan-Slavism promotes cultural or political unity among Slavic peoples. Its versions ranged from Russian imperialism to liberation movements.

examples.text: Slavic congresses promoting shared culture expressed Pan-Slavism.
examples.note: Common language and ancestry linked communities.

commonMisreadings: It was never one agreed political program.

concepts.name: Panentheism
concepts.summary: Panentheism says the world exists within God while God exceeds the world.
concepts.body: Panentheism says the world exists within God while God exceeds the world. It combines divine immanence with divine transcendence.

examples.text: A theologian saying the universe is in God but not all of God is panentheistic.
examples.note: The claim includes nature without exhausting divinity.

commonMisreadings: It differs from pantheism.

concepts.name: Panexperientialism
concepts.summary: Panexperientialism attributes experience or proto-experience to all entities.
concepts.body: Panexperientialism attributes experience or proto-experience to all entities. It is associated with process philosophy and primitive feeling.

examples.text: A process philosopher may assign an electron minimal experience.
examples.note: The experience is rudimentary, not reflective.

commonMisreadings: It does not give every object a human mind.

concepts.name: Panpsychism
concepts.summary: Panpsychism holds that mentality or consciousness is fundamental and widespread in nature.
concepts.body: Panpsychism holds that mentality or consciousness is fundamental and widespread in nature. Many versions attribute minimal experience to fundamental entities.

examples.text: Treating particles as having basic phenomenal properties is panpsychism.
examples.note: Physical particles receive a mental aspect.

commonMisreadings: It is not necessarily animism.

concepts.name: Pantheism
concepts.summary: Pantheism identifies God with the universe or totality of reality.
concepts.body: Pantheism identifies God with the universe or totality of reality. It treats divinity as immanent rather than a distinct external creator.

examples.text: Calling the whole of nature divine expresses pantheism.
examples.note: The universe and divine reality are equated.

commonMisreadings: It differs from panentheism because it denies a divine excess.

concepts.name: Paraconsistent logic
concepts.summary: Paraconsistent logic allows contradictions without entailing every proposition.
concepts.body: Paraconsistent logic allows contradictions without entailing every proposition. It supports controlled reasoning from inconsistent information.

examples.text: A database can contain both fire and no-fire reports without proving the moon is cheese.
examples.note: Contradiction does not cause explosion.

commonMisreadings: It does not make every contradiction harmless or true.

concepts.name: Paradigm
concepts.summary: A paradigm is a shared model or framework guiding inquiry in a field.
concepts.body: A paradigm is a shared model or framework guiding inquiry in a field. Kuhn's paradigm includes methods, standards, problems, and examples.

examples.text: Classical mechanics organized motion research before relativity.
examples.note: It structured questions and acceptable solutions.

commonMisreadings: It is more than one isolated theory.

concepts.name: Paradigm shift
concepts.summary: A paradigm shift transforms a field's basic problems, methods, and explanatory framework.
concepts.body: A paradigm shift transforms a field's basic problems, methods, and explanatory framework. Kuhn said shifts can change how observations are classified.

examples.text: Relativity transformed concepts of space, time, and motion.
examples.note: The new framework reorganized basic categories.

commonMisreadings: It is not a minor improvement.

concepts.name: Paradox of fiction
concepts.summary: The paradox of fiction asks how fictional characters can cause genuine emotions despite nonexistence.
concepts.body: The paradox of fiction asks how fictional characters can cause genuine emotions despite nonexistence. Responses invoke imagination, quasi-emotion, or non-belief-based affect.

examples.text: A reader fears for Anna Karenina while knowing she is fictional.
examples.note: Knowledge and emotion coexist in the case.

commonMisreadings: The reader need not believe the character is real.

concepts.name: Paradox of hedonism
concepts.summary: The paradox of hedonism says directly pursuing pleasure can prevent obtaining it.
concepts.body: The paradox of hedonism says directly pursuing pleasure can prevent obtaining it. Sidgwick linked the problem to making happiness one's sole conscious goal.

examples.text: Monitoring every moment's pleasure can reduce enjoyment.
examples.note: Attention to the goal interferes with the desired state.

commonMisreadings: It does not show pleasure lacks value.

concepts.name: Paradox of tolerance
concepts.summary: The paradox of tolerance says unlimited tolerance may permit intolerant forces to destroy tolerance.
concepts.body: The paradox of tolerance says unlimited tolerance may permit intolerant forces to destroy tolerance. Popper argued that tolerant societies may restrict movements seeking coercive domination.

examples.text: Banning a group planning to abolish elections presents the dilemma.
examples.note: Restriction protects institutions from anti-tolerant capture.

commonMisreadings: It does not justify suppressing every unpopular view.

concepts.name: Pareto efficiency
concepts.summary: Pareto efficiency is a state where no feasible change benefits someone without harming someone else.
concepts.body: Pareto efficiency is a state where no feasible change benefits someone without harming someone else. It measures non-waste, not equality or justice.

examples.text: One owner holding two houses can be Pareto-efficient if transfer harms that owner.
examples.note: No improvement is possible without a loss under the options.

commonMisreadings: Efficiency does not imply fairness.

concepts.name: Parfit's repugnant conclusion
concepts.summary: Parfit's repugnant conclusion says some assumptions rank a huge population with barely worthwhile lives above a smaller flourishing population.
concepts.body: Parfit's repugnant conclusion says some assumptions rank a huge population with barely worthwhile lives above a smaller flourishing population. Parfit derived it through population comparisons under total welfare.

examples.text: Billions with minimally positive welfare can outrank millions with excellent lives.
examples.note: Adding positive lives drives the comparison.

commonMisreadings: Parfit presented it as troubling, not endorsed.

concepts.name: Part-list cueing effect
concepts.summary: The part-list cueing effect is reduced recall of unprompted items after some studied items are presented as cues.
concepts.body: The part-list cueing effect is reduced recall of unprompted items after some studied items are presented as cues. The cues can create retrieval competition or inhibition.

examples.text: Seeing apple and pear can impair recall of other studied fruits.
examples.note: The presented subset disrupts access to the remainder.

commonMisreadings: It is not ordinary forgetting alone.

concepts.name: Partiality
concepts.summary: Partiality gives special consideration to particular people, groups, or relationships.
concepts.body: Partiality gives special consideration to particular people, groups, or relationships. Partialist ethics can treat family and friendship duties as legitimate.

examples.text: A parent aiding their child before strangers acts partially.
examples.note: The special relationship grounds priority.

commonMisreadings: Partiality need not be unjustified bias.

concepts.name: Participatory democracy
concepts.summary: Participatory democracy gives citizens an active role in making political decisions.
concepts.body: Participatory democracy gives citizens an active role in making political decisions. It can use assemblies, participatory budgeting, and workplace democracy.

examples.text: Residents directly allocating part of a city budget practice it.
examples.note: Citizens decide policy rather than only electing officials.

commonMisreadings: It can coexist with representative democracy.

concepts.name: Particular
concepts.summary: A particular is one specific entity, contrasted with a repeatable universal.
concepts.body: A particular is one specific entity, contrasted with a repeatable universal. Individual objects and events can be particulars.

examples.text: This red apple is a particular, unlike redness itself.
examples.note: It has a unique history despite shared color.

commonMisreadings: A particular need not be physical in every theory.

concepts.name: Paternalism
concepts.summary: Paternalism interferes with a person's choice to protect that person's welfare.
concepts.body: Paternalism interferes with a person's choice to protect that person's welfare. Soft forms target ignorance or incapacity, while hard forms override informed choice.

examples.text: Mandatory motorcycle helmets are defended as paternalistic safety rules.
examples.note: The restriction protects the chooser rather than others.

commonMisreadings: Not every safety law is paternalistic.

concepts.name: Path dependence
concepts.summary: Path dependence means present outcomes depend strongly on the sequence of earlier events.
concepts.body: Path dependence means present outcomes depend strongly on the sequence of earlier events. Switching costs, increasing returns, and institutional inertia can sustain it.

examples.text: QWERTY's persistence despite alternative layouts is a common example.
examples.note: Early adoption made later change costly.

commonMisreadings: It is more than mere historical influence.

concepts.name: Patient-centered ethics
concepts.summary: Patient-centered ethics prioritizes a patient's values, preferences, interests, and informed participation.
concepts.body: Patient-centered ethics prioritizes a patient's values, preferences, interests, and informed participation. It treats the patient as a person rather than only as a disease case.

examples.text: A clinician selecting treatment through discussion of the patient's goals follows it.
examples.note: The patient's conception of a good outcome guides care.

commonMisreadings: It remains constrained by safety and professional duties.

concepts.name: Patriotism
concepts.summary: Patriotism is attachment and concern for one's country expressed through loyalty or service.
concepts.body: Patriotism is attachment and concern for one's country expressed through loyalty or service. It can be critical, supporting national principles while opposing injustice.

examples.text: A citizen opposing an unjust law to defend constitutional ideals shows critical patriotism.
examples.note: Opposition is motivated by concern for the country's character.

commonMisreadings: It need not be nationalism or superiority.

concepts.name: Peer disagreement
concepts.summary: Peer disagreement is conflict between people similarly competent, informed, and sincere.
concepts.body: Peer disagreement is conflict between people similarly competent, informed, and sincere. It can provide evidence that one's own reasoning may be mistaken.

examples.text: Two equally trained astronomers disagreeing over the same data are epistemic peers.
examples.note: Comparable expertise makes revision relevant.

commonMisreadings: Any disagreement is not automatically peer disagreement.

concepts.name: Perception
concepts.summary: Perception is organized sensory acquisition of an environment's objects and events.
concepts.body: Perception is organized sensory acquisition of an environment's objects and events. It may be direct or inferential depending on philosophical theory.

examples.text: Seeing a tree combines light stimulation with an experienced object at a location.
examples.note: Sensory input is organized into world-directed experience.

commonMisreadings: Perception is not raw sensation alone.

concepts.name: Perdurantism
concepts.summary: Perdurantism says an object persists by having distinct temporal parts.
concepts.body: Perdurantism says an object persists by having distinct temporal parts. It treats a persisting thing as extended through time like a whole with spatial parts.

examples.text: Seed, sapling, and mature tree can be temporal parts of one tree.
examples.note: Stages compose one four-dimensional object.

commonMisreadings: It differs from endurantism, where the whole is present at each time.

concepts.name: Perennialism
concepts.summary: Perennialism holds that enduring spiritual truths recur across different traditions.
concepts.body: Perennialism holds that enduring spiritual truths recur across different traditions. Comparative perennialists seek a common transcendent unity beneath doctrines.

examples.text: A scholar identifying one mystical truth in Hindu, Christian, and Sufi texts is perennialist.
examples.note: The comparison emphasizes shared essence.

commonMisreadings: It is stronger than ordinary religious pluralism.

concepts.name: Perfect duty
concepts.summary: A perfect duty is a strict moral requirement allowing no discretion about whether to perform it.
concepts.body: A perfect duty is a strict moral requirement allowing no discretion about whether to perform it. Kant treats false promises as examples of perfect duties.

examples.text: A borrower cannot break a repayment promise merely for convenience.
examples.note: The duty excludes choosing whether to honor it.

commonMisreadings: It concerns strictness, not guaranteed outcomes.

concepts.name: Performative utterance
concepts.summary: A performative utterance performs an action in being appropriately spoken.
concepts.body: A performative utterance performs an action in being appropriately spoken. Austin analyzed promises, apologies, naming, and declarations through felicity conditions.

examples.text: Saying I apologize in the right context performs an apology.
examples.note: The speech act changes a social situation rather than reporting one.

commonMisreadings: It can fail when context is inappropriate.

concepts.name: Persistence
concepts.summary: Persistence is continued existence or identity across different times.
concepts.body: Persistence is continued existence or identity across different times. Theories include endurantism, perdurantism, and stage theory.

examples.text: A river persists despite replacement of its water.
examples.note: Organizational continuity supports identity.

commonMisreadings: Persistence is not mere resemblance.

concepts.name: Personal identity
concepts.summary: Personal identity concerns what makes a person at one time the same person later.
concepts.body: Personal identity concerns what makes a person at one time the same person later. Candidates include bodily, psychological, memory, brain, and narrative continuity.

examples.text: Retained memories and intentions support psychological identity.
examples.note: Mental relations connect the later person to the earlier one.

commonMisreadings: It is not identical to unchanged personality.

concepts.name: Personalism
concepts.summary: Personalism treats the person as a fundamental bearer of dignity and moral agency.
concepts.body: Personalism treats the person as a fundamental bearer of dignity and moral agency. It emphasizes freedom, responsibility, and relationality.

examples.text: Rejecting use of a patient solely for institutional efficiency is personalist.
examples.note: The patient remains an end with intrinsic dignity.

commonMisreadings: It differs from individualism because persons can be relational.

concepts.name: Personhood
concepts.summary: Personhood is the status of being a person with associated rights, duties, or moral consideration.
concepts.body: Personhood is the status of being a person with associated rights, duties, or moral consideration. Criteria may include consciousness, rationality, self-awareness, biology, or recognition.

examples.text: A corporation's legal personhood is juridical rather than biological.
examples.note: The corporation receives legal standing without being human.

commonMisreadings: Personhood and humanity are not identical in every context.

concepts.name: Perspectivism
concepts.summary: Perspectivism says knowledge and interpretation are situated from particular standpoints.
concepts.body: Perspectivism says knowledge and interpretation are situated from particular standpoints. It need not say all perspectives are equally good.

examples.text: A participant and archivist may give differently informative accounts of an event.
examples.note: Each account reflects position and available information.

commonMisreadings: It is not automatically relativism.

concepts.name: Phenomenal consciousness
concepts.summary: Phenomenal consciousness is the felt qualitative character of experience.
concepts.body: Phenomenal consciousness is the felt qualitative character of experience. Examples include pain, redness, and the taste of coffee.

examples.text: The painful feel of touching a hot pan is phenomenal consciousness.
examples.note: The focus is subjective experience, not withdrawal behavior.

commonMisreadings: It differs from access consciousness.

concepts.name: Phenomenalism
concepts.summary: Phenomenalism analyzes physical objects through actual or possible sensory experiences.
concepts.body: Phenomenalism analyzes physical objects through actual or possible sensory experiences. A table may be defined by stable patterns of possible visual and tactile experience.

examples.text: The table exists as what would be experienced under suitable conditions.
examples.note: Counterfactual experience supplies object stability.

commonMisreadings: It does not require objects to vanish when unobserved.

concepts.name: Phenomenology
concepts.summary: Phenomenology studies structures and meanings of lived first-person experience.
concepts.body: Phenomenology studies structures and meanings of lived first-person experience. It examines intentionality, embodiment, temporality, and perception.

examples.text: Analyzing how a remembered melody unfolds is phenomenology.
examples.note: The temporal structure of experience is described.

commonMisreadings: It is not merely introspective psychology.

concepts.name: Philosophical behaviorism
concepts.summary: Philosophical behaviorism analyzes mental states as behavior or dispositions to behave.
concepts.body: Philosophical behaviorism analyzes mental states as behavior or dispositions to behave. Ryle used it to challenge the mind as a hidden separate substance.

examples.text: A belief can be described through how someone reasons and responds.
examples.note: Behavioral criteria replace an occult inner object.

commonMisreadings: It does not eliminate mental vocabulary.

concepts.name: Philosophical pessimism
