concepts.summary: Philosophical pessimism holds that suffering or frustration fundamentally outweighs or conditions life's value.
concepts.body: Philosophical pessimism holds that suffering or frustration fundamentally outweighs or conditions life's value. Schopenhauer linked desire to recurring dissatisfaction.

examples.text: Treating ordinary striving as a cycle of need expresses pessimism.
examples.note: The judgment concerns existence's structure, not one setback.

commonMisreadings: It is not clinical depression.

concepts.name: Philosophical quietism
concepts.summary: Philosophical quietism dissolves philosophical problems through clarification rather than substantive theory.
concepts.body: Philosophical quietism dissolves philosophical problems through clarification rather than substantive theory. It often identifies words used outside their ordinary practical roles.

examples.text: Showing that where has different senses can dissolve a mind-location puzzle.
examples.note: Linguistic clarification removes the apparent problem.

commonMisreadings: It is not intellectual inactivity.

concepts.name: Philosophical zombie
concepts.summary: A philosophical zombie is physically human-like but lacks phenomenal consciousness.
concepts.body: A philosophical zombie is physically human-like but lacks phenomenal consciousness. Chalmers uses the thought experiment to question physical entailment of experience.

examples.text: A zombie reports pain and behaves normally while feeling nothing.
examples.note: Physical duplication is stipulated without subjective experience.

commonMisreadings: It is not merely an unusual person.

concepts.name: Philosophy of liberation
concepts.summary: Philosophy of liberation analyzes oppression from marginalized standpoints and seeks emancipatory transformation.
concepts.body: Philosophy of liberation analyzes oppression from marginalized standpoints and seeks emancipatory transformation. Latin American versions emphasize coloniality, exclusion, and victims.

examples.text: Beginning ethics from colonized people's poverty and exclusion is liberation philosophy.
examples.note: Oppressed experience guides diagnosis and theory.

commonMisreadings: It is philosophy as well as activism.

concepts.name: Philosophy of literature
concepts.summary: Philosophy of literature studies literature's nature, interpretation, value, and cognitive or ethical significance.
concepts.body: Philosophy of literature studies literature's nature, interpretation, value, and cognitive or ethical significance. It addresses fiction, metaphor, authorship, imagination, and literary value.

examples.text: Asking whether novels provide moral knowledge is philosophy of literature.
examples.note: The question concerns literature's philosophical contribution.

commonMisreadings: It is not every form of literary criticism.

concepts.name: Philosophy of religion
concepts.summary: Philosophy of religion critically examines religious concepts and arguments.
concepts.body: Philosophy of religion critically examines religious concepts and arguments. It addresses God, faith, evil, revelation, and religious experience.

examples.text: The argument from evil is a philosophy-of-religion problem.
examples.note: It tests compatibility between divine goodness and suffering.

commonMisreadings: It differs from theology's usual internal commitment.

concepts.name: Philosophy of science
concepts.summary: Philosophy of science studies science's concepts, methods, foundations, and rational structure.
concepts.body: Philosophy of science studies science's concepts, methods, foundations, and rational structure. It examines explanation, confirmation, laws, models, and realism.

examples.text: Asking whether successful theories are literally true is philosophy of science.
examples.note: The issue concerns what scientific success warrants.

commonMisreadings: It is not merely scientific history.

concepts.name: Physicalism
concepts.summary: Physicalism says everything is physical or wholly dependent on the physical.
concepts.body: Physicalism says everything is physical or wholly dependent on the physical. Reductive and nonreductive versions disagree about mental properties.

examples.text: A physicalist may say consciousness depends completely on neural state.
examples.note: Mind is included in a physically complete ontology.

commonMisreadings: It is not identical to behaviorism.

concepts.name: Picture-superiority effect
concepts.summary: The picture-superiority effect is better memory for pictures than equivalent words.
concepts.body: The picture-superiority effect is better memory for pictures than equivalent words. Pictures support richer perceptual and associative encoding.

examples.text: A bicycle drawing is often recalled better than the word bicycle.
examples.note: The image supplies visual features as well as meaning.

commonMisreadings: It is a tendency, not an exceptionless law.

concepts.name: Placebo effect
concepts.summary: The placebo effect is an outcome change produced by treatment context, expectation, or conditioning rather than active ingredients.
concepts.body: The placebo effect is an outcome change produced by treatment context, expectation, or conditioning rather than active ingredients. It can alter pain reports and some bodily processes without treating every disease.

examples.text: An inert pill described as analgesic may reduce a patient's pain.
examples.note: Expectation and context influence pain experience.

commonMisreadings: It does not show illness is imaginary.

concepts.name: Platonism
concepts.summary: Platonism holds that abstract entities exist independently of human minds.
concepts.body: Platonism holds that abstract entities exist independently of human minds. Mathematical Platonism treats numbers as discovered rather than invented.

examples.text: Saying seven exists without humans is mathematical Platonism.
examples.note: The number is mind-independent and abstract.

commonMisreadings: Modern Platonism need not reproduce all of Plato's philosophy.

concepts.name: Pluralism in metaphysics
concepts.summary: Metaphysical pluralism holds that reality has multiple irreducible fundamental kinds or principles.
concepts.body: Metaphysical pluralism holds that reality has multiple irreducible fundamental kinds or principles. It may treat physical, mental, abstract, and normative facts as distinct.

examples.text: A theory refusing to reduce minds and numbers to matter is pluralist.
examples.note: Several basic ontological categories remain.

commonMisreadings: It concerns reality, not political pluralism.

concepts.name: Political obligation
concepts.summary: Political obligation is an alleged moral duty to obey laws or support political authority.
concepts.body: Political obligation is an alleged moral duty to obey laws or support political authority. Arguments invoke consent, fair play, natural duty, or social cooperation.

examples.text: Paying taxes because a just cooperative scheme creates duties invokes it.
examples.note: Membership and cooperation explain the requirement.

commonMisreadings: Legal obligation and moral obligation can diverge.

concepts.name: Political representation
concepts.summary: Political representation is acting, speaking, or deciding on behalf of constituents.
concepts.body: Political representation is acting, speaking, or deciding on behalf of constituents. It may be electoral, descriptive, symbolic, or substantive.

examples.text: An elected legislator voting for district interests represents constituents.
examples.note: The official decides under an authorized relationship.

commonMisreadings: Representation does not require personal resemblance.

concepts.name: Political sovereignty
concepts.summary: Political sovereignty is supreme authority within a political community or territory.
concepts.body: Political sovereignty is supreme authority within a political community or territory. It can belong to a monarch, state, people, or constitution.

examples.text: A constitution locating final authority in citizens expresses popular sovereignty.
examples.note: Citizens are the ultimate source of binding authority.

commonMisreadings: Sovereignty need not mean unlimited practical power.

concepts.name: Polytheism
concepts.summary: Polytheism recognizes multiple gods or divine beings.
concepts.body: Polytheism recognizes multiple gods or divine beings. Gods may have distinct domains, powers, and relationships.

examples.text: Greek worship of Zeus, Athena, and Apollo is polytheistic.
examples.note: Several divine agents occupy one religious system.

commonMisreadings: It is more specific than belief in many supernatural beings.

concepts.name: Populism
concepts.summary: Populism frames politics as a morally pure people against a corrupt elite.
concepts.body: Populism frames politics as a morally pure people against a corrupt elite. It can attach to left or right substantive ideologies.

examples.text: A party claiming only it represents ordinary citizens uses populism.
examples.note: People-versus-elite rhetoric supplies the core frame.

commonMisreadings: It is not identical to democracy.

concepts.name: Positive liberty
concepts.summary: Positive liberty is effective capacity to pursue purposes and exercise agency.
concepts.body: Positive liberty is effective capacity to pursue purposes and exercise agency. It contrasts with freedom from interference.

examples.text: Public education can increase positive liberty by developing capabilities.
examples.note: Resources expand what people can actually do.

commonMisreadings: It need not dictate a person's ends.

concepts.name: Positivism
concepts.summary: Positivism grounds reliable knowledge in observation, scientific method, or formal analysis.
concepts.body: Positivism grounds reliable knowledge in observation, scientific method, or formal analysis. Logical positivism also used verificationist and anti-metaphysical criteria.

examples.text: Rejecting an unverifiable assertion as non-scientific applies positivism.
examples.note: Empirical or logical testability sets the standard.

commonMisreadings: It is stronger than merely respecting science.

concepts.name: Positivity offset
concepts.summary: The positivity offset is a tendency toward slightly more positive than negative affect in ordinary neutral conditions.
concepts.body: The positivity offset is a tendency toward slightly more positive than negative affect in ordinary neutral conditions. Stress, illness, personality, and context can alter it.

examples.text: Mild contentment during an uneventful day illustrates the offset.
examples.note: Positive affect occurs without a special happy event.

commonMisreadings: It differs from optimism about the future.

concepts.name: Possible world
concepts.summary: A possible world is a complete way reality could have been.
concepts.body: A possible world is a complete way reality could have been. Modal semantics uses worlds to evaluate necessity, possibility, and counterfactuals.

examples.text: A world where it rains can make it could have rained true.
examples.note: The structured scenario represents an alternative condition.

commonMisreadings: It need not be a parallel physical universe.

concepts.name: Post-anarchism
concepts.summary: Post-anarchism revises anarchist opposition to domination using poststructuralist accounts of power and identity.
concepts.body: Post-anarchism revises anarchist opposition to domination using poststructuralist accounts of power and identity. It rejects fixed revolutionary subjects while retaining anti-hierarchical resistance.

examples.text: Decentralized activists analyzing produced identities exemplify post-anarchism.
examples.note: Anti-authoritarian politics combines with nonessentialist theory.

commonMisreadings: It extends rather than simply abandons anarchism.

concepts.name: Post-Marxism
concepts.summary: Post-Marxism revises Marxism in response to changes in capitalism, culture, and class politics.
concepts.body: Post-Marxism revises Marxism in response to changes in capitalism, culture, and class politics. It emphasizes discourse, contingency, hegemony, and multiple antagonisms.

examples.text: Explaining coalition politics through race, gender, discourse, and class is post-Marxist.
examples.note: Conflict remains without one economic foundation.

commonMisreadings: It is not simply anti-Marxism.

concepts.name: Post-positivism
concepts.summary: Post-positivism accepts evidence and testing while rejecting strong claims of neutral certainty.
concepts.body: Post-positivism accepts evidence and testing while rejecting strong claims of neutral certainty. It treats knowledge as fallible, theory-laden, and revisable.

examples.text: Treating an experiment as support rather than proof is post-positivist.
examples.note: Empirical method is combined with fallibilism.

commonMisreadings: It is not relativism.

concepts.name: Postcolonialism
concepts.summary: Postcolonialism studies continuing political, cultural, economic, and epistemic effects of colonial rule.
concepts.body: Postcolonialism studies continuing political, cultural, economic, and epistemic effects of colonial rule. It examines representation, hybridity, resistance, and coloniality after independence.

examples.text: Critiquing a museum's European portrayal of colonized peoples is postcolonial analysis.
examples.note: Colonial power persists through knowledge and representation.

commonMisreadings: It includes colonial histories, not only post-independence events.

concepts.name: Posthumanism
concepts.summary: Posthumanism questions human exceptionalism and boundaries among humans, animals, machines, and environments.
concepts.body: Posthumanism questions human exceptionalism and boundaries among humans, animals, machines, and environments. It critiques the autonomous human subject as the sole center of value.

examples.text: Including animals and ecosystems in theories of agency is posthumanist.
examples.note: Moral and political analysis extends beyond isolated humans.

commonMisreadings: It need not be anti-human.

concepts.name: Postmodernism
concepts.summary: Postmodernism questions universal foundations, grand narratives, stable meaning, and straightforward progress.
concepts.body: Postmodernism questions universal foundations, grand narratives, stable meaning, and straightforward progress. It appears in philosophy, art, architecture, literature, and social theory.

examples.text: An eclectic building rejecting one governing style is often postmodern.
examples.note: Plurality and irony shape its design.

commonMisreadings: It is not simply anything contemporary.

concepts.name: Poststructuralism
concepts.summary: Poststructuralism questions stable structures, fixed identities, and transparent language.
concepts.body: Poststructuralism questions stable structures, fixed identities, and transparent language. Derrida, Foucault, and Deleuze analyze discourse, difference, and power.

examples.text: Showing madness categories are institutionally produced is poststructuralist.
examples.note: A supposed essence is treated as historically constructed.

commonMisreadings: It studies structures rather than denying all structure.

concepts.name: Potentiality and actuality
concepts.summary: Potentiality and actuality distinguish what a thing can become from what it currently realizes.
concepts.body: Potentiality and actuality distinguish what a thing can become from what it currently realizes. Aristotle uses them to explain change and development.

examples.text: An acorn is potentially an oak, while the mature tree is actual.
examples.note: Capacity and realized form illustrate the distinction.

commonMisreadings: Potentiality is more than bare logical possibility.

concepts.name: Power
concepts.summary: Power is the capacity to influence actions, outcomes, resources, or conduct.
concepts.body: Power is the capacity to influence actions, outcomes, resources, or conduct. It can operate through coercion, incentives, norms, knowledge, or dependence.

examples.text: A legislature has power when its laws change citizens' choices.
examples.note: Authority and enforcement alter conduct.

commonMisreadings: Power is broader than physical force.

concepts.name: Practical reason
concepts.summary: Practical reason deliberates about what to do, which ends to pursue, and how to achieve them.
concepts.body: Practical reason deliberates about what to do, which ends to pursue, and how to achieve them. It differs from theoretical reason, which primarily seeks truth.

examples.text: Choosing the fastest route to arrive before noon uses practical reason.
examples.note: Means are evaluated relative to an intended end.

commonMisreadings: It can assess ends as well as calculate means.

concepts.name: Pragmatic encroachment
concepts.summary: Pragmatic encroachment is the view that practical stakes can affect whether a person knows or is justified in believing a proposition.
concepts.body: Pragmatic encroachment is the view that practical stakes can affect whether a person knows or is justified in believing a proposition. On this view, the same evidence may suffice for knowledge in a low-stakes setting but not when an error would be costly.

examples.text: A bank customer may know the bank is open when merely passing by but not before risking a large payment.
examples.note: The costly decision raises the practical standard relevant to the knowledge judgment.

commonMisreadings: It does not mean that truth itself changes with a person's interests.

concepts.name: Pragmaticism
concepts.summary: Pragmaticism is Charles Sanders Peirce's version of pragmatism, linking a concept's meaning to its conceivable practical effects.
concepts.body: Pragmaticism is Charles Sanders Peirce's version of pragmatism, linking a concept's meaning to its conceivable practical effects. Peirce renamed his doctrine to distinguish it from broader uses of the word pragmatism.

examples.text: The meaning of hardness includes what would happen under relevant tests of scratching or pressure.
examples.note: Those possible experimental consequences express the concept's practical meaning.

commonMisreadings: It is not simply the advice to choose whatever works in an immediate situation.

concepts.name: Pragmatics
concepts.summary: Pragmatics is the study of how context affects the interpretation and use of language.
concepts.body: Pragmatics is the study of how context affects the interpretation and use of language. It examines implicature, presupposition, deixis, speech acts, and conversational norms.

examples.text: The sentence “Can you pass the salt?” usually functions as a request rather than a question about ability.
examples.note: The conversational setting supplies the intended force beyond the literal wording.

commonMisreadings: Pragmatics differs from semantics, which studies meaning encoded by linguistic expressions.

concepts.name: Pragmatism
concepts.summary: Pragmatism is a philosophical tradition that evaluates beliefs partly by their practical consequences, inquiry, and problem-solving success.
concepts.body: Pragmatism is a philosophical tradition that evaluates beliefs partly by their practical consequences, inquiry, and problem-solving success. Classical pragmatists include Peirce, William James, and John Dewey, although they developed distinct versions.

examples.text: A scientist treats a theory as warranted when sustained inquiry and testing support its predictions.
examples.note: Its practical success is evidence within inquiry, not a license to call every useful belief true.

commonMisreadings: Pragmatism is not identical to short-term usefulness or opportunism.

concepts.name: Precautionary principle
concepts.summary: The precautionary principle holds that lack of complete scientific certainty should not automatically delay measures against serious or irreversible harm.
concepts.body: The precautionary principle holds that lack of complete scientific certainty should not automatically delay measures against serious or irreversible harm. Its strongest formulations place the burden of proof on activities that pose substantial environmental or health risks.

examples.text: A government may restrict a persistent chemical before long-term ecological effects are fully known.
examples.note: The restriction responds to potentially irreversible damage under uncertainty.

commonMisreadings: The principle does not require banning every activity that has any conceivable risk.

concepts.name: Predicate
concepts.summary: A predicate is an expression that attributes a property or relation to one or more arguments and thereby forms a sentence when completed.
concepts.body: A predicate is an expression that attributes a property or relation to one or more arguments and thereby forms a sentence when completed. In “Socrates is mortal,” “is mortal” is a one-place predicate applied to Socrates.

examples.text: In “Mira admires Lee,” “admires” is a two-place predicate relating Mira and Lee.
examples.note: The verb requires two arguments to express the stated relation.

commonMisreadings: A predicate is not the same thing as a complete proposition.

concepts.name: Predictive processing
concepts.summary: Predictive processing is a framework in which the brain is modeled as continuously generating predictions and updating them from sensory prediction errors.
concepts.body: Predictive processing is a framework in which the brain is modeled as continuously generating predictions and updating them from sensory prediction errors. Perception can result from combining top-down expectations with bottom-up signals weighted by estimated precision.

examples.text: A faint spoken word may be heard differently depending on the surrounding sentence.
examples.note: Contextual expectations help explain the perceptual interpretation of ambiguous input.

commonMisreadings: The framework does not claim that perception is conscious guesswork in the ordinary sense.

concepts.name: Preference utilitarianism
concepts.summary: Preference utilitarianism evaluates actions by how well they satisfy the preferences of all affected beings.
concepts.body: Preference utilitarianism evaluates actions by how well they satisfy the preferences of all affected beings. Unlike classical hedonistic utilitarianism, it treats a fulfilled preference as valuable even when it is not a pleasure.

examples.text: Keeping a competent patient's informed refusal of treatment can count positively because it respects the patient's preference.
examples.note: The outcome satisfies an autonomous preference rather than maximizing felt enjoyment.

commonMisreadings: A preference must still be relevant and informed enough to carry moral weight in the theory.

concepts.name: Premise
concepts.summary: A premise is a proposition offered as support for a conclusion in an argument.
concepts.body: A premise is a proposition offered as support for a conclusion in an argument. An argument can contain explicit premises and additional assumptions that remain unstated.

examples.text: “Every mammal breathes air; whales are mammals; therefore whales breathe air” has two premises.
examples.note: Each premise contributes inferential support for the conclusion.

commonMisreadings: A premise need not be true merely because it appears in an argument.

concepts.name: Presentism in metaphysics
concepts.summary: Presentism is the metaphysical view that only presently existing objects and events are real.
concepts.body: Presentism is the metaphysical view that only presently existing objects and events are real. According to presentism, past entities no longer exist and future entities do not yet exist.

examples.text: On a presentist view, Julius Caesar exists only as a present fact or representation, not as a past object.
examples.note: The past is treated as no longer part of reality itself.

commonMisreadings: Presentism differs from eternalism, which regards past, present, and future entities as equally real.

concepts.name: Presupposition
concepts.summary: A presupposition is information a speaker takes for granted when uttering a sentence and that often survives negation.
concepts.body: A presupposition is information a speaker takes for granted when uttering a sentence and that often survives negation. The sentence “Leah stopped smoking” presupposes that Leah smoked before.

examples.text: “Leah did not stop smoking” normally preserves the assumption that she previously smoked.
examples.note: The background assumption remains in both the affirmative and negative forms.

commonMisreadings: A presupposition is distinct from an entailment that disappears under ordinary negation.

concepts.name: Primacy effect
concepts.summary: The primacy effect is the tendency for items encountered early in a sequence to be remembered or influential more than later items.
concepts.body: The primacy effect is the tendency for items encountered early in a sequence to be remembered or influential more than later items. In free recall, early list items often receive more rehearsal and transfer into long-term memory.

examples.text: A person may remember the first names in a meeting's introduction especially well.
examples.note: Early items benefited from additional encoding opportunities.

commonMisreadings: It is not the same as the recency effect, which favors the last items.

concepts.name: Priming
concepts.summary: Priming is a change in the processing of a stimulus caused by prior exposure to a related or preceding stimulus.
concepts.body: Priming is a change in the processing of a stimulus caused by prior exposure to a related or preceding stimulus. Semantic priming can make a person recognize “doctor” faster after seeing “nurse.”

examples.text: Reading the word “yellow” can speed recognition of “banana” in a lexical decision task.
examples.note: The first word activates related representations before the second judgment.

commonMisreadings: Priming need not involve deliberate memory or conscious recollection.

concepts.name: Principal–agent problem
concepts.summary: The principal–agent problem arises when an agent acts for a principal but has different interests or better information about the relevant action.
concepts.body: The principal–agent problem arises when an agent acts for a principal but has different interests or better information about the relevant action. Monitoring and incentive contracts are used to reduce the agent's opportunity to exploit this information gap.

examples.text: A company shareholder may struggle to ensure that an executive pursues long-term firm value.
examples.note: The executive controls daily decisions while the shareholder bears much of the resulting risk.

commonMisreadings: It is not merely any disagreement between two people.

concepts.name: Principle of charity
concepts.summary: The principle of charity instructs an interpreter to understand an argument or statement in its strongest reasonable form.
concepts.body: The principle of charity instructs an interpreter to understand an argument or statement in its strongest reasonable form. It discourages attributing obvious errors to a speaker when a coherent interpretation is available.

examples.text: A critic interprets “all birds fly” as referring to typical birds rather than deliberately ignoring flightless species.
examples.note: The charitable restriction produces a more plausible claim for evaluation.

commonMisreadings: Charity does not permit changing a claim so much that the speaker's position disappears.

concepts.name: Principle of sufficient reason
concepts.summary: The principle of sufficient reason states that every fact or occurrence has an adequate reason, explanation, or ground.
concepts.body: The principle of sufficient reason states that every fact or occurrence has an adequate reason, explanation, or ground. Leibniz used it as a foundational metaphysical principle alongside the principle of contradiction.

examples.text: A falling glass is explained by its being pushed, gravity, and the surrounding physical conditions.
examples.note: Those conditions provide an account of why the event occurred rather than another event.

commonMisreadings: The principle is stronger than the modest claim that many events have discoverable causes.

concepts.name: Prioritarianism
concepts.summary: Prioritarianism is a consequentialist view that gives extra moral weight to benefits received by people who are worse off.
concepts.body: Prioritarianism is a consequentialist view that gives extra moral weight to benefits received by people who are worse off. It uses a concave value function so that an equal benefit matters more at a lower welfare level.

examples.text: Giving a medical treatment to a severely ill patient can outweigh giving the same treatment to a mildly ill patient.
examples.note: The benefit to the worse-off patient has greater moral value under the weighting rule.

commonMisreadings: Prioritarianism differs from egalitarianism because it need not value equality as such.

concepts.name: Prisoner's dilemma
concepts.summary: The prisoner's dilemma is a game in which individually rational choices produce a worse result for both players than mutual cooperation would.
concepts.body: The prisoner's dilemma is a game in which individually rational choices produce a worse result for both players than mutual cooperation would. Each player has a dominant strategy to defect when the standard payoff ordering holds.

examples.text: Two suspects separately choose whether to confess, and both receive harsher sentences if both confess.
examples.note: Each confession is safer for the individual given the other's choice, but mutual confession is jointly worse.

commonMisreadings: The dilemma is not simply any conflict between individual and collective interests.

concepts.name: Private language argument
concepts.summary: The private-language argument is Wittgenstein's argument that a language understandable only by one person cannot have meaning fixed by purely private inner references.
concepts.body: The private-language argument is Wittgenstein's argument that a language understandable only by one person cannot have meaning fixed by purely private inner references. It emphasizes public criteria and practices for distinguishing correct from incorrect applications of signs.

examples.text: A diary mark meaning “my private sensation S” would lack an independent standard for checking whether it is used correctly.
examples.note: Without criteria beyond seeming right, correctness collapses into mere inclination.

commonMisreadings: The argument does not deny that people have private experiences.

concepts.name: Private property
concepts.summary: Private property is a system in which specified individuals or organizations hold socially recognized rights to control, use, exclude others from, and transfer resources.
concepts.body: Private property is a system in which specified individuals or organizations hold socially recognized rights to control, use, exclude others from, and transfer resources. Property rights are legal and institutional relations rather than simple physical possession.

examples.text: A homeowner may exclude trespassers and sell a house under the applicable law.
examples.note: The legal system assigns control and transfer powers to the owner.

commonMisreadings: Private property does not imply that every resource must be privately owned.

concepts.name: Problem of evil
concepts.summary: The problem of evil is the challenge of reconciling the existence of suffering and wrongdoing with an all-powerful, all-knowing, and perfectly good deity.
concepts.body: The problem of evil is the challenge of reconciling the existence of suffering and wrongdoing with an all-powerful, all-knowing, and perfectly good deity. The logical version argues that certain divine attributes and evil are inconsistent, while evidential versions argue that evil makes theism less probable.

examples.text: A child's severe pain can be cited as evidence against the claim that a perfectly good and powerful God governs the world.
examples.note: The suffering appears difficult to explain as necessary for a greater good.

commonMisreadings: The problem concerns both natural evil and moral evil, not only human wrongdoing.

concepts.name: Problem of other minds
concepts.summary: The problem of other minds is the epistemological difficulty of knowing whether other beings have conscious experiences rather than merely observable behavior.
concepts.body: The problem of other minds is the epistemological difficulty of knowing whether other beings have conscious experiences rather than merely observable behavior. A person has direct access to their own experiences but ordinarily infers another person's experience from behavior and context.

examples.text: Seeing someone recoil and cry supports the belief that they feel pain, but does not provide direct access to that pain.
examples.note: The inference moves from publicly observed signs to privately experienced states.

commonMisreadings: The problem does not imply that belief in other minds is irrational or avoidable.

concepts.name: Problem of religious diversity
concepts.summary: The problem of religious diversity asks how widespread, persistent disagreement among religions affects claims that one religious belief is uniquely justified.
concepts.body: The problem of religious diversity asks how widespread, persistent disagreement among religions affects claims that one religious belief is uniquely justified. Different traditions often offer incompatible doctrines while presenting sincere and apparently comparable forms of testimony.

examples.text: A Christian, Muslim, and Hindu may each inherit a different religious framework and find its practices evidentially compelling.
examples.note: The variation makes cultural location and epistemic access relevant to religious justification.

commonMisreadings: The problem is about disagreement and justification, not merely the existence of many rituals.

concepts.name: Problem of the criterion
concepts.summary: The problem of the criterion asks how we can identify reliable methods of knowledge without already knowing which particular beliefs are true, or identify true beliefs without a reliable method.
concepts.body: The problem of the criterion asks how we can identify reliable methods of knowledge without already knowing which particular beliefs are true, or identify true beliefs without a reliable method. It presents a circular choice among skepticism, foundationalism, and accepting a starting point without independent proof.

examples.text: To test a perceptual method, one may need trusted perceptions to judge the test's result.
examples.note: The attempted validation uses the very capacity whose reliability is under examination.

commonMisreadings: It is not just a complaint that some standards are difficult to agree on.

concepts.name: Procedural justice
concepts.summary: Procedural justice concerns whether the processes used to make decisions are fair, consistent, impartial, and respectful.
concepts.body: Procedural justice concerns whether the processes used to make decisions are fair, consistent, impartial, and respectful. People often judge an outcome as more legitimate when they had a voice and were treated with dignity during the procedure.

examples.text: A court can provide procedural justice by allowing both parties to present evidence before an impartial judge.
examples.note: The opportunity for a fair hearing supports the legitimacy of the decision process.

commonMisreadings: Procedural justice differs from distributive justice, which evaluates the allocation of outcomes.

concepts.name: Process philosophy
concepts.summary: Process philosophy treats becoming, change, events, and relations as fundamental features of reality rather than reducing them to static substances.
concepts.body: Process philosophy treats becoming, change, events, and relations as fundamental features of reality rather than reducing them to static substances. Alfred North Whitehead developed a major process metaphysics in which actual occasions are basic units of existence.

examples.text: A living organism is understood as an ongoing pattern of activity rather than an unchanging thing that merely undergoes changes.
examples.note: The organism's identity is explained through continuity of process and relation.

commonMisreadings: Process philosophy does not mean that every change is random or unstructured.

concepts.name: Process theology
concepts.summary: Process theology applies process philosophy to theology, portraying God and the world as dynamically related rather than God as an entirely immutable controller.
concepts.body: Process theology applies process philosophy to theology, portraying God and the world as dynamically related rather than God as an entirely immutable controller. In Whiteheadian forms, God influences possibilities and responds to the world's actual events but does not unilaterally determine them.

examples.text: A process theologian may say that God persuades a community toward compassion while creatures retain genuine freedom.
examples.note: Divine action is conceived as persuasive rather than coercive control.

commonMisreadings: Process theology differs from classical theism on divine power and immutability.

concepts.name: Processing fluency
concepts.summary: Processing fluency is the subjective ease with which information is perceived, understood, or retrieved.
concepts.body: Processing fluency is the subjective ease with which information is perceived, understood, or retrieved. Fluent information can feel more familiar, truthful, or aesthetically pleasing even when fluency comes from irrelevant factors.

examples.text: People may rate a statement printed in clear high-contrast type as more believable than the same statement in difficult type.
examples.note: The easier presentation creates a positive fluency signal that can bias judgment.

commonMisreadings: Fluency is not evidence that the statement is actually true.

concepts.name: Progressivism
concepts.summary: Progressivism is a political orientation that favors social reform, expanded inclusion, and public action to address economic or political inequalities.
concepts.body: Progressivism is a political orientation that favors social reform, expanded inclusion, and public action to address economic or political inequalities. Its policies commonly include labor protections, civil rights, regulation, and broader democratic participation.

examples.text: A progressive campaign may support a minimum-wage increase and stronger workplace safety enforcement.
examples.note: Both measures use public policy to improve workers' social and economic conditions.

commonMisreadings: Progressivism is a broad political tradition rather than one fixed platform.

concepts.name: Proof
concepts.summary: A proof is a sequence of logically connected steps that establishes a conclusion from accepted premises, definitions, or inference rules.
concepts.body: A proof is a sequence of logically connected steps that establishes a conclusion from accepted premises, definitions, or inference rules. In mathematics, a proof must make its inferential dependencies explicit enough for competent readers to check.

examples.text: From “n is even” and the definition of evenness, one can prove that n equals 2k for some integer k.
examples.note: The definition supplies the exact form required for the conclusion.

commonMisreadings: A persuasive example or empirical measurement is not automatically a proof.

concepts.name: Proof by cases
concepts.summary: Proof by cases establishes a conclusion by dividing the possibilities into exhaustive cases and proving the conclusion in each case.
concepts.body: Proof by cases establishes a conclusion by dividing the possibilities into exhaustive cases and proving the conclusion in each case. The cases may overlap, but together they must cover every situation allowed by the premises.

examples.text: To prove an integer is divisible by 2 or odd, one considers the cases where it is even and where it is not even.
examples.note: Every integer falls into one of the two cases, and each yields the target conclusion.

commonMisreadings: The method fails if an unconsidered case remains.

concepts.name: Proof by contradiction
concepts.summary: Proof by contradiction assumes the negation of the desired conclusion and derives an impossibility.
concepts.body: Proof by contradiction assumes the negation of the desired conclusion and derives an impossibility. The contradiction shows that the assumption cannot be true, so the original conclusion follows under classical logic.

examples.text: To prove that there is no greatest prime, assume a greatest prime list and construct a number that yields a new prime divisor.
examples.note: The constructed divisor contradicts the claim that the list was complete.

commonMisreadings: A contradiction proof is not the same as showing that the conclusion is merely unlikely.

concepts.name: Proof theory
concepts.summary: Proof theory is the study of formal proofs as mathematical objects, including their syntax, structure, and consistency.
concepts.body: Proof theory is the study of formal proofs as mathematical objects, including their syntax, structure, and consistency. It analyzes formal systems through concepts such as derivability, normalization, cut elimination, and proof-theoretic strength.

examples.text: Gentzen's consistency proof for arithmetic studies transformations of formal derivations.
examples.note: The proof itself becomes the object whose structure and permitted transformations are examined.

commonMisreadings: Proof theory differs from model theory, which studies interpretations and structures satisfying sentences.

concepts.name: Proper name
concepts.summary: A proper name is a linguistic expression conventionally used to refer to a particular individual, place, object, or institution.
concepts.body: A proper name is a linguistic expression conventionally used to refer to a particular individual, place, object, or institution. Proper names such as “Ada Lovelace” can continue referring to their bearer even when speakers associate different descriptions with the name.

examples.text: “Mount Everest” refers to one particular mountain rather than to mountains generally.
examples.note: The expression has a conventional reference to that geographic individual.

commonMisreadings: A proper name is not automatically synonymous with a definite description.

concepts.name: Property
concepts.summary: A property is a feature or attribute that can be predicated of an object or instantiated by multiple objects.
concepts.body: A property is a feature or attribute that can be predicated of an object or instantiated by multiple objects. Being red, having mass, and being triangular are standard examples of properties.

examples.text: The property of being electrically conductive is instantiated by copper and many other materials.
examples.note: Different objects share the same general attribute.

commonMisreadings: A property differs from a relation, which connects two or more entities.

concepts.name: Property dualism
concepts.summary: Property dualism holds that the mental and physical are distinct kinds of properties even if there is only one underlying kind of substance.
concepts.body: Property dualism holds that the mental and physical are distinct kinds of properties even if there is only one underlying kind of substance. It can accept physical substance monism while denying that phenomenal consciousness is reducible to physical properties.

examples.text: A brain state may have neural properties and also the phenomenal property of producing a particular pain experience.
examples.note: The two property types are attributed to the same physical system but are not identified.

commonMisreadings: Property dualism differs from substance dualism, which posits distinct kinds of substances.

concepts.name: Property rights
concepts.summary: Property rights are legally or socially enforceable claims concerning the use, control, exclusion, income, and transfer of a resource.
concepts.body: Property rights are legally or socially enforceable claims concerning the use, control, exclusion, income, and transfer of a resource. A property-rights bundle can divide powers among an owner, tenant, lender, and government.

examples.text: A tenant may possess a right to occupy an apartment while the landlord retains the right to sell it.
examples.note: Different parties hold different incidents of the overall property arrangement.

commonMisreadings: Property rights are not limited to absolute ownership of a physical object.

concepts.name: Proportionality
concepts.summary: Proportionality is the principle that a response, restriction, or penalty should be appropriately related in severity to the aim, harm, or violation at issue.
concepts.body: Proportionality is the principle that a response, restriction, or penalty should be appropriately related in severity to the aim, harm, or violation at issue. Constitutional and international law often use proportionality tests to assess whether rights limitations go beyond what is necessary.

examples.text: A minor administrative error ordinarily should not receive the same penalty as deliberate fraud.
examples.note: The unequal seriousness of the conduct calls for an unequal sanction.

commonMisreadings: Proportionality does not mean that the response must be numerically identical to the harm.

concepts.name: Proposition
concepts.summary: A proposition is an abstract content that can be expressed by a declarative sentence and evaluated as true or false.
concepts.body: A proposition is an abstract content that can be expressed by a declarative sentence and evaluated as true or false. Different sentences can express the same proposition when they have the same truth-conditional content.

examples.text: “Snow is white” and “La neige est blanche” can express one proposition in different languages.
examples.note: The wording differs while the asserted content remains equivalent.

commonMisreadings: A proposition is not the physical sentence token used to express it.

concepts.name: Propositional logic
concepts.summary: Propositional logic is a formal system that represents whole propositions as variables and combines them with truth-functional connectives.
concepts.body: Propositional logic is a formal system that represents whole propositions as variables and combines them with truth-functional connectives. Its basic operators include negation, conjunction, disjunction, and conditional implication.

examples.text: The formula “P and Q” is true exactly when both component propositions are true.
examples.note: Its truth value depends on the values assigned to P and Q.

commonMisreadings: Propositional logic does not analyze the internal subjects and predicates of atomic propositions.

concepts.name: Prospect theory
concepts.summary: Prospect theory describes decision-making under risk using reference points, loss aversion, and nonlinear weighting of probabilities.
concepts.body: Prospect theory describes decision-making under risk using reference points, loss aversion, and nonlinear weighting of probabilities. It predicts that losses usually feel larger than equivalent gains and that small probabilities may be overweighted.

examples.text: A person may reject a fair gamble to avoid a possible loss but buy lottery tickets because the tiny chance of winning feels salient.
examples.note: The two choices reflect different distortions around losses and unlikely outcomes.

commonMisreadings: Prospect theory is descriptive of observed judgments rather than a rule for ideal rational choice.

concepts.name: Protectionism
concepts.summary: Protectionism is the use of tariffs, quotas, subsidies, or regulations to shield domestic producers from foreign competition.
concepts.body: Protectionism is the use of tariffs, quotas, subsidies, or regulations to shield domestic producers from foreign competition. These measures can support selected industries while raising prices or reducing competitive pressure for consumers.

examples.text: A country may impose a tariff on imported steel to protect its domestic steel mills.
examples.note: The tariff makes foreign steel more expensive relative to local production.

commonMisreadings: Protectionism is not the same as any policy that regulates international trade.

concepts.name: Pseudoscience
concepts.summary: Pseudoscience is a purported field or practice that presents itself as scientific while lacking adequate empirical support, reliable methods, or openness to testing.
concepts.body: Pseudoscience is a purported field or practice that presents itself as scientific while lacking adequate empirical support, reliable methods, or openness to testing. It often uses scientific-sounding language while resisting falsification and ignoring contrary evidence.

examples.text: Astrology is commonly classified as pseudoscience because its broad claims have not shown reliable predictive validity under controlled testing.
examples.note: The practice retains its claims despite weak and nonreproducible evidence.

commonMisreadings: Pseudoscience is distinguished from a genuine scientific hypothesis that remains uncertain but testable.

concepts.name: Psychological egoism
concepts.summary: Psychological egoism is the descriptive theory that all human actions are ultimately motivated by self-interest.
concepts.body: Psychological egoism is the descriptive theory that all human actions are ultimately motivated by self-interest. It interprets apparently altruistic behavior as serving a desire of the agent, such as avoiding guilt or gaining satisfaction.

examples.text: A person who anonymously donates may be said to act for the satisfaction of helping others.
examples.note: The theory treats the donor's personal motive as self-interested even though the beneficiary gains.

commonMisreadings: Psychological egoism describes motivation and does not by itself say that selfishness is morally right.

concepts.name: Public goods
concepts.summary: Public goods are goods that are non-excludable and non-rivalrous, so people can use them without preventing others' use and are difficult to exclude from.
concepts.body: Public goods are goods that are non-excludable and non-rivalrous, so people can use them without preventing others' use and are difficult to exclude from. Their features create free-rider problems because individuals can benefit without voluntarily paying.

examples.text: National defense protects residents broadly and does not become depleted when one resident benefits.
examples.note: The same protection can be enjoyed by many people at once without ordinary exclusion.

commonMisreadings: A publicly provided good is not necessarily a public good if users can be excluded or consumption competes.

concepts.name: Public reason
concepts.summary: Public reason is the idea that coercive political rules should be justifiable to citizens through reasons they can reasonably share despite deep private or religious disagreement.
concepts.body: Public reason is the idea that coercive political rules should be justifiable to citizens through reasons they can reasonably share despite deep private or religious disagreement. Rawls uses public reason to constrain arguments about constitutional essentials and basic justice.

examples.text: A legislator defending a tax law may appeal to equal civic rights and public welfare rather than only to a sectarian revelation.
examples.note: The stated reason can be assessed by citizens with different comprehensive doctrines.

commonMisreadings: Public reason does not require citizens to abandon private religious motivations.

concepts.name: Pygmalion effect
concepts.summary: The Pygmalion effect is the tendency for higher expectations from an authority or teacher to improve a person's performance.
concepts.body: The Pygmalion effect is the tendency for higher expectations from an authority or teacher to improve a person's performance. Expectations can alter attention, feedback, opportunities, and interaction quality, which then affect outcomes.

examples.text: Students identified to a teacher as likely to show intellectual growth may later perform better.
examples.note: The teacher's changed treatment can help produce the expected improvement.

commonMisreadings: The effect is not proof that expectations alone determine achievement in every case.

concepts.name: Pyrrhonism
concepts.summary: Pyrrhonism is an ancient skeptical tradition that suspends judgment when opposing arguments appear equipollent.
concepts.body: Pyrrhonism is an ancient skeptical tradition that suspends judgment when opposing arguments appear equipollent. Pyrrhonist practice aims at tranquillity by avoiding dogmatic commitment rather than asserting that every belief is false.

examples.text: A Pyrrhonist may withhold judgment about whether a disputed metaphysical entity exists after comparing balanced arguments.
examples.note: Suspension follows the apparent equality of support for the competing claims.

commonMisreadings: Pyrrhonism differs from dogmatic skepticism, which asserts that knowledge is impossible.

concepts.name: Pythagoreanism
concepts.summary: Pythagoreanism is a philosophical and religious tradition associated with Pythagoras that emphasizes mathematical structure, harmony, and disciplined communal life.
concepts.body: Pythagoreanism is a philosophical and religious tradition associated with Pythagoras that emphasizes mathematical structure, harmony, and disciplined communal life. Ancient Pythagoreans linked numerical ratios to musical harmony and sometimes treated numbers as fundamental principles.

examples.text: The octave's musical ratio of 2:1 was used as evidence that mathematical relations underlie harmony.
examples.note: The audible consonance corresponds to a simple numerical proportion.

commonMisreadings: Pythagoreanism is broader than the modern theorem about right triangles.

concepts.name: Qualia
concepts.summary: Qualia are the subjective, phenomenal qualities of conscious experience, such as how red looks or pain feels.
concepts.body: Qualia are the subjective, phenomenal qualities of conscious experience, such as how red looks or pain feels. The term is used in debates about whether physical descriptions exhaust the character of experience.

examples.text: The felt bitterness of tasting a lemon is a candidate quale.
examples.note: It identifies the first-person character of that tasting episode.

commonMisreadings: Qualia are not simply external physical properties such as a lemon's chemical composition.

concepts.name: Quantifier
concepts.summary: A quantifier is a logical operator that specifies how many objects in a domain satisfy a condition.
concepts.body: A quantifier is a logical operator that specifies how many objects in a domain satisfy a condition. The universal quantifier means “for every,” while the existential quantifier means “for at least one.”

examples.text: In “Every cat is mortal,” the word “every” quantifies over cats.
examples.note: It requires the predicate “mortal” to hold for each object in the quantified class.

commonMisreadings: A quantifier differs from an ordinary numerical adjective because its logical scope matters.

concepts.name: Radical democracy
concepts.summary: Radical democracy is a political approach that seeks to deepen popular self-government by expanding participation and contesting entrenched power relations.
concepts.body: Radical democracy is a political approach that seeks to deepen popular self-government by expanding participation and contesting entrenched power relations. It often treats democratic conflict and institutional transformation as ongoing rather than aiming at final social unanimity.

examples.text: A radical-democratic assembly may let affected residents directly shape a city's housing policy.
examples.note: The people subject to the policy gain an active role in determining it.

commonMisreadings: Radical democracy does not necessarily mean violent revolution or simple majority rule.

concepts.name: Radical empiricism
concepts.summary: Radical empiricism is William James's view that experience includes both relations among things and the things related, rather than only discrete sensations.
concepts.body: Radical empiricism is William James's view that experience includes both relations among things and the things related, rather than only discrete sensations. It treats experienced relations as directly given aspects of experience instead of as additions imposed by thought.

examples.text: The felt continuity between two moments of a melody is part of experience for a radical empiricist.
examples.note: The relation of succession is experienced along with the individual notes.

commonMisreadings: Radical empiricism is not merely an insistence on using laboratory experiments.

concepts.name: Radical feminism
concepts.summary: Radical feminism analyzes women's oppression as rooted in patriarchal social structures, especially the organization of sexuality, reproduction, and power.
concepts.body: Radical feminism analyzes women's oppression as rooted in patriarchal social structures, especially the organization of sexuality, reproduction, and power. It argues that changing formal laws may be insufficient if intimate and cultural institutions continue to reproduce male dominance.

examples.text: A radical-feminist analysis may examine how sexual violence and reproductive control maintain gender hierarchy.
examples.note: The practices are treated as structural mechanisms rather than isolated personal incidents.

commonMisreadings: Radical feminism is not defined simply by having extreme opinions about gender.

concepts.name: Rational choice theory
concepts.summary: Rational choice theory models agents as selecting actions that best satisfy their preferences given available information and constraints.
concepts.body: Rational choice theory models agents as selecting actions that best satisfy their preferences given available information and constraints. It is used in economics, political science, and sociology to explain behavior through preferences, incentives, and strategic interaction.

examples.text: A voter may choose the candidate whose policies provide the greatest expected benefit under the voter's beliefs.
examples.note: The choice follows an assumed ranking of outcomes and an assessment of probabilities.

commonMisreadings: The theory's “rationality” is formal consistency, not necessarily wisdom or moral goodness.

concepts.name: Rational egoism
concepts.summary: Rational egoism is the normative view that an agent ought to act in accordance with their own long-term self-interest.
concepts.body: Rational egoism is the normative view that an agent ought to act in accordance with their own long-term self-interest. It differs from psychological egoism because it prescribes conduct rather than describing every actual motive.

examples.text: A rational egoist may reject a profitable fraud because legal punishment would undermine long-term welfare.
examples.note: The action is judged by the agent's durable interests rather than immediate gain.

commonMisreadings: Rational egoism does not entail that all short-term selfish impulses are rational.

concepts.name: Rationalism
concepts.summary: Rationalism is the epistemological view that reason, conceptual insight, or a priori knowledge can provide substantial knowledge independently of sensory experience.
concepts.body: Rationalism is the epistemological view that reason, conceptual insight, or a priori knowledge can provide substantial knowledge independently of sensory experience. Early modern rationalists such as Descartes, Spinoza, and Leibniz emphasized necessary truths and rational principles.

examples.text: Knowledge that all triangles have three sides can be justified by conceptual analysis rather than measuring triangles.
examples.note: The claim holds for the concept of a triangle before any particular observation.

commonMisreadings: Rationalism does not require denying that experience supplies useful knowledge.

concepts.name: Rationality
concepts.summary: Rationality is the capacity or standard of forming beliefs and choosing actions in accordance with reasons, evidence, goals, or valid norms.
concepts.body: Rationality is the capacity or standard of forming beliefs and choosing actions in accordance with reasons, evidence, goals, or valid norms. Theoretical rationality concerns belief, while practical rationality concerns action and deliberation.

examples.text: Updating a weather belief after receiving a reliable forecast is an instance of theoretical rationality.
examples.note: The belief changes in response to relevant evidence.

commonMisreadings: Rationality is not identical to intelligence, success, or agreement with another person.

concepts.name: Reactionary politics
concepts.summary: Reactionary politics seeks to restore or preserve a perceived earlier social, political, or religious order in response to reform or revolutionary change.
concepts.body: Reactionary politics seeks to restore or preserve a perceived earlier social, political, or religious order in response to reform or revolutionary change. Reactionaries typically regard recent transformations as sources of disorder and treat inherited institutions as politically authoritative.

examples.text: A movement demanding the return of an abolished hereditary privilege is reactionary.
examples.note: Its goal is reversal toward a prior hierarchy rather than incremental improvement of the current system.

commonMisreadings: Reactionary politics is distinct from conservatism when it explicitly seeks restoration of a past order.

concepts.name: Reactivity
concepts.summary: Reactivity is the tendency of a person, system, or measurement to change because it is being observed, tested, or acted upon.
concepts.body: Reactivity is the tendency of a person, system, or measurement to change because it is being observed, tested, or acted upon. In social research, participants may alter their behavior when they know they are part of a study.

examples.text: Employees may work faster during a monitored trial than during ordinary unobserved shifts.
examples.note: The observation procedure itself changes the behavior being measured.

commonMisreadings: Reactivity is not simply responsiveness to any stimulus; the observation or intervention must affect the result.

concepts.name: Realism
concepts.summary: Realism is the view that some entities, facts, or truths exist independently of our beliefs, descriptions, or conceptual schemes.
concepts.body: Realism is the view that some entities, facts, or truths exist independently of our beliefs, descriptions, or conceptual schemes. Scientific realism, for example, treats well-confirmed unobservable entities such as electrons as real rather than merely useful instruments.

examples.text: A realist may say that electrons existed before scientists developed the concept of them.
examples.note: The claim makes electron existence independent of human recognition.

commonMisreadings: Realism is opposed to some forms of anti-realism, not to every form of interpretation.

concepts.name: Recency effect
concepts.summary: The recency effect is the tendency for the most recently encountered items in a sequence to be recalled or influence judgment more strongly.
concepts.body: The recency effect is the tendency for the most recently encountered items in a sequence to be recalled or influence judgment more strongly. In immediate free recall, final list items can remain active in short-term memory.

examples.text: A listener may remember the last points in a presentation better immediately afterward.
examples.note: The final items have had the shortest interval to decay or be displaced.

commonMisreadings: The recency effect differs from primacy, which favors early items.

concepts.name: Reciprocity
concepts.summary: Reciprocity is a norm or pattern in which benefits, favors, obligations, or harms are returned in kind between parties.
concepts.body: Reciprocity is a norm or pattern in which benefits, favors, obligations, or harms are returned in kind between parties. It can support cooperation by making current assistance likely to be answered with future assistance.

examples.text: A neighbor waters another neighbor's plants after receiving help with a home repair.
examples.note: The returned favor reflects an expectation of mutual exchange.

commonMisreadings: Reciprocity is not identical to altruism, which can occur without expecting a return.

concepts.name: Reconstructionism
concepts.summary: Reconstructionism is the attempt to rebuild an institution, tradition, or social order after major disruption by reinterpreting and reorganizing its elements.
concepts.body: Reconstructionism is the attempt to rebuild an institution, tradition, or social order after major disruption by reinterpreting and reorganizing its elements. The term can describe theological, educational, or political movements that seek renewal through deliberate reconstruction.

examples.text: A school adopting reconstructionist education may redesign its curriculum around democratic problem-solving after a social crisis.
examples.note: The institution is rebuilt to address changed conditions rather than simply restored unchanged.

commonMisreadings: Reconstructionism differs from restorationism, which aims to recover an earlier form.

concepts.name: Recursive definition
concepts.summary: A recursive definition specifies a class or function through base cases and rules that define new cases from earlier ones.
concepts.body: A recursive definition specifies a class or function through base cases and rules that define new cases from earlier ones. It is valid only when the recursion is grounded and the defining process determines the intended objects.

examples.text: The factorial function is defined by 0! = 1 and (n+1)! = (n+1)n!.
examples.note: Each later factorial is determined from a previously defined smaller one.

commonMisreadings: A recursive definition is not an informal repetition without a base case.

concepts.name: Red-team reasoning
concepts.summary: Red-team reasoning deliberately searches for weaknesses, counterexamples, hidden assumptions, and failure modes in a proposal.
concepts.body: Red-team reasoning deliberately searches for weaknesses, counterexamples, hidden assumptions, and failure modes in a proposal. It improves decisions by assigning someone or a group to challenge the favored plan rather than merely endorse it.

examples.text: Before launching software, a red team tries to exploit an authentication design and document how it could fail.
examples.note: The adversarial test targets vulnerabilities that ordinary implementation review might overlook.

commonMisreadings: Red-team reasoning is structured criticism, not opposition for its own sake.

concepts.name: Reductio ad impossibile
concepts.summary: Reductio ad impossibile is an argument that assumes a claim and derives an impossible result, thereby rejecting the claim or establishing its contrary.
concepts.body: Reductio ad impossibile is an argument that assumes a claim and derives an impossible result, thereby rejecting the claim or establishing its contrary. It is a broad contradiction-based method used in mathematics and philosophy.

examples.text: Assuming that a smallest positive rational number exists leads to a smaller positive rational by dividing it by two.
examples.note: The derived object contradicts the assumed minimality.

commonMisreadings: It is not limited to arguments whose contradiction is a formal logical inconsistency.

concepts.name: Reductionism
concepts.summary: Reductionism is the explanatory view that complex phenomena can be understood through simpler components, levels, or mechanisms.
concepts.body: Reductionism is the explanatory view that complex phenomena can be understood through simpler components, levels, or mechanisms. A reduction can be ontological, claiming only the lower-level entities are fundamental, or explanatory, linking higher-level behavior to lower-level processes.

examples.text: A reductionist account of digestion explains it through organs, cells, chemical reactions, and physical interactions.
examples.note: The higher-level process is analyzed by its constituent mechanisms.

commonMisreadings: Reductionism does not always require denying that higher-level descriptions are useful.

concepts.name: Reductionist physicalism
concepts.summary: Reductionist physicalism is the view that mental phenomena are physical and can in principle be identified with or explained completely by physical states and processes.
concepts.body: Reductionist physicalism is the view that mental phenomena are physical and can in principle be identified with or explained completely by physical states and processes. It differs from nonreductive physicalism, which accepts physical dependence while denying identity or reduction of mental properties.

examples.text: A reductionist physicalist may identify pain with a neural state type or with a function realized physically.
examples.note: The mental property is treated as nothing over and above an appropriate physical basis.

commonMisreadings: The view is stronger than the claim that mental events depend causally on brains.

concepts.name: Reference
concepts.summary: Reference is the relation by which a linguistic expression, symbol, or representation stands for an object, individual, kind, or state of affairs.
concepts.body: Reference is the relation by which a linguistic expression, symbol, or representation stands for an object, individual, kind, or state of affairs. Reference can depend on convention, context, causal history, or descriptive content depending on the theory.

examples.text: The name “Tokyo” refers to a particular city in ordinary English use.
examples.note: The expression systematically picks out that city in relevant contexts.

commonMisreadings: Reference is not the same as sense, which concerns an expression's mode of presentation or conceptual content.

concepts.name: Reflective equilibrium
concepts.summary: Reflective equilibrium is a method of justifying principles by bringing considered judgments, general principles, and background theories into mutual coherence through revision.
concepts.body: Reflective equilibrium is a method of justifying principles by bringing considered judgments, general principles, and background theories into mutual coherence through revision. The method can be narrow within one domain or wide when it incorporates broader empirical and philosophical commitments.

examples.text: A person may revise a punishment judgment after comparing it with a general commitment against cruel treatment.
examples.note: The judgment and principle are adjusted until the resulting set is more coherent.

commonMisreadings: Reflective equilibrium is not mere consistency with one's first intuitions.

concepts.name: Reformism
concepts.summary: Reformism is the political strategy of pursuing substantial social change through gradual legal, institutional, or electoral reforms rather than revolutionary overthrow.
concepts.body: Reformism is the political strategy of pursuing substantial social change through gradual legal, institutional, or electoral reforms rather than revolutionary overthrow. Reformists may seek to transform economic or political relations while retaining portions of existing institutions.

examples.text: A labor movement may pursue universal healthcare through legislation and elections instead of abolishing the state.
examples.note: Its incremental means are directed toward a larger structural improvement.

commonMisreadings: Reformism differs from conservatism because its aim is deliberate change.

concepts.name: Relation
concepts.summary: A relation is a property or structure that connects two or more entities in a specified way.
concepts.body: A relation is a property or structure that connects two or more entities in a specified way. Relations can be symmetric or asymmetric, and one-place relations are often treated as properties.

examples.text: Being taller than relates one person to another in an ordered comparison.
examples.note: The relation cannot be fully specified by describing either person alone.

commonMisreadings: A relation is not necessarily a physical object located between its relata.

concepts.name: Relationalism about space
concepts.summary: Relationalism about space holds that spatial facts consist in relations among objects or events rather than in an independently existing container of space.
concepts.body: Relationalism about space holds that spatial facts consist in relations among objects or events rather than in an independently existing container of space. On this view, distances and directions are grounded in the arrangement of material things or possible relations.

examples.text: A universe containing only two objects could have a spatial distance because of their relative separation.
examples.note: The spatial fact is explained through the objects' relation rather than an empty absolute space.

commonMisreadings: Relationalism contrasts with substantivalism, which treats space as an entity or structure existing independently.

concepts.name: Relevance logic
concepts.summary: Relevance logic is a family of nonclassical logics designed to require a meaningful connection between premises and conclusions in valid inference.
concepts.body: Relevance logic is a family of nonclassical logics designed to require a meaningful connection between premises and conclusions in valid inference. It rejects some classical principles, such as unrestricted implication, when they allow irrelevant premises to entail a conclusion.

examples.text: From a contradiction, relevance logic does not automatically infer every unrelated proposition.
examples.note: The inference is blocked because the arbitrary conclusion lacks the required relevance to the premises.

commonMisreadings: Relevance logic is not a theory of conversational relevance alone.

concepts.name: Reliabilism
concepts.summary: Reliabilism is an epistemological theory that treats a belief as justified or knowledge-producing when it results from a reliably truth-conducive process.
concepts.body: Reliabilism is an epistemological theory that treats a belief as justified or knowledge-producing when it results from a reliably truth-conducive process. A reliable process is one that yields true beliefs at a sufficiently high rate in appropriate conditions.

examples.text: A normally functioning visual system can justify the belief that a tree is present when the person sees a tree in daylight.
examples.note: The perceptual process usually produces true beliefs in that environment.

commonMisreadings: Reliabilism need not require the believer to know or articulate why the process is reliable.

concepts.name: Religious nationalism
concepts.summary: Religious nationalism is an ideology that identifies a nation or state with a particular religion and seeks political authority or identity on that basis.
concepts.body: Religious nationalism is an ideology that identifies a nation or state with a particular religion and seeks political authority or identity on that basis. It can use religious symbols, narratives, laws, or membership boundaries to define national belonging.

examples.text: A party may argue that the state should privilege one faith because it allegedly expresses the nation's sacred heritage.
examples.note: Religious identity is made part of the political definition of the nation.

commonMisreadings: Religious nationalism is not the same as ordinary private religious patriotism.

concepts.name: Religious pluralism
concepts.summary: Religious pluralism is the view that multiple religious traditions can possess genuine value, truth, or legitimate paths to the transcendent.
concepts.body: Religious pluralism is the view that multiple religious traditions can possess genuine value, truth, or legitimate paths to the transcendent. Some pluralists claim that religions are culturally diverse responses to a reality no single tradition fully captures.

examples.text: A pluralist may regard Christian, Buddhist, and Muslim practices as distinct but potentially authentic forms of religious orientation.
examples.note: The traditions are not reduced to mere error simply because they disagree.

commonMisreadings: Pluralism differs from relativism if it makes substantive claims about shared religious value.

concepts.name: Reminiscence bump
concepts.summary: The reminiscence bump is the tendency for adults to recall a disproportionately large number of autobiographical memories from adolescence and early adulthood.
concepts.body: The reminiscence bump is the tendency for adults to recall a disproportionately large number of autobiographical memories from adolescence and early adulthood. The pattern is often associated with identity formation, novel experiences, and enduring cultural milestones during those years.

examples.text: A seventy-year-old may remember many events from ages fifteen to thirty but fewer routine events from middle age.
examples.note: The earlier period contains memorable transitions that remain highly accessible.

commonMisreadings: The bump is a distributional pattern in autobiographical memory, not proof that all early memories are accurate.

concepts.name: Reparative justice
concepts.summary: Reparative justice seeks to address past wrongdoing by repairing material, political, or social harm suffered by victims or their descendants.
concepts.body: Reparative justice seeks to address past wrongdoing by repairing material, political, or social harm suffered by victims or their descendants. It can involve compensation, restitution, institutional reform, public acknowledgment, or measures against continuing disadvantage.

examples.text: A state may provide restitution and educational support to a community dispossessed through an unlawful land seizure.
examples.note: The measures respond to a concrete historical injury and its ongoing effects.

commonMisreadings: Reparative justice is broader than an apology without material or institutional repair.

concepts.name: Replication
concepts.summary: Replication is the repeated performance of a study, experiment, or analysis to determine whether its findings recur under the same or closely related conditions.
concepts.body: Replication is the repeated performance of a study, experiment, or analysis to determine whether its findings recur under the same or closely related conditions. A successful replication increases confidence that a result is not a chance outcome or artifact of one procedure.

examples.text: An independent laboratory repeats a psychology experiment using the published protocol and tests whether the reported effect appears.
examples.note: The new test examines the original claim beyond the first research team.

commonMisreadings: Replication does not require every study to reproduce an effect exactly in every context.

concepts.name: Representationalism
concepts.summary: Representationalism is the theory that perception or mental states involve internal representations that stand for objects, properties, or states of affairs.
concepts.body: Representationalism is the theory that perception or mental states involve internal representations that stand for objects, properties, or states of affairs.
