Perceptual experience is explained partly by the content and causal role of a representation rather than by direct possession of the external object.

examples.text: A visual system represents a red apple through neural states that guide recognition and action.
examples.note: The internal state carries information about the apple without being the apple itself.

commonMisreadings: Representationalism does not entail that all representations are conscious images.

concepts.name: Republican liberty
concepts.summary: Republican liberty is freedom understood as non-domination, meaning protection from arbitrary or uncontrolled power by another person or institution.
concepts.body: Republican liberty is freedom understood as non-domination, meaning protection from arbitrary or uncontrolled power by another person or institution. A person can be interfered with rarely yet lack republican liberty if someone else has unchecked power to interfere at will.

examples.text: A benevolent master may leave a slave's choices alone while retaining arbitrary authority over the slave.
examples.note: The standing dependence itself constitutes domination even without constant interference.

commonMisreadings: Republican liberty differs from negative liberty defined only as actual non-interference.

concepts.name: Republicanism
concepts.summary: Republicanism is a political tradition that values self-government, civic participation, public virtue, and freedom from domination.
concepts.body: Republicanism is a political tradition that values self-government, civic participation, public virtue, and freedom from domination. Classical and modern republican theories often emphasize institutions that prevent arbitrary power through law and civic accountability.

examples.text: A republic may require elected officials to publish decisions and face regular public scrutiny.
examples.note: Accountability limits rulers' ability to exercise uncontrolled authority.

commonMisreadings: Republicanism is not defined simply by having a nonhereditary head of state.

concepts.name: Resistance
concepts.summary: Resistance is opposition to a force, authority, policy, or social condition that seeks to prevent, limit, or reverse its effects.
concepts.body: Resistance is opposition to a force, authority, policy, or social condition that seeks to prevent, limit, or reverse its effects. Resistance can be individual or collective and can use legal protest, civil disobedience, strikes, or armed action.

examples.text: Workers who strike against unsafe conditions resist the employer's demand to continue operating without safeguards.
examples.note: Their coordinated refusal aims to change the imposed conditions.

commonMisreadings: Resistance is not necessarily violent or morally justified merely because it opposes authority.

concepts.name: Respect
concepts.summary: Respect is an attitude or practice of recognizing another person's dignity, standing, rights, or legitimate claims.
concepts.body: Respect is an attitude or practice of recognizing another person's dignity, standing, rights, or legitimate claims. Respect can require allowing autonomy, using appropriate regard, and avoiding treatment that humiliates or instrumentalizes a person.

examples.text: A doctor respects a competent patient's decision by explaining options and honoring an informed refusal.
examples.note: The patient is treated as an agent entitled to decide about their body.

commonMisreadings: Respect is distinct from admiration, which requires positive evaluation of a person's qualities.

concepts.name: Restorative justice
concepts.summary: Restorative justice is an approach to wrongdoing that seeks to repair relationships and harm through accountability, participation, and community-based resolution.
concepts.body: Restorative justice is an approach to wrongdoing that seeks to repair relationships and harm through accountability, participation, and community-based resolution. It may bring victims, responsible parties, and affected community members together to discuss harm and agree on repair.

examples.text: A victim and an offender may participate in a facilitated conference that results in restitution and a public apology.
examples.note: The process addresses the victim's injury and the offender's responsibility directly.

commonMisreadings: Restorative justice is not simply leniency or the absence of consequences.

concepts.name: Retributive justice
concepts.summary: Retributive justice holds that proportionate punishment is justified because a wrongdoer deserves it for committing a culpable wrong.
concepts.body: Retributive justice holds that proportionate punishment is justified because a wrongdoer deserves it for committing a culpable wrong. Its central concern is desert and proportionality rather than rehabilitation or compensation alone.

examples.text: A court imposes a proportionate sentence on a person convicted of deliberate assault.
examples.note: The punishment is justified by the offender's culpable violation and its seriousness.

commonMisreadings: Retributive justice differs from revenge because it requires principled and proportionate judgment.

concepts.name: Retrieval-induced forgetting
concepts.summary: Retrieval-induced forgetting is the tendency for retrieving some items from memory to impair later recall of related items that were not retrieved.
concepts.body: Retrieval-induced forgetting is the tendency for retrieving some items from memory to impair later recall of related items that were not retrieved. The effect is often explained by inhibitory control that suppresses competing memories during selective retrieval.

examples.text: Practicing recall of some fruits from a studied list can make unpracticed related fruits harder to remember later.
examples.note: Retrieval strengthens the practiced items while reducing access to competitors.

commonMisreadings: It differs from ordinary forgetting caused only by the passage of time.

concepts.name: Revolutionary socialism
concepts.summary: Revolutionary socialism is the view that socialism requires a fundamental transformation of capitalist property and political relations, often through mass political rupture.
concepts.body: Revolutionary socialism is the view that socialism requires a fundamental transformation of capitalist property and political relations, often through mass political rupture. It rejects the idea that gradual reforms within existing institutions alone can establish a socialist order.

examples.text: A revolutionary socialist organization may seek worker control of industry through a mass strike and seizure of production.
examples.note: The proposed change removes capitalist ownership rather than merely regulating it.

commonMisreadings: Revolutionary socialism does not necessarily prescribe one specific form of post-revolutionary government.

concepts.name: Rhyme-as-reason effect
concepts.summary: The rhyme-as-reason effect is the tendency for rhyming statements to seem more truthful or persuasive than equivalent non-rhyming statements.
concepts.body: The rhyme-as-reason effect is the tendency for rhyming statements to seem more truthful or persuasive than equivalent non-rhyming statements. The effect can arise because rhyme increases processing fluency and makes a slogan easier to remember.

examples.text: “Woes unite foes” may sound more credible than “Woes unite enemies” despite similar content.
examples.note: The rhyming version is processed and recalled more smoothly, influencing judgment.

commonMisreadings: The effect shows a bias in perceived truth, not evidence that rhyming claims are actually better supported.

concepts.name: Right-libertarianism
concepts.summary: Right-libertarianism is a political position emphasizing strong individual property rights, voluntary exchange, limited government, and self-ownership.
concepts.body: Right-libertarianism is a political position emphasizing strong individual property rights, voluntary exchange, limited government, and self-ownership. It commonly permits state action mainly to protect persons and property against force, fraud, and rights violations.

examples.text: A right-libertarian may oppose compulsory taxation for broad redistribution while supporting courts and police against theft.
examples.note: The position treats redistributive coercion as a significant interference with ownership.

commonMisreadings: Right-libertarianism differs from left-libertarianism over the distribution or ownership of natural resources.

concepts.name: Rights
concepts.summary: Rights are justified claims or entitlements that place duties, permissions, or protections on other persons or institutions.
concepts.body: Rights are justified claims or entitlements that place duties, permissions, or protections on other persons or institutions. Rights may be moral, legal, civil, political, positive, or negative depending on their source and required duties.

examples.text: A legal right to vote obliges the state to provide eligible citizens a non-discriminatory opportunity to cast ballots.
examples.note: The entitlement correlates with an institutional duty to protect access.

commonMisreadings: A right is not merely a strong personal preference.

concepts.name: Rigid designator
concepts.summary: A rigid designator is a term that refers to the same object in every possible world in which that object exists.
concepts.body: A rigid designator is a term that refers to the same object in every possible world in which that object exists. Saul Kripke used the concept to distinguish names such as “Aristotle” from descriptions that may pick out different individuals in other possible situations.

examples.text: “Water” is rigid if used as a name for the substance H2O, since it refers to H2O in relevant possible worlds.
examples.note: The reference remains fixed even when a world's watery substance differs.

commonMisreadings: A definite description such as “the teacher of Alexander” need not be rigid.

concepts.name: Ring of Gyges
concepts.summary: The Ring of Gyges is Plato's thought experiment about an invisibility ring that allows its wearer to act without being detected.
concepts.body: The Ring of Gyges is Plato's thought experiment about an invisibility ring that allows its wearer to act without being detected. In the Republic, Glaucon uses it to challenge the claim that people are just for its own sake rather than for reputation or consequences.

examples.text: A person who could become invisible might steal without fear of punishment or social condemnation.
examples.note: The case removes ordinary external incentives that support just behavior.

commonMisreadings: The thought experiment asks about the nature of justice, not about actual invisibility technology.

concepts.name: Risk
concepts.summary: Risk is the possibility of an unwanted outcome combined with uncertainty about whether or when it will occur, often represented using probabilities.
concepts.body: Risk is the possibility of an unwanted outcome combined with uncertainty about whether or when it will occur, often represented using probabilities. Unlike mere ambiguity, risk permits at least some assessment of possible outcomes and their likelihoods.

examples.text: An insurer faces a calculable risk of a house fire based on historical claim rates.
examples.note: Past data allow an estimate of the probability even though the individual fire is uncertain.

commonMisreadings: Risk differs from uncertainty in strict Knightian usage, where probabilities are not known.

concepts.name: Robustness
concepts.summary: Robustness is the ability of a method, system, claim, or conclusion to remain reliable when conditions, assumptions, data, or implementation details vary.
concepts.body: Robustness is the ability of a method, system, claim, or conclusion to remain reliable when conditions, assumptions, data, or implementation details vary. A robust statistical result persists across reasonable model specifications and samples rather than depending on one fragile choice.

examples.text: A policy effect that remains after excluding outliers and using several plausible regressions is statistically robust.
examples.note: The conclusion survives relevant analytic changes.

commonMisreadings: Robustness is not the same as being invulnerable to every possible disturbance.

concepts.name: Romanticism
concepts.summary: Romanticism was an intellectual and artistic movement that emphasized emotion, imagination, individuality, nature, and the sublime in reaction to some ideals of Enlightenment rationalism and industrial modernity.
concepts.body: Romanticism was an intellectual and artistic movement that emphasized emotion, imagination, individuality, nature, and the sublime in reaction to some ideals of Enlightenment rationalism and industrial modernity. It influenced literature, painting, music, philosophy, and ideas of national culture during the late eighteenth and nineteenth centuries.

examples.text: Wordsworth's poetry presents encounters with nature as sources of intense feeling and insight.
examples.note: The poem gives imaginative experience and nature a central cultural role.

commonMisreadings: Romanticism is not simply any work that depicts romantic love.

concepts.name: Rule consequentialism
concepts.summary: Rule consequentialism evaluates actions by the consequences of following a system of rules whose general acceptance would produce the best results.
concepts.body: Rule consequentialism evaluates actions by the consequences of following a system of rules whose general acceptance would produce the best results. It differs from act consequentialism by assessing rules rather than calculating each isolated act directly.

examples.text: Keeping a rule against lying can be justified if general adherence builds trust and produces better social outcomes.
examples.note: The rule's beneficial effects across cases determine its justification.

commonMisreadings: Rule consequentialism is not identical to obeying any existing legal rule.

concepts.name: Rule of law
concepts.summary: The rule of law is the principle that public power must operate through publicly known, stable, general, and fairly applied laws rather than arbitrary commands.
concepts.body: The rule of law is the principle that public power must operate through publicly known, stable, general, and fairly applied laws rather than arbitrary commands. It commonly requires legal equality, due process, independent courts, and limits on official discretion.

examples.text: A government follows the rule of law when officials can be challenged in court for violating a published statute.
examples.note: The same legal standards constrain officeholders and ordinary citizens.

commonMisreadings: The rule of law is not satisfied merely because a government issues many rules.

concepts.name: Rule utilitarianism
concepts.summary: Rule utilitarianism judges actions by rules whose general acceptance would maximize well-being.
concepts.body: Rule utilitarianism judges actions by rules whose general acceptance would maximize well-being. It evaluates rules by their general consequences rather than each act separately.

examples.text: Keeping promises is normally required because promise-keeping sustains trust.
examples.note: The practice benefits social cooperation even when one breach might help.

commonMisreadings: It is not act utilitarianism, which evaluates each individual act directly.

concepts.name: Rule-following problem
concepts.summary: The rule-following problem asks what makes an application conform to a rule.
concepts.body: The rule-following problem asks what makes an application conform to a rule. Wittgenstein held that practices of training and correction help determine future applications.

examples.text: A pupil continues 2, 4, 6, 8 with 10 when applying addition.
examples.note: Shared mathematical practice fixes the relevant continuation.

commonMisreadings: It is not merely difficulty remembering a rule.

concepts.name: Russell's paradox
concepts.summary: Russell's paradox is the contradiction arising from the set of all sets that are not members of themselves.
concepts.body: Russell's paradox is the contradiction arising from the set of all sets that are not members of themselves. Membership in that set requires both membership and nonmembership.

examples.text: R = {x | x is not a member of x} yields R ∈ R iff R ∉ R.
examples.note: Each possible status produces its opposite.

commonMisreadings: It differs from the liar paradox, which concerns sentence truth.

concepts.name: Russell's teapot
concepts.summary: Russell's teapot is an analogy that an unsupported unfalsifiable claim does not merit belief merely because it cannot be disproved.
concepts.body: Russell's teapot is an analogy that an unsupported unfalsifiable claim does not merit belief merely because it cannot be disproved. The imagined teapot orbits between Earth and Mars beyond detection.

examples.text: Someone claims that a tiny undetectable teapot circles Mars.
examples.note: The claimant supplies no evidence for the claim.

commonMisreadings: It does not prove every extraordinary claim false.

concepts.name: Sacrifice
concepts.summary: Sacrifice is deliberately surrendering a valued good for a goal, duty, relationship, or commitment.
concepts.body: Sacrifice is deliberately surrendering a valued good for a goal, duty, relationship, or commitment. It may involve resources, safety, comfort, opportunity, or life.

examples.text: A firefighter enters a burning building to rescue a trapped resident.
examples.note: The firefighter gives up safety to protect another person.

commonMisreadings: Sacrifice does not require receiving no benefit or recognition.

concepts.name: Samkhya
concepts.summary: Samkhya is an Indian system distinguishing consciousness from material nature.
concepts.body: Samkhya is an Indian system distinguishing consciousness from material nature. Classical Samkhya calls passive consciousness purusha and evolving nature prakriti.

examples.text: Liberation occurs when purusha is recognized as distinct from prakriti.
examples.note: This ends identification with mental and material transformations.

commonMisreadings: It is not Advaita Vedanta's nondual metaphysics.

concepts.name: Samsara
concepts.summary: Samsara is the recurring cycle of birth, death, and rebirth in several Indian traditions.
concepts.body: Samsara is the recurring cycle of birth, death, and rebirth in several Indian traditions. It is commonly linked with karma, dissatisfaction, and the need for liberation.

examples.text: In Buddhism, craving and ignorance condition continued rebirth.
examples.note: Those causes sustain the cycle that awakening aims to end.

commonMisreadings: Samsara is not simply ordinary life in every tradition.

concepts.name: Satisfiability
concepts.summary: Satisfiability is the property of a formula having at least one interpretation that makes it true.
concepts.body: Satisfiability is the property of a formula having at least one interpretation that makes it true. A satisfiable formula need not be true under every assignment.

examples.text: P ∨ Q is satisfiable because assigning P true makes it true.
examples.note: One successful valuation establishes satisfiability.

commonMisreadings: It differs from validity, which requires truth under all interpretations.

concepts.name: Scholasticism
concepts.summary: Scholasticism is a medieval and early modern method using systematic questions, objections, replies, and argument.
concepts.body: Scholasticism is a medieval and early modern method using systematic questions, objections, replies, and argument. It integrated authorities with distinctions and formal reasoning, especially in universities.

examples.text: Thomas Aquinas presents objections before answering whether God's existence can be demonstrated.
examples.note: The structure tests a claim against competing arguments.

commonMisreadings: It is not simply any medieval philosophy or blind appeal to authority.

concepts.name: Schrodinger's cat
concepts.summary: Schrodinger's cat is a thought experiment about applying quantum superposition to a macroscopic system.
concepts.body: Schrodinger's cat is a thought experiment about applying quantum superposition to a macroscopic system. A quantum event is imagined entangled with alternatives associated with a cat's condition before observation.

examples.text: A sealed box contains a cat and a decay-triggered lethal device.
examples.note: The case illustrates the measurement problem rather than proposing an experiment.

commonMisreadings: It does not show that everyday cats are literally half-dead.

concepts.name: Scientific anti-realism
concepts.summary: Scientific anti-realism denies or suspends commitment to theories describing observer-independent unobservable reality.
concepts.body: Scientific anti-realism denies or suspends commitment to theories describing observer-independent unobservable reality. Some anti-realists treat theoretical entities as instruments for organizing predictions.

examples.text: An instrumentalist uses electrons to calculate observations without claiming electrons exist.
examples.note: Predictive success is accepted without literal commitment to hidden objects.

commonMisreadings: It is not necessarily denial that observations are real.

concepts.name: Scientific explanation
concepts.summary: Scientific explanation accounts for why a phenomenon occurs through causes, mechanisms, laws, models, or patterns.
concepts.body: Scientific explanation accounts for why a phenomenon occurs through causes, mechanisms, laws, models, or patterns. Different sciences use causal, statistical, mechanistic, and historical forms.

examples.text: Germ theory explains infection through microorganisms damaging tissue.
examples.note: The mechanism connects illness with an underlying process.

commonMisreadings: Explanation is not merely a successful prediction or restatement.

concepts.name: Scientific method
concepts.summary: The scientific method is a family of practices for forming, testing, revising, and communicating empirical claims.
concepts.body: The scientific method is a family of practices for forming, testing, revising, and communicating empirical claims. It commonly uses observation, measurement, controlled comparison, replication, and criticism.

examples.text: Researchers compare randomized treatment and control groups in a drug trial.
examples.note: The comparison helps separate treatment effects from chance and confounding.

commonMisreadings: There is no single rigid sequence for every science.

concepts.name: Scientific realism
concepts.summary: Scientific realism holds that successful theories often describe real structures, entities, and processes independent of observation.
concepts.body: Scientific realism holds that successful theories often describe real structures, entities, and processes independent of observation. It explains mature theories' success partly through approximate truth about unobservables.

examples.text: A realist treats bacteria as real causes of disease.
examples.note: The bacterial mechanism is part of the world's structure.

commonMisreadings: It does not require every current theory to be exactly true.

concepts.name: Scientism
concepts.summary: Scientism holds that scientific methods or authority should dominate or exclusively determine legitimate knowledge and belief.
concepts.body: Scientism holds that scientific methods or authority should dominate or exclusively determine legitimate knowledge and belief. The term often criticizes extending experimental standards to value and meaning questions.

examples.text: Someone says moral judgments are meaningless unless laboratory-measurable.
examples.note: The claim applies scientific measurement beyond its direct domain.

commonMisreadings: Scientism is not simply respect for scientific evidence.

concepts.name: Scotism
concepts.summary: Scotism is the philosophical and theological tradition associated with John Duns Scotus.
concepts.body: Scotism is the philosophical and theological tradition associated with John Duns Scotus. It emphasizes univocity of being, formal distinction, haecceity, and aspects of will.

examples.text: Scotus explains an individual's distinctness through haecceity, or thisness.
examples.note: Thisness accounts for individuation beyond shared nature.

commonMisreadings: Scotism is not every medieval discussion of Scotus.

concepts.name: Second-order logic
concepts.summary: Second-order logic quantifies over properties, relations, or sets as well as individual objects.
concepts.body: Second-order logic quantifies over properties, relations, or sets as well as individual objects. Its greater expressive power can characterize the natural numbers categorically under standard semantics.

examples.text: A formula says every property containing zero and closed under successor contains every natural number.
examples.note: The quantifier ranges over properties or sets.

commonMisreadings: It is not first-order logic with more individual variables.

concepts.name: Second-order thinking
concepts.summary: Second-order thinking evaluates indirect, delayed, and systemic consequences as well as immediate results.
concepts.body: Second-order thinking evaluates indirect, delayed, and systemic consequences as well as immediate results. It asks how others respond and what those responses cause later.

examples.text: A rent cap may lower current prices but reduce future rental supply.
examples.note: The supply response is an effect of the intervention.

commonMisreadings: It is not simply thinking about a second topic.

concepts.name: Secularism
concepts.summary: Secularism limits religious control of public institutions or separates religious authority from state authority.
concepts.body: Secularism limits religious control of public institutions or separates religious authority from state authority. It can protect religious freedom while preventing establishment of one faith.

examples.text: A constitution permits several religions and bars an official church.
examples.note: Citizenship is separated from religious membership.

commonMisreadings: It is not necessarily hostility to religion.

concepts.name: Selection effect
concepts.summary: A selection effect occurs when observed cases are chosen through a process that makes them differ systematically from the target population.
concepts.body: A selection effect occurs when observed cases are chosen through a process that makes them differ systematically from the target population. Selection can create or hide associations because inclusion depends on relevant traits.

examples.text: A hospital study overrepresents severe disease because mild cases stay home.
examples.note: The sampling process changes the apparent disease distribution.

commonMisreadings: It is not an effect caused by the treatment itself.

concepts.name: Self
concepts.summary: The self is the subject or entity regarded as bearer of experiences, thoughts, actions, or identity.
concepts.body: The self is the subject or entity regarded as bearer of experiences, thoughts, actions, or identity. Theories treat it variously as substance, psychological pattern, narrative, or process.

examples.text: A person remembers childhood experiences as belonging to the present individual.
examples.note: Memory supports one account of personal continuity.

commonMisreadings: The self is not automatically body, brain, personality, or soul.

concepts.name: Self-consciousness
concepts.summary: Self-consciousness is awareness of oneself as oneself or of one's own states and actions.
concepts.body: Self-consciousness is awareness of oneself as oneself or of one's own states and actions. It involves representing oneself as the object of thought or perception.

examples.text: Seeing a mark in a mirror and recognizing it as one's own displays self-recognition.
examples.note: The observed body is represented as the observer's body.

commonMisreadings: It is not identical to consciousness without self-awareness.

concepts.name: Self-determination
concepts.summary: Self-determination is the capacity or right to direct one's own life, political status, or collective affairs.
concepts.body: Self-determination is the capacity or right to direct one's own life, political status, or collective affairs. Politically, it can mean choosing government without external domination.

examples.text: A colonized population votes on independence from an empire.
examples.note: The vote expresses collective control over political status.

commonMisreadings: It does not mean every preference overrides law or others' rights.

concepts.name: Self-evidence
concepts.summary: Self-evidence is seeming true through understanding a proposition itself without inferential proof.
concepts.body: Self-evidence is seeming true through understanding a proposition itself without inferential proof. A proposition may seem self-evident to one rational agent while others misunderstand it.

examples.text: After grasping the terms, one sees that a whole exceeds any proper part.
examples.note: The concepts appear to provide immediate warrant.

commonMisreadings: It is not identical to subjective certainty or agreement.

concepts.name: Self-generation effect
concepts.summary: The self-generation effect is improved memory for information produced or completed by the learner.
concepts.body: The self-generation effect is improved memory for information produced or completed by the learner. Generation creates richer retrieval cues than passive reading.

examples.text: A student recalls an antonym better after producing it than after seeing it.
examples.note: The student's own activity strengthens encoding.

commonMisreadings: It does not mean no external information was used.

concepts.name: Self-reference effect
concepts.summary: The self-reference effect is improved memory when information is encoded in relation to oneself.
concepts.body: The self-reference effect is improved memory when information is encoded in relation to oneself. Personal relevance promotes elaboration and distinctive retrieval cues.

examples.text: A person remembers "reliable" better after judging whether it describes them.
examples.note: The self-related judgment gives personal meaning.

commonMisreadings: It is not merely seeing the word self.

concepts.name: Semantic consequence
concepts.summary: Semantic consequence is the relation in which every model satisfying premises also satisfies the conclusion.
concepts.body: Semantic consequence is the relation in which every model satisfying premises also satisfies the conclusion. It is written Γ ⊨ φ and concerns truth under interpretations.

examples.text: P and P → Q semantically entail Q.
examples.note: Every valuation satisfying both premises satisfies Q.

commonMisreadings: It differs from derivability, which concerns formal proofs.

concepts.name: Semantic externalism
concepts.summary: Semantic externalism holds that meaning depends partly on factors outside an individual's internal state.
concepts.body: Semantic externalism holds that meaning depends partly on factors outside an individual's internal state. Causal history, social practice, and environment can determine content.

examples.text: Twin Earth's liquid can differ in meaning from Earth's water despite identical appearances.
examples.note: The external substance helps determine reference.

commonMisreadings: It does not deny all internal contributions to meaning.

concepts.name: Semantic holism
concepts.summary: Semantic holism holds that an expression's meaning depends on its relations to a broad network of expressions or beliefs.
concepts.body: Semantic holism holds that an expression's meaning depends on its relations to a broad network of expressions or beliefs. Changing one network element can alter meanings of connected terms.

examples.text: Electron's meaning depends on relations to charge, fields, and measurement.
examples.note: The term gains content from its theoretical role.

commonMisreadings: It does not require identical meanings for every speaker.

concepts.name: Semantic internalism
concepts.summary: Semantic internalism holds that meaning is determined by factors internal to the speaker or linguistic system.
concepts.body: Semantic internalism holds that meaning is determined by factors internal to the speaker or linguistic system. Candidates include conceptual roles, mental representations, and computational structures.

examples.text: An internalist says a water concept is fixed by cognitive representation despite environmental change.
examples.note: Internal representational organization grounds the content.

commonMisreadings: It does not deny all influence from social language.

concepts.name: Semantics
concepts.summary: Semantics is the study of meaning in language, formal systems, and representational systems.
concepts.body: Semantics is the study of meaning in language, formal systems, and representational systems. It examines reference, truth conditions, entailment, and interpreted content.

examples.text: Formal semantics assigns "Snow is white" a condition involving snow and whiteness.
examples.note: The condition states what makes the sentence true.

commonMisreadings: It differs from syntax, which studies structure without meaning.

concepts.name: Semiotics
concepts.summary: Semiotics is the study of signs and processes by which something stands for or communicates something else.
concepts.body: Semiotics is the study of signs and processes by which something stands for or communicates something else. It analyzes words, images, gestures, objects, codes, and contexts.

examples.text: A red traffic light signifies that drivers must stop.
examples.note: A shared code links the color to the required action.

commonMisreadings: It is broader than study of written language.

concepts.name: Sense and reference
concepts.summary: Sense and reference are Frege's distinction between an expression's mode of presentation and its object.
concepts.body: Sense and reference are Frege's distinction between an expression's mode of presentation and its object. Expressions can share reference while differing in cognitive significance.

examples.text: Morning star and evening star both refer to Venus but present it differently.
examples.note: Learning their co-reference can therefore be informative.

commonMisreadings: Sense is not simply a private image.

concepts.name: Sense data
concepts.summary: Sense data are purported immediate mental contents given in perception, such as visual patches or felt qualities.
concepts.body: Sense data are purported immediate mental contents given in perception, such as visual patches or felt qualities. Sense-data theories use them to explain directly presented perceptual knowledge.

examples.text: A red oval appearance in hallucination is sense data without a red object.
examples.note: The appearance is experienced without its ordinary external object.

commonMisreadings: Sense data are not straightforwardly physical objects.

concepts.name: Sentience
concepts.summary: Sentience is the capacity for subjective experience, especially pleasure, pain, or awareness.
concepts.body: Sentience is the capacity for subjective experience, especially pleasure, pain, or awareness. It is often a basis for moral consideration because suffering can make things worse for a being.

examples.text: A dog withdraws its paw after a painful stimulus and may whine.
examples.note: The behavior is evidence relevant to felt experience.

commonMisreadings: It is not identical to intelligence or self-consciousness.

concepts.name: Sentientism
concepts.summary: Sentientism makes conscious experience the fundamental basis of moral consideration.
concepts.body: Sentientism makes conscious experience the fundamental basis of moral consideration. It rejects species, intelligence, or language as sufficient grounds for ignoring suffering.

examples.text: A sentientist objects to severe pain inflicted on a pig unable to use human language.
examples.note: The pig's capacity for suffering matters morally.

commonMisreadings: It need not assign identical rights to all sentient beings.

concepts.name: Separatism
concepts.summary: Separatism advocates political, cultural, religious, or social separation between groups or institutions.
concepts.body: Separatism advocates political, cultural, religious, or social separation between groups or institutions. Political separatism may seek an independent state, while institutional separatism seeks distinct organizations.

examples.text: A region campaigns to leave a federation and become independent.
examples.note: The goal is territorial political separation.

commonMisreadings: It is not automatically isolationism.

concepts.name: Sequent calculus
concepts.summary: Sequent calculus is a proof system in which sequents represent relations between premise and conclusion collections.
concepts.body: Sequent calculus is a proof system in which sequents represent relations between premise and conclusion collections. Inference rules transform sequents until axioms or desired sequents are reached.

examples.text: P, P → Q ⊢ Q can be derived in a sequent calculus.
examples.note: The proof records that Q follows from assumptions.

commonMisreadings: A sequent is not itself a true-or-false sentence.

concepts.name: Serial-position effect
concepts.summary: The serial-position effect is different recall performance according to an item's position in a list.
concepts.body: The serial-position effect is different recall performance according to an item's position in a list. Early items often show primacy and late items recency, with weaker middle recall.

examples.text: People recall first and last words more often than middle words.
examples.note: Sequence position predicts recall probability.

commonMisreadings: It does not require identical effects in every list.

concepts.name: Shinto
concepts.summary: Shinto is a Japanese tradition centered on kami, ritual purity, ancestral ties, and relationships with places and communities.
concepts.body: Shinto is a Japanese tradition centered on kami, ritual purity, ancestral ties, and relationships with places and communities. Practices include shrine rituals, offerings, purification, and festivals rather than one creed.

examples.text: A visitor washes at a shrine fountain and offers a prayer to a kami.
examples.note: Purification and offering constitute ritual participation.

commonMisreadings: It is not simply folklore or one philosophical doctrine.

concepts.name: Ship of Theseus
concepts.summary: The Ship of Theseus puzzle asks whether an object remains the same after all its parts are gradually replaced.
concepts.body: The Ship of Theseus puzzle asks whether an object remains the same after all its parts are gradually replaced. It becomes harder when removed original parts are reassembled into another ship.

examples.text: A museum replaces every plank over decades until none is original.
examples.note: The case separates material continuity from identity criteria.

commonMisreadings: Counting changed parts alone does not solve it.

concepts.name: Signaling
concepts.summary: Signaling is communication in which an observable act or trait conveys information about a hidden state or intention.
concepts.body: Signaling is communication in which an observable act or trait conveys information about a hidden state or intention. Signals may be costly, conventional, reliable, deceptive, or incentive-shaped.

examples.text: A peacock's elaborate tail can signal condition to mates while imposing survival costs.
examples.note: Cost can make the display harder for weak individuals to sustain.

commonMisreadings: It is not identical to intentional verbal communication.

concepts.name: Sikh philosophy
concepts.summary: Sikh philosophy centers on one formless God, remembrance, ethical action, equality, and service.
concepts.body: Sikh philosophy centers on one formless God, remembrance, ethical action, equality, and service. It emphasizes householder life, honest work, sharing, and overcoming ego in community.

examples.text: Langar provides a shared meal to people from different social backgrounds.
examples.note: The practice expresses service and rejects caste exclusion.

commonMisreadings: It is not reducible to generic monotheism.

concepts.name: Simulation hypothesis
concepts.summary: The simulation hypothesis proposes that conscious observers might inhabit an artificial computational simulation.
concepts.body: The simulation hypothesis proposes that conscious observers might inhabit an artificial computational simulation. Its plausibility depends on assumptions about advanced civilizations, consciousness, and computational capacity.

examples.text: A future civilization runs conscious ancestor simulations whose inhabitants experience a physical-seeming world.
examples.note: If common, simulated observers could outnumber original-world observers.

commonMisreadings: Virtual imitation alone does not establish the hypothesis.

concepts.name: Simulation theory of mind
concepts.summary: Simulation theory of mind explains other minds by imagining or modeling how one would respond in another's situation.
concepts.body: Simulation theory of mind explains other minds by imagining or modeling how one would respond in another's situation. It contrasts with mindreading based primarily on an internal theory of psychological laws.

examples.text: To understand a friend's choice, one imagines having the friend's information and preferences.
examples.note: The simulated decision process supports an attribution.

commonMisreadings: It does not require duplicating the other person's brain.

concepts.name: Situation ethics
concepts.summary: Situation ethics holds that particular circumstances and love should guide moral judgment rather than exceptionless rules.
concepts.body: Situation ethics holds that particular circumstances and love should guide moral judgment rather than exceptionless rules. Joseph Fletcher's version treats agapeic concern as the governing principle.

examples.text: Breaking a promise may be justified to prevent serious harm.
examples.note: Concrete human consequences guide the decision over formal rule status.

commonMisreadings: It does not make every felt preference morally sufficient.

concepts.name: Skeptical theism
concepts.summary: Skeptical theism holds that human limits weaken inferences from apparently pointless suffering against a morally perfect God.
concepts.body: Skeptical theism holds that human limits weaken inferences from apparently pointless suffering against a morally perfect God. Humans may be unable to survey possible reasons available to an omniscient being.

examples.text: Seeing no reason for a child's illness does not prove no sufficient reason exists.
examples.note: The absence of an accessible explanation is weak evidence under the view.

commonMisreadings: It neither explains suffering nor proves God's existence.

concepts.name: Skepticism
concepts.summary: Skepticism is a family of positions questioning whether knowledge, certainty, or justification is attainable in some domain.
concepts.body: Skepticism is a family of positions questioning whether knowledge, certainty, or justification is attainable in some domain. Arguments may challenge perception, memory, induction, testimony, or the external world.

examples.text: A brain-in-a-vat scenario asks how experience could distinguish reality from computer-generated experience.
examples.note: It targets evidence available from within experience.

commonMisreadings: It need not mean refusing all practical belief.

concepts.name: Sleeping Beauty problem
concepts.summary: The Sleeping Beauty problem asks what probability Beauty should assign after awakening without knowing which experiment day it is.
concepts.body: The Sleeping Beauty problem asks what probability Beauty should assign after awakening without knowing which experiment day it is. The one-half versus one-third debate concerns self-locating information and sampling structure.

examples.text: Beauty wakes once after heads and twice on separate days after tails, with memory erased.
examples.note: On waking she assesses the probability of heads.

commonMisreadings: It is not merely a question about ordinary sleep.

concepts.name: Social anarchism
concepts.summary: Social anarchism seeks society without coercive hierarchy, organized through voluntary cooperation and mutual aid.
concepts.body: Social anarchism seeks society without coercive hierarchy, organized through voluntary cooperation and mutual aid. It emphasizes collective institutions, shared resources, and equality more than individualist anarchism.

examples.text: A worker cooperative governs a factory without a permanent managerial class.
examples.note: Production is coordinated through collective control.

commonMisreadings: It does not mean no organization or rules.

concepts.name: Social constructivism
concepts.summary: Social constructivism holds that knowledge, meaning, identity, or institutions form through interaction and shared practices.
concepts.body: Social constructivism holds that knowledge, meaning, identity, or institutions form through interaction and shared practices. Language, norms, roles, and history can make apparently natural arrangements socially dependent.

examples.text: A banknote functions as money through collectively maintained monetary rules.
examples.note: Social practice assigns and sustains its status.

commonMisreadings: Construction does not imply unreality or total arbitrariness.

concepts.name: Social contract
concepts.summary: The social contract is a theory that political authority or obligations arise from agreement or hypothetical agreement among people.
concepts.body: The social contract is a theory that political authority or obligations arise from agreement or hypothetical agreement among people. Theories use it to justify sovereignty, limited government, rights, or cooperation.

examples.text: People accept common laws in exchange for protection by political authority.
examples.note: Reciprocal terms explain political obligation.

commonMisreadings: It is often hypothetical rather than a signed historical document.

concepts.name: Social democracy
concepts.summary: Social democracy combines representative democracy and regulated capitalism with extensive social protections.
concepts.body: Social democracy combines representative democracy and regulated capitalism with extensive social protections. It commonly supports public services, labor rights, progressive taxation, and redistribution.

examples.text: A state funds universal healthcare while private firms continue operating.
examples.note: Markets remain while insecurity and inequality are reduced.

commonMisreadings: It is not abolition of private productive ownership.

concepts.name: Social epistemology
concepts.summary: Social epistemology studies how knowledge and justified belief are produced and shared among people and institutions.
concepts.body: Social epistemology studies how knowledge and justified belief are produced and shared among people and institutions. It examines testimony, expertise, disagreement, group inquiry, power, and epistemic institutions.

examples.text: Scientists use peer criticism and replication to check a claim.
examples.note: Interaction can reveal errors an isolated investigator misses.

commonMisreadings: It does not reduce truth to group opinion.

concepts.name: Social justice
concepts.summary: Social justice concerns fair distribution of benefits, burdens, rights, opportunities, and recognition.
concepts.body: Social justice concerns fair distribution of benefits, burdens, rights, opportunities, and recognition. It addresses inequality, discrimination, participation, status, and institutional procedures.

examples.text: Removing a transit barrier can expand access to jobs and education.
examples.note: The change addresses a structural obstacle rather than private charity.

commonMisreadings: It is broader than charity because it evaluates institutions.

concepts.name: Social liberalism
concepts.summary: Social liberalism combines individual rights and liberties with public action securing social and economic opportunity.
concepts.body: Social liberalism combines individual rights and liberties with public action securing social and economic opportunity. It accepts markets while supporting regulation, welfare, and public goods when needed for effective freedom.

examples.text: Government provides education and healthcare so deprivation does not nullify formal liberty.
examples.note: Public provision increases practical ability to exercise rights.

commonMisreadings: It differs from laissez-faire liberalism.

concepts.name: Social movement
concepts.summary: A social movement is a sustained collective effort seeking or resisting significant social, cultural, or political change.
concepts.body: A social movement is a sustained collective effort seeking or resisting significant social, cultural, or political change. Movements use networks, campaigns, protest, organizing, and public claims outside routine procedures.

examples.text: The civil rights movement used boycotts, marches, litigation, and voter registration drives.
examples.note: Coordinated action pursued legal and institutional transformation.

commonMisreadings: One spontaneous protest is not necessarily a movement.

concepts.name: Socialism
concepts.summary: Socialism is a family of views favoring social or collective control of productive resources and reduced class domination.
concepts.body: Socialism is a family of views favoring social or collective control of productive resources and reduced class domination. Proposals range from worker cooperatives and market socialism to public planning.

examples.text: A factory is owned and governed by its workers, who decide how surplus is used.
examples.note: Production control is shared by workers rather than private owners.

commonMisreadings: It is not identical to one historical economic system.

concepts.name: Solidarity
concepts.summary: Solidarity is mutual support and shared responsibility among people recognizing common interests or conditions.
concepts.body: Solidarity is mutual support and shared responsibility among people recognizing common interests or conditions. It can motivate collective action without identical identities or immediate benefits.

examples.text: Workers in separate departments strike together against discriminatory dismissal.
examples.note: They accept shared costs because the treatment is a common concern.

commonMisreadings: Solidarity is more than agreement or sympathy.

concepts.name: Sophism
concepts.summary: Sophism is reasoning associated with Greek sophists and often criticized for prioritizing persuasive victory over truth.
concepts.body: Sophism is reasoning associated with Greek sophists and often criticized for prioritizing persuasive victory over truth. Later philosophers used the term for deceptive or eristic argument.

examples.text: A speaker exploits verbal ambiguity to make a weak case appear decisive.
examples.note: The apparent refutation depends on equivocation.

commonMisreadings: It does not mean every sophist's argument was false.

concepts.name: Soteriology
concepts.summary: Soteriology is the study of salvation, liberation, or deliverance from sin, suffering, death, or ignorance.
concepts.body: Soteriology is the study of salvation, liberation, or deliverance from sin, suffering, death, or ignorance. Traditions propose different remedies, including grace, faith, practice, knowledge, ritual, or awakening.

examples.text: Christian soteriology studies reconciliation with God through Christ.
examples.note: It analyzes the nature and means of salvation.

commonMisreadings: It is not limited to afterlife theories.

concepts.name: Soundness of a proof system
concepts.summary: A proof system is sound when every formula it proves is valid under its intended semantics.
concepts.body: A proof system is sound when every formula it proves is valid under its intended semantics. Soundness prevents formal derivations from establishing semantically false conclusions.

examples.text: A classical calculus proving P ∨ ¬P must prove a classically valid formula.
examples.note: The rules preserve validity from axioms.

commonMisreadings: It differs from completeness, which concerns proving every valid formula.

concepts.name: Soundness of an argument
concepts.summary: An argument is sound when it is valid and all its premises are true.
concepts.body: An argument is sound when it is valid and all its premises are true. Soundness guarantees a true conclusion, while validity alone concerns conditional preservation.

examples.text: All mammals are warm-blooded, whales are mammals, therefore whales are warm-blooded.
examples.note: The form is valid and both premises are true.

commonMisreadings: A valid argument with a false premise is not sound.

concepts.name: Spacing effect
concepts.summary: The spacing effect is improved long-term retention when study sessions are distributed over time.
concepts.body: The spacing effect is improved long-term retention when study sessions are distributed over time. Spacing supplies repeated retrieval opportunities and varied encoding contexts.

examples.text: Reviewing vocabulary for ten minutes on four days usually beats one forty-minute session.
examples.note: Distributed practice supports durable recall.

commonMisreadings: It is not merely a longer single session.

concepts.name: Speciesism
concepts.summary: Speciesism is unjustified differential treatment based solely on species membership.
concepts.body: Speciesism is unjustified differential treatment based solely on species membership. It resembles discrimination when a group boundary disregards morally relevant interests.

examples.text: Refusing to relieve a cow's severe suffering while relieving equivalent dog suffering solely by species is speciesist.
examples.note: The unequal treatment tracks species rather than suffering.

commonMisreadings: It does not require treating all species identically.

concepts.name: Speculative realism
concepts.summary: Speculative realism is a contemporary movement criticizing philosophies that limit reality to human access or correlation.
concepts.body: Speculative realism is a contemporary movement criticizing philosophies that limit reality to human access or correlation. Its thinkers develop diverse realist accounts of objects, materiality, and worlds independent of thought.

examples.text: An object-oriented philosopher treats a tree as more than its human appearance.
examples.note: The tree has relations and properties not exhausted by encounter.

commonMisreadings: It is not one unified doctrine.

concepts.name: Speech act
concepts.summary: A speech act is an action performed in or through speaking, such as asserting, promising, requesting, or apologizing.
concepts.body: A speech act is an action performed in or through speaking, such as asserting, promising, requesting, or apologizing. Theory distinguishes utterance, performed act, and effects on an audience.

examples.text: Saying "I apologize" can perform an apology rather than describe one.
examples.note: The utterance changes a social relation by undertaking the act.

commonMisreadings: Speech acts are not limited to true-or-false statements.

concepts.name: Spinozism
concepts.summary: Spinozism is Spinoza's system identifying God or Nature as one infinite substance.
concepts.body: Spinozism is Spinoza's system identifying God or Nature as one infinite substance. Finite minds and bodies are modes or attributes within this necessary natural order.

examples.text: A human mind and body are two ways of understanding one finite mode.
examples.note: Mental and bodily descriptions belong to one order.

commonMisreadings: It is not conventional theism with a separate creator.

concepts.name: Spiritualism
concepts.summary: Spiritualism is an orientation emphasizing spirit, nonmaterial reality, or communication with the dead.
concepts.body: Spiritualism is an orientation emphasizing spirit, nonmaterial reality, or communication with the dead. The nineteenth-century movement used séances and mediums to claim contact with departed persons.

examples.text: A séance seeks messages from a deceased person through a medium.
examples.note: The practice treats consciousness as surviving bodily death.

commonMisreadings: It is broader than one ghost claim.

concepts.name: Stalinism
concepts.summary: Stalinism is the system associated with Stalin's rule, marked by party control, collectivization, repression, and state planning.
concepts.body: Stalinism is the system associated with Stalin's rule, marked by party control, collectivization, repression, and state planning. It used purges, censorship, coercive policing, industrialization, and a leadership cult.

examples.text: Forced collectivization transferred peasant farms into state-directed collective production.
examples.note: State power reorganized agriculture with severe human costs.

commonMisreadings: It is not a neutral synonym for all socialism.

concepts.name: Standpoint epistemology
concepts.summary: Standpoint epistemology holds that social positions shape access to knowledge and patterns of ignorance.
concepts.body: Standpoint epistemology holds that social positions shape access to knowledge and patterns of ignorance. Marginalized positions may reveal structures dominant positions overlook, but no standpoint guarantees truth.

examples.text: Workers may notice exploitative practices managers rarely encounter.
examples.note: Their location provides evidence about institutional effects.

commonMisreadings: Identity alone does not make every belief correct.

concepts.name: State
concepts.summary: A state is a political institution claiming authority over territory and population through law, administration, and coercion.
concepts.body: A state is a political institution claiming authority over territory and population through law, administration, and coercion. Modern states commonly possess sovereignty, taxation, bureaucracy, and a claimed legitimate monopoly of force.

examples.text: France maintains courts, borders, taxation, and administration over its territory.
examples.note: These institutions exercise organized authority.

commonMisreadings: A state is not identical to a temporary government.

concepts.name: State capitalism
concepts.summary: State capitalism is an economy where the state owns or directs major enterprises while retaining capitalist accumulation or markets.
concepts.body: State capitalism is an economy where the state owns or directs major enterprises while retaining capitalist accumulation or markets. State ownership can coexist with wage labor, competition, and profit.

examples.text: A government oil company sells petroleum for profit internationally.
examples.note: Public ownership coexists with commercial accumulation.

commonMisreadings: It is not any economy with regulation or taxes.

concepts.name: State of nature
concepts.summary: The state of nature is a hypothetical condition without established political authority used to analyze rights and government.
concepts.body: The state of nature is a hypothetical condition without established political authority used to analyze rights and government. Hobbes, Locke, and Rousseau describe it differently for different arguments.

examples.text: Hobbes imagines people lacking a common judge and facing insecurity.
examples.note: Without shared authority, conflict and uncertainty become central.

commonMisreadings: It need not be a verified historical period.

concepts.name: State socialism
concepts.summary: State socialism is a system where the state owns or centrally directs most productive resources for socialist goals.
concepts.body: State socialism is a system where the state owns or centrally directs most productive resources for socialist goals. It commonly uses public planning, state enterprises, and administrative allocation.

examples.text: A planning agency sets factory output targets and allocates inputs.
examples.note: The state directs production rather than private markets.

commonMisreadings: It is not every capitalist economy with welfare policies.

concepts.name: State-dependent memory
concepts.summary: State-dependent memory is improved recall when retrieval occurs in a physiological or psychological state resembling encoding.
concepts.body: State-dependent memory is improved recall when retrieval occurs in a physiological or psychological state resembling encoding. Mood, intoxication, arousal, and other internal conditions can serve as context cues.

examples.text: Material learned while mildly anxious may be recalled more easily in similar anxiety.
examples.note: The state recreates cues linked to learning.

commonMisreadings: It differs from mood-congruent memory.

concepts.name: Statism
concepts.summary: Statism assigns the state a dominant or extensive role in social, economic, or political organization.
concepts.body: Statism assigns the state a dominant or extensive role in social, economic, or political organization. It can support strong administration, public ownership, regulation, or central authority.

examples.text: A government centrally controls licensing and most major industries.
examples.note: The state is the primary coordinating instrument.

commonMisreadings: Statism is not one single ideology.

concepts.name: Steelmanning
concepts.summary: Steelmanning reformulates an opponent's argument in its strongest plausible form before criticism.
concepts.body: Steelmanning reformulates an opponent's argument in its strongest plausible form before criticism. It preserves the actual commitments while adding charitable clarity.

examples.text: A critic presents the strongest environmental case before discussing policy costs.
examples.note: The response addresses a serious position rather than a caricature.

commonMisreadings: It is not agreement or changing the thesis.

concepts.name: Stereotype threat
concepts.summary: Stereotype threat is the risk that awareness of a negative group stereotype impairs performance in a relevant setting.
concepts.body: Stereotype threat is the risk that awareness of a negative group stereotype impairs performance in a relevant setting. Concern about confirming the stereotype can consume attention and increase stress.

examples.text: A student reminded of a mathematics stereotype performs worse than in a neutral setting.
examples.note: Situational threat can disrupt working memory and focus.

commonMisreadings: It does not explain every performance gap.

concepts.name: Stoicism
concepts.summary: Stoicism is an ancient philosophy holding virtue to be the good and rational response to control to be central to flourishing.
concepts.body: Stoicism is an ancient philosophy holding virtue to be the good and rational response to control to be central to flourishing. Stoics distinguish judgments and actions from external outcomes not fully controlled by an agent.

examples.text: After losing a promotion, someone focuses on acting honestly and wisely.
examples.note: Character is evaluated rather than an uncontrollable result.

commonMisreadings: Stoicism is not emotional numbness.

concepts.name: Strong artificial intelligence
concepts.summary: Strong artificial intelligence holds that a suitably designed artificial system could genuinely have mind, understanding, or consciousness.
concepts.body: Strong artificial intelligence holds that a suitably designed artificial system could genuinely have mind, understanding, or consciousness. It concerns real mental states, not only humanlike outputs.

examples.text: A defender may say a future robot understands language through its computational organization.
examples.note: Understanding is treated as real rather than imitation.

commonMisreadings: It is not simply making software perform hard tasks.

concepts.name: Stroop effect
concepts.summary: The Stroop effect is slower or less accurate responding when an automatic response conflicts with the required task.
concepts.body: The Stroop effect is slower or less accurate responding when an automatic response conflicts with the required task. Naming ink color is delayed when the printed word names an incongruent color.

examples.text: The word blue printed in red creates conflict when saying the ink color.
examples.note: Automatic reading competes with color naming.

commonMisreadings: It is not simply unfamiliar-word slowing.

concepts.name: Structural injustice
concepts.summary: Structural injustice is disadvantage produced by ordinary institutions and processes rather than one isolated wrongful act.
concepts.body: Structural injustice is disadvantage produced by ordinary institutions and processes rather than one isolated wrongful act. It can persist when people follow accepted rules whose combined effects burden a group.

examples.text: Cumulative zoning places affordable housing far from transit and jobs.
examples.note: No single decision need intend exclusion for the pattern to restrict opportunity.

commonMisreadings: Individual responsibility can still matter.

concepts.name: Structural linguistics
concepts.summary: Structural linguistics studies language as a relational system whose elements gain value through contrasts and combinations.
concepts.body: Structural linguistics studies language as a relational system whose elements gain value through contrasts and combinations. Saussure distinguished the social language system from individual speech events.

examples.text: The phoneme p contrasts with b in pat and bat.
examples.note: The contrast gives each sound linguistic value.

commonMisreadings: It does not deny language history or variation.

concepts.name: Structural realism
concepts.summary: Structural realism holds that science may correctly describe relational structure even when entity interpretations change.
concepts.body: Structural realism holds that science may correctly describe relational structure even when entity interpretations change. It explains continuity in theory change by preserving mathematical or relational patterns.

examples.text: A later theory retains an earlier theory's equations while reinterpreting its entities.
examples.note: Relations survive revision of object descriptions.

commonMisreadings: It is not full realism about every unobservable nature.

concepts.name: Structuralism
concepts.summary: Structuralism explains phenomena through underlying systems of relations rather than isolated elements or intentions.
concepts.body: Structuralism explains phenomena through underlying systems of relations rather than isolated elements or intentions. It influenced linguistics, anthropology, literary theory, and philosophy in varied forms.

examples.text: An anthropologist analyzes myth through recurring nature-culture oppositions.
examples.note: Each element gets significance from its relational position.

commonMisreadings: It is not one unchanged cross-disciplinary theory.

concepts.name: Subjective well-being
concepts.summary: Subjective well-being is self-reported life evaluation and experience, including satisfaction and positive or negative affect.
concepts.body: Subjective well-being is self-reported life evaluation and experience, including satisfaction and positive or negative affect. It is commonly measured through questionnaires rather than inferred only from income or health.

examples.text: A survey asks respondents about life satisfaction and recent happiness or distress.
examples.note: The measures target experienced and evaluated quality of life.

commonMisreadings: It is not identical to momentary pleasure or objective conditions.

concepts.name: Sublime
concepts.summary: The sublime is an aesthetic experience of overwhelming magnitude, power, or difficulty exceeding ordinary comprehension.
concepts.body: The sublime is an aesthetic experience of overwhelming magnitude, power, or difficulty exceeding ordinary comprehension. Kant connects vastness in nature with reflection on reason's capacity beyond sensory measurement.

examples.text: A vast storm at sea evokes fear, awe, and reflection on human reason.
examples.note: The scene exceeds comfortable sensory grasp while stimulating thought.

commonMisreadings: It differs from beauty's harmony and proportion.

concepts.name: Subsidiarity
concepts.summary: Subsidiarity says decisions should be made at the lowest competent level while higher authorities support rather than replace it.
concepts.body: Subsidiarity says decisions should be made at the lowest competent level while higher authorities support rather than replace it. The principle balances local autonomy with coordination and assistance.

examples.text: National disaster funding supports local neighborhood distribution.
examples.note: Higher authority supplies capacity without taking over competent local tasks.

commonMisreadings: It does not require every decision to stay local.

concepts.name: Substance
concepts.summary: Substance is a metaphysical entity or underlying reality existing in itself rather than merely as a property.
concepts.body: Substance is a metaphysical entity or underlying reality existing in itself rather than merely as a property. It contrasts with accidents or modes that depend on a bearer.

examples.text: An Aristotelian individual horse is substance while its color is an accident.
examples.note: The horse bears properties that depend on it.

commonMisreadings: Philosophers disagree about which entities are substances.

concepts.name: Substance dualism
concepts.summary: Substance dualism holds that mind and body are distinct kinds of substance.
concepts.body: Substance dualism holds that mind and body are distinct kinds of substance. It treats conscious thought as irreducible to an extended material body.

examples.text: Descartes argues that a thinking mind can be conceived separately from a spatial body.
examples.note: The distinction is taken to indicate distinct substances.

commonMisreadings: It is stronger than property dualism.

concepts.name: Substance self
concepts.summary: The substance-self theory grounds personal identity in a persisting underlying self or soul.
concepts.body: The substance-self theory grounds personal identity in a persisting underlying self or soul. It explains continuity through a bearer of mental states rather than only memory or psychology.

examples.text: A soul theory says the same immaterial soul persists from childhood to adulthood.
examples.note: The soul remains through physical and psychological change.

commonMisreadings: It is not merely the claim that personality remains stable.

concepts.name: Substratum theory
concepts.summary: Substratum theory says properties inhere in an underlying bearer not identical with any one property.
concepts.body: Substratum theory says properties inhere in an underlying bearer not identical with any one property. The substratum explains how a thing remains one substance while qualities change.

examples.text: A red round apple is said to have a bearer of its redness, shape, and taste.
examples.note: The bearer unifies the properties in one object.

commonMisreadings: A substratum is not another observable property.

concepts.name: Sufficient condition
concepts.summary: A sufficient condition guarantees the occurrence or truth of another condition.
concepts.body: A sufficient condition guarantees the occurrence or truth of another condition. It need not be necessary because the result may arise in other ways.

examples.text: Being a square is sufficient for being a rectangle.
examples.note: Every square is a rectangle, though not every rectangle is a square.

commonMisreadings: Sufficiency guarantees but does not require the result.

concepts.name: Sufficientarianism
concepts.summary: Sufficientarianism says justice primarily requires ensuring everyone has enough of a relevant good.
concepts.body: Sufficientarianism says justice primarily requires ensuring everyone has enough of a relevant good. Crossing a sufficiency threshold matters more than eliminating all inequality above it.

examples.text: A health policy prioritizes people below a minimum standard over already well-served patients.
examples.note: The threshold sets initial distributional priority.

commonMisreadings: It need not deny that inequalities above the threshold matter.

concepts.name: Suffix effect
concepts.summary: The suffix effect is impaired immediate serial recall after an irrelevant spoken item follows a list.
concepts.body: The suffix effect is impaired immediate serial recall after an irrelevant spoken item follows a list. The spoken suffix disrupts auditory representation of the list's ending and recency.

examples.text: Digits followed by the word zero are recalled less well than digits followed by silence.
examples.note: The suffix interferes with auditory short-term memory.

commonMisreadings: It is not simply forgetting from a long delay.

concepts.name: Sufism
concepts.summary: Sufism is a diverse Islamic tradition emphasizing purification, remembrance of God, disciplined practice, and experiential knowledge.
concepts.body: Sufism is a diverse Islamic tradition emphasizing purification, remembrance of God, disciplined practice, and experiential knowledge. Paths may include guides, dhikr, ethical refinement, poetry, and devotional practice.

examples.text: A practitioner repeats divine names in dhikr to overcome ego and cultivate remembrance.
examples.note: Repetition functions as spiritual transformation.

commonMisreadings: It is not a separate religion from Islam.

concepts.name: Supererogation
concepts.summary: Supererogation is morally good action that is not required and whose omission is not blameworthy.
concepts.body: Supererogation is morally good action that is not required and whose omission is not blameworthy. Such acts exceed ordinary duty while remaining praiseworthy.

examples.text: A passerby risks safety to rescue a stranger from a dangerous river.
examples.note: The rescue is admirable even if omission is not culpable.

commonMisreadings: It is not merely permissible morally neutral action.

concepts.name: Supervenience
concepts.summary: Supervenience is a dependence relation where no difference in one property set occurs without a difference in another.
concepts.body: Supervenience is a dependence relation where no difference in one property set occurs without a difference in another. If mind supervenes on body, physically identical systems cannot differ mentally under that relation.

examples.text: Two physically identical objects cannot differ in color if color supervenes on physical properties.
examples.note: A higher-level difference requires a base-level difference.

commonMisreadings: Supervenience alone supplies no mechanism or reduction.

concepts.name: Sustainability
concepts.summary: Sustainability is maintaining human and ecological well-being without exhausting conditions needed by future generations.
concepts.body: Sustainability is maintaining human and ecological well-being without exhausting conditions needed by future generations. It considers environmental limits, social needs, economic practice, and intergenerational effects together.

examples.text: Catch limits let a fishery's breeding population replenish.
examples.note: The policy preserves the ecological basis for future harvests.

commonMisreadings: It is broader than short-term efficiency or isolated conservation.

concepts.name: Swampman
concepts.summary: Swampman is a thought experiment about personal identity in which a person is destroyed and an exact physical duplicate appears by chance from swamp lightning.
concepts.body: Swampman is a thought experiment about personal identity in which a person is destroyed and an exact physical duplicate appears by chance from swamp lightning. The case challenges whether psychological continuity, physical continuity, or causal history is necessary for someone to be the same person.

examples.text: If Davidson's body dissolves and an indistinguishable Davidson emerges from a swamp, the new being remembers his life but has no causal connection to it.
examples.note: The duplicate has the original's apparent memories and character but lacks the ordinary history that produced them.

commonMisreadings: Swampman is not simply a clone, because the thought experiment emphasizes instantaneous accidental duplication without reproductive or technological copying.

concepts.name: Syllogism
concepts.summary: A syllogism is a deductive argument with premises and a conclusion arranged so that the conclusion follows from the premises by a stated logical form.
concepts.body: A syllogism is a deductive argument with premises and a conclusion arranged so that the conclusion follows from the premises by a stated logical form. A categorical syllogism typically contains three propositions involving a major term, a minor term, and a middle term.

examples.text: All mammals are animals and all whales are mammals, so all whales are animals, is a valid syllogism.
examples.note: The middle term links the premises while disappearing from the conclusion, preserving the inferential structure.

commonMisreadings: A syllogism is not any argument with two premises, since validity depends on its logical form rather than its premise count.

concepts.name: Syndicalism
concepts.summary: Syndicalism is a socialist movement that treats labor unions as the main instruments for worker emancipation and social transformation.
concepts.body: Syndicalism is a socialist movement that treats labor unions as the main instruments for worker emancipation and social transformation. Revolutionary syndicalists commonly advocate direct action, including strikes and boycotts, rather than relying primarily on parliamentary parties.

examples.text: The Industrial Workers of the World organized across trades and promoted worker control through industrial unionism.
examples.note: Its organizing model seeks to unite workers as a class capable of taking over production.

commonMisreadings: Syndicalism is not identical to ordinary trade unionism, because it assigns unions a broader revolutionary and governing role.

concepts.name: Syntax
concepts.summary: Syntax is the system of rules governing how words or symbols combine into well-formed expressions.
concepts.body: Syntax is the system of rules governing how words or symbols combine into well-formed expressions. In natural language, syntax concerns constituent structure and relations such as subject, object, and agreement.

examples.text: The English sentences "The dog chased the cat" and "The cat chased the dog" use similar words but different syntax to express different events.
examples.note: Changing constituent order changes grammatical roles and therefore the proposition conveyed.

commonMisreadings: Syntax is not the same as meaning, although syntactic structure can constrain and help determine meaning.

concepts.name: Systems thinking
concepts.summary: Systems thinking analyzes phenomena as interconnected wholes whose behavior arises from relationships, feedback, and patterns over time.
concepts.body: Systems thinking analyzes phenomena as interconnected wholes whose behavior arises from relationships, feedback, and patterns over time. It often distinguishes reinforcing feedback, which amplifies change, from balancing feedback, which counteracts change.
