examples.text: A public-health planner may model how vaccination, infection rates, hospital capacity, and public behavior affect one another.
examples.note: The model treats an outbreak as a dynamic network rather than as an isolated sequence of individual decisions.

commonMisreadings: Systems thinking is not merely considering many factors, because it specifically studies interactions, feedback, and emergent behavior.

concepts.name: Taste
concepts.summary: Taste is the sensory capacity by which substances dissolved in saliva produce gustatory experiences through receptors in the mouth.
concepts.body: Taste is the sensory capacity by which substances dissolved in saliva produce gustatory experiences through receptors in the mouth. Human taste commonly distinguishes sweet, sour, salty, bitter, and umami, while smell contributes substantially to flavor perception.

examples.text: Glutamate in a savory broth can activate umami taste receptors.
examples.note: Glutamate is a tastant whose characteristic savory quality is detected by gustatory receptors.

commonMisreadings: Taste is not identical to flavor or aesthetic preference, both of which include additional sensory or evaluative elements.

concepts.name: Tautology
concepts.summary: A tautology is a proposition or formula that is true under every permitted interpretation of its variables.
concepts.body: A tautology is a proposition or formula that is true under every permitted interpretation of its variables. In propositional logic, a statement such as p or not-p is a tautology because no truth assignment makes it false.

examples.text: The formula "It is raining or it is not raining" is tautological in classical logic.
examples.note: The disjunction covers both truth possibilities for the same proposition.

commonMisreadings: A tautology is not simply a repetitive sentence in ordinary speech, where the term often means verbal redundancy.

concepts.name: Technocracy
concepts.summary: Technocracy is a political ideal in which trained experts and technical procedures play a central role in governing society.
concepts.body: Technocracy is a political ideal in which trained experts and technical procedures play a central role in governing society. Technocratic arguments usually claim that specialized knowledge can improve decisions about complex economic or infrastructural systems.

examples.text: A government agency that delegates energy-grid planning to engineers and systems analysts exemplifies a technocratic arrangement.
examples.note: The policy authority is assigned according to technical expertise rather than electoral popularity alone.

commonMisreadings: Technocracy is not rule by all educated people in general, since it specifically privileges technical expertise in administration.

concepts.name: Teleology
concepts.summary: Teleology explains a process, object, or action by reference to an end, purpose, or goal.
concepts.body: Teleology explains a process, object, or action by reference to an end, purpose, or goal. A teleological explanation can describe an organ by the function it performs or an action by the agent's intended aim.

examples.text: A biologist may say that roots grow toward water because acquiring water is the function served by that growth.
examples.note: The explanation identifies an outcome or function toward which the process is directed.

commonMisreadings: Teleology is not necessarily a claim that nature has conscious intentions, since functions can be discussed without attributing minds.

concepts.name: Teletransportation paradox
concepts.summary: The teletransportation paradox asks whether a person survives when a machine scans their structure, destroys the original, and reconstructs an exact copy elsewhere.
concepts.body: The teletransportation paradox asks whether a person survives when a machine scans their structure, destroys the original, and reconstructs an exact copy elsewhere. It separates questions about bodily continuity, psychological continuity, and numerical identity.

examples.text: If a teleporter recreates Alice on Mars while the Earth body is destroyed, it is unclear whether Alice traveled or a duplicate began there.
examples.note: The recreated person has Alice's memories and personality, making psychological survival plausible while leaving identity disputed.

commonMisreadings: The paradox is not simply a problem about transport technology, because its central issue is the criterion for personal identity.

concepts.name: Temperance
concepts.summary: Temperance is the virtue of regulating appetites and emotions so that desires remain proportionate to reason and circumstances.
concepts.body: Temperance is the virtue of regulating appetites and emotions so that desires remain proportionate to reason and circumstances. Classical virtue ethics treats temperance as self-command rather than total abstinence from bodily pleasures.

examples.text: A temperate diner stops eating when satisfied even though highly palatable food remains available.
examples.note: The choice permits pleasure while preventing appetite from dictating action.

commonMisreadings: Temperance is not the same as suppression, because it aims at appropriate desire rather than elimination of desire.

concepts.name: Temporal parts
concepts.summary: Temporal parts are time-indexed portions of an enduring object, each existing during a particular interval in a four-dimensional account of persistence.
concepts.body: Temporal parts are time-indexed portions of an enduring object, each existing during a particular interval in a four-dimensional account of persistence. The temporal-parts view allows one object to have different properties at different times without one part literally changing its intrinsic properties.

examples.text: A person-at-age-five and that person's-at-age-fifty can be treated as distinct temporal parts of one spacetime worm.
examples.note: Each stage has its own location and age while belonging to the same temporally extended entity.

commonMisreadings: Temporal parts are not ordinary physical pieces, because they differ by time rather than by simultaneous spatial separation.

concepts.name: Term
concepts.summary: A term is a linguistic expression that can function as a subject or predicate in an argument or proposition.
concepts.body: A term is a linguistic expression that can function as a subject or predicate in an argument or proposition. In traditional logic, a term names or signifies an entity, class, or property without itself asserting a complete proposition.

examples.text: In "Socrates is mortal," "Socrates" and "mortal" function as terms.
examples.note: Each expression contributes an element to the proposition but does not independently make a complete assertion there.

commonMisreadings: A term is not necessarily a single word, since phrases such as "the first person on the Moon" can function as terms.

concepts.name: Testimonial injustice
concepts.summary: Testimonial injustice occurs when a speaker receives reduced credibility because of prejudice associated with the speaker's social identity.
concepts.body: Testimonial injustice occurs when a speaker receives reduced credibility because of prejudice associated with the speaker's social identity. The injustice concerns a credibility deficit in an exchange where the hearer treats relevant testimony as less trustworthy than it deserves.

examples.text: A court dismissing a witness's account because of a racist stereotype can commit testimonial injustice.
examples.note: The stereotype lowers the witness's credibility independently of the evidence supplied.

commonMisreadings: Testimonial injustice is not every mistaken evaluation of testimony, because prejudice must contribute to the credibility distortion.

concepts.name: Testimony
concepts.summary: Testimony is information or belief acquired from another person's assertion, report, or communicative act.
concepts.body: Testimony is information or belief acquired from another person's assertion, report, or communicative act. Testimonial knowledge depends on factors such as the speaker's competence, sincerity, and the hearer's ability to assess those factors.

examples.text: A traveler learns that a museum is closed by believing the curator's announcement.
examples.note: The traveler obtains the information through the curator's communicated assertion rather than direct observation.

commonMisreadings: Testimony is not limited to sworn courtroom evidence, since ordinary conversation also transmits testimony.

concepts.name: Testing effect
concepts.summary: The testing effect is the finding that actively retrieving information from memory improves later retention more than merely restudying the information.
concepts.body: The testing effect is the finding that actively retrieving information from memory improves later retention more than merely restudying the information. Retrieval practice strengthens access to a memory and can reveal gaps that passive review leaves hidden.

examples.text: Students who answer practice questions after reading a chapter often recall it better later than students who reread the chapter for the same time.
examples.note: The practice test requires retrieval, which exercises the memory route used in later recall.

commonMisreadings: The testing effect does not mean every test improves learning, because feedback, timing, and test design affect the result.

concepts.name: Theism
concepts.summary: Theism is belief in or philosophical commitment to the existence of at least one god, often understood as a personal creator or sustainer.
concepts.body: Theism is belief in or philosophical commitment to the existence of at least one god, often understood as a personal creator or sustainer. Many theistic traditions attribute intelligence, agency, and moral significance to God or gods.

examples.text: Classical Christian theism holds that one God created the world and can act within it.
examples.note: The claim includes a divine reality with agency rather than an impersonal first principle alone.

commonMisreadings: Theism is not synonymous with a particular religion, because several religions and philosophical positions are theistic.

concepts.name: Theocracy
concepts.summary: A theocracy is a political order in which divine authority, religious law, or clerical leadership is treated as a primary source of government legitimacy.
concepts.body: A theocracy is a political order in which divine authority, religious law, or clerical leadership is treated as a primary source of government legitimacy. The term can describe rule by clergy or rule by officials who claim to implement a deity's commands.

examples.text: In a theocratic system, a supreme religious council may approve laws according to its interpretation of sacred law.
examples.note: Political decisions are institutionally subordinated to a religious authority or norm.

commonMisreadings: Theocracy is not simply a state whose citizens are religious, because the defining feature is governmental authority grounded in religion.

concepts.name: Theodicy
concepts.summary: A theodicy is an attempt to explain how an omnipotent, omniscient, and perfectly good God can permit evil.
concepts.body: A theodicy is an attempt to explain how an omnipotent, omniscient, and perfectly good God can permit evil. Theodicies may appeal to free will, soul-making, cosmic order, or limitations on human understanding.

examples.text: A free-will theodicy argues that moral evil is possible because genuine freedom requires the ability to choose wrongly.
examples.note: The proposed justification connects the existence of evil with a greater good or necessary condition.

commonMisreadings: A theodicy is not merely the claim that evil exists, since it addresses the compatibility of evil with divine goodness and power.

concepts.name: Theory of mind
concepts.summary: Theory of mind is the capacity to attribute beliefs, desires, intentions, and other mental states to oneself and other agents.
concepts.body: Theory of mind is the capacity to attribute beliefs, desires, intentions, and other mental states to oneself and other agents. It includes recognizing that another person's representation of the world can differ from reality or from one's own representation.

examples.text: A child who expects Sally to search where she last left a toy, despite the toy having been moved, demonstrates false-belief understanding.
examples.note: The child tracks Sally's belief rather than substituting the child's own knowledge.

commonMisreadings: Theory of mind is not identical to empathy, because representing another's mental state need not involve sharing that person's emotion.

concepts.name: Theory underdetermination
concepts.summary: Theory underdetermination is the condition in which available evidence is compatible with more than one explanatory theory.
concepts.body: Theory underdetermination is the condition in which available evidence is compatible with more than one explanatory theory. Underdetermination can persist even when rival theories make the same predictions for all currently observed cases.

examples.text: Two physical theories may account equally well for existing measurements while differing about unobserved particles.
examples.note: The evidence fails to select one theory uniquely because both accommodate the data.

commonMisreadings: Theory underdetermination is not proof that all theories are equally good, since simplicity, scope, and future evidence can still distinguish them.

concepts.name: Theory-ladenness
concepts.summary: Theory-ladenness is the dependence of observation, description, or interpretation on prior concepts, expectations, or theoretical commitments.
concepts.body: Theory-ladenness is the dependence of observation, description, or interpretation on prior concepts, expectations, or theoretical commitments. It means that what investigators treat as relevant evidence can be shaped by the frameworks through which they examine phenomena.

examples.text: A trained astronomer identifies a faint point as a variable star while an untrained observer sees only a moving light.
examples.note: Background concepts affect classification and attention without making the physical stimulus arbitrary.

commonMisreadings: Theory-ladenness does not imply that observations are wholly subjective or unconstrained by the world.

concepts.name: Theravada Buddhism
concepts.summary: Theravada Buddhism is a Buddhist tradition that emphasizes the Pali Canon, monastic discipline, meditation, and liberation as arahantship.
concepts.body: Theravada Buddhism is a Buddhist tradition that emphasizes the Pali Canon, monastic discipline, meditation, and liberation as arahantship. It is historically prominent in Sri Lanka and mainland Southeast Asia and preserves a major lineage of early Buddhist teachings.

examples.text: A Theravada monastery may train monks in vipassana meditation and recite passages from the Pali Canon.
examples.note: The practices and textual tradition express its emphasis on disciplined cultivation and insight.

commonMisreadings: Theravada Buddhism is not simply a synonym for all early Buddhism, because it is a living historical tradition with its own institutions and developments.

concepts.name: Thisness
concepts.summary: Thisness is the property or principle that makes an individual entity the particular entity it is rather than another entity.
concepts.body: Thisness is the property or principle that makes an individual entity the particular entity it is rather than another entity. Medieval and early modern philosophers used related notions of haecceity to distinguish individuals that share all general properties.

examples.text: The thisness of a particular oak would distinguish it from a qualitatively identical oak grown beside it.
examples.note: The distinction depends on numerical identity rather than on a differing observable quality.

commonMisreadings: Thisness is not the same as a unique description, because an entity could have thisness even if no description uniquely identifies it.

concepts.name: Thomism
concepts.summary: Thomism is the philosophical and theological tradition based on the work of Thomas Aquinas and later interpreters.
concepts.body: Thomism is the philosophical and theological tradition based on the work of Thomas Aquinas and later interpreters. It combines Aristotelian metaphysics with Christian doctrines about creation, God, natural law, and human flourishing.

examples.text: A Thomist argument may explain change through act and potency and then relate those concepts to a doctrine of creation.
examples.note: The analysis uses Aquinas's Aristotelian framework to address theological questions.

commonMisreadings: Thomism is not identical to medieval scholasticism as a whole, since scholasticism includes rival traditions such as Scotism and nominalism.

concepts.name: Time
concepts.summary: Time is the dimension or ordering through which events are related as earlier, simultaneous, or later.
concepts.body: Time is the dimension or ordering through which events are related as earlier, simultaneous, or later. Philosophical theories disagree about whether time exists independently, whether only the present is real, and whether temporal passage is fundamental.

examples.text: The eruption of Mount Vesuvius in 79 CE precedes a present-day observation of its archaeological remains.
examples.note: The events stand in an ordered relation even though the eruption and observation are not simultaneous.

commonMisreadings: Time is not simply change, because some theories treat change as occurring in time while distinguishing the two concepts.

concepts.name: Tip-of-the-tongue phenomenon
concepts.summary: The tip-of-the-tongue phenomenon is the temporary inability to retrieve a known word despite a strong feeling that its retrieval is imminent.
concepts.body: The tip-of-the-tongue phenomenon is the temporary inability to retrieve a known word despite a strong feeling that its retrieval is imminent. People in this state can often recall partial information such as the word's initial sound, syllable count, or meaning.

examples.text: A speaker unable to say "hibiscus" may report that the word begins with h and has several syllables.
examples.note: Partial access shows that semantic or phonological information can be available without complete word production.

commonMisreadings: The phenomenon is not ordinary forgetting, because the person retains a metacognitive sense that the word is known.

concepts.name: Titoism
concepts.summary: Titoism is the form of communist politics associated with Josip Broz Tito's Yugoslavia, especially its independence from Soviet direction and worker self-management.
concepts.body: Titoism is the form of communist politics associated with Josip Broz Tito's Yugoslavia, especially its independence from Soviet direction and worker self-management. It combined one-party socialist rule with a non-aligned foreign policy and a more decentralized economic system than the Soviet model.

examples.text: Yugoslav enterprises were governed through workers' councils under the self-management system.
examples.note: The arrangement gave workers an institutional role in management while retaining socialist political authority.

commonMisreadings: Titoism is not simply nationalism, because it remained a communist project with international and economic doctrines of its own.

concepts.name: Tolerance
concepts.summary: Tolerance is the deliberate acceptance or noninterference toward beliefs, practices, or identities one disapproves of, within specified limits.
concepts.body: Tolerance is the deliberate acceptance or noninterference toward beliefs, practices, or identities one disapproves of, within specified limits. Political tolerance protects disagreement by restraining coercion rather than requiring approval or indifference.

examples.text: A university may permit a controversial student association to distribute lawful literature despite administrators' personal disagreement.
examples.note: The institution allows expression without endorsing the association's views.

commonMisreadings: Tolerance is not unlimited acceptance, because liberal toleration can exclude conduct that violates others' rights.

concepts.name: Totalitarianism
concepts.summary: Totalitarianism is a form of political rule seeking comprehensive control over public and private life through ideology, coercion, and mass organization.
concepts.body: Totalitarianism is a form of political rule seeking comprehensive control over public and private life through ideology, coercion, and mass organization. Totalitarian regimes commonly attempt to eliminate independent institutions, monopolize communication, and mobilize citizens around an official worldview.

examples.text: Nazi Germany used propaganda, secret police, party organizations, and terror to penetrate many areas of social life.
examples.note: The state pursued ideological conformity through coordinated institutions and coercive surveillance.

commonMisreadings: Totalitarianism is not merely dictatorship, because it involves an ambition to transform and control society as a whole.

concepts.name: Traditionalism
concepts.summary: Traditionalism is the disposition to preserve inherited beliefs, practices, institutions, or authorities because of their historical continuity or perceived wisdom.
concepts.body: Traditionalism is the disposition to preserve inherited beliefs, practices, institutions, or authorities because of their historical continuity or perceived wisdom. Traditionalist reasoning gives epistemic or moral weight to established customs, though it need not reject all change.

examples.text: A community that retains an inherited initiation ceremony while adapting its materials practices traditionalism.
examples.note: The ceremony is preserved because its lineage and meaning are treated as reasons for continuation.

commonMisreadings: Traditionalism is not identical to reactionary politics, since a person can value tradition while accepting substantial reform.

concepts.name: Tragedy
concepts.summary: Tragedy is a dramatic form in which serious conflict leads to suffering, loss, or catastrophe and exposes limits in human action or knowledge.
concepts.body: Tragedy is a dramatic form in which serious conflict leads to suffering, loss, or catastrophe and exposes limits in human action or knowledge. Classical tragedy often centers on a protagonist whose choices and circumstances interact in ways that produce a reversal or downfall.

examples.text: In Sophocles' Oedipus Rex, Oedipus's determination to discover the truth contributes to the revelation that destroys his standing.
examples.note: The pursuit of knowledge is both admirable and bound to a devastating recognition.

commonMisreadings: Tragedy is not simply any sad story, because its structure turns suffering into an exploration of conflict, agency, and human limits.

concepts.name: Tragedy of the commons
concepts.summary: The tragedy of the commons is the tendency for individuals pursuing private benefit to overuse a shared resource, damaging it for everyone.
concepts.body: The tragedy of the commons is the tendency for individuals pursuing private benefit to overuse a shared resource, damaging it for everyone. The problem arises when users receive the full immediate benefit of extraction while distributing the long-term cost across the community.

examples.text: Several fishing fleets can deplete a shared fishery when each gains by catching more fish before others do.
examples.note: Each fleet has an incentive to increase its catch even though aggregate overfishing collapses the resource.

commonMisreadings: The tragedy is not inevitable for every common resource, because rules, monitoring, and shared governance can prevent depletion.

concepts.name: Transcendence
concepts.summary: Transcendence is existence or activity that goes beyond an ordinary domain, limit, category, or condition.
concepts.body: Transcendence is existence or activity that goes beyond an ordinary domain, limit, category, or condition. In religious philosophy, transcendence often describes a divine reality not contained within the created or empirical world.

examples.text: A theist who says God is transcendent means that God is not merely one finite object among others.
examples.note: The claim places the divine outside the ordinary order of finite entities.

commonMisreadings: Transcendence is not the same as physical distance, because something can transcend a category without being spatially far away.

concepts.name: Transcendental idealism
concepts.summary: Transcendental idealism is Kant's view that objects as experienced are structured by the conditions of human sensibility and understanding, while things in themselves are not known as they are independently of those conditions.
concepts.body: Transcendental idealism is Kant's view that objects as experienced are structured by the conditions of human sensibility and understanding, while things in themselves are not known as they are independently of those conditions. Space and time are forms of intuition and categories such as causality are conditions through which experience is organized.

examples.text: Kant argues that every experienced event is represented as occurring in time and under causal relations.
examples.note: These structures belong to the conditions of possible experience rather than being inferred from experience as raw properties.

commonMisreadings: Transcendental idealism is not the claim that external objects are imaginary, since it affirms empirically real appearances.

concepts.name: Transcendentalism
concepts.summary: Transcendentalism was a nineteenth-century American intellectual movement emphasizing intuition, individual conscience, nature, and spiritual insight beyond established institutions.
concepts.body: Transcendentalism was a nineteenth-century American intellectual movement emphasizing intuition, individual conscience, nature, and spiritual insight beyond established institutions. Its writers argued that direct experience and inward reflection could disclose truths not exhausted by conventional authority.

examples.text: Ralph Waldo Emerson's essay "Nature" presents the natural world as a source of spiritual and intellectual renewal.
examples.note: Nature functions as a medium through which the individual can encounter meaning and insight.

commonMisreadings: American transcendentalism is not identical to Kant's transcendental idealism, despite sharing language about going beyond ordinary experience.

concepts.name: Transhumanism
concepts.summary: Transhumanism is a movement advocating the responsible use of science and technology to enhance human capacities and overcome limitations such as disease, aging, and cognitive impairment.
concepts.body: Transhumanism is a movement advocating the responsible use of science and technology to enhance human capacities and overcome limitations such as disease, aging, and cognitive impairment. Its proposals range from genetic and prosthetic enhancement to life extension and possible mind uploading.

examples.text: An implant that restores hearing and later provides frequency ranges unavailable to ordinary hearing is a transhumanist enhancement example.
examples.note: The technology first repairs a disability and then extends a human capacity beyond the typical biological range.

commonMisreadings: Transhumanism is not simply medical treatment, because it also considers elective enhancement and transformation of human nature.

concepts.name: Trolley problem
concepts.summary: The trolley problem is a family of moral thought experiments in which a person must choose whether to redirect harm from one group to another.
concepts.body: The trolley problem is a family of moral thought experiments in which a person must choose whether to redirect harm from one group to another. It tests how people weigh consequences, intention, action, omission, and the use of persons as means.

examples.text: In the standard switch case, pulling a lever diverts a runaway trolley from five people onto a track with one person.
examples.note: The decision compares saving more lives with directly causing one person's death through redirection.

commonMisreadings: The trolley problem is not a single settled puzzle, since variations alter the morally relevant features and produce different judgments.

concepts.name: Trope theory
concepts.summary: Trope theory is the metaphysical view that properties and relations are particular instances rather than repeatable universals.
concepts.body: Trope theory is the metaphysical view that properties and relations are particular instances rather than repeatable universals. On this view, the redness of one apple and the redness of another are numerically distinct tropes that resemble each other.

examples.text: The specific redness located on a red apple is a trope attached to that individual object.
examples.note: Its particular location and bearer distinguish it from the redness trope of another apple.

commonMisreadings: Trope theory is not nominalism in every form, because some trope theorists use resemblance relations or compresence to explain shared categories.

concepts.name: Trotskyism
concepts.summary: Trotskyism is a Marxist tradition associated with Leon Trotsky that emphasizes permanent revolution, internationalism, and opposition to bureaucratic Stalinism.
concepts.body: Trotskyism is a Marxist tradition associated with Leon Trotsky that emphasizes permanent revolution, internationalism, and opposition to bureaucratic Stalinism. Trotskyists argue that socialist revolution cannot remain securely isolated in one country and that workers' democracy must be defended.

examples.text: A Trotskyist organization may support international revolutionary coordination while criticizing the Soviet bureaucracy.
examples.note: The position connects the success of socialism to international extension and political control by workers.

commonMisreadings: Trotskyism is not simply any anti-Stalinist communism, because it includes distinctive theories of permanent revolution and transitional politics.

concepts.name: Truth
concepts.summary: Truth is the property of a proposition, belief, or statement when it accurately represents or otherwise satisfies the relevant standard of reality or correctness.
concepts.body: Truth is the property of a proposition, belief, or statement when it accurately represents or otherwise satisfies the relevant standard of reality or correctness. Competing theories explain truth through correspondence, coherence, deflationary equivalence, or pragmatic success.

examples.text: The statement "Perth is in Western Australia" is true because Perth is located in that state.
examples.note: The fact described by the statement matches the statement's asserted condition.

commonMisreadings: Truth is not identical to belief or consensus, since a widely held belief can be false.

concepts.name: Truth conditions
concepts.summary: Truth conditions are the circumstances under which a statement would be true or false.
concepts.body: Truth conditions are the circumstances under which a statement would be true or false. A semantic theory can explain a sentence's meaning by specifying what the world would have to be like for the sentence to be true.

examples.text: The truth condition of "Snow is white" is that snow is white.
examples.note: The sentence is true exactly when the stated condition obtains, under the relevant interpretation.

commonMisreadings: Truth conditions are not the same as evidence for truth, because conditions describe what makes a statement true rather than how we know it.

concepts.name: Truth table
concepts.summary: A truth table is a tabular method that lists the truth value of a compound proposition for every possible assignment of truth values to its components.
concepts.body: A truth table is a tabular method that lists the truth value of a compound proposition for every possible assignment of truth values to its components. It can be used to test whether a formula is a tautology, contradiction, or contingent proposition.

examples.text: A table for p and q shows that their conjunction is true only in the row where both p and q are true.
examples.note: The rows exhaust the possible classical truth assignments and the conjunction column records the resulting value.

commonMisreadings: A truth table is not a table of empirical observations, because it evaluates logical combinations rather than measured cases.

concepts.name: Truth value
concepts.summary: A truth value is the status assigned to a proposition in a logical system, commonly true or false in classical logic.
concepts.body: A truth value is the status assigned to a proposition in a logical system, commonly true or false in classical logic. Some nonclassical logics add values such as indeterminate, both, or neither, depending on their treatment of contradiction and vagueness.

examples.text: The proposition "2 plus 2 equals 4" has the classical truth value true.
examples.note: Its truth status follows from the arithmetic relation asserted by the proposition.

commonMisreadings: A truth value is not the proposition itself, because it is the status attributed to the proposition.

concepts.name: Truth-conditional semantics
concepts.summary: Truth-conditional semantics explains linguistic meaning by specifying the conditions under which sentences are true or false.
concepts.body: Truth-conditional semantics explains linguistic meaning by specifying the conditions under which sentences are true or false. It typically assigns meanings to simpler expressions and composes them into truth conditions for larger sentences.

examples.text: The semantics of "Ava opened the door" includes the condition that Ava performed the relevant opening action on the relevant door.
examples.note: The sentence's interpretation is characterized by the state of affairs required for its truth.

commonMisreadings: Truth-conditional semantics is not a claim that speakers always know explicit truth conditions when they understand a sentence.

concepts.name: Truthmaker
concepts.summary: A truthmaker is the entity, fact, state of affairs, or feature of reality that makes a proposition true.
concepts.body: A truthmaker is the entity, fact, state of affairs, or feature of reality that makes a proposition true. Truthmaker theory explains truth by relating true propositions to aspects of the world that account for their correctness.

examples.text: The presence of snow on a particular mountain can serve as a truthmaker for "Snow is on that mountain."
examples.note: The actual snowy state explains why the proposition is true rather than false.

commonMisreadings: A truthmaker is not necessarily a cause, because a fact can make a proposition true without temporally producing it.

concepts.name: Twin Earth
concepts.summary: Twin Earth is a thought experiment by Hilary Putnam in which a planet like Earth has a substance superficially like water but with a different chemical composition, XYZ.
concepts.body: Twin Earth is a thought experiment by Hilary Putnam in which a planet like Earth has a substance superficially like water but with a different chemical composition, XYZ. It argues that the meanings or referents of words can depend partly on the external environment rather than on mental states alone.

examples.text: An Earth speaker and a Twin Earth speaker may both use "water" while referring to H2O and XYZ respectively.
examples.note: The different substances fix different external references despite identical apparent experiences and linguistic behavior.

commonMisreadings: Twin Earth is not a claim that such a planet has been observed, but a philosophical argument about externalism in semantics.

concepts.name: Tyranny
concepts.summary: Tyranny is oppressive rule that exercises power arbitrarily or without adequate regard for law, rights, or the common good.
concepts.body: Tyranny is oppressive rule that exercises power arbitrarily or without adequate regard for law, rights, or the common good. Classical political thought often contrasts tyranny with legitimate rule by noting whether authority serves the ruler's private interest.

examples.text: A ruler who imprisons critics without trial and changes laws solely to retain personal power acts tyrannically.
examples.note: The ruler uses public authority as an instrument of arbitrary personal control.

commonMisreadings: Tyranny is not simply unpopular government, because its defining feature is oppressive and arbitrary exercise of power.

concepts.name: Ubuntu
concepts.summary: Ubuntu is an African ethical and philosophical concept often expressed as the idea that a person's humanity is realized through relationships with other people.
concepts.body: Ubuntu is an African ethical and philosophical concept often expressed as the idea that a person's humanity is realized through relationships with other people. It emphasizes mutual recognition, solidarity, compassion, and communal responsibility rather than isolated self-sufficiency.

examples.text: A community restorative-justice process that reintegrates an offender while acknowledging victims can be interpreted through ubuntu.
examples.note: The process treats social repair and shared human dignity as central to justice.

commonMisreadings: Ubuntu is not reducible to generic kindness, because it presents personhood and obligation as fundamentally relational.

concepts.name: Ultranationalism
concepts.summary: Ultranationalism is an extreme form of nationalism that treats the nation as superior, demands intense loyalty, and often legitimizes domination or exclusion.
concepts.body: Ultranationalism is an extreme form of nationalism that treats the nation as superior, demands intense loyalty, and often legitimizes domination or exclusion. It commonly combines mythic national identity with hostility toward minorities, foreigners, or alleged internal enemies.

examples.text: A movement that calls for ethnic purification and territorial expansion in the nation's name exemplifies ultranationalism.
examples.note: National belonging is made absolute and used to justify coercion against groups defined as outside it.

commonMisreadings: Ultranationalism is not ordinary patriotism, because patriotism need not assert national superiority or endorse aggression.

concepts.name: Uncertainty
concepts.summary: Uncertainty is a condition in which the available information does not determine a single definite belief, prediction, or outcome.
concepts.body: Uncertainty is a condition in which the available information does not determine a single definite belief, prediction, or outcome. It can arise from incomplete evidence, randomness, measurement limits, or ambiguity in the relevant model.

examples.text: A weather forecast assigning a 40 percent chance of rain represents uncertainty about tomorrow's precipitation.
examples.note: The probability expresses incomplete determination of the event from current information.

commonMisreadings: Uncertainty is not identical to ignorance, because a person can quantify uncertainty without lacking all relevant knowledge.

concepts.name: Unconscious
concepts.summary: The unconscious is the domain of mental processes, representations, or motives that are not currently accessible to conscious awareness.
concepts.body: The unconscious is the domain of mental processes, representations, or motives that are not currently accessible to conscious awareness. Different psychological theories use the term for automatic processing, repressed conflict, implicit memory, or other nonconscious activity.

examples.text: A person may automatically recognize a familiar face without being able to report the visual computations involved.
examples.note: The processing influences behavior while remaining unavailable to introspective awareness.

commonMisreadings: The unconscious is not necessarily the same as the Freudian system of repression, because contemporary theories use the term more broadly.

concepts.name: Underdetermination
concepts.summary: Underdetermination is the situation in which the available evidence or premises do not uniquely determine a conclusion among multiple possibilities.
concepts.body: Underdetermination is the situation in which the available evidence or premises do not uniquely determine a conclusion among multiple possibilities. It may concern scientific theories, causal explanations, interpretation, or practical decisions.

examples.text: The same observed correlation between ice-cream sales and drownings can fit several causal explanations, including a common seasonal cause.
examples.note: The data alone do not select one causal story because different models predict the observation.

commonMisreadings: Underdetermination is not mere uncertainty about one known answer, since it concerns multiple compatible answers or explanations.

concepts.name: Universal
concepts.summary: A universal is a repeatable property, relation, or kind that can be instantiated by multiple particular things.
concepts.body: A universal is a repeatable property, relation, or kind that can be instantiated by multiple particular things. Realist theories treat universals as features shared by particulars, while nominalist theories deny that such entities exist independently.

examples.text: The property of being triangular is a universal instantiated by many distinct triangles.
examples.note: Different triangles can possess one repeatable geometric property despite being separate objects.

commonMisreadings: A universal is not the same as a set of instances, because the philosophical question concerns what explains their commonality.

concepts.name: Universal quantification
concepts.summary: Universal quantification is the logical operation of asserting that a predicate holds for every object in a specified domain.
concepts.body: Universal quantification is the logical operation of asserting that a predicate holds for every object in a specified domain. It is represented in predicate logic by the symbol ∀ and is sensitive to the chosen domain of quantification.

examples.text: ∀x(Human(x) → Mortal(x)) says that every human is mortal.
examples.note: The conditional restricts the claim to objects that satisfy the predicate Human.

commonMisreadings: Universal quantification does not assert that the domain contains humans unless existence is separately stated.

concepts.name: Universals problem
concepts.summary: The universals problem asks whether properties and relations shared by many particulars are real entities, mental concepts, linguistic names, or only resemblances.
concepts.body: The universals problem asks whether properties and relations shared by many particulars are real entities, mental concepts, linguistic names, or only resemblances. Realism, nominalism, and conceptualism offer competing accounts of why different objects can be classified under one predicate.

examples.text: The redness of several apples raises the question of whether one universal redness exists in them or whether they merely resemble one another.
examples.note: The case requires an account of common predication across distinct particulars.

commonMisreadings: The universals problem is not just the problem of defining a word, because it concerns the metaphysical status of what words generalize over.

concepts.name: Upaya
concepts.summary: Upaya, often translated as skillful means, is the Buddhist idea that a teaching or practice may be adapted to a person's circumstances to aid liberation.
concepts.body: Upaya, often translated as skillful means, is the Buddhist idea that a teaching or practice may be adapted to a person's circumstances to aid liberation. Its usefulness is judged by whether it helps overcome attachment and ignorance rather than by rigid adherence to one presentation.

examples.text: A teacher may give a simple meditation instruction to a beginner and a more technical instruction to an advanced student.
examples.note: The different teachings serve the learners' conditions while aiming at transformative insight.

commonMisreadings: Upaya does not mean that any deception is automatically acceptable, because the means must be skillful and oriented toward liberation.

concepts.name: Utilitarianism
concepts.summary: Utilitarianism is the ethical view that actions, rules, or institutions should be assessed by their consequences for overall well-being or utility.
concepts.body: Utilitarianism is the ethical view that actions, rules, or institutions should be assessed by their consequences for overall well-being or utility. Classical utilitarianism commonly seeks the greatest aggregate happiness or welfare for all affected.

examples.text: A utilitarian hospital policy may allocate scarce organs to patients according to expected total life-years saved.
examples.note: The policy compares outcomes across all patients rather than privileging one patient's claim by status.

commonMisreadings: Utilitarianism is not simply consequentialism in general, because it specifies welfare or utility as the relevant value.

concepts.name: Utility
concepts.summary: Utility is the value, benefit, satisfaction, or preference-fulfillment that an agent receives from an option in a decision or ethical model.
concepts.body: Utility is the value, benefit, satisfaction, or preference-fulfillment that an agent receives from an option in a decision or ethical model. In economics, utility functions represent preferences and can rank alternatives without requiring pleasure as the only source of value.

examples.text: A commuter may assign greater utility to a reliable train than to a cheaper but frequently delayed bus.
examples.note: The ranking represents the commuter's relative preference among available options.

commonMisreadings: Utility is not necessarily monetary profit, because an option can have utility through time, comfort, safety, or other valued outcomes.

concepts.name: Utopian socialism
concepts.summary: Utopian socialism is a nineteenth-century socialist tradition that proposed ideal cooperative communities as models for overcoming exploitation and social conflict.
concepts.body: Utopian socialism is a nineteenth-century socialist tradition that proposed ideal cooperative communities as models for overcoming exploitation and social conflict. Its proponents often emphasized moral persuasion, planned communal living, and exemplary institutions rather than class struggle as a historical necessity.

examples.text: Robert Owen's New Harmony project attempted to establish a cooperative community in Indiana.
examples.note: The settlement sought to demonstrate a different social order through organized communal practice.

commonMisreadings: Utopian socialism is not the claim that every ideal society is impossible, because the label refers to a specific reform tradition and Marxist criticism of it.

concepts.name: Vagueness
concepts.summary: Vagueness is a lack of sharp boundaries in the application conditions of an expression, producing borderline cases.
concepts.body: Vagueness is a lack of sharp boundaries in the application conditions of an expression, producing borderline cases. A vague predicate can be clearly applicable to some cases and clearly inapplicable to others while leaving intermediate cases unsettled.

examples.text: The adjective "bald" is vague because no precise number of hairs determines every borderline case.
examples.note: Hair loss changes gradually while ordinary language does not fix an exact cutoff for baldness.

commonMisreadings: Vagueness is not ambiguity, because ambiguity involves multiple distinct meanings rather than one meaning with indeterminate boundaries.

concepts.name: Vaisheshika
concepts.summary: Vaisheshika is an ancient Indian philosophical school that analyzes reality through categories such as substance, quality, motion, universality, particularity, and inherence.
concepts.body: Vaisheshika is an ancient Indian philosophical school that analyzes reality through categories such as substance, quality, motion, universality, particularity, and inherence. It developed an atomist account of physical substances and was later closely integrated with Nyaya logic and epistemology.

examples.text: A Vaisheshika analysis can explain a clay pot through its substance, qualities, motion, and relation of inherence to its parts.
examples.note: The object is understood by classifying its constituents and the relations connecting them.

commonMisreadings: Vaisheshika is not simply Indian atomism, because its system also includes a detailed ontology of properties and relations.

concepts.name: Validity
concepts.summary: Validity is the property of an argument whose conclusion follows necessarily from its premises under the relevant logical interpretation.
concepts.body: Validity is the property of an argument whose conclusion follows necessarily from its premises under the relevant logical interpretation. An argument can be valid even when one or more premises are false, because validity concerns form rather than actual truth.

examples.text: If all birds are mammals and all robins are birds, then all robins are mammals is valid despite its false first premise.
examples.note: If the premises were true, the conclusion could not be false given the argument's structure.

commonMisreadings: Validity is not soundness, because soundness additionally requires true premises.

concepts.name: Value
concepts.summary: Value is the worth, importance, or desirability attributed to an object, state, action, or outcome.
concepts.body: Value is the worth, importance, or desirability attributed to an object, state, action, or outcome. Philosophers distinguish intrinsic value, valuable for its own sake, from instrumental value, valuable as a means.

examples.text: A friendship may be valued intrinsically, while a train ticket may be valued instrumentally for enabling travel.
examples.note: The friendship is treated as worth having in itself and the ticket as useful for a further end.

commonMisreadings: Value is not identical to price, because market price measures exchange under conditions rather than all forms of worth.

concepts.name: Value of information
concepts.summary: The value of information is the expected improvement in decision quality or outcome produced by obtaining additional information before acting.
concepts.body: The value of information is the expected improvement in decision quality or outcome produced by obtaining additional information before acting. It is high when information can change the choice and the benefits of a better choice exceed the cost of acquiring it.

examples.text: A farmer may pay for a frost forecast if knowing the temperature will determine whether to protect a crop.
examples.note: The forecast has value because it can prevent a costly mistake and alter the farming decision.

commonMisreadings: Value of information is not the same as information quantity, because abundant information can be irrelevant or costly.

concepts.name: Value pluralism
concepts.summary: Value pluralism is the view that multiple fundamental values exist and may be genuinely distinct, partly incompatible, and not reducible to one common scale.
concepts.body: Value pluralism is the view that multiple fundamental values exist and may be genuinely distinct, partly incompatible, and not reducible to one common scale. Pluralists argue that choices can involve real trade-offs among values such as liberty, equality, justice, and happiness.

examples.text: A policy may increase equality while restricting liberty, with neither value simply convertible into units of the other.
examples.note: The conflict is treated as a genuine normative trade-off rather than a failure to calculate one master value.

commonMisreadings: Value pluralism is not moral relativism, because pluralists can defend objective values while denying that one value governs all cases.

concepts.name: Variable
concepts.summary: A variable is a symbol or expression whose value can vary over a specified domain or during a calculation.
concepts.body: A variable is a symbol or expression whose value can vary over a specified domain or during a calculation. In logic and mathematics, variables are assigned values by interpretations, substitutions, or quantifiers.

examples.text: In the equation x plus 2 equals 5, x is a variable that receives the value 3 in the solution.
examples.note: The symbol stands for a value that is constrained by the equation rather than fixed by its spelling.

commonMisreadings: A variable is not an unknown in every context, because it can also range over many values or represent a parameter.

concepts.name: Vedanta
concepts.summary: Vedanta is a family of Indian philosophical traditions grounded in the Upanishads, the Bhagavad Gita, and the Brahma Sutras.
concepts.body: Vedanta is a family of Indian philosophical traditions grounded in the Upanishads, the Bhagavad Gita, and the Brahma Sutras. Its schools debate the relationship among Brahman, the self, the world, knowledge, and liberation, with Advaita, Vishishtadvaita, and Dvaita offering distinct answers.

examples.text: Advaita Vedanta holds that ultimate reality is nondual Brahman and that ignorance misidentifies the self as separate.
examples.note: The doctrine explains liberation as knowledge overcoming the appearance of fundamental separateness.

commonMisreadings: Vedanta is not one uniform doctrine, because its major schools disagree about the reality of difference and the status of the world.

concepts.name: Veil of ignorance
concepts.summary: The veil of ignorance is Rawls's device of choosing principles of justice without knowing one's position, abilities, wealth, or social identity in the resulting society.
concepts.body: The veil of ignorance is Rawls's device of choosing principles of justice without knowing one's position, abilities, wealth, or social identity in the resulting society. It is used in the original position to prevent bargaining based on knowledge of personal advantage.

examples.text: Behind the veil, a chooser does not know whether they will be born rich or poor and must select fair social rules.
examples.note: The uncertainty makes the chooser assess institutions from every possible social position.

commonMisreadings: The veil of ignorance is not a demand for permanent ignorance, because it is a hypothetical condition for selecting principles.

concepts.name: Verification theory of meaning
concepts.summary: The verification theory of meaning holds that the meaning of a statement is connected to the conditions or procedures that would verify it.
concepts.body: The verification theory of meaning holds that the meaning of a statement is connected to the conditions or procedures that would verify it. Logical positivists used versions of the theory to distinguish empirically testable statements from formal truths and metaphysical assertions.

examples.text: The statement "There is iron in this sample" has meaning under a verificationist approach through specified chemical tests that could confirm it.
examples.note: The testing procedure supplies an empirical route for determining the statement's truth.

commonMisreadings: The verification theory of meaning is not simply the claim that verified statements are true, because it concerns meaning and criteria of significance.

concepts.name: Verificationism
concepts.summary: Verificationism is the epistemological and semantic doctrine that a claim is cognitively meaningful only if it is empirically verifiable or analytically true, in a suitably qualified sense.
concepts.body: Verificationism is the epistemological and semantic doctrine that a claim is cognitively meaningful only if it is empirically verifiable or analytically true, in a suitably qualified sense. It was influential in logical positivism as a way to reject metaphysical claims that seemed to lack possible tests.

examples.text: A verificationist may treat "The thermometer reads 20 degrees" as meaningful because an observation can check it.
examples.note: The claim has an identifiable observational procedure connecting language to evidence.

commonMisreadings: Verificationism is not ordinary fact-checking, because it is a general theory about what makes assertions meaningful.

concepts.name: Violence
concepts.summary: Violence is the intentional or threatened use of physical force, or in broader accounts coercive harm, against persons, bodies, or communities.
concepts.body: Violence is the intentional or threatened use of physical force, or in broader accounts coercive harm, against persons, bodies, or communities. Definitions differ over whether structural deprivation and symbolic domination count as violence in addition to direct bodily force.

examples.text: A person who strikes another to injure them commits direct physical violence.
examples.note: The case involves deliberate bodily force producing or threatening harm.

commonMisreadings: Violence is not identical to all coercion, because some coercive acts do not use force or threaten physical harm under narrower definitions.

concepts.name: Virtue
concepts.summary: A virtue is a stable and valuable disposition to perceive, feel, choose, and act well in relevant circumstances.
concepts.body: A virtue is a stable and valuable disposition to perceive, feel, choose, and act well in relevant circumstances. Virtues are typically developed through habituation and practical judgment rather than acquired as isolated rules.

examples.text: A courageous firefighter enters a burning building to rescue someone while appropriately recognizing the danger.
examples.note: The action expresses a settled disposition that balances concern for safety with the urgent need to help.

commonMisreadings: Virtue is not the same as a single heroic act, because the concept concerns a developed character trait.

concepts.name: Virtue epistemology
concepts.summary: Virtue epistemology explains knowledge and justified belief partly through intellectual virtues or competences of the knower.
concepts.body: Virtue epistemology explains knowledge and justified belief partly through intellectual virtues or competences of the knower. It emphasizes reliable cognitive abilities, responsible inquiry, or intellectual character traits such as open-mindedness and courage.

examples.text: A scientist who carefully tests an unexpected result and revises a favored hypothesis exercises intellectual humility and reliability.
examples.note: The belief-forming process is creditable because it results from competent and responsible inquiry.

commonMisreadings: Virtue epistemology is not simply virtue ethics applied to knowledge, because it addresses epistemic justification, knowledge, and cognitive success.

concepts.name: Virtue ethics
concepts.summary: Virtue ethics is an approach to morality that evaluates character and practical wisdom as central to living and acting well.
concepts.body: Virtue ethics is an approach to morality that evaluates character and practical wisdom as central to living and acting well. Rather than deriving every duty from a rule or outcome, it asks what a virtuous person would perceive and do in context.

examples.text: A virtue ethicist deciding whether to disclose a painful truth considers honesty, compassion, timing, and practical judgment together.
examples.note: The response is assessed through the agent's character and the situation's morally relevant features.

commonMisreadings: Virtue ethics is not the claim that consequences or rules never matter, because virtues guide judgment about both.

concepts.name: Virtue of wu wei
concepts.summary: The virtue of wu wei is the Daoist ideal of effortless or non-forcing action that accords with the patterns of circumstances.
concepts.body: The virtue of wu wei is the Daoist ideal of effortless or non-forcing action that accords with the patterns of circumstances. It involves responsive spontaneity and skillful restraint rather than passivity or refusal to act.

examples.text: An experienced craftsperson cuts along the natural grain of wood with minimal force and adjustment.
examples.note: The action succeeds by following the material's tendencies instead of imposing brute resistance.

commonMisreadings: Wu wei is not laziness, because it can involve highly trained and timely action that feels unforced.

concepts.name: Volition
concepts.summary: Volition is the faculty or process involved in choosing, intending, and initiating an action.
concepts.body: Volition is the faculty or process involved in choosing, intending, and initiating an action. Philosophical accounts of volition examine whether conscious choice is free, causally determined, or constrained by reasons and desires.

examples.text: A person who forms the intention to raise a hand and then raises it exercises volition.
examples.note: The movement is connected to an adopted intention rather than occurring as a mere reflex.

commonMisreadings: Volition is not identical to desire, because an agent can desire something without choosing to pursue it.

concepts.name: Voluntarism
concepts.summary: Voluntarism is a family of views that gives will, choice, or voluntary commitment priority in explaining action, value, knowledge, or religious authority.
concepts.body: Voluntarism is a family of views that gives will, choice, or voluntary commitment priority in explaining action, value, knowledge, or religious authority. In ethics and political thought, voluntarist positions often emphasize consent and self-determination over imposed ends.

examples.text: A voluntarist theory of contract treats an agreement as legitimate because parties freely consent to it.
examples.note: The binding force is explained by voluntary authorization rather than by status alone.

commonMisreadings: Voluntarism is not simply free will, because the term covers broader doctrines about the explanatory priority of will.

concepts.name: Von Restorff effect
concepts.summary: The von Restorff effect is the tendency for an item that differs markedly from surrounding items to be remembered better.
concepts.body: The von Restorff effect is the tendency for an item that differs markedly from surrounding items to be remembered better. Distinctiveness increases the salience and encoding of the isolated item within an otherwise uniform set.

examples.text: A red word in a list of black words is often recalled more readily than the black words.
examples.note: The color difference makes the item stand out during encoding and retrieval.

commonMisreadings: The effect is not a guarantee of perfect memory, because distinctiveness can be weakened by distraction or poor encoding.

concepts.name: Welfare capitalism
concepts.summary: Welfare capitalism is a capitalist system in which markets and private ownership coexist with state or employer programs that protect social welfare.
concepts.body: Welfare capitalism is a capitalist system in which markets and private ownership coexist with state or employer programs that protect social welfare. It can include social insurance, public services, labor protections, and benefits intended to reduce insecurity without abolishing capitalism.

examples.text: Postwar Sweden combined private firms with public health care, pensions, unemployment insurance, and redistribution.
examples.note: The economy retained markets while institutions provided broad social protection.

commonMisreadings: Welfare capitalism is not socialism, because productive property and market exchange remain central rather than being comprehensively socialized.

concepts.name: Well-being
concepts.summary: Well-being is a person's condition of living or faring well, according to a theory that may emphasize pleasure, preference satisfaction, capabilities, or objective goods.
concepts.body: Well-being is a person's condition of living or faring well, according to a theory that may emphasize pleasure, preference satisfaction, capabilities, or objective goods. Philosophical theories disagree about whether well-being is wholly subjective or includes goods such as health, relationships, and understanding.

examples.text: A person with secure housing, meaningful relationships, good health, and opportunities for agency has several dimensions of well-being.
examples.note: The example includes conditions that support a life going well beyond momentary pleasure.

commonMisreadings: Well-being is not identical to happiness, because someone can be happy briefly while lacking health, security, or valued opportunities.

concepts.name: Well-formed formula
concepts.summary: A well-formed formula is an expression constructed according to the formation rules of a formal language.
concepts.body: A well-formed formula is an expression constructed according to the formation rules of a formal language. Well-formedness is syntactic and does not by itself determine whether the formula is true or provable.

examples.text: In propositional logic, (p and q) is a well-formed formula, whereas and p q is not under standard infix notation.
examples.note: The first expression follows the language's connective and parenthesis rules while the second does not.

commonMisreadings: A well-formed formula is not automatically a true statement, because syntactic correctness precedes semantic evaluation.

concepts.name: Yoga philosophy
concepts.summary: Yoga philosophy is the set of Indian philosophical teachings associated with yoga practice, especially the discipline and psychology articulated in Patanjali's Yoga Sutras.
concepts.body: Yoga philosophy is the set of Indian philosophical teachings associated with yoga practice, especially the discipline and psychology articulated in Patanjali's Yoga Sutras. It describes liberation through ethical restraint, concentration, meditation, and discriminative insight, with a distinction between consciousness and material nature.

examples.text: The eight-limbed path begins with ethical yamas and niyamas before progressing toward meditative absorption.
examples.note: The sequence treats conduct and mental discipline as supports for transformative knowledge.

commonMisreadings: Yoga philosophy is not merely physical exercise, because its classical aim is liberation from suffering and misidentification.

concepts.name: Yogacara
concepts.summary: Yogacara is a Mahayana Buddhist philosophical tradition that analyzes experience, cognition, consciousness, and the construction of subject-object duality.
concepts.body: Yogacara is a Mahayana Buddhist philosophical tradition that analyzes experience, cognition, consciousness, and the construction of subject-object duality. It is associated with ideas such as the storehouse consciousness and the three natures, though interpretations vary across its history.

examples.text: A Yogacara analysis may explain a perceived external object through habitual cognitive processes that structure experience.
examples.note: The account investigates how consciousness organizes the appearance of a world rather than simply denying experience.

commonMisreadings: Yogacara is not adequately reduced to subjective idealism, because its texts develop complex Buddhist accounts of causation, practice, and emptiness.

concepts.name: Zeigarnik effect
concepts.summary: The Zeigarnik effect is the tendency for interrupted or incomplete tasks to remain more accessible in memory than completed tasks.
concepts.body: The Zeigarnik effect is the tendency for interrupted or incomplete tasks to remain more accessible in memory than completed tasks. The unfinished task can maintain cognitive activation until it is completed or mentally resolved.

examples.text: A student may keep thinking about an interrupted proof more readily than about a proof finished earlier.
examples.note: The unresolved goal remains active and continues to draw attention or recall.

commonMisreadings: The Zeigarnik effect is not universal for every interruption, because motivation, task structure, and experimental conditions influence it.

concepts.name: Zen Buddhism
concepts.summary: Zen Buddhism is a Mahayana Buddhist tradition emphasizing meditation, direct insight, disciplined practice, and awakening beyond attachment to conceptual fixation.
concepts.body: Zen Buddhism is a Mahayana Buddhist tradition emphasizing meditation, direct insight, disciplined practice, and awakening beyond attachment to conceptual fixation. It developed in China as Chan and later spread to Korea, Japan, Vietnam, and elsewhere, with lineages using teachings, meditation, and sometimes koan practice.

examples.text: A Zen practitioner may sit in zazen and investigate a koan under guidance from a teacher.
examples.note: The practice combines sustained attention with an inquiry intended to disrupt habitual conceptual patterns.

commonMisreadings: Zen Buddhism is not simply mindfulness or aesthetic minimalism, because it is a religious tradition with ethical, institutional, and doctrinal dimensions.

concepts.name: Zeno's paradoxes
concepts.summary: Zeno's paradoxes are arguments that use apparently plausible assumptions about motion, plurality, or space to generate contradictions or infinite regress.
concepts.body: Zeno's paradoxes are arguments that use apparently plausible assumptions about motion, plurality, or space to generate contradictions or infinite regress. The Achilles paradox suggests that a faster runner cannot overtake a slower runner if infinitely many intermediate points must first be reached.

examples.text: Achilles must reach the tortoise's previous position, then its next position, and so on through infinitely many stages.
examples.note: The sequence appears to require completing infinitely many subjourneys before overtaking can occur.

commonMisreadings: The paradoxes are not empirical proof that motion is impossible, because mathematical theories of convergent infinite series offer ways to analyze the apparent problem.

concepts.name: Zionism
concepts.summary: Zionism is a modern Jewish national movement supporting Jewish self-determination in the historic Land of Israel, with diverse religious, cultural, and political forms.
concepts.body: Zionism is a modern Jewish national movement supporting Jewish self-determination in the historic Land of Israel, with diverse religious, cultural, and political forms. It emerged in the late nineteenth century amid European nationalism and antisemitism, and the State of Israel was established in 1948.

examples.text: Theodor Herzl's political Zionism advocated organized international efforts toward a Jewish homeland.
examples.note: The movement linked Jewish political security and national self-determination to a territorial project.

commonMisreadings: Zionism is not a single uniform ideology, because religious, socialist, revisionist, cultural, and other forms have differed sharply.
